chapters.title: Foreword
paragraphs: _I spent several years thinking about the subject of this book. At last, by the grace of God, I have been able to write it, and I enjoyed the work so much that I will be well satisfied if you find even a part of that same joy in reading it._

_While I followed this history, I kept thinking about the high and noble spirit that moved these excellent men to do what they did. They gave us such a perfect picture of courage and humility that anyone would do very well to copy their ways, as far as he can._

_I believe King Arthur was the most honorable and gentle Knight who ever lived in all the world. His fellows of the Round Table looked to him as the mirror of chivalry, and together they formed such a company of noble knights that we can hardly hope to see their like again. For this reason it gave me extraordinary pleasure to watch how those famous knights acted whenever they were called upon to take up their quests._

_And so, in the year of grace nineteen hundred and two, I began writing this history of King Arthur and his Knights of the Round Table. If I am able, I will gladly finish it later in another book, and I hope it will please everyone who cares to read the story._

chapters.title: The Book of King Arthur: Prologue
paragraphs: Long ago there lived a very noble King named Uther-Pendragon, who became ruler over all of Britain. Two men gave him great help in winning the crown of the realm. One was a powerful enchanter and prophet whom people called Merlin the Wise, and he gave Uther-Pendragon very good advice. The other was an excellent and famous knight named Ulfius. Many people thought him the greatest war leader alive in those days, and he helped and advised Uther-Pendragon in battle. So, with the help of Merlin and Sir Ulfius, Uther-Pendragon defeated all his enemies and became King of the whole realm.

After Uther-Pendragon had ruled for a number of years, he married a beautiful and gentle lady named Igraine. She was the widow of Gerlois, the Duke of Tintegal, and by him she had two daughters. One was named Margaise and the other Morgana le Fay, who was a famous sorceress. After the Queen married the mighty King, she brought her daughters to his Court. There Margaise was married to King Urien of Gore, and Morgana le Fay was married to King Lot of Orkney.

Some time later, Uther-Pendragon and Queen Igraine had a son. He was very handsome, and big and strong for his age. While the baby still lay wrapped in his swaddling clothes in a cradle of gold and ultramarine, Merlin came to Uther-Pendragon with the spirit of prophecy strong upon him, as often happened. Speaking in that spirit, he said, “Lord, I have been given a vision. Soon you will fall sick with a fever, and you may die of the violent sweating that follows. If that sad thing happens, this young child, who is truly the hope of the whole realm, will be in great danger. Many enemies will surely rise up to seize him for the sake of his inheritance. Either he will be killed, or he will be held captive, and he could hardly hope to escape. So I beg you, Lord, to let Sir Ulfius and me carry the child away now to a safe refuge. There he can be hidden in secret until he grows to manhood and can protect himself from any danger that threatens him.”

When Merlin had finished speaking, Uther-Pendragon answered him calmly and firmly. “Merlin, as for my own death, when my time comes to die, I believe God will give me the grace to meet my end cheerfully. Truly, I am no different in that from any other man born of woman. But as for this young child, if your prophecy is true, then his danger is very great. It would be good to carry him away to some safe shelter, as you advise. So I ask you to do as you think best in this matter, and to keep in your heart that the child is the most precious inheritance I will leave to this land.”

Uther-Pendragon said all this with great calm and a peaceful spirit. Merlin did as he had advised. He and Sir Ulfius carried the child away by night, and no one but they knew where the baby had been taken. Soon afterward Uther-Pendragon fell sick just as Merlin had foretold, and he died exactly as Merlin had feared. So it was very good that the child had been taken to a safe place.

After Uther-Pendragon had died, everything happened as Merlin had feared, and the whole realm fell into great disorder. Each lesser king fought against his neighbor for the overlordship. Wicked knights and barons raided the highways as they pleased and cruelly forced helpless travelers to pay tolls. Some travelers they took prisoner and held for ransom, and others they killed because they had no ransom to pay. It became a common sight to find a dead man lying by the roadside if you set out on a journey for any business at all. So, after a while, that whole sorrowful land groaned under its troubles.

Nearly eighteen years passed in this great misery. Then one day the Archbishop of Canterbury called Merlin to him and said, “Merlin, people say you are the wisest man in all the world. Can you not find some way to heal the troubles of this unhappy realm? Turn your wisdom to this matter and choose a king who will be a fit overlord for us. Then we may live happily once more, as we did in the days of Uther-Pendragon.”

Then Merlin raised his face to the Archbishop and said, “My lord, the spirit of prophecy that rests upon me sometimes moves me to speak. I see that this country will soon have a king who will be wiser, greater, and more worthy of praise than even Uther-Pendragon was. He will bring order and peace where there is now disorder and war. I can also tell you that this King will be of Uther-Pendragon’s own royal blood.”

The Archbishop replied, “What you tell me, Merlin, is wonderfully strange. But in this spirit of prophecy, can you not foretell when this King will come? And how will we know him when he appears among us? Many lesser kings would gladly be overlord of this land, and many of them think themselves fit to rule over all the others. How will we tell the true King from those who may name themselves the rightful king?”

“My lord Archbishop,” said Merlin, “if you give me leave to use my magic, I will set a task. If any man achieves it, all the world will know at once that he is the rightful King and overlord of this realm.” The Archbishop answered, “Merlin, I tell you to do whatever seems right to you in this matter.” And Merlin said, “I will do so.”

So Merlin used magic to make a huge four-sided marble stone suddenly appear in an open place before the cathedral door. On top of the marble he made an anvil stand, and into the anvil he thrust a great naked sword, halfway up the blade. It was the most wonderful sword anyone had ever seen. The blade was of blue steel, extraordinarily bright and shining. The hilt was of gold, carved with wonderful skill and set with a great number of precious stones, so that it flashed brilliantly in the sunlight. And around the sword these words were written in letters of gold:—

Whoever Pulls This Sword from the Anvil
Is the Rightful Born King of England.
A great many people came and gazed at the sword and marveled at it, for nothing like it had ever been seen on earth.

When Merlin had worked this miracle, he told the Archbishop to call together all the leading people of the land at Christmastime. He told him to order every man to try to draw out the sword, for the one who succeeded in pulling it from the anvil would be the rightful King of Britain.

The Archbishop followed Merlin’s instructions. Such was the marvel of the marble stone and the anvil. Anyone who wants to can read the whole tale in a very old book by Robert de Boron, titled Le Roman de Merlin.

When the Archbishop’s command went out, calling all the chief people of the land to try this miracle, the whole realm was stirred up. (It truly was a miracle to draw a sword blade out of an anvil of solid iron.) Every man asked his neighbor, “Who will draw out that sword, and who will be our King?” Some thought it would be King Lot, and others thought it would be King Urien of Gore, who were both sons-in-law of Uther-Pendragon. Some thought it would be King Leodegrance of Camiliard, and others King Ryence of North Wales. Some thought it would be this king and some that king, and the whole world split into parties, each believing as it liked.

As Christmastime came near, it seemed that the entire world was making its way to London Town. The highways and byways filled with travelers: kings, lords, knights, ladies, squires, pages, and men-at-arms. All of them were heading to the place where the sword and anvil would be tried. Every inn and castle was packed so full that it was a wonder so many people could fit inside. Tents and pavilions were pitched everywhere along the roadsides for those who could not find shelter indoors.

But when the Archbishop saw the crowds gathering, he said to Merlin, “Merlin, it would be very strange if, among all these great kings and noble lords, we could not find one worthy to be King of this realm.”

Merlin smiled and said, “Do not be surprised, my lord, if none of those who seem so worthy turns out to be worthy. And do not be surprised if, among those no one knows, one rises up who proves himself entirely worthy.”
The Archbishop thought over Merlin’s words, and so this story begins.

chapters.title: The Winning of Kinghood: Chapter 1
paragraphs: _Here begins the story of the sword, the anvil, and the marble stone, and of how a young man nobody had heard of, who had won no fame in arms and held no high rank, first won that sword._
_So listen to what I have written below._
_Sir Kay takes part in a great tournament at London Town, and his sword breaks. Arthur then finds him a new one._

Among the worthy men who were called to London Town by the Archbishop’s command, as told above, there was a certain knight of high rank and great honor. His name was Sir Ector of Bonmaison. He was called the Trustworthy Knight, because he faithfully kept the secrets of those who confided in him. He also did for every man, high or low, exactly what he had promised to do, without ever falling short. So this noble and excellent knight was held in great respect by all who knew him. He was honorable in his conduct, and he was also very wealthy and powerful. He owned seven castles in Wales and in the lands just north of it. He also owned fertile stretches of farmland with villages belonging to them, and several vast forests, both in the north country and in the west. This noble knight had two sons. The elder was Sir Kay, a young knight of great courage and promise, who was already well known in the courts of chivalry for several honorable deeds he had done in arms. The younger was a lad of eighteen named Arthur, who at that time served Sir Kay with a good reputation as his squire.

When Sir Ector of Bonmaison received the Archbishop’s command by messenger, he called his two sons to him at once and told them to get ready to go with him to London Town, and they did so. In the same way he told a great number of his servants, squires, and pages to make ready, and they did so too. So Sir Ector of Bonmaison set out for London Town in obedience to the Archbishop’s orders, with a very large company of armed men and a great display of splendor.

When he arrived, he made camp in a certain field where many other noble knights and mighty lords had already settled. There he set up a very fine pavilion of green silk and raised his banner, which showed the emblem of his house: a black griffin on a field of green.

The field held a great many other pavilions of many different colors, and above each one flew the pennant and banner of the mighty lord it belonged to. Because there were so many pennants and banners, the sky was almost hidden in places by the bright colors of the fluttering flags.

Among the great lords who had come at the Archbishop’s call were many famous kings, queens, and noblemen of high rank. There was King Lot of Orkney, who had married a stepdaughter of Uther-Pendragon. There was King Uriens of Gore, who had married another stepdaughter of that great king. There were also King Ban, King Bors, King Ryance, King Leodegrance, and many others of the same rank. In all there were no fewer than twelve kings and seven dukes. With all the lords, ladies, squires, and pages who came with them, London had hardly ever seen such a crowd before that day.

The Archbishop of Canterbury kept in mind how extraordinary this occasion was, since so many kings, dukes, and high lords had gathered for the adventure of the sword and the anvil. So he ordered a grand and noble tournament to be announced. He ordered that this contest of arms be held in a certain field near the great cathedral, three days before the trial of the sword and the anvil, which was to take place on Christmas Day, as told above. All knights of suitable birth, rank, and quality were invited to take part. Very many noble knights applied to enter, and in such numbers that three heralds were kept busy checking their claims to the right to fight. These heralds examined the coats of arms and family records of every applicant with great care.

When Sir Kay heard about this tournament, he went to his father. Standing before him, he spoke like this: “Father, I am your son, and I have inherited from you a very high rank and fortune. I find that I badly want to risk my body in this tournament. If I can prove my worth as a knight before this college of heralds, it may bring great honor and credit to you and to our house if I take part. So I ask your leave to do as I wish.”

Sir Ector answered him: “My son, you have my leave to enter this honorable contest. I hope God will give you great strength, and also such a good spirit that you win honor for yourself and credit for us who share your blood.”

So Sir Kay left, filled with great joy, and went at once to the gathering of heralds and presented his claims to them. After they had carefully examined his right to knighthood, they entered his name as a knight in the contest, as he wished. At this Sir Kay was filled with satisfaction and happiness.

When his name had been entered on the list of fighters, Sir Kay chose his young brother Arthur to be his squire. Arthur would carry his spear and pennant before him onto the field of battle. Arthur, too, was delighted at the honor that had come to him and his brother.

When the day of the tournament arrived, a huge crowd gathered to watch that noble and courtly clash of arms. London was, as I have said, packed with nobles and knights. It was reckoned that no fewer than twenty thousand lords and ladies, not counting the twelve kings and seven dukes and their courts, filled the stands around the field of battle to watch the chosen knights. These noble people sat so close together, and so filled the seats and benches set aside for them, that a solid wall of people seemed to surround the meadow where the fighting would take place. Any knight might well be moved to do his very best on such a great occasion, with so many beautiful ladies and noble lords watching him. So the hearts of all the knights present swelled with eagerness to throw their opponents down into the dust.

In the center of this wonderful crowd of lords and ladies stood the seat and throne of the Archbishop himself. Above the throne was a canopy of purple cloth decorated with silver lilies. The throne itself was hung all around with purple velvet, embroidered in turn with the figure of St. George in gold and with silver crosses of St. George surrounded by golden halos. There the Archbishop sat in great state and splendor, surrounded by a noble court of high-ranking clerks and honorable knights. The whole center of the field glittered with gold and silver embroidery, and it was beautiful with the colors of rich clothing and bright with fine armor of excellent workmanship. Everything was so stately that very few of those present had ever seen so grand a preparation for battle as the one they now saw.

When the whole great crowd had taken their places and everything was ready, a herald came and stood before the Archbishop’s throne and blew a loud, strong blast on a trumpet. At that signal the gates of the lists were thrown open, and two parties of knights entered, one at the northern end of the field and the other at the southern end. At once the whole wide field glittered as the sunlight shone on polished armor and gear. The two parties took up their positions, each in the place given to it, one to the north and the other to the south.

The party Sir Kay had joined stood at the north of the field, and it numbered ninety-three. The other party stood at the south end of the field, and it numbered ninety-six. Although Sir Kay’s party had three fewer men, it was somewhat the stronger, because it included a number of knights of great strength and fame. Two of those knights later became honored companions of the Round Table, and it is worth mentioning them here. They were Sir Mador de la Porte and Sir Bedevere, and Sir Bedevere was the last man to see King Arthur alive on this earth.

When everything was ready as the rules of the tournament required, the knights had prepared themselves in every necessary way. They had readied their spears and shields as knights should before a serious battle. Then the herald put his trumpet to his lips a second time and blew it with all his strength. After sounding this blast, he waited a little while and then blew the trumpet again.

At that blast, each party of knights left its place and charged at the other in great uproar. They came with such noise and fury that the whole earth groaned beneath the feet of the war-horses and trembled and shook as if in an earthquake.

The two companies met in the middle of the field, and the crash of breaking lances was so terrible that those who heard it were stunned and frightened. Several fair ladies fainted with fear at the noise, and others cried out. Besides the great uproar, the air was full of flying splinters of ash wood.

In that famous charge, seventy noble and honorable knights were thrown down, and many of them were trampled under the horses’ hoofs. When the two companies drew back to their places, the ground could be seen covered all over with broken pieces of lances and fragments of armor. Many knights lay sadly in the middle of all that wreckage. Some of them tried to get up and could not, while others lay quite still as if dead. Many squires and pages ran to them, lifted up the fallen men, and carried them away to safe places. Other attendants ran and gathered up the pieces of armor and the broken spears and carried them off to the barriers. Soon the field was completely cleared once more.
Then everyone who looked down on that meadow cheered loudly and joyfully, for such a noble and glorious friendly contest of arms had hardly ever been seen in all that kingdom before.

Now let us turn to Sir Kay. In this charge he had done so well that no knight there had done better, and perhaps none had done as well. Two opponents had aimed their spears at him at once, yet he had resisted both attacks. One of the two he struck so hard in the middle of his defenses that he lifted that attacker clean over the back of his horse. He flung him to the ground half a spear’s length behind his steed, and the fallen knight rolled over three times in the dust before he stopped.
When the men of Sir Kay’s party who were near him saw what he had done, they cheered him loudly and wildly, so much so that Sir Kay was very well pleased and glad at heart.

It should be said that at that time there was hardly any knight in all the world as skilled in deeds of arms as Sir Kay. Knights of much greater fame and more glorious achievement came later, as will be told in good time. But at that time many people counted Sir Kay among the most powerful knights in all that kingdom, whether in wandering adventures or in battle.

So that round of the combat ended to the great pleasure and satisfaction of everyone who saw it, and above all of Sir Kay and his friends. When it was over, the two parties in battle order went back to their assigned places.

When they arrived there, each knight handed his spear to his squire. The next round was to be fought with swords, so all lances and other weapons were to be put away. Such was the rule of that courteous and gentle contest of arms.

So when the herald blew his trumpet again, each knight drew his weapon so readily that the air was full of flashing blades all at once. When the herald blew a second time, each party pressed forward into the fight with noble hearts and eager spirits. Every knight meant to face his opponent with all the strength he had.

At once such a fierce battle began that even if those knights had been bitter enemies of long standing instead of friendly contestants, the blows they struck at one another could not have been stronger or more astonishing to watch.

In this fight, too, Sir Kay proved himself so remarkable a champion that his equal could be found nowhere on that field. He struck down five knights, one after the other, before anyone stopped his advance.
Seeing him do such work, several knights of the other party tried to reach him and meet him in his advance.

Among them was a certain knight named Sir Balamorgineas, who was so huge that he rode with his head and shoulders above every other knight. He was so extraordinarily strong that people believed he could withstand the attack of three ordinary knights at once. When this knight saw what Sir Kay was doing, he cried out to him, “Ho! ho! Sir Knight of the black griffin, turn this way and fight me!”

When Sir Kay saw that Sir Balamorgineas meant to come against him in that way, threatening and ready to fight, he turned toward his enemy in great good cheer. At that time Sir Kay was full of youthful fire, and he thought nothing of attacking any opponent who challenged him.

(So it was at that time. But later, when he became Seneschal and other, mightier knights appeared at the King’s court, he would sometimes avoid a fight with a knight such as Sir Launcelot, Sir Pellias, Sir Marhaus, or Sir Gawaine, if he could do so without hurting his honor.)

So, full of the spirit of youth, he turned toward him with a bold heart, burning with the eagerness and fury of battle. He cried out in a great voice, “Very well, I will fight you, and I will throw you down like your fellows!” With that he struck at Sir Balamorgineas with wonderful fierceness and with all his might. Sir Balamorgineas took the blow on his helmet and was completely dazed by its force, for he had never felt anything like it before. His head spun so badly that he had to hold on to the horn of his saddle to keep from falling.

It was a great misfortune for Sir Kay that his sword snapped off at the hilt from the force of his blow. The blade flew so high into the air that it seemed to rise above the towers of the cathedral. But that is what happened, and so Sir Kay was left without a weapon. People thought that, because of that stroke, he had Sir Balamorgineas completely at his mercy. If he could have struck one more blow with his sword, they said, he might easily have defeated him.

But as things stood, Sir Balamorgineas soon recovered enough to see that his enemy was now helpless. He was filled with rage over the blow he had received, and he pressed hard against Sir Kay, meaning to strike him down in a fierce attack.

Things might have gone very badly for Sir Kay at that moment. But three of his fellow knights saw the terrible danger he was in, and they pushed in between him and Sir Balamorgineas. They meant to take the attack of that knight upon themselves and so save Sir Kay from being thrown down. They did this so well that Sir Kay was able to push his way out of the crowd and reach the barriers without any further harm from his enemies.

When he reached the barrier, his squire, young Arthur, came running to him with a cup of spiced wine. Sir Kay lifted the visor of his helmet to drink, for he was terribly thirsty. And behold, his face was covered with blood and sweat, and he was so parched from the battle that his tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth and he could not speak. But when he had drunk the wine that Arthur gave him, his tongue was loosened, and he called out to the young man in a loud and angry voice: “Ho! ho! Brother, get me another sword so that I can go on fighting, for I am surely winning great glory for our family this day!” And Arthur said, “Where shall I get you a sword?” And Kay said, “Hurry to our father’s tent and bring me another sword from there, for the one I have is broken.” And Arthur said, “I will do so as fast as I can.” Then he put his hand on the barrier and leaped over it into the lane beyond. He ran down the lane as fast as he could, meaning to do what his brother had told him. With the same speed he ran to the tent that his father had set up in the meadows.

But when he came to Sir Ector’s tent, he found no one there, for all the servants had gone to the tournament. He could not find any sword that would suit his brother, either, and he was at a loss to know what to do.

In this difficulty he remembered the sword that was stuck in the anvil before the cathedral, and it seemed to him that such a sword would suit his brother very well. So he said to himself, “I will go there and get that sword if I can, for it will serve my brother well to finish his battle with.” Then he ran as fast as he could to the cathedral. When he got there, he found that no one was guarding the block of marble, as there had been before, for all the guards had gone to watch the contest of arms that was going on. The anvil and the sword stood within his reach. With no one there to stop young Arthur, he leaped up onto the block of marble and laid his hands on the hilt of the sword. He bent his body and pulled hard on the sword, and behold, it came out of the anvil with wonderful smoothness and ease. He held the sword in his hand, and it was his.

Once the sword was his, he hid it under his cloak so that nobody could see it, because it gleamed with a dazzling light. Then he jumped down from the marble block and hurried back to the tournament field with it.

When Arthur came back into the meadow, he found Sir Kay waiting for him with great impatience. As soon as Sir Kay saw him, he cried out eagerly, “Have you got a sword?” And Arthur said, “Yes, I have one here.” Then he opened his cloak and showed Sir Kay the sword he had brought.

When Sir Kay saw the sword, he knew it at once. He did not know what to think or what to say, and for a while he stood like a man turned to stone, staring at that sword. After a time he said, in a very strange voice, “Where did you get that sword?” Arthur looked at his brother and saw that his face was greatly troubled and as white as wax. And he said, “Brother, what is wrong with you, that you look so strange? I will tell you the whole truth. I could find no sword in our father’s tent, so I remembered the sword that stood in the anvil on the marble block before the cathedral. I went there and tried to pull it out, and it came out with wonderful ease. When I had drawn it out, I wrapped it in my cloak and brought it here to you, as you see.”

Then Sir Kay turned his thoughts inward and said to himself, “Behold, my brother Arthur is hardly more than a child. He is also very innocent. So he does not know what he has done in this, or what the doing of it means. Now, since he has won this weapon, why should I not claim that deed for myself, and so gain the glory that goes with it?” Then he roused himself and said to Arthur, “Give the sword and the cloak to me,” and Arthur did as his brother commanded. When he had done so, Sir Kay said to him, “Tell no one of this, but keep it secret in your own heart. Meanwhile, go to our father where he sits at the lists, and ask him to come at once to the tent where we are staying.”

Arthur did as Sir Kay told him, though he was filled with wonder that his brother should be so troubled in spirit. He did not know what he had done in drawing that sword out of the anvil. Nor did he know what great things would come from that small act. So it is in this world that a man sometimes proves himself worthy of a great trust, and yet, in his humility, he does not know that he is worthy of it at all. And so it was with young Arthur at that time.

chapters.title: The Winning of Kinghood: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How Arthur Performed the Miracle of the Sword Twice in Front of Sir Ector, and How the Truth About His Birth Was Revealed to Him._

So Arthur hurried to the part of the lists where Sir Ector sat with the people of his household. He stood before his father and said, “Sir, my brother Kay sent me here to ask you to come at once to the pavilion where we are staying. Truly, I think something very strange has happened, because my brother Kay has a look on his face that I have never seen before.”

Sir Ector wondered greatly why Sir Kay would leave the fighting and call for him at such a time. So he got up from his seat and went with Arthur. They walked to the pavilion, and when he arrived, he saw Sir Kay standing in the middle of it. Sir Ector saw that his son’s face was as white as wood ashes and that his eyes shone with a strange brightness. Sir Ector said, “My son, what is wrong?” Sir Kay answered, “Sir, here is something truly wonderful.” With that, he took his father by the hand and led him to the table that stood in the pavilion. A cloak lay on the table, and something was wrapped inside it. Then Sir Kay opened the cloak, and there lay the sword of the anvil! Both its hilt and its blade gleamed with dazzling splendor.

Sir Ector knew that sword at once, and he knew where it had come from. He was so astonished that he did not know what to do. For a while he could not speak. Then at last he found his voice and cried out loudly, “What is this that I see before me!”
Sir Kay answered, “Sir, I have the sword that stood a short while ago in the anvil, on the block of marble before the great cathedral. So I ask you to tell me what this means.”
Then Sir Ector said, “How did you come by that sword?”
For a while Sir Kay was silent. Then he said, “Sir, I broke my sword in the battle I fought just now, and so I found this sword to use in its place.”

Sir Ector was utterly bewildered and hardly knew whether to believe what he had heard. After a while he said, “If you really drew this sword out of the anvil, then you must be the rightful King of Britain, for that is what the writing on the sword declares. But if you truly drew it out of the anvil, then you will be just as able to push it back into the place you took it from.”

At this, Sir Kay was deeply troubled, and he cried out loudly, “Who could do such a thing? Who could work so great a miracle as to thrust a sword into solid iron?” Sir Ector answered, “That miracle is no greater than the one you worked in drawing it out. Who ever heard of a man who could pull a sword out of a place and yet could not put it back where he found it?”

Sir Kay did not know what to say to his father, and he was afraid that he would not be able to work that miracle. Still, he tried to comfort himself, saying, “If my young brother Arthur could work this miracle, why should I not do the same? Surely I am no less worthy than he is. If he drew the sword out so easily, perhaps I can push it back just as easily.” So he took what comfort he could from these thoughts.

Then he wrapped the sword in the cloak again. He and Sir Ector left the pavilion and made their way to the marble stone and the anvil in front of the cathedral. Arthur went along with his father and his brother, and they did not forbid him. When they came to the place where the sword had been, Sir Kay climbed onto the block of marble and looked at the top of the anvil. The top of the anvil was perfectly smooth, without a single scratch or mark. Sir Kay said to himself, “What is my father asking me to do! Who in all the world could push a sword blade into a solid iron anvil?” But he could not back out of that impossible task. He was forced to try the miracle, so he set the point of the sword against the iron and pressed on it with all his strength. But he could not do it. He struggled with all his might, pressing the sword against the anvil, yet he did not pierce the iron even as deep as the width of a hair.
After he had tried for a long while, he finally gave up and came down from where he stood. He said to his father, “Sir, no man alive can work that miracle.”
Sir Ector answered, “How is it possible, then, that you could have pulled out that sword as you say, and yet you cannot put it back?”

Then young Arthur spoke up and said, “Father, may I speak?” Sir Ector said, “Speak, my son.” Arthur said, “I would like to try holding that sword.” Sir Ector replied, “By what right would you hold that sword?” Arthur said, “Because I was the one who drew that sword out of the anvil for my brother. And as you say, drawing it out is no harder than pushing it back in. So I believe I can set it back into the iron it came from.”

Then Sir Ector looked at young Arthur so strangely that Arthur did not know why he was staring at him that way. So he cried out, “Sir, why do you look at me so strangely? Are you angry with me?” Sir Ector answered, “Before God, my son, I am not angry with you.” Then he said, “If you wish to hold the sword, you may certainly try that miracle.”

So Arthur took the sword from his brother Kay and leaped up onto the marble stone. He set the point of the sword on the anvil and pressed down hard. And the sword slid smoothly into the middle of the anvil until it stood halfway in, and there it held fast. After he had worked that miracle, he drew the sword out again quickly and easily, and then he pushed it back in once more, just as he had done before.

When Sir Ector saw what Arthur had done, he cried out in a very loud voice, “Lord! Lord! What a miracle my eyes have seen!” And when Arthur came down from the block of marble, Sir Ector knelt before him and pressed his hands together, palm to palm.
When Arthur saw what his father was doing, he cried out like someone in great pain, and he said, “Father! Father! Why are you kneeling to me?”

Sir Ector answered him, “I am not your father. Now it is clear that you are surely of very noble birth and that the blood of kings runs in your veins. Otherwise you could not have handled that sword as you have.”
Then Arthur began to weep uncontrollably, and he cried out in deep anguish, “Father! Father! What are you saying? Please get up and do not kneel to me.”
So Sir Ector rose from his knees and stood facing Arthur. He said, “Arthur, why are you weeping?” And Arthur said, “Because I am afraid.”
All this time Sir Kay had stood close by, unable to move or speak. He stood like a man in a trance, and he said to himself, “What is this? Is my brother a King?”
Then Sir Ector spoke. He said, “Arthur, the time has come for you to know who you are, for the true story of your life has been kept hidden from you until now.

“I will confess everything to you. Eighteen years ago a man came to me who was very wise and highly favored by Uther-Pendragon, and that man was the Enchanter Merlin. Merlin showed me the signet ring of Uther-Pendragon. By the power of that ring, he ordered me to be at a certain place at a certain time that he named. The place was the back gate of Uther-Pendragon’s castle, and the time was midnight of that very day.
“He ordered me to tell no one anything about what he told me, and I kept his secret as he asked.

“So I went to that back gate at midnight, as Merlin had commanded. There Merlin came to me with another man, and the other man was Sir Ulfius, the chief knight of Uther-Pendragon’s household. I tell you that these two men were closer to Uther-Pendragon than any other men in the world.

“When those two came up to me, I saw that Merlin was carrying something in his arms, wrapped in a scarlet mantle of fine cloth. He opened the folds of the mantle, and there I saw a newborn child wrapped in swaddling clothes. I saw the child by the light of a lantern that Sir Ulfius carried. He was very fair of face and large of bone—and you were that child.

“Then Merlin gave me my orders. I was to take the child and raise him as my own. He said the child was to be named Arthur, and that no one in all the world was to know anything except that the child was mine. I told Merlin I would do as he wished, and I took the child and carried him home with me. I announced that the child was my own, and everyone believed my words, so no one ever knew anything except that you were my own son. The lady who was my wife took that secret with her to Paradise when she died. Since then, until now, no one in the world has known about this matter except me and those two men I told you of.

“Until now I have never known who your father was. But now I suspect who he was, and that you have very high and kingly blood in your veins. I think that perhaps your father was Uther-Pendragon himself. For who but the son of Uther-Pendragon could have drawn that sword out of the anvil as you have?”

When Arthur heard his father say this, he cried out in a loud and violent voice, “Woe! Woe! Woe!” He said those words three times. Sir Ector said, “Arthur, why are you so sorrowful?” And Arthur said, “Because I have lost my father, and I would rather have my father than be a King!”

While these things were happening, two men came to that place. They were very tall and had a noble and proud bearing. When the two men came near, Arthur, Sir Ector and Sir Kay saw that one of them was the Enchanter Merlin and the other was Sir Ulfius. Both men were famous and well known all over the world. When the two had reached the three, Merlin said, “How goes it?” Sir Ector answered, “It goes in a most wonderful way. Look, Merlin! This is the child you brought to me eighteen years ago, and you can see that he has grown into a man.”

Then Merlin said, “Sir Ector, I know very well who this young man is, for I have watched over him carefully all this time. I know that Britain’s hope lies in him. Moreover, I tell you that even today, in the surface of an enchanted mirror, I have seen everything he has done since morning. I know how he drew the sword from the anvil and how he pushed it back in. I know how he drew it out and pushed it back a second time. I also know everything you have been telling him just now, and so I declare that you have told him the plain truth. And now the spirit of prophecy is upon me, and I can see into the future. You, Arthur, will become the greatest and most famous King who ever lived in Britain. I see that many knights of extraordinary excellence will gather around you, and that men will tell of their marvelous deeds as long as this land lasts. I see that through these knights your reign will be full of splendor and glory. I see that the most marvelous adventure of the Holy Grail will be achieved by three of the knights of your Court. This will bring you lasting fame, for you will be the King in whose reign the holy cup is won. All these things I foresee. And now the time is near when the glory of your House will be shown to the world again, and all the people of this land will rejoice in you and your kingship. So, Sir Ector, for these next three days, I charge you to guard this young man as the apple of your eye, for the hope and safety of this whole realm lie in him.”

Then Sir Ector raised his voice and cried to Arthur, “A boon! A boon!” Arthur said, “Alas! What is this? Do you, my father, ask a boon of me? I can give you anything in the world that is mine. Ask what you wish, and it is yours!” Then Sir Ector said, “I beg this of you: that when you are King, your brother Kay may be Seneschal of this whole realm.” Arthur said, “It shall be as you ask.” And he said, “As for you, it shall be better still, for you shall be my father until the end!” With these words, he took Sir Ector’s head in his hands and kissed him on the forehead and on both cheeks, and so he sealed his promise.

All this while Sir Kay had stood as if struck by thunder. He did not know whether to be lifted to the skies or cast down into the depths, because his young brother had passed him by and been raised to such an astonishing height of fortune. So he stood like someone who had lost all life and movement.

Let it be said here that Arthur kept everything he had promised his father. In later times he made Sir Kay his Seneschal, and Sir Ector was a father to him until the day he died, which happened five years after this.
That is how the royal blood of Arthur first came to light. Now listen, and you will hear how it was proved to the whole world.

chapters.title: The Winning of Kinghood: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How Several Kings and High Dukes Tried and Failed to Pull the Sword Out of the Anvil, and How Arthur Tried It and Won._
When the morning of Christmas day came, many thousands of people of every rank, both noble and common, gathered in front of the cathedral to watch the trial of that sword.

A canopy of embroidered cloth in many colors had been spread above the sword and the anvil, and a platform had been built all around the block of marble. Close by, a throne had been set up for the Archbishop. He was to oversee the trial and make sure that everything was done fairly and with proper care.

By midmorning the Archbishop himself arrived in great state and took his seat on the high throne that had been prepared for him. His whole court of clerks and knights gathered around him, so that he made a very proud and splendid sight, full of courtly dignity.

Nineteen kings and sixteen dukes had gathered for the trial. Each of them was of such noble and high rank that he hoped to be proven that very day before the whole world to be the rightful king and overlord of all Britain. So after the Archbishop had settled on his throne, several of them came and demanded that he put the matter to the test at once. The Archbishop ordered his herald to sound a trumpet and call everyone who had the right to try the sword to come forward for that adventure. The herald did as the Archbishop commanded.

As soon as the herald had sounded his trumpet, the first of the kings came forward to try the sword. He was King Lot of Orkney and the Isles. Eleven knights and five esquires came with King Lot, so that he looked very noble in the eyes of all. When King Lot reached the place, he climbed onto the platform. First he bowed to the Archbishop, and then he laid his hands on the pommel of the sword in full sight of everyone. He bent his body and pulled on the sword with great strength. But he could not move the blade in the anvil even by the width of a hair. It stood as firm as the iron it was set in. After that first attempt he tried three more times, but still he could not move the blade in the iron. Then, having tried four times, he gave up and came down from the platform. He was filled with great anger that he had not succeeded.

After King Lot came his brother-in-law, King Urien of Gore, and he made his attempt in the same way that King Lot had done. But he did no better than the first king. After King Urien came King Fion of Scotland, and after King Fion came King Mark of Cornwall. After King Mark came King Ryence of North Wales, and after King Ryence came King Leodegrance of Cameliard. After him came all the other kings and dukes who have been named, and not one of them could move the blade. Some of these high and mighty lords were filled with anger that they had failed. Others were ashamed that they had failed before the eyes of everyone watching. But whether they were angry or ashamed, it did them no good at all.

When all the kings and dukes had failed in this adventure, the people there were astonished, and they said to one another, “How can this be? If all these kings and dukes of such high rank have failed, who can hope to succeed? Every man most worthy of this great honor has been here, and all have tried to draw the sword, and all have failed. Who is left to come after them and hope to succeed?”

The kings and dukes talked together in the same way. After a while six of the most worthy came forward. They were King Lot, King Urien, King Pellinore, King Ban, King Ryence, and Duke Clarence of Northumberland. They stood before the Archbishop’s throne and spoke to him like this: “Sir, all the kings and dukes of this realm have struggled before you to draw out that sword, and look! Not one of those who tried has succeeded. What can we think, then, except that the enchanter Merlin set up this adventure to bring shame and disgrace on all of us here, and on you, the head of the church in this realm? For who in all the world could hope to pull a sword blade out of a bed of solid iron? Look! It is beyond the power of any man. Is it not plain to see that Merlin has made a fool of us all? Now, so that this great crowd will not have been called here for nothing, we beg you in your wisdom to choose at once the one best fitted to be overlord of this realm, from among the kings gathered here. When you have chosen him, we promise to obey him in everything he commands. Truly, such a choice will be better worth our while than wasting time on this foolish task. No man in all the world can pull a sword out of an anvil.”

The Archbishop was deeply troubled, for he said to himself, “Can it be true that Merlin has deceived me, and made a fool of me and of all these kings and noble people? Surely this cannot be. Merlin is very wise, and he would not make a fool of the whole realm for the sake of so poor a joke as this. Surely he has some purpose in this that we know nothing about, since we are less wise than he. So I will be patient a while longer.” Having thought this over, he spoke aloud to the seven high lords. “Messires,” he said, “I still have faith that Merlin has not deceived us, so I ask you to be patient for one short while longer. Wait for the time it takes a man to count five hundred twice over. If no one comes forward to do this task by then, at your request I will choose one of you and proclaim him King and Overlord of all.” For the Archbishop believed that Merlin was about to name a king before them all at any moment.
Now we will leave these men and turn to Arthur and his father and brother.

Merlin had told those three to wait in their pavilion until he thought the time was right for them to come out. That time had now come, and Merlin and Sir Ulfius went to the pavilion of Sir Ector. Merlin said, “Arthur, get up and come out, for now the hour has come for you to try, before the whole world, the miracle that you performed in private not long ago.” So Arthur did as Merlin told him. He came out of the pavilion with his father and his brother, and look! He was like someone walking in a dream.

So the five of them went down toward the cathedral and the place of the trial. When they came to the crowd gathered there, the people made way for them, marveling and saying to one another, “Who are these people with the enchanter Merlin and Sir Ulfius, and where do they come from? For all the world knew Merlin and Sir Ulfius, and the people knew that something very extraordinary was about to happen. Arthur was dressed all in flame-colored clothing embroidered with silver thread, so that others in the crowd said, “Truly, that youth is very fair to look upon. Who can he be?”

But Merlin said nothing to anyone. He brought Arthur through the crowd to the place where the Archbishop sat, and the crowd made way for him so that he was not held back. When the Archbishop saw Merlin coming with these others, he stood up and said, “Merlin, who are these people you bring to us, and what is their business here?” Merlin said, “Lord, here is one who has come to try that sword over there.” The Archbishop said, “Which one is he?” and Merlin said, “This is he,” and he laid his hand on Arthur.

Then the Archbishop looked at Arthur and saw that the youth had a very handsome face, so his heart went out to Arthur and he loved him very much. The Archbishop said, “Merlin, by what right does this young man come here?” Merlin answered, “Lord, he comes here by the best right there is in the world. The one who stands before you dressed in red is the true son of Uther-Pendragon and of his lawful wife, Queen Igraine.”

The Archbishop cried out in great surprise. Those standing close by, who heard Merlin’s words, were so astonished that they could not tell what to think. The Archbishop said, “Merlin, what are you telling me? Until this day, who in all the world ever heard that Uther-Pendragon had a son?”

Merlin answered, “No one has ever known of it until now, except a very few. This is how it happened. When this child was born, the spirit of prophecy came upon me, and I saw that Uther-Pendragon would die before very long. So I feared that the King’s enemies would lay violent hands on the young child for the sake of his inheritance. At the King’s command, another man and I took the young child from his mother and gave him to a third man. That man took the royal child and has raised him ever since as his own son. There are others here who can swear that all this is true. The man who was with me when the child was taken from his mother was Sir Ulfius, and the man to whom the child was given was Sir Ector of Bonmaison. These two witnesses, who are above all reproach, will swear to the truth of what I have said, for here they stand before you to confirm my words.”
Sir Ulfius and Sir Ector said, “Everything Merlin has said is true, and we give our most faithful and sacred word of honor on it.”
The Archbishop answered, “Who could doubt the word of such honorable witnesses?” Then he looked at Arthur with a smile.
Then Arthur said, “Lord, do I have your leave to take hold of that sword?” The Archbishop said, “You have my leave, and may the grace of God go with you as you try.”

Then Arthur went to the block of marble and laid his hands on the hilt of the sword that was thrust into the anvil. He bent his body and pulled hard, and look! The sword came out with great ease and very smoothly. When he had the sword in his hands, he swung it around his head so that it flashed like lightning. After he had swung it three times around his head, he set the point against the face of the anvil and pressed down hard. And behold! The sword slid smoothly back into the place where it had stood before, and when it was halfway in, it held fast. In this way Arthur completed the marvelous miracle of the sword in the eyes of all the world.

When the people gathered there saw this miracle performed before their faces, they all lifted their voices together. They shouted so fiercely and with such a huge uproar that it seemed the whole earth rocked and trembled with the sound.

While they were shouting, Arthur took hold of the sword again, drew it out, swung it, and drove it back into the anvil. Then he drew it out a third time and did the same thing as before. In this way everyone there saw the miracle performed three times over.

All the kings and dukes who were there were filled with amazement. They did not know what to think or say when they saw someone who was little more than a boy do the very thing at which the best of them had failed. Some of them, having seen the miracle, were willing to accept Arthur because of it, but others would not. These withdrew and stood apart, and as they stood there they said among themselves, “What is this? Who can believe such a thing, that a beardless boy should be set before us all and made King and overlord of this great realm to rule over us? No! No! We will have none of him for our King.” Others said, “Is it not clear that Merlin and Sir Ulfius are lifting up this unknown boy so that they may raise themselves up along with him?” So these discontented kings spoke among themselves, and the most bitter of them all were King Lot and King Urien, who were related to Arthur by marriage.

When the Archbishop saw the discontent of these kings and dukes, he said to them, “What is this, Messires! Are you not satisfied?” They said, “We are not satisfied.” The Archbishop said, “What do you want?” They said, “We want a different sort of king for Britain than a beardless boy whom no one knows, and whose birthright only three men can vouch for.” The Archbishop said, “What of that? Has he not done the miracle that you yourselves tried and failed to do?”
But these high and mighty lords would not be satisfied. With angry faces turned away, they left that place, filled with rage.

But other kings and dukes came and bowed to Arthur and paid him honor, wishing him joy of what he had done. The foremost of those who came to him in friendship was King Leodegrance of Cameliard. All the crowd acknowledged him and pressed around the place, shouting so that it sounded like thunder.

All this while Sir Ector and Sir Kay had stood to one side. They were weighed down by sorrow, for it seemed to them that Arthur had suddenly been lifted so far above their rank that they could never hope to come near him again. Now he was of kingly importance and they were only common knights. After a while Arthur saw them standing there with downcast looks. He went straight to them, took each one by the hand in turn, and kissed each on the cheek. Then they were glad again to be raised up to him in this way.

When Arthur left that place, great crowds of people followed him, so that the streets were completely filled with people pressing close. The crowd kept loudly hailing him as the chosen King of England, and those nearest to him tried to touch the hem of his clothes. Arthur’s heart was lifted up with great joy and gladness, so that his soul took wing and flew like a bird into the sky.

That day, then, Arthur won the adventure of the sword and took up his birthright as king. May God bless every one of you, so that you too may do well in all you set out to do. Any man can be a king in whatever life he is given, if he can draw the sword of success out of the iron of circumstance. So when your own time of trial comes, I hope it goes for you as it went for Arthur that day. May you win success that fully satisfies you, with great glory and perfect happiness. Amen.

chapters.title: The Winning of Kinghood: Conclusion
paragraphs: After these events, there was a great deal of talk among the people, along with confusion and uproar. Some of the kings and nearly all of the common people said, “Look! A king has come to us, as if from Heaven itself, to bring peace to our troubled land.” But other kings, and they were the greater number, said, “Who is this beardless boy who comes claiming to be High King of Britain? Who ever heard of him before? We want nothing to do with him unless he proves himself further and offers better evidence.” So, for the sake of peace, the Archbishop ordered that the sword be tested once more at Candlemas. Again everyone who tried to pull out the sword failed, but Arthur drew it out several times, very easily, in front of everyone. Then a third trial was held at Easter, and after that a fourth trial at Pentecost. At every one of these trials Arthur pulled the sword out of the anvil again and again, and no one but he could draw it out.

After that fourth trial, several of the kings, many of the lesser barons and knights, and all of the common people cried out that there had been trials enough. They said that Arthur had surely proven himself to be the rightful King, and so they demanded that he be made King in truth, so that he could rule over them. Wherever Arthur went, great crowds followed him, hailing him as the true son of Uther-Pendragon and the rightful overlord of Britain. So the Archbishop saw how the people loved Arthur and how greatly they wanted him as their King. He ordered that Arthur be anointed and crowned with royal honor, and this was done at the great Cathedral. Some say that the Cathedral was St. Paul’s, and some say that it was not.

But once Arthur had been crowned, all those who opposed his Kingship left in great anger and immediately began to prepare for war against him. The people, however, stood with Arthur and joined him, and so did several Kings and many of the lesser barons and knights. With Merlin’s advice, Arthur made friends and allies of several other kings, and together they fought two great wars against his enemies and won both. In the second war a very famous battle was fought near the Forest of Bedegraine, which is why it was called the Battle of Bedegraine. In that battle Arthur defeated his enemies so completely that they could never hope to unite against him in war again.

From King Lot, his brother-in-law, King Arthur took two of his sons to live at Court and serve as hostages for peace afterward. These two were Gawaine and Geharris, and after a while they became very famous and accomplished knights. From King Urien, his other brother-in-law, Arthur took one son, Ewaine, to keep at Court as a hostage for peace. He, too, became in time a very famous and accomplished knight. Because of these hostages, there was peace between those three kingly brothers from then on. A certain very famous king and knight named King Pellinore was one of Arthur’s enemies. Arthur drove him out of his lands, away from the homes of men, and into the forest. King Ryence was another of his enemies, and Arthur drove him into the mountains of North Wales. Other kings who were his enemies he forced to bend to his will. As a result, the whole land was at such peace as it had not known since the days of Uther-Pendragon.

King Arthur made Sir Kay his Seneschal, as he had promised to do. He made Sir Ulfius his Chamberlain, Merlin his Counsellor, and Sir Bodwain of Britain his Constable. These men were all of the kind who greatly added to the glory and fame of his reign and set him on his throne with complete security.

Now the reign of King Arthur was firmly established, and word of his greatness began to spread through the world. Many men of noble souls, generous spirit, and great knightly skill wanted above all things to win glory in arms at Courts of Chivalry. They saw that great honor and a higher standing were likely to be won under such a king. So from all parts, little by little, a Court of noble, honorable knights began to gather around King Arthur. It was a Court such as no one had ever seen before, and perhaps no one will ever see again.

People all over the world still know the story of these good knights today. The names of many kings and emperors have faded away and been forgotten, yet men still remember Sir Galahad, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Tristram of Lyonesse, Sir Percival of Gales, Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Bors de Ganis, and many others of that noble household and worthy brotherhood. I believe that for as long as people write books, the deeds of these worthy men will be remembered.

In this history, which is still to be written, I have set myself the task of telling the reader of this book about many of these adventures. I will also tell him a number of circumstances that I do not believe everyone knows. Later, when I tell of the founding of the Round Table, I will set out a list of many of those worthy men who gathered at the Court of Arthur at this time. They were chosen to found the order of the Round Table, and for that reason they were called “The Ancient and Honorable Companions of the Round Table.”

Although this entire book is mainly about King Arthur, the fame of these great and honorable knights belonged to him, and his fame belonged to them. For that reason, no one can speak of the greatness of King Arthur without also speaking of the greatness of the noble gentlemen I have named.

chapters.title: The Winning of a Sword: Chapter 1
paragraphs: _This part of the story tells of certain adventures of Arthur after he became King. It tells how, with great knightly courage and skill, he fought a fierce and bloody battle with a Sable Knight. It also tells how, because of that battle, he won a Sword so famous and glorious that its fame will last as long as our language is spoken. No sword like it had ever been seen in the world before that time, and none has been seen since. Its name was Excalibur._

_If you choose to read this story, I believe it will entertain you very well. I am sure it will lift your spirits, because of the remarkable courage those two famous and worthy knights showed when they fought that great battle. You will also find much delight in reading about a wonderful land of Faerie, where King Arthur wandered. There he found a Lake of Enchantment and spoke with a gentle and beautiful lady of that land, who told him how to win the famous sword I have mentioned._

_Writing these things has given me such pleasure that at times my heart seemed to overflow with pure joy. So I hope you will find as much pleasure in them as I have. Now I ask you to listen to what follows._
_A Wounded Knight Arrives at King Arthur’s Court; a Young Knight of the Court Sets Out to Avenge Him and Fails; and the King Then Takes the Challenge on Himself._

One pleasant day in the springtime, King Arthur and his Court were traveling in royal style through the part of Britain that lies near the Forests of the Usk. The weather was very warm, so the King and his Court stopped in the forest, under the trees, in the cool and pleasant shade. There the King rested for a while on a couch of rushes spread with scarlet cloth.

The knights at the Court then were Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Kay, Sir Pellias, Sir Bedevere, Sir Caradoc, Sir Geraint, Sir Bodwin of Britain, Sir Constantine of Cornwall, Sir Brandiles, and Sir Mador de la Porte. You could not have found a company of nobler or finer knights anywhere in the world.

The King lay half asleep, and these fine knights sat talking cheerfully together. Suddenly there was a great bustle and stir at the edge of the Court, and a sad and sorrowful sight appeared. A badly wounded knight came toward them, held up on his horse by a golden-haired page dressed in white and blue. The knight’s clothes and the trappings of his horse were also white and blue. On his shield he bore a single silver lily on a field of pure blue.

The knight was in a terrible state. His face was as pale as wax, and his head hung down on his chest. His eyes were glazed and saw nothing that passed around him. His fine white and blue clothes were all red with the blood that ran from a great wound in his side. As they came along, the young page wept and cried out so sadly that it broke the heart to hear him.

As they came near, King Arthur woke and cried out, “Alas! What sorrowful sight is this that I see? Hurry, my lords, and help that knight. And you, Sir Kay, go quickly and bring that young page here, so that we may hear from his own lips what has happened to his lord.”

So several of the knights hurried at the King’s command and gave the wounded knight every help. They carried him to King Arthur’s own pavilion, which had been set up a little way off. When he was there, the King’s surgeon came to care for him. His wounds were so bad, however, that he could not hope to live much longer.

Meanwhile, Sir Kay brought the young page before the King, where he sat. The King thought he had hardly ever seen a more beautiful face. The King said, “Please tell me, Sir Page, who is your master, and how did he come to be in the sad and pitiful state we have just seen?”

“I will do so, my Lord,” said the youth. “My master is called Sir Myles of the White Fountain, and he comes from the country to the north, a long way from here. In that country he is lord of seven castles and many noble estates, so, as you can see, he is a man of great importance. Two weeks ago, perhaps stirred by the lively spirit of springtime, he set out with only me as his squire. He wished to seek adventure, as a good knight who wanders in search of it should. We had several adventures, and in all of them my lord was completely successful. He defeated six knights in different places and sent them all to his castle to tell his lady of his bravery.

“At last, this morning, a long way from here, we came upon a fair castle in the forest. It stood in a valley surrounded by open stretches of smooth lawn, decked with many flowers of different kinds. There we saw three lovely damsels tossing a golden ball from one to another. The damsels were dressed all in flame-colored satin, and their hair was the color of gold. As we came near, they stopped their play. The one who seemed to be their leader called out to my lord and asked where he was going and what his business was.

“My lord answered that he was a knight wandering in search of adventure. At this the three damsels laughed, and the one who had spoken first said, ‘If you are looking for adventure, Sir Knight, perhaps I can help you find one that will satisfy you completely.’
“My master answered, ‘Please, fair damsel, tell me what that adventure is, so that I may try it at once.’

“Then the lady told my master to take a certain path and follow it for a league or a little more. He would then come to a stone bridge over a rushing stream, and she promised him that there he would find enough adventure to satisfy any man.

“So my master and I went that way, as the damsel had told us, and soon we came to the bridge she had spoken of. And there, beyond the bridge, stood a lonely castle with a tall, straight tower. In front of the castle was a wide, level lawn of well-trimmed grass. Just past the bridge was an apple tree hung with a great many shields. In the middle of the bridge hung a single shield, entirely black, and beside it hung a brass hammer. Beneath the shield these words were written in red letters:

Whoever Strikes This Shield
Does So At His Own Risk.
“When my master, Sir Myles, read those words, he went straight to the shield. He seized the hammer that hung beside it and struck the shield such a blow that it rang like thunder.

“At once, as if in answer, the castle’s portcullis was let down, and a knight came out, dressed from head to foot in black armor. His clothes, the trappings of his horse, and all his gear were black as well.

“When the Sable Knight saw my master, he came riding swiftly across the meadow to the other end of the bridge. There he drew rein, saluted my master, and cried out, ‘Sir Knight, why did you strike that shield? Because of your boldness, I will take your own shield from you and hang it on that apple tree, where you see all those other shields hanging.’ My master answered, ‘You will not do that unless you can defeat me, knight against knight.’ And at once he raised his shield and made ready for combat.

“So my master and the Sable Knight, once they were ready, charged together with all their might. They met in the middle of the course, and my master’s spear burst into splinters. But the spear of the Sable Knight held. It pierced Sir Myles’s shield and went into his side, so that both he and his horse were thrown violently into the dust. He was so badly wounded that he could not get up from the ground where he lay.

“Then the Sable Knight took my master’s shield and hung it in the branches of the apple tree with the other shields. After that, without paying any more attention to my master or asking how badly he was hurt, he rode back into his castle, and the portcullis was shut behind him at once.

“After he had gone, I got my master onto his horse with great difficulty and took him away from there. I did not know where I might find shelter for him until I came to this place. And that, my lord King, is the true story of how my master got the deadly wound he suffers from.”

“Ha! By the glory of Paradise!” cried King Arthur. “I think it a great shame that strangers in my Kingdom, and so near my Court, should be treated as rudely as Sir Myles has been. It is certainly discourteous to leave a fallen knight on the ground without stopping to ask how badly he is hurt. It is even more discourteous to take the shield of a fallen knight who has fought well.”
All the knights in the King’s Court cried shame on the Sable Knight for such rude behavior.

Then an esquire who served the King, named Griflet, came forward. He was much loved by his royal master. He knelt before the King and cried out in a loud voice, “I ask a favor of you, my lord King! I beg you to grant it to me!”
King Arthur looked kindly on the youth as he knelt before him, and said, “Ask, Griflet, and your favor will be granted.”

Then Griflet said, “This is what I ask. I beg you to make me a knight right away and let me go out and punish this unkind knight. I will overthrow him and win back the shields he has hung on that apple tree.”

King Arthur was very troubled in his mind, for Griflet was still only an esquire and had never been tested in arms. So he said, “Look, you are still too young to face so mighty a knight as this black champion must be. He has overthrown so many knights without being hurt himself. Please, dear Griflet, think again and ask some other favor.”
But young Griflet only cried out all the more, “A favor! A favor! And you have granted it to me.”
Then King Arthur said, “You shall have your favor, though my heart tells me you will suffer great pain and misfortune from this adventure.”

So that night Griflet kept watch over his armor in a chapel in the forest. In the morning, after receiving the Sacrament, he was made a knight by King Arthur’s own hand, and no knight could have had a greater honor than that. Then King Arthur fastened the golden spurs to Sir Griflet’s heels with his own hand.
So Griflet was made a knight. He mounted his war-horse and rode straight off on his adventure, full of joy and singing for pure pleasure.

It was around this time that Sir Myles died from his wound. Life is often like this: some people meet death and misfortune, while others laugh and sing in hope and joy, as if sorrow and death, those terrible things, could never touch the world they live in.

That afternoon King Arthur sat waiting anxiously for news of the young knight, but there was none until toward evening. Then some of his attendants came hurrying to him, saying that Sir Griflet was returning, but without his shield, and looking as though some great misfortune had struck him. Right after them came Sir Griflet himself, held up on his horse by Sir Constantine on one side and Sir Brandiles on the other. And look! Sir Griflet’s head hung down on his chest, and his fine new armor was all broken and stained with blood and dust. He looked so sorrowful that King Arthur’s heart tightened with grief to see that young knight in such a pitiful state.

At King Arthur’s command, they took Sir Griflet to the Royal Pavilion and laid him down on a soft couch. Then the King’s surgeon examined his wounds. He found that the head of a spear and part of its shaft were still stuck in Sir Griflet’s side, so that he was in terrible and bitter pain.
When King Arthur saw how dangerously Sir Griflet lay, he cried out, “Alas! My dear young knight, what has happened to you, to bring you to this sad state that I see?”

Then Sir Griflet, speaking in a very weak voice, told King Arthur how he had fared. He said that he had ridden through the forest until he found the three beautiful damsels that the page of Sir Myles had spoken of. He said these damsels had told him how to go about his adventure. He said he had found the bridge where the shield and the brass hammer hung, and had seen the apple tree hung full of shields there. He said he struck the shield of the Sable Knight with the brass hammer, and the Sable Knight came riding out against him. He said that this knight did not seem to want to fight him. Instead, the knight told him very nobly that he was too young and too untried in arms to face a seasoned knight, and he advised Sir Griflet to give up the adventure before it was too late. But in spite of this advice, Sir Griflet would not give up. He declared that he would certainly fight that other knight in black. At the very first charge, Sir Griflet’s spear burst into pieces, but the spear of the Sable Knight held and pierced through Sir Griflet’s shield and into his side, causing the grievous wound he now suffered. And Sir Griflet said that the Sable Knight had then, most courteously, lifted him onto his horse again. The knight had kept Sir Griflet’s shield, however, and hung it on the tree with the others there. Then he had sent Sir Griflet on his way, so that he had managed to ride back here, though in great pain and sorrow.

Then King Arthur became furious and was greatly troubled in his mind, for he loved Sir Griflet very dearly. So he declared that he himself would go out to punish that Sable Knight and humble him with his own hand. The knights of his Court tried to talk him out of the adventure, but he declared that he would humble that proud knight with his own hand. With God’s grace, he said, he would undertake the adventure the very next day.

He was so upset that he could hardly eat his food that evening for anger, and he would not go to his couch to sleep. Instead, he asked Sir Griflet very closely where he might find that valley of flowers and those three damsels. Then he spent the night walking up and down his pavilion, waiting for the day to dawn.

As soon as the birds began to chirp and the east grew bright with the coming daylight, King Arthur called his two esquires. With their help he put on his armor and mounted a milk-white war-horse. Then he set off at once on the adventure he had decided upon.

It is a very pleasant thing to ride out at dawn on a spring day. The little birds sing their sweetest songs then, all joining in one happy chorus, so that you can hardly tell one note from another. The growing things of the earth smell their sweetest in the freshness of early morning—the flowers, the shrubs, and the blossoms on the trees. The dew sparkles over all the grass like countless jewels of every color. The whole world seems sweet and clean and new, as if it had just been created for the person who came out to wander so early in the morning.
So King Arthur’s heart swelled with joy, and he sang a quaint old song as he rode through the forest on his knightly quest.

About noon he came to the part of the forest that he had heard about several times before. All at once he saw a wide, gently sloping valley in front of him, and down it ran a stream as bright as silver. The valley was covered with countless fair and fragrant flowers of many kinds. In the middle of the valley stood a handsome castle with tall red roofs and many bright windows, and King Arthur thought it a very fine castle indeed. On a smooth green lawn he saw the three damsels dressed in flame-colored satin, the ones that the page of Sir Myles and Sir Griflet had spoken of. They were playing ball with a golden ball, and the hair of each of them was the color of gold. As he drew near, it seemed to King Arthur that they were the most beautiful damsels he had ever seen in all his life.
As King Arthur came up to them, the three stopped tossing the ball. The one who was the fairest of all the damsels asked him where he was going and what errand he was on.

Then King Arthur replied, “Ah, fair lady! Where should a belted knight ride on a day like this, and on what business, other than the search for adventure? That is just what suits a knight who is strong in heart and body and wishes to be a knight errant.”

Then the three damsels smiled at the King, for he had a very handsome face and they liked him well. “Alas, Sir Knight!” said the one who had spoken first, “please do not be in such a hurry to take on a dangerous adventure. Stay with us instead for a day or two or three, to feast and be merry with us. Good cheer does a great deal to lift the heart, and we would gladly enjoy the company of such a gallant knight as you seem to be. That castle over there is ours, and all this happy valley is ours. Those who have visited it are so pleased by its gaiety that they call it the Valley of Delight. So stay with us a little while, and do not be in such haste to go on.”

“No,” said King Arthur, “I cannot stay with you, fair ladies, for I am set on an adventure. You will understand it well when I tell you that I am seeking the Sable Knight, who has defeated so many other knights and taken away their shields. So I beg you, of your kindness, to tell me where I may find him.”

“Heaven help us!” cried the one who spoke for the others, “this is truly a sorry adventure you are seeking, Sir Knight! In these last two days, two knights have already fought that knight, and both have fallen into great pain and disgrace. Even so, if you will take on this danger, you will not go until you have eaten and refreshed yourself.” With that, she lifted a little ivory whistle that hung from her neck on a golden chain, and blew a shrill note on it.

In answer to this call, three fair young pages came out of the castle, all dressed in flame-colored clothes. Between them they carried a silver table covered with a white cloth. After them came five other pages dressed the same way, carrying flagons of white wine and red, dried fruits, sweets, and loaves of fine white bread.

King Arthur gladly got down from his war-horse, because he was very hungry and thirsty. He took a seat at the table, with the damsels on either side of him, and ate heartily. All the while he chatted pleasantly with the ladies, who listened to him cheerfully. He never told them his name, though they kept wondering who this noble warrior could be, who had arrived in their valley.

When he had satisfied his hunger and thirst, King Arthur mounted his steed again, and the three damsels led him a little way across the valley, he riding his horse and they walking beside him. Before long he saw a dark path that led into the farther side of the forest. When he had come to it, the lady who had spoken to him before said, “That is the way you must take if you want to enter upon this adventure. So farewell, and may good fortune go with you, for truly you are the most courteous knight who has come this way for a long time.”
Then King Arthur bowed to the ladies with great courtesy and rode away, full of joy at the pleasant adventure he had just passed through.

After King Arthur had gone some distance, he came to a place where charcoal burners worked at their trade. There were many mounds of earth there, all smoking from the smoldering logs inside them, and the whole air was filled with the smell of the damped fires.

As the King came near this spot, he saw that something was going on that was very wrong. In the open clearing he saw three sooty fellows with long knives in their hands, chasing one old man whose beard was as white as snow. The respectable old man was richly dressed in black, and his horse stood a little way off. He was running this way and that, as if to escape from those wicked men, and he seemed to be very hard pressed and in great danger of his life.

“By heaven!” said the young King to himself, “here is someone in bitter need of help.” Then he cried out in a great voice, “Stop, villains! What do you think you are doing?” With that he spurred his horse, lowered his spear, and charged down upon them with a noise as loud as thunder.

The three wicked fellows saw the armed Knight come thundering toward them. They threw down their knives at once and fled in all directions, shouting in fear. They did not stop until they had vanished into the thick brush of the forest, where no rider could hope to follow.
