Having driven away those wicked fellows, King Arthur rode up to the man he had rescued, meaning to comfort him. And behold! When he came close, he saw that the old man was the Enchanter Merlin. The King could not understand where Merlin had so suddenly come from, since only a short while before he had been at the King’s Court at Carleon. Nor could he understand what Merlin was doing in that place. So he spoke to the Enchanter and said, “Ha! Merlin, it seems to me that I have saved your life. Surely you would not have escaped from those wicked men if I had not happened to come this way just now.”

“Do you think so, my lord?” said Merlin. “Now let me tell you that I may have seemed to be in danger, but I could have saved myself very easily if I had wished to. Just as you saw me in this seeming danger, so you should know that a real danger, far greater than this, lies ahead of you, and there will be no knight errant to rescue you from it. So I beg you, my lord, to take me with you on this adventure you have set out upon. I tell you that you will certainly suffer great grief and pain in it.”

“Merlin,” said King Arthur, “even if I were to face my death, I would not turn back from this adventure. But as for the advice you give me, it seems to me that it will be very good to take you with me, if such danger lies ahead of me as you say.”
And Merlin said, “Yes, it would be very good for you to do so.”
So Merlin mounted his palfrey, and he and King Arthur set out from that place to pursue the adventure that the King had undertaken.

chapters.title: The Winning of a Sword: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How King Arthur fought the Sable Knight and was badly wounded, and how Merlin carried him safely away from the battlefield._

King Arthur and Merlin rode together through the forest for a long while. At last they saw that they must be getting close to the place where the Sable Knight lived, the knight the King was so eager to find. The forest had been wild, deep and mossy until then, but now it grew thinner and more open, as though people lived nearby.

Soon they saw a fierce stream rushing through a dark and gloomy valley. A stone bridge crossed the stream. On the far side of the bridge lay a smooth, level lawn of green grass, a fine place for knights to joust. Beyond the lawn stood a tall and grim castle with smooth walls and a straight tower. It was built on the rocks so well that it seemed to be part of the stone itself. So they knew this must be the castle the page and Sir Griflet had told them about.

Halfway across the bridge hung a black shield and a brass mallet, just as the page and Sir Griflet had said. On the far side of the stream stood an apple tree, and among its leaves hung a great many shields with different emblems, just as those two had described. Some of the shields were clean and bright, and some were dirty and stained with blood. Some were whole and unbroken, and some were split as though in a fight between two knights. All of them belonged to knights whom the Sable Knight, who lived in the castle, had defeated in combat with his own hand.

“By the splendor of Paradise!” said King Arthur. “He must be a truly brave knight, to have defeated so many other knights by his strength alone. Indeed, Merlin, there must be a hundred shields hanging in that tree!”
Merlin answered him, “And you, my Lord, may be very glad if your shield is not hanging there too before the sun goes down this evening.”

“That,” said King Arthur, with a steady face, “will be as God wills. Truly, I want more than ever to test my strength against that knight. Think what honor I would win if I beat so brave a warrior as this Sable Champion seems to be, since he has beaten so many other good knights.”
Having said this, King Arthur at once urged his horse forward. As he came onto the bridge, he clearly read the challenge written in red letters beneath the shield:

Whoever Strikes This Shield
Does So At His Own Risk.

Having read the words, the King grabbed the brass mallet and hit the shield so hard that the noise bounced back. It came back from the castle’s smooth walls, from the rocks beneath them, and from the edge of the forest all around, as if twelve other shields had been struck in those places.

At the sound, the portcullis of the castle was let fall at once, and a knight came out, huge in size and dressed all in black armor. All his clothing and all the trappings of his horse were black too, so that he looked very grim and frightening. The Sable Knight crossed the smooth green meadow with a stately and dignified pace. He rode neither in haste nor slowly, but with great pride and a haughty look, as a champion should who perhaps had never yet been beaten in battle. When he reached the end of the bridge, he pulled in his reins and greeted King Arthur with great dignity, and with great arrogance too. “Ha! Sir Knight!” he said. “Why did you strike my shield after reading the words written there? I tell you that, because of your rudeness, I will now take your shield from you and hang it on that apple tree, where you see all those other shields hanging. So either hand your shield over to me without more talk, or get ready to defend it with your body. If you choose that, you will certainly suffer great pain and injury.”

“Thank you for the choice you give me,” said King Arthur. “But as for taking away my shield, I believe that will be as Heaven wills, and not as you will. Know, unkind knight, that I came here for no other purpose than to fight you, and to win back with my own body all those shields that hang on that apple tree. So get ready at once, so that I can face you, perhaps to your great disadvantage.”

“I will do that,” replied the Sable Knight. Then he turned his horse’s head and rode back some distance across the level lawn, and took his place where he thought best. King Arthur also rode out onto the lawn and took his place where he thought best.
Each knight leveled his spear and braced his shield for the charge. Then each called out to his war-horse and dug his spurs deep into its sides.

The two noble horses rushed forward like lightning, racing across the ground so fast that the earth shook and trembled beneath them as in an earthquake. The two knights met squarely in the very middle of the field and crashed together like a thunderbolt. They struck each other so hard that the spears burst into splinters all the way down to the hand guard and the broken stump. The horses staggered back from the shock, and only the great skill of the riders kept them from falling.
But with great spirit, each knight lifted his horse up with his own courage, and so finished his ride safely.

King Arthur was very amazed that he had not knocked his opponent down. As has been said, he was thought to be the best knight in all of Britain, the one most proven in deeds of arms. So he wondered at the strength and skill of this knight, who had not been thrown down by so great a blow against his defenses. When they met again in the middle of the field, King Arthur greeted the knight and spoke to him with great courtesy. He said, “Sir Knight, I do not know who you are, but I give you my word as a knight that you are the mightiest knight I have ever met in all my life. Now I ask you to get down from your horse at once. Let us fight this battle with swords and on foot, for it would be a pity to let it end this way.”

“No,” said the Sable Knight, “I will not fight this battle on foot until one of us two has been knocked down.” Then he shouted, “Ho! Ho!” in a very loud voice. At once the castle gate opened, and two tall squires came running out, dressed all in black with crimson patches. Each squire carried a great spear of ash wood, new and well seasoned, never yet strained in battle.
Each knight took a spear: King Arthur chose one and the Sable Knight took the other. Then each of them went back to the place from which he had started his charge before.

Once again each knight drove his horse forward to the attack, and once again each struck the other so squarely in the middle of his defense that the spears were splintered. Only the hand guard and the stump of each spear were left in the knight’s grip.

As before, King Arthur wanted to fight the battle out with swords on foot, but again the Sable Knight refused. He called out to those inside the castle, and two other squires came out at once with fresh new spears of ash wood. Each knight took a spear again, and when he was armed with it, each chose his place on that fair, level lawn of grass.

For the third time the two fine knights made ready and hurled themselves at one another in a furious charge. As twice before, King Arthur hit the Sable Knight dead center, and his spear burst into splinters. This time, though, the Sable Knight’s spear did not break. It held firm, and his blow landed on King Arthur’s shield with such force that the spear went straight through its middle. The girths of the King’s saddle snapped under that mighty blow, and the King and his horse were hurled backward. King Arthur might have been knocked to the ground, but he leaped clear of his saddle with extraordinary skill. So, though his horse was overthrown, he himself kept his footing and did not fall into the dust. Even so, the blow he received was so violent that for a little while he lost his senses, and everything whirled around before his eyes.

But when his sight returned, he was filled with such a fierce anger that it seemed as though all the blood in his heart rushed into his head. He saw nothing but red before his eyes. When this also passed, he saw the Sable Knight sitting on his horse not far away. King Arthur ran to him at once, caught the bridle of his horse, and cried out fiercely to the Sable Knight, “Come down, you black knight! Fight me on foot, with your sword.”

“I will not do that,” said the Sable Knight, “for, look! I have knocked you down. So hand over your shield to me, so that I may hang it on that apple tree, and go on your way as others have done before you.”

“I will not!” cried King Arthur in great passion. “I will not give up, and I will not leave, until one of us has completely beaten the other.” With that he thrust the Sable Knight’s horse backward by the bridle so hard that the other was forced to leap from his saddle to save himself from falling to the ground.

Now each knight was as furious as the other. Each drew his sword and raised his shield, and they rushed together like two wild bulls fighting. They thrust, they struck, they slashed, they parried, they struck again and again, and the sound of their blows crashing and clashing together filled the whole place with an enormous uproar. No one can fully imagine how fierce that fight was. The blows were so violent that whole pieces of armor were hacked from their bodies, and many deep and terrible wounds were given and received. The armor of each knight was stained red with the blood that ran down over it.

At last King Arthur, almost mad with rage, swung a blow so fierce that no armor could have stood against it had it landed squarely. Instead his sword snapped off at the hilt, and the blade spun up into the air in three pieces. Even so, the blow was so mighty that the Sable Knight groaned, reeled, and stumbled around in a circle like a blind man who does not know which way to go.

Soon, however, he steadied himself. King Arthur stood close by, and the Sable Knight did not realize that his enemy had no sword left to protect himself. He flung away his shield, gripped his sword with both hands, and swung it with a terrible stroke. It split King Arthur’s shield and his helmet and bit down to the bone of his skull.

King Arthur believed he had been killed. His head swam, his legs shook, and he sank to his knees. Blood and sweat mixed in the darkness of his helmet and ran down in a lather into his eyes, so that he could not see. The Sable Knight saw how badly he was hurt and shouted at him to give up and hand over his shield, since he was too badly wounded to fight on.

But King Arthur refused to yield. He caught the other knight by the sword-belt and pulled himself to his feet. Now that he had partly shaken off his daze, he wrapped both arms around the other knight and set his knee behind the Sable Knight’s thigh. He threw him to the ground so hard that the fall was astonishing to hear. The Sable Knight lay senseless for a while. King Arthur at once unlaced his helmet and saw his face. Although blood still ran down his own face in streams, he knew who it was. The knight was King Pellinore, who was named earlier in this history. He had twice made war against King Arthur. (It has already been told how King Arthur drove that other king away from the homes of men and into the forests. That is why Pellinore now lived in this poor, gloomy castle, and from it made war on every knight who came to that place.)

Now King Arthur saw who his opponent was, and he shouted, “Ha! Pellinore, is it you? Give up, for I have you completely in my power.” Then he pulled out his dagger and held its point against King Pellinore’s throat.

Meanwhile King Pellinore had mostly recovered from his fall. He saw the blood pouring from beneath his enemy’s helmet and understood that the blow he had struck must have wounded the other badly. He grabbed King Arthur’s wrist and pushed the dagger’s point away from his throat, so it no longer threatened him much.

Indeed, between his painful wound and the loss of blood, King Arthur had now grown very sick and faint, and it seemed to him that he was near death. So it was not hard for King Pellinore to heave himself up suddenly from the ground and overthrow his enemy, until King Arthur lay beneath his knees.

King Pellinore was wild with rage from the hard fight. His eyes were bloodshot like a wild boar’s, and foam, like a boar’s, clung to the beard around his mouth. He wrenched the dagger out of his enemy’s hand and at once began to unlace his helmet, meaning to kill him where he lay. But at that moment Merlin came hurrying up, crying out, “Stop! Stop! Sir Pellinore, what are you doing? Hold back your wicked hand! For the man who lies beneath you is none other than Arthur, King of this whole realm!”

King Pellinore was stunned. For a little while he said nothing. Then he shouted, “Is that what you say, old man? Then your words have sealed this man’s death. No one in all the world has ever suffered such harm and such wrongs as I have suffered from him. Look! He has taken from me my power, my kingship, my honors and my lands, and has left me only this gloomy, dismal castle in the forest to live in. Now that he is in my power, he will die at once. If for no other reason, he will die because, if I let him go free now, he will surely take revenge on me when he has recovered from all the harm he has suffered at my hands.”

Then Merlin said, “No! He will not die by your hand, for I myself will save him.” Then he lifted his staff and hit King Pellinore across the shoulders. King Pellinore dropped at once and lay face down on the ground like a man struck dead.

At this, King Arthur raised himself on his elbow and saw his enemy lying there as if dead. He cried out, “Ha! Merlin! What have you done? I am deeply sorry, for I see that with your magic arts you have killed one of the best knights in all the world.”

“Not so, my lord King!” said Merlin. “Truly, I tell you that you are much closer to death than he is. He is only asleep and will wake soon. But you are in such a state that it would take only a very little to make you die.”

And indeed King Arthur was terribly sick, even to the heart, from the painful wound he had received. It was only with great effort that Merlin could help him up onto his horse. When that was done, Merlin hung the King’s shield on the horn of the saddle. Then he led the wounded man across the bridge at once, guiding the horse by the bridle, and took him away into the forest.

Now I must tell you that in that part of the forest lived a certain hermit. He was so holy that the wild birds of the woodland would come and rest on his hand while he read his prayer book. He was so gentle and blessed that the wild does would come right to the door of his hermitage and stand there while he milked them for his meal. The hermit lived so far from the homes of people that when he rang the bell for morning or evening prayers, there was hardly ever anyone to hear it except the wild creatures nearby. Even so, royal folk and others of high rank would sometimes come to this remote and lonely place, as if on a pilgrimage, because the hermit was so very saintly.

So Merlin brought King Arthur to this sanctuary. When they arrived, he and the hermit lifted the wounded man down from his saddle, while the hermit spoke many words of pity and sorrow. Together they carried him into the holy man’s cell. There they laid him on a couch of moss, unlaced his armor, and searched his wounds. They bathed them with pure water and bandaged his hurts, for the hermit was a very skilled healer. For all that day and part of the next, King Arthur lay on the hermit’s bed like a man about to die. He saw everything around him as though through thin water. His breath hung and fluttered on his lips, and he could not even lift his head from the bed because of the weakness that lay upon him.

Now on the afternoon of the second day, a great noise and bustle broke out in that part of the forest. The Lady Guinevere of Cameliard had come on a pilgrimage to the holy man, together with her Court of ladies and knights. The fame of his saintliness had reached even the place where she lived. The lady had a favorite page who was very sick with a fever. She hoped the holy man might give her some charm or amulet that could cure him. So she had come to that place with her whole Court, and all that part of the forest was bright with fine clothing. The silence there was filled with the sound of talk and laughter, songs, the chattering of many voices, and the neighing of horses. The Lady Guinevere rode in the midst of her damsels and her Court. Her beauty outshone theirs as the morning star outshines all the lesser stars around it. Then and ever afterward, all the Courts of Chivalry held her to be the most beautiful lady in the world.

When the Lady Guinevere reached that place, she saw King Arthur’s milk-white war-horse standing near the hermitage, cropping the green grass of the open glade. She also saw Merlin standing beside the door of the cell. She asked him whose noble war-horse it was that grazed in that lonely place, and who lay inside the cell. Merlin answered her, “Lady, the one who lies within is a knight. He is so badly wounded that he is sick almost to death!”

“Heaven have pity!” cried the Lady Guinevere. “What a sad thing you tell me! Now I beg you to lead me to that knight at once so that I may see him. For I have in my Court a very skilled healer, who is well used to curing the hurts that knights receive in battle.”

So Merlin brought the lady into the cell, and there she saw King Arthur stretched out on the bed. She did not know who he was. Yet it seemed to her that in all her life she had never seen a knight of such noble appearance as the one who lay badly wounded in that lonely place. King Arthur looked up to where she stood beside his bed of pain, surrounded by her maidens. In his great weakness he did not know whether the one he saw was a mortal lady or some tall, stately angel. Perhaps she had come down from one of the lordly Courts of Paradise to visit him in his pain and trouble. The Lady Guinevere was filled with pity at the sight of King Arthur’s sorrowful state. So she called the skilled healer who was with her Court. She told him to bring a certain alabaster box of very precious balsam. She commanded him to examine the knight’s wounds and to anoint them with the balsam, so that he might be healed of his hurts as quickly as possible.

So the wise and skilled healer did as the Lady Guinevere commanded, and at once King Arthur felt all his aches fade away and his spirit grow content. When the Lady and her Court had gone, he found his heart greatly lifted. Three days later he was completely healed, and he was as well and strong and lively as he had ever been in all his life.

This was the first time King Arthur ever saw that beautiful lady, the Lady Guinevere of Cameliard. From that time on he never forgot her, and she was almost always in his thoughts. So when he had recovered, he said to himself, “I will forget that I am a king, and I will cherish the thought of this lady. I will serve her faithfully, as a good knight may serve the lady he has chosen.”
And so he did, as you will hear later in this book.

chapters.title: The Winning of a Sword: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How King Arthur Found a Noble Sword in a Wonderful Way, and How He Fought Again With It and Won That Battle._

As soon as the strange balsam had healed the terrible wounds King Arthur received in his battle with King Pellinore, he felt a strong desire to meet his enemy again. He wanted to try the fight once more and win back the honor he had lost. On the morning of the fourth day he was completely well. After he had eaten breakfast, he walked along the edge of the forest to refresh himself, listening to the woodbirds singing their morning songs as loudly as they could. Merlin walked beside him, and Arthur told Merlin that he meant to fight King Pellinore again. He said, “Merlin, it troubles me deeply that I came off so badly in my recent fight with King Pellinore. Truly, he is the best knight I have ever faced in all the world. Still, things might have gone differently if my sword had not broken and left me with no defense. However that may be, I want to try this adventure again, and I will do so as soon as I can.”

Merlin answered, “You are surely a brave man to be so eager for battle, when you came so close to death not even four days ago. But how can you hope to try this adventure without preparing? Look, you have no sword and no spear, and you do not even have your dagger to fight with. How can you hope to take on this adventure?”
King Arthur said, “That I do not know, but I will find some weapon as soon as I can. Even if I had nothing better than an oak club, I would still fight this battle again with a tool as poor as that.”

“Ha! My lord,” said Merlin, “I see that you are set on renewing this quarrel. So I will not try to stop you, but will do everything I can to help you get what you wish. To that end I must tell you about a part of this forest, which is a very strange place indeed. There is a woodland there that is sometimes called Arroy and sometimes the Forest of Adventure, because no knight ever enters it without some adventure coming to him. Close to Arroy lies a land of enchantment that has been seen several times. It is a wonderful land, for it holds a wide and spacious lake, and that lake is enchanted too. For some time now, people have seen what looks like a woman’s arm rising from the middle of that lake. The arm is very beautiful and is dressed in white silk, and its hand holds a sword so excellent and so lovely that no eye has ever seen its equal. The sword is called Excalibur, a name given to it by those who have seen it because of its marvelous brightness and beauty. Several knights have already seen that sword and tried to win it for themselves, but until now no one has been able to touch it, and many have lost their lives in the attempt. When anyone comes near it, he either sinks into the lake, or the arm vanishes completely, or it is pulled down beneath the water. That is why no one has ever been able to take that sword. Now, I can lead you to that Lake of Enchantment, and there you can see Excalibur with your own eyes. Once you have seen it, you may want to win it. If you can do that, you will have a sword well suited for fighting.”

“Merlin,” said the King, “this is a very strange thing you tell me. I want more than I can say to try to win this sword for myself, so I beg you to take me at once to this enchanted lake you speak of.” And Merlin said, “I will.”

So that morning King Arthur and Merlin said goodbye to the holy hermit, and the King knelt in the grass to receive his blessing. Then they left that place and went once more into the deeper forest, making their way to the part that was known as Arroy.

After a while they came to Arroy, and it was about noon. As they entered those woodlands they came to a small clearing, and there they saw a white doe with a golden collar around its neck. King Arthur said, “Look, Merlin, what a wonderful sight!” And Merlin said, “Let us follow that doe.” At this the doe turned, and they followed it. Before long they came to a gap in the trees where there was a small lawn of sweet, soft grass. There they saw a bower, and in front of the bower stood a table covered with a fine snow-white cloth and set with food: white bread, wine, and several kinds of meat. At the door of the bower stood a page dressed all in green. His hair was as black as ebony, and his eyes were as black as jet and very bright. When the page saw King Arthur and Merlin, he greeted them and welcomed the King warmly. He said, “Ha! King Arthur, you are welcome to this place. I beg you, get down from your horse and refresh yourself before going farther.”

King Arthur was unsure at first whether this might be some enchantment meant to harm him, for he was astonished that a page in the deep forest should know him so well. But Merlin told him to be of good cheer. He said, “Indeed, my lord, you may freely take this food, which I can tell you was prepared especially for you. What is more, you may take it as a sign that this adventure will end very happily.”

So King Arthur sat down at the table with a glad heart, for he was hungry. That page and another like him waited on him, serving all the food on silver plates and all the wine in golden goblets, just as he was used to being served in his own court. But these things were much more skillfully made, and more beautiful, than the tableware in the King’s court.

When he had eaten his fill, he washed his hands in a silver basin that the first page held out to him, and dried them on a fine linen napkin that the other page brought. Merlin refreshed himself too, and then they went on their way, delighted with this pleasant adventure. To the King it seemed to promise a good end to his undertaking.

About the middle of the afternoon King Arthur and Merlin suddenly came out of the forest onto a fair, level plain. It was covered with so many flowers that no one could imagine how many there were or how beautiful they were.

This was a wonderful land, for all the air seemed to be made of gold, it was so bright and shining. Here and there on the plain stood trees in full blossom, and their fragrance was so sweet that the King had never smelled anything like it. In the branches of those trees sat many birds of different colors, and their singing delighted the heart of anyone who heard it. In the middle of the plain lay a lake as bright as silver, and all around its edges grew great numbers of lilies and daffodils. Yet although the place was so lovely, there was not a single sign of human life anywhere. It seemed as lonely as the empty sky on a summer day. Because of the marvelous beauty of the place, and its strangeness and complete solitude, King Arthur understood that he must have come into a land of powerful enchantment. Happily, a fairy of very high rank lived there. A kind of fear wrapped around his spirit as he pushed his great milk-white war-horse through the long, fair grass dotted with flowers, and he did not know what strange things were about to happen to him.

When he reached the edge of the lake, he saw the wonder that Merlin had told him about. In the middle of the water was a beautiful arm, like a woman’s, dressed in white silk. Several bracelets of worked gold circled the arm, and the hand held a sword of marvelous workmanship up in the air above the water. Neither the arm nor the sword moved even a hair’s breadth. They were as still as a carved statue on the surface of the lake. The sun of that strange land shone down on the hilt of the sword, which was pure gold set with jewels of several kinds. The hilt and the bracelets on the arm glittered in the middle of the lake like a strange and splendid star. King Arthur sat on his war-horse and gazed from a distance at the arm and the sword, and he wondered greatly at them. But he did not know how he could reach the sword, for the lake was very wide and deep, and he could not tell how to get there and make the sword his own. As he sat thinking about this, he suddenly noticed a strange lady coming toward him through the tall flowers that bloomed along the shore. When he saw her, he quickly got down from his war-horse and went forward to meet her, with the bridle over his arm. When he came close to her, he saw that she was extraordinarily beautiful. Her face was as clear as wax, and her eyes were perfectly black, as bright and shining as two jewels set in ivory. Her hair was like silk, as black as black could be, and so long that it reached the ground as she walked. The lady was dressed all in green, except that a fine cord of crimson and gold was woven into the braids of her hair. Around her neck hung a lovely necklace of several strands of opals and emeralds set in skillfully worked gold, and around her wrists were bracelets of the same kind, opals and emeralds set in gold. When King Arthur saw her wonderful appearance, which was like an ivory statue of great beauty dressed in green, he at once knelt before her among all those flowers. He said, “Lady, I can plainly see that you are no mortal maiden, but one of the Fay. And I see that this place, because of its great beauty, can be nothing other than a land of Faerie that I have wandered into.”

And the Lady replied, “King Arthur, you speak truly, for I am indeed of Faerie. I may also tell you that my name is Nymue, and that I am the chief of those Ladies of the Lake you may have heard people speak of. You should know too that what you see over there as a wide lake is really a plain like this one, covered with flowers. In the middle of that plain stands a castle of white marble and deep blue, decorated with gold. But so that mortal eyes would not see our home, my sisters and I have spread the look of a lake over the whole castle, so that it is completely hidden. No mortal man can cross that lake except in one way, or he will surely die in it.”
“Lady,” said King Arthur, “what you tell me fills me with wonder. And I fear that in coming here I have done wrong to break in on the peace of your home.”

“No, not at all, King Arthur,” said the Lady of the Lake, “for truly you are very welcome here. I may also tell you that I feel more friendship for you and the noble knights of your court than you can easily guess. But I ask you, out of courtesy, to tell me what brings you to our land.”

“Lady,” said the King, “I will tell you the whole truth. Not long ago I fought a battle with a certain black knight, in which I was badly and painfully wounded. I broke my spear, snapped my sword, and even lost my dagger, so that I had no weapon left at all. In this need Merlin, here, told me about Excalibur, and how an arm in the middle of this magic lake always holds it up. So I came here and, behold, I find it just as he said. Now, Lady, if it is possible, I would gladly win that excellent sword, so that I could fight my battle to its end.”

“Ha! My lord King,” said the Lady of the Lake, “that sword is not easy to win, and I must tell you that several knights have lost their lives trying to do what you have in mind. Truly, no man can win that sword unless he is without fear and without reproach.”

“Alas, Lady!” said King Arthur, “that is sad news for me. Although I do not lack a knight’s courage, there are many things for which I blame myself. Still, I would gladly try this, even at great risk to myself. So I beg you, tell me how I can best take on this adventure.”

“King Arthur,” said the Lady of the Lake, “I will do what I have said to help you in this matter.” Then she lifted a single emerald that hung from a small golden chain at her belt, and the emerald was skillfully carved in the shape of a whistle. She put the whistle to her lips and blew on it sharply. At once something shining brightly appeared on the water, far away. It came toward them very fast, and as it drew near, it turned out to be a boat made entirely of carved brass. The front of the boat was carved in the shape of a beautiful woman’s head, and on each side were wings like a swan’s wings. The boat glided over the water like a swan, so swiftly that long lines like silver threads stretched out behind it across the water, which was otherwise as smooth as glass. When the brass boat reached the shore, it stopped there and did not move again.

Then the Lady of the Lake told King Arthur to get into the boat, and he did. As soon as he was aboard, the boat moved away from the shore as swiftly as it had come. Merlin and the Lady of the Lake stood at the water’s edge and watched King Arthur and the brass boat go.
King Arthur saw that the boat floated swiftly across the lake to the place where the arm held up the sword, and that the arm and the sword did not move but stayed just where they were.
Then King Arthur reached out and took the sword in his hand. At once the arm sank beneath the water, and King Arthur held the sword, with its scabbard and its belt, in his hand. They were his own.

Then his heart swelled with joy, as if it would burst inside his chest, for Excalibur was a hundred times more beautiful than he had thought possible. His heart nearly broke from pure happiness at having won that magic sword.

Then the brass boat carried him quickly back to land, and he stepped ashore where the Lady of the Lake and Merlin stood. Standing on the shore, he thanked the Lady beyond measure for all she had done to help him in his great undertaking, and she answered him with cheerful and gracious words.

Then King Arthur bowed to the lady, as was proper. He mounted his war-horse, and Merlin mounted his palfrey, and they rode away to go about their business. The King’s heart was still swelling with pure delight at having that beautiful sword for his own—the most beautiful and the most famous sword in all the world.

That night King Arthur and Merlin stayed with the holy hermit at his sanctuary in the forest. When morning came, the King bathed in the ice-cold forest fountain and felt wonderfully refreshed. Then they left, thanking the saintly man for the shelter he had given them.

Soon, around noon, they reached the valley of the Sable Knight. Everything was arranged exactly as it had been when King Arthur was there before: the gloomy castle, the lawn of smooth grass, the apple tree covered with shields, and the bridge where that single black shield hung.

“Now, Merlin,” said King Arthur, “this time I strictly forbid you to interfere in this quarrel. And if you value my favor, you must not use any of your magic on my behalf. So listen to what I say, and obey it with all possible care.”

Right away the King rode out onto the bridge. He seized the brass mallet and struck the black shield with all his strength. At once the portcullis of the castle dropped, just as before, and the Sable Knight rode out, already dressed and armed for the fight, as he had done the other time. He came to the head of the bridge, and King Arthur spoke to him like this: “Sir Pellinore, we know each other quite well now, and each of us believes he has a reason to quarrel with the other. You believe that I, for reasons of my own that seemed right to me, took away your kingly rank and drove you into this lonely forest. I believe that you set yourself up here to insult and harm knights, lords, and other people of my kingdom. So, since I am here as a wandering knight, I challenge you to fight me, man to man, until one of us has defeated the other.”

King Pellinore bowed his head in obedience at these words. Then he turned his horse, rode a short distance away, and took the place where he had stood before. King Arthur also rode a short distance away and took the place where he had stood before. At the same moment one of those tall pages dressed all in black and crimson came out of the castle. He gave King Arthur a good, sturdy spear of ash wood, well seasoned and not yet used in battle. When the two knights were ready, they shouted and drove their horses together. Each struck the other so squarely in the middle of his defenses that both spears shattered in their hands, bursting into small splinters as they had before.

Then each of the two knights skillfully leaped from his horse and drew his sword. They began to fight so fiercely and so violently that two wild bulls in the mountains could not have fought a more desperate battle.

But now that King Arthur had Excalibur to help him, he soon overcame his enemy. He gave King Pellinore several wounds and received none himself. Not a single drop of his blood was shed in that whole fight, though his enemy’s armor was soon stained crimson. At last King Arthur struck such a mighty blow that King Pellinore was stunned. His sword and shield dropped from his hands, his legs trembled beneath him, and he sank to his knees on the ground. Then he begged King Arthur for mercy, saying, “Spare my life and I will surrender to you.”

King Arthur said, “I will spare you, and I will do more than that. Now that you have surrendered to me, see! I will give back your power and your rank. I bear you no ill will, Pellinore. Still, I cannot tolerate rebels against my rule in this kingdom. As God is my judge, I declare that I think only of the good of the people of my kingdom. So whoever is against me is also against them, and whoever is against them is also against me. But now I will require a pledge of your good faith toward me in the future. You must send me your two eldest sons as hostages of your good will, namely Sir Aglaval and Sir Lamorack. Your young son, Dornar, you may keep with you for your comfort.”
So those two young knights came to the Court of King Arthur. They became very famous knights, and in time they were made fellows of the Round Table, with great honor.

King Arthur and King Pellinore went together into King Pellinore’s castle, and there King Pellinore’s wounds were bandaged and he was made comfortable. That night King Arthur stayed in King Pellinore’s castle. When morning came, he and Merlin went back to the King’s Court, which was waiting for him in the forest at the place where he had set it up.

King Arthur felt very great pleasure as he and Merlin rode back together through the forest. It was the leafiest time of the year, when the woodlands dressed themselves in their best clothes of clear, bright green. Every wooded hollow and little valley was full of the scent of the thickets. In every tangled depth the small birds sang with all their might, as though they would burst their little throats with the melody. The ground under the horses’ feet was so soft with fragrant moss that no sound of hoofbeats could be heard on the earth. The bright yellow sunlight came down through the leaves, so that the ground was scattered with a great many trembling circles like pure yellow gold. Now and then that sunlight would fall on the armed knight as he rode, so that his armor seemed to catch fire with a great glory, shining like a sudden bright star among the dark shadows of the woods.

So King Arthur took great joy in that forest land. He had no ache or pain of any kind, and his heart was lifted high by the wonderful success of the adventure he had undertaken. In that adventure he had not only turned a very bitter enemy into a friend who would be of great use and comfort to him, but he had also gained a sword like none the world had ever seen. Whenever he thought of that splendid sword hanging at his side, and whenever he remembered the land of Faëry he had wandered into and what had happened to him there, his heart filled with such pure joy that he hardly knew how to hold himself together. So great was the delight that filled his whole chest.

Indeed, I can think of no greater good to wish for you in all your life than that you might enjoy the happiness that comes to a person when he has done his very best and has completely succeeded in what he set out to do. Then all the world seems filled with a bright, shining light, and the body feels so lifted up that the feet are freed from heaviness and touch the earth very lightly, because of the lightness of the spirit within. So if it were in my power to give you the very best the world has to give, I would wish that you might win your battle as King Arthur won his battle at that time. I would wish that you might ride homeward in the same triumph and joy that filled him that day, and that the sunlight might shine around you as it shone around him. I would wish that the breezes might blow and all the little birds might sing with all their might as they sang for him, and that your heart might also sing its song of rejoicing in the pleasantness of the world in which you live.

As they rode through the forest together, Merlin said to the King, “My Lord, which would you rather have, Excalibur or the sheath that holds him?” King Arthur answered, “Ten thousand times I would rather have Excalibur than his sheath.” “In that you are wrong, my Lord,” said Merlin, “for let me tell you something. Excalibur is of such great temper that he can cut in two either a feather or a bar of iron. Yet his sheath is of such a kind that whoever wears it can suffer no wound in battle, and he cannot lose a single drop of blood. As proof, you may remember that in your recent battle with King Pellinore you suffered no wound and lost no blood.”

Then King Arthur turned a look of great displeasure on his companion and said, “Now, Merlin, I declare that you have taken from me all the glory of the battle I have just fought. What credit can there be for a knight who fights his enemy by means of enchantment such as you describe? Indeed, I am inclined to take this glorious sword back to that magic lake and throw it in, where it belongs. I believe a knight should fight by his own strength and not by magic.”

“My Lord,” said Merlin, “you are quite right in what you believe. But you must remember that you are not an ordinary wandering knight. You are a King, and your life does not belong to you but to your people. So you have no right to put it in danger, and you should do everything in your power to protect it. Therefore you should keep that sword, so that it may guard your life.”

Then King Arthur thought about those words in silence for a long while, and when he spoke it was like this: “Merlin, you are right in what you say. For the sake of my people, I will keep both Excalibur, to fight for them, and his sheath, to protect my life for their sake. Still, I will never use him again except in serious battle.” King Arthur kept to that promise, so that afterward he fought no mock battles except with a lance and on horseback.

King Arthur kept Excalibur as the greatest treasure of all his possessions. He said to himself, “A sword like this is fit for a king above other kings and a lord above other lords. God has seen fit to place that sword in my keeping in such a marvelous way, so He must mean for me to be His servant and do unusual things. Therefore I will treasure this noble weapon, not only for its excellent worth, but because it will be a sign to me of the great things that God, in His mercy, has plainly chosen me to do in His service.”

So King Arthur had a strong chest made for Excalibur. It was bound all around with many bands of wrought iron, studded all over with great iron nails, and locked with three great padlocks. In this strongbox he kept Excalibur lying on a cushion of crimson silk and wrapped in fine linen. Very few people ever saw the sword in its glory, except when it flashed like a sudden flame in the uproar of battle.

When the time came for King Arthur to defend his realm or his subjects against their enemies, he would take out the sword and fasten it at his side. When he did so, he looked like a hero of God wearing a blade of shining lightning. Yes, at such times Excalibur shone with such terrible brightness that the very sight of it would shake the spirit of every wrongdoer with such great fear that he would, in a way, feel the pangs of death before the edge of the blade ever touched his flesh.

So King Arthur treasured Excalibur, and the sword stayed with him all his life, so that the name of Arthur and the name of Excalibur are one. I believe that sword is the most famous of any that was ever seen or heard of in all the Courts of Chivalry.

As for the sheath of the blade, King Arthur lost it through the treachery of one who should by rights have been his dearest friend (as you will hear soon). In the end the loss of that miraculous sheath caused him a very great deal of pain and sorrow.
You will read about all of that, too, God willing, in due time.

So ends the story of the winning of Excalibur. May God grant you in your life that you may have His truth to help you, like a shining sword, to overcome your enemies. May He give you Faith (for Faith holds Truth as a scabbard holds its sword), and may that Faith heal all your wounds of sorrow as the sheath of Excalibur healed all the wounds of the one who wore that excellent weapon. For with Truth and Faith belted on, you will be as well able to fight all your battles as that noble hero of old, whom men called King Arthur.

chapters.title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 1
paragraphs: _I have told you how King Arthur won the excellent sword Excalibur to defend himself with. Now I will tell of many other noble and knightly adventures, through which he won a most beautiful and gentle lady to be his Queen._
_Everyone in the world knows the fame of the gracious Lady Guinevere. Yet I do not think the whole story of the adventures by which King Arthur won her good favor has ever been told._

_This tale tells of that courtship. It also tells of an enchanted disguise that King Arthur put on for his purpose, and of several adventures of daring knighthood that he undertook. So I hope that whoever reads what I have written will find it both pleasant and entertaining._
_How King Arthur Went to Tintagalon with Four of His Court, and How He Disguised Himself for a Certain Purpose._

One day King Arthur announced a great feast, to be held at Carleon upon Usk. Many noble guests were invited, and a splendid Court gathered at the King’s castle. At that feast seven kings and five queens sat in royal state. There were also high lords and beautiful ladies of rank, sixty-seven in number. And there were many of the famous knights of the King’s Court, who were counted the most renowned in arms in all of Christendom. Of all this great gathering of kings, lords, and knights, not one man looked unkindly at his neighbor, and all were united in good fellowship. So the young King looked around him and saw such peace and friendship among these noble lords, where before there had been quarrels and ill will. “Truly,” he said to himself, “it is wonderful how my reign has bound men together in kindness and good fellowship!” These thoughts lifted his spirit like a bird, and it sang within him.
While the King sat at the feast, a herald-messenger suddenly arrived from the west country. The herald came and stood before the King, and said: “Greetings to you, King Arthur!”
Then the King said: “Speak, and tell me, what is your message?”

The herald answered: “I come from King Leodegrance of Cameliard, who is in great trouble. This is how it stands. His enemy and yours, King Ryence of North Wales, is the same man who once insulted you by commanding you to send him your beard to trim his mantle. Now he makes certain demands of my master, King Leodegrance, and King Leodegrance is very unwilling to meet them. King Ryence of North Wales threatens to bring war into Cameliard because King Leodegrance will not give in at once. King Leodegrance no longer has the many knights and armed men he once gathered around him to defend his kingdom against attack. You, in your majesty, have brought peace to this realm and broken the power of all those kings under you. So the knights who once made King Leodegrance’s Court so famous have gone elsewhere. They seek better chances for their courage and skill at arms than his peaceful Court can offer. And so my master, King Leodegrance, begs help from you, who are his King and Overlord.”

King Arthur and all the Court that feasted with him listened to the herald-messenger in complete silence. The King’s face, which had been bright with cheerfulness, grew dark and clouded with anger. “Ha!” he cried, “this is truly no good news that you have brought to our feast. I will give your master, King Leodegrance, what help I can in this need, and I will do it quickly. But tell me, sir herald, what are the things that King Ryence demands of your master?”

“I will tell you, my Lord,” said the herald-messenger. “First, King Ryence demands a large part of the lands of Cameliard that lie along the borders of North Wales. Second, he demands that the Lady Guinevere, the King’s daughter, be given in marriage to Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, who is a relative of King Ryence. That Duke is a mighty warrior, but he is so ugly to look at and so violent in temper that I believe there is no one like him for ugliness or for madness of mood in all the world.”

When King Arthur heard what the messenger said, he was seized at once with a terrible rage. His eyes seemed to shoot out sparks of pure light, his face blazed like fire, and he ground his teeth together like the stones of a mill. Then he rose from the chair where he sat and left the place. All who saw his anger shuddered and turned their eyes away from his face.

King Arthur went alone into an inner room of the castle and walked up and down there for a long time. In all that time none of his household dared to come near him. The reason for the King’s wrath was this. Ever since he had lain wounded and sick, close to death, in the forest, he had kept in mind how the Lady Guinevere had suddenly appeared before him. She had seemed like a tall, straight, shining angel come down to him out of Paradise, full of pity and wonderfully beautiful. So the thought of that wicked, mad Duke Mordaunt of North Umber demanding to marry her filled him with a rage so violent that it shook his spirit like a mighty wind.
So for a long while he paced up and down in his anger, as I have said. No one dared come near him, but all stood far off and watched him from a distance.

After a while he gave orders that Merlin, Sir Ulfius, and Sir Kay should come to him where he was. When they had come, he talked with them for some time. He told Merlin to get ready to go on a journey with him. He told Sir Ulfius and Sir Kay to gather a large army of chosen knights and armed men, and to bring that army at once to the lands near the royal castle of Tintagalon, which stands close to the borders of North Wales and of Cameliard.

So Sir Ulfius and Sir Kay went to do as King Arthur commanded, and Merlin did so too. The next day King Arthur and Merlin set out for Tintagalon across the forest land of Usk. With them went certain famous knights of the King’s Court, the best proven in arms of all those around him. They were Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine, who were nephews of the King, and Sir Pellias and Sir Geraint, the son of Erbin.

They traveled all that day and part of the next, and nothing good or bad happened to them on the way. At last they came to the large and noble castle named Tintagalon, which guards the country bordering Cameliard and North Wales. Here King Arthur was welcomed with great rejoicing, for wherever the King went the people loved him dearly. So the people of Tintagalon were very glad when he came to them.

The morning after King Arthur came to Tintagalon, the summer night had been very warm, and he and Merlin were glad to get up early and go outside to enjoy the dewy freshness of the early day. In the cool of the morning they walked together in the garden, which was a very pleasant place, in the shadow of a tall, straight tower. All around were many trees with good shade, where the little birds sang sweetly in the cheerful summer weather.

There King Arthur spoke very freely to Merlin. He said: “Merlin, I believe the Lady Guinevere is the fairest lady in all the world. My heart seems always to be filled with love for her. I think of her all day long, whether I am eating, or drinking, or walking, or sitting still, or going about my business, and I dream of her many nights as well. It has been so with me, Merlin, ever since a month ago, when I lay sick in that hermit’s cell in the forest and she came and stood beside me like a shining angel out of Paradise. So I will not allow any other man but me to have her for his wife.

“Now I know very well that you are wonderfully skilled in the arts of magic that can change a man’s appearance, so that even those who know him best cannot recognize him. So I ask you very earnestly to disguise me, so that I may go into Cameliard unknown to anyone, and may live there in such a way that I can see the Lady Guinevere every day. I tell you truly that I want to see her in such a way that she does not know of my regard for her. I would also like to see for myself how great the dangers are that surround King Leodegrance, for the King is my good friend.”
“My Lord King,” said Merlin, “it shall be as you wish. This morning I will have you so disguised that no one in all the world will be able to tell who you are.”

That morning, a little before the first hour of the day, Merlin came to the King where he was and gave him a little cap. The cap was such that when the King set it on his head, he took on at once the look of a rough country fellow. Then the King ordered a jerkin of coarse frieze to be brought to him. He covered his royal and knightly clothes with it, and he hid the golden collar with its hanging jewel, which he always wore around his neck. Then he set the cap on his head, and at once he looked like a peasant farmhand.
Thus entirely disguised, he left Tintagalon unknown to anyone and went on foot to the town of Cameliard.

Toward the end of the day, as the sun was sinking, he drew near the place. He saw before him a large and important town of many pretty houses with red walls and shining windows. The houses of the town all sat on a high, steep hill, one above the other, and the town was surrounded by a great wall, high and strong. A great castle guarded the town, and the castle had very many towers and roofs. All around the castle were many fair gardens and lawns and meadows, and several orchards and groves of trees with thick and pleasant shade. At that time of day the sky behind the castle was one blaze of fire, so that the towers and battlements of the castle and its roofs and chimneys stood black against the bright light. Great flocks of pigeons circled the towers of the castle in constant flight against that fiery sky. King Arthur was tired from walking all day, and it seemed to him that he had hardly ever seen in all his life so fair and pleasing a place as that excellent castle with its gardens and lawns and groves of trees.
So King Arthur came to the castle of Cameliard in the disguise of a poor peasant from the countryside, and no one in all the world knew who he was.

When he reached the castle, he asked for the head gardener. When he spoke with the gardener, he begged to be taken into service in that part of the garden that belonged to the home of the Lady Guinevere. The gardener looked at him and saw that he was tall and strong and well built. He liked him very well and took him into service as he asked.
And that is how King Arthur of Britain became a gardener’s boy at Cameliard.

The King was very glad to be in that garden. In that pleasant summer season the Lady Guinevere came every day to walk among the flowers with her damsels, and King Arthur, disguised as a peasant gardener boy, saw her many times when she came there.
So King Arthur stayed at that place for more than a week. He did not mind that in all that time he enjoyed none of his kingly rank, but was only a gardener’s boy in the castle garden of Cameliard.

One day, when the weather was very warm, one of the damsels who attended the Lady Guinevere got up early in the morning, while the air was still cool and fresh. She left the Lady Guinevere still sleeping. This damsel, whose name was Mellicene of the White Hand, went into the ante-room, opened the window, and looked out into the rose garden that lay next to the Lady Guinevere’s bower.

In that place there was a carved marble figure of a youth, holding a marble pitcher in his arms. A fountain of water, as clear as crystal, flowed out of the pitcher into a marble basin. The figure, the fountain, and the marble basin lay in the shade of a linden-tree. All around was a thick growth of roses, so that the place was completely hidden, except from the windows of the castle high above.

So it happened that as the damsel looked down from the window, she saw a very wonderful sight. A strange knight was kneeling beside the fountain and bathing his face and chest in the crystal water. The damsel saw that the sunlight fell down through the leaves of the linden-tree and lay upon that strange knight. She saw that his hair and beard were the color of red gold, shining brilliantly in the bright morning. She saw that his brow and throat and chest were white as alabaster. And she saw that around his neck and shoulders hung a golden collar of marvelous beauty, so that when the sunlight shone on it, it flashed like pure lightning.

The damsel Mellicene saw this strange sight, which seemed like a vision, and stood for a long while entranced with wonder and delight. She did not know whether what she saw was a dream or not, nor whether the one who sat there was a spirit or a man of flesh and blood.

After a while she recovered somewhat from her astonishment. She drew back softly from the window, turned around, and ran lightly down the turret stairs, and so came out into the fair and blooming garden at the foot of the tower. She ran through the garden as fast and as quietly as she could. She came down a garden path to the marble fountain, the linden-trees, and the rose-trees where she had just seen that strange knight bathing in the crystal water.

But King Arthur had heard the damsel coming and had quickly put the cap back on his head. So when the damsel Mellicene arrived, she found no one by the fountain but the gardener’s boy. She asked him: “Who are you, fellow? And why do you sit here by the fountain?”
And he answered her: “I am the gardener’s lad who came a short time ago to work at this place.”

“Then tell me, fellow,” she said, “and tell me truly. Who was that young knight who was here beside the fountain just now, and where has he gone?” “Lady,” he said, “no one has been at this fountain today but me.”

“No, fellow,” she cried, “you are deceiving me. I assure you that I saw with my own eyes, just now, a strange young knight sitting here bathing in the waters of this fountain.” And the gardener’s boy said, “Lady, what I have told you is the plain truth, for no one has been here this morning but me. So if you think you saw anyone else, you are surely mistaken.”

At this, the damsel looked at him in great confusion. She was amazed, for she could not completely disbelieve him. Yet she could not fully believe him either, because her own eyes had seen what they had seen, and she knew she had not been mistaken. So she did not know what to think, and in her confusion she felt a deep anger toward that gardener’s boy. “Truly,” she said, “if you are deceiving me, I will make you suffer a great deal of pain, for I will have you whipped with cords.” Then she turned and left that place, still wondering at the strange sight and what it could mean.

That morning she told Lady Guinevere everything she had seen. But Lady Guinevere only laughed at her and teased her, saying she must have been asleep and dreaming when she saw that vision. In fact, the damsel herself had begun to think that this must be so. Even so, from then on she looked out of her window every morning, though she saw nothing for a long while, because King Arthur did not come back to that place soon.

Then, on another morning, she looked out of the window and, behold, the strange knight was sitting by the fountain once more, just as he had sat before. He bathed his face and his chest in the water as he had done before. He looked as handsome and as noble as ever, and his hair and his young beard shone like gold in the sun, as they had shone before. This time she saw that his golden collar lay on the edge of the fountain beside him, and it sparkled brilliantly in the sunlight while he bathed. After the damsel had watched him for some time, she ran as fast as she could to the room where Lady Guinevere still lay, and she cried out loudly, “Lady! Lady! Get up and come with me! That same young knight I saw before is bathing at the fountain under the linden tree right now.”
Then Lady Guinevere, full of wonder, got up very quickly. She dressed in all haste and went with the damsel to the window that looked out over that part of the garden.

There she saw the young knight herself, as he washed at the fountain. She saw that his hair and his beard shone like gold in the sunlight. She saw that his undershirt was of purple linen woven with gold thread. And she saw that beside him lay the skillfully made golden collar, set with many jewels of different colors, shining brilliantly where it rested on the marble edge of the fountain.

For a while she gazed at him in great astonishment. Then she commanded the damsel Mellicene to come with her, and she turned and went down the turret stairs and out into the garden, just as her damsel had done before. Then, as that damsel had done, she hurried as fast as she could along the path toward the fountain.

But when she arrived, behold, she found no young knight there, only the gardener’s boy, exactly as had happened with the damsel Mellicene before. For King Arthur had heard her coming and had at once put the enchanted cap on his head. Lady Guinevere was greatly amazed to find only the gardener’s boy, and she did not know what to think of so strange a thing. So she asked him, just as Mellicene had done, where the young knight had gone whom she had just seen at the fountain. And the gardener’s boy answered her as before: “Lady! No one has been at this place at all this morning, except me.”

Now when King Arthur put on his cap at the Lady’s coming, he had been in such a hurry that he forgot his golden collar. Guinevere saw it lying there, shining brightly, beside the edge of the fountain. “What is this!” she said. “Do you dare to make fun of me? Now tell me, fellow, do gardeners’ boys in the land you come from wear golden collars around their necks like the one that lies there beside the fountain? If I had you well whipped, it would be no more than you deserve. But take that trinket and give it to the one it truly belongs to. And tell him from me that it does not suit a true belted knight to hide himself in a lady’s private gardens.” Then she turned away with the damsel Mellicene, left that place, and went back to her chamber.

Yet all that day, as she sat over her embroidery, she kept wondering how that strange young knight could have vanished so suddenly and left only the poor gardener’s boy in his place. For a long time she could not solve the riddle.

Then, suddenly, at the hour when the heat of the day was giving way to the cooler part of the afternoon, she roused herself because a thought had come to her in an instant. So she called the damsel Mellicene to her and told her to go and tell the gardener’s boy to bring her at once a basket of fresh roses to decorate her tower room.

So Mellicene went and did as she was told, and after some time the gardener’s boy came carrying a large basket of roses. And behold, he was wearing his cap on his head. All the damsels who attended Lady Guinevere cried out at him when they saw that he wore his cap in her presence, and Mellicene of the White Hand demanded of him, “What! What is this, Sir peasant! Do you know so little of the respect owed to a king’s daughter that you wear your cap even in the presence of Lady Guinevere? Now I order you to take your cap off your head at once.”
And King Arthur answered her, “Lady, I cannot take off my cap.”
Lady Guinevere said, “And why can you not take off your cap, you rude fellow?”
“Lady,” he said, “I cannot take off my cap, because I have an ugly sore on my head.”
“Then keep your cap on,” said Lady Guinevere. “Just bring the roses to me.”

And so, at her command, he brought the roses to her. But when he had come close to the lady, she suddenly snatched at the cap and pulled it off his head. Then, behold, he was changed in an instant. In place of the gardener’s boy, there stood before Lady Guinevere and her damsel the figure of a noble young knight, with hair and beard like threads of gold. He let his basket of roses fall, so that the flowers scattered all over the floor, and he stood and looked at everyone there. Some of the damsels attending Lady Guinevere shrieked, and others stood frozen with amazement, hardly able to believe what their eyes saw. But not one of those ladies knew that the man they saw was King Arthur. Still, Lady Guinevere remembered that this was the knight she had found so badly wounded, lying in the hermit’s cell in the forest.
Then she laughed and threw his cap back to him. “Take your cap,” she said, “and go on your way, you gardener’s boy with the ugly sore on his head.” She said this because she meant to mock him.

But King Arthur made no reply to her. Instead, with a very serious face, he put his cap on his head again. Taking on his humble disguise once more, he turned and left that place, leaving the roses scattered over the floor just as they had fallen.

And after that, whenever Lady Guinevere came upon the gardener’s boy in the garden, she would say to her damsel, in a voice loud enough for him to hear, “Look! There is the gardener’s boy who has an ugly sore on his head, so that he must always wear his cap to hide it.”
She spoke openly like this, mocking him. But in private she told her damsels to say nothing about these things and to keep to themselves everything that had happened.

chapters.title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How King Ryence came to Cameliard, and how King Arthur fought with the Duke of North Umber._

One day around this time, a messenger came to the court of King Leodegrance. He brought news that King Ryence of North Wales and Duke Mordaunt of North Umber were coming, and that they were bringing a large and splendid company of knights and lords. King Leodegrance was deeply troubled by this news. He did not know what the visit meant, but he greatly feared it meant trouble for him. So on the day King Ryence and the Duke of North Umber appeared before the castle, King Leodegrance went out to greet them. The three of them met in the meadows below the castle walls of Cameliard.
There King Leodegrance welcomed the two visitors in the proper manner. He asked them to come into the castle with him, so that he could entertain them as their rank deserved.

But King Ryence gave no friendly answer to this courtesy. “No,” he said, “we will not go with you into your castle, King Leodegrance, until we learn whether you are our friend or our enemy. Right now we are certainly not such good friends with you that we want to sit at your table and eat your bread and salt. And we cannot be anything but your enemies until you have met our demands. You must give me the lands I am asking for, and you must give the Lady Guinevere to my cousin, Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, to be his wife. It is in your power to make us either your friends or your enemies. So we will stay here, outside your castle, for five days. In that time you can decide on your answer, and then we will know whether we are friends or enemies.”

“And in the meantime,” said Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, “I am ready to fight for my right to the hand of the Lady Guinevere against any knight of your court who wants to deny my just claim. And if you have no knight in your whole court who can face me in a bout of arms, you can hardly hope to defend yourself against the great army of knights King Ryence has gathered to bring against you, if you refuse what we ask.”

King Leodegrance was greatly discouraged. He feared those proud lords, and he did not know what to say to them. So he turned and walked back into his castle, weighed down with worry and sorrow. King Ryence and Duke Mordaunt and their court of lords and knights set up their pavilions in the meadows across from the castle, until the whole plain was covered with tents. There they made camp with great rejoicing, with the sounds of feasting and singing and merrymaking, for King Ryence had gathered a very noble court around him.

When the next morning came, Duke Mordaunt of North Umber went out dressed in armor that no weapon could pierce. He rode up and down the field before the castle and loudly challenged those inside, daring any knight to come out and meet him in a knightly fight. “Ho!” he cried. “What now, you Knights of Cameliard! Is there no one to come out and meet me? How can you hope to stand against the Knights of North Wales, if you are afraid to face one single Knight from North Umber?” He mocked them in his pride, and no one dared to come out from Cameliard against him. The Duke of North Umber was one of the most famous knights of his day, and he was very strong and had won many fights. In these peaceful times, no one at King Leodegrance’s court was able to face a warrior of such proven skill and courage. So no one took up the challenge that the Duke of North Umber gave to the court of Cameliard. Meanwhile, many people gathered on the walls of Cameliard and looked down at the proud and haughty duke in his splendid armor. All of them were grieved and ashamed that no one in that peaceful town could go out against him. All the lords and knights of King Ryence’s court came and stood in front of the King’s pavilion. They laughed and clapped their hands and cheered Duke Mordaunt as he rode up and down before them. The more they swelled with laughter, the more ashamed the people of Cameliard felt. “Ho! Ho!” cried the proud Duke. “What now! Will no one come out to meet me? How can you of Cameliard hope to face the King of North Wales and all his army of knights, when I am only one man among them?” And the people of Cameliard, gathered on the walls, listened to him with shame and sorrow.

All this time King Arthur had been digging in the garden. But he knew very well everything that was happening, and how the Duke of North Umber rode up and down so proudly before the castle walls. Suddenly he felt that he could not bear it any longer. So he put down his spade and slipped out by a small back gate, and went up into the town.

There was in Cameliard a very rich merchant named Ralph of Cardiff. The fame of his wealth and high standing had reached even King Arthur’s ears at Carleon. So King Arthur made his way to this man’s house.

In a narrow lane, not far from the merchant’s house, he took off his magic cap of disguise and took on something of his noble appearance again. He now wanted to show his knightliness to those who looked at him. So when he stood before the rich merchant in his private room, and the merchant looked up into his face, the merchant did not know what to think. Here was a lord of such noble bearing, dressed all in rough wool. King Arthur was a stranger to the good man, who did not know his face. Even so, the merchant knew that this was no ordinary knight. He must surely be a man of high rank and authority, even though he wore coarse cloth.

Then King Arthur opened the breast of his jerkin and showed the merchant the gold collar that hung around his neck. Under the rough woolen coat he also showed an undergarment of fine purple silk embroidered with gold. Then he showed the good man his own signet ring, and when the merchant saw it, he knew it was the ring of the King of Britain. Seeing these signs of high and lordly authority, the merchant rose, stood before the King, and took off his cap.

“Sir Merchant,” said the King, “know that I am a strange knight in disguise in this place. Even so, I can tell you that I am a very good friend to King Leodegrance and wish him well. Surely you know how the Duke of North Umber rides up and down before the King’s castle all the time, challenging anyone inside to come out and fight him for the Lady Guinevere. Now I mean to take up that fight myself, and I hope very much that I will uphold the honor of Cameliard and bring shame upon its enemies.

“Sir Merchant, I know very well that you have several suits of fine armor in your treasury. Their fame has reached my ears, though I live a good distance from here. So I ask you to outfit me in the best way you can, so that I may fight that Duke of North Umber right away. I give you my knightly word that you will be fully repaid for the best suit of armor you can lend me, and that it will be very soon.”

“My Lord,” said Master Ralph, “I can see that you are no ordinary wandering knight, but a man of very high rank. It is a great pleasure to carry out all your wishes. But even if you were someone other than you are, I would gladly give you armor, since you wish to ride out against that duke.”

With this he rang a little silver bell that stood near him, and several attendants came at once in answer to its sound. He placed the King in their hands and told them to show him the greatest honor. Some of the attendants prepared a bath of lukewarm water for the King, perfumed with ambergris, which felt very pleasant. After he had bathed and been dried with soft linen towels, other attendants led him to a hall hung all over with tapestries and embroideries. There a noble feast had been laid out for his refreshment. The lordly merchant himself looked after the King’s needs. He served him many kinds of fine, delicate meats, and also fine white bread. He poured him wines from various countries, some as red as rubies and others as yellow as gold. Indeed, the King had hardly ever enjoyed a better feast than the one Ralph of Cardiff spread for him.

When he had eaten and was fully refreshed, six pages came in, richly dressed in blue silk. They took the King to a grand room and dressed him in a suit of Spanish armor, very skillfully made and inlaid with gold. Its like could hardly be found anywhere in the land. The tunic worn over the armor and all the other trappings were of satin, as white as milk. The shield was white too, with no painted emblem or design of any kind. Then the attendants led the King into the courtyard, where a noble war-horse stood, as white as milk. All its trappings were of milk-white cloth, with no emblem or decoration of any kind. Its bridle and reins were studded all over with silver knobs.

The attendants helped King Arthur mount this horse. Then the lordly merchant came forward and gave him many words of encouragement. The King said farewell and rode away, shining in white and glittering in fine armor, so that he looked like the full moon in harvest season.
As he rode down the stony streets of the town, the people turned and gazed after him, for he made a very noble sight as he passed along the narrow way between the houses.

King Arthur rode to the back gate of the castle. There he got down from his horse and tied it. Then he went straight into the garden, and finding an attendant there, he asked to speak with the Lady Guinevere at once. The attendant, amazed at his lordly appearance, went and gave the message. Soon the Lady Guinevere came, full of wonder, and walked along a gallery with several of her damsels until she was above the place where King Arthur stood. When King Arthur looked up and saw her above him, he loved her very much. And he said to her, “Lady, I greatly wish to do you the honor I am able. I am going out now to fight that Duke of North Umber who rides up and down before this castle. I hope, and truly believe, that I will bring about his downfall. So I ask you for some token, such as a lady may give to a knight to wear when he rides out to do her honor.”

Then the Lady Guinevere said, “Truly, Sir Knight, I wish I knew who you are. Yet even though I do not know, I am quite willing to take you as my champion, as you offer. As for the token you speak of, if you tell me what you would like, I will gladly give it to you.”
“If that is so, Lady,” said King Arthur, “I would like the necklace you wear around your throat. It seems to me that if I had it tied around my arm, my courage would grow much greater.”

“By my faith, Sir Knight,” said the Lady, “you will surely have what you ask of me.” As she spoke, she took the necklace of pearls from her long, smooth neck and dropped it down to King Arthur where he stood.

King Arthur took the necklace and tied it around his arm, and he thanked her warmly. Then he bowed to the Lady Guinevere with true knightly grace, and she bowed to him. Then he went out from that place at once, his heart swelling with joy that the Lady Guinevere had shown him such favor.

By now the word had gone around Cameliard that a knight was going out to fight the Duke of North Umber. So great crowds gathered on the walls. King Leodegrance and the Lady Guinevere and the whole court came to the part of the castle walls that overlooked the meadow where the Duke of North Umber waited. Soon so great a crowd had gathered that any knight would be encouraged to do his very best before the many watchers looking down on the field.

Then suddenly the portcullis of the castle was raised and the drawbridge was let down, and the White Champion rode out to the fight he had taken on. As he rode across the narrow bridge, the hoofs of his war-horse struck the boards with a noise like thunder. When he came out into the sunlight, behold, his armor flashed like lightning, and when the people saw him, they shouted aloud.

When the Duke of North Umber saw a knight dressed all in white, he rode straight up to him and spoke words of knightly greeting. “Messire,” he said, “I see that you wear no crest on your helmet and no emblem on your shield, so I do not know who you are. Even so, I believe you are a knight of good quality and proven courage, or you would not have come to this place.”
“Truly, Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I am of a rank equal to your own. And as for my courage, I believe it has been proven in as many fights as yours has.”

“Sir Knight,” said the Duke of Umber, “you speak with a very bold spirit. Even so, you may say whatever prayers you can, for I will soon knock you from your saddle so that you will never rise again. I have done the same to better men than you could ever hope to be.”
King Arthur answered this with great calm: “That will be as Heaven wills, Sir Knight, and not as you will.”

Then each knight saluted the other and rode to his place. There each one set his spear and shield and made himself ready for the fight. A silence fell over everyone, so deep that a man could hear his own heart beating. For a short while each knight sat like a statue made of iron.
