Then suddenly each one shouted to his war-horse, dug his spurs into its side, and shot forward from his place. They met in the middle of the course with a noise like a violent thunderclap. And behold, the spear of the Duke of North Umber burst into splinters, down to the very stump. But the spear of King Arthur did not break. It held firm, and the Duke was thrown out of his saddle like a windmill, whirling in the air. He struck the earth so hard that the ground shook beneath him. Indeed, he rolled over and over three full times before he stopped.
Then all the people on the wall shouted with all their might, so that the noise was astonishing. They had hardly hoped that their champion would prove so extraordinarily strong and skillful.

Meanwhile, the men of King Ryence’s court ran at once to the Duke of Umber where he lay on the ground, and they quickly unlaced his helmet to give him air. At first they thought he was dead, and then they thought he was about to die, for behold, he lay without any life or movement. He did not wake from that swoon for a full two hours and more.

While the attendants were busy with Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, King Arthur sat quietly on his horse and watched everything they did. Then he saw that his enemy was not dead. He turned his horse around and rode away from that place.

He did not go back to Cameliard at that time. He felt that he was not yet finished with these enemies of the peace of his realm. So he decided not to return the horse and armor to the merchant yet, but to keep them for a while in case he needed them again.

He remembered that on his way to Cameliard he had passed through a part of the forest where some woodcutters were chopping down trees. He thought he would go there and leave his horse and armor with those rough folk until he needed them again. So he rode off into the countryside. He left behind him the town, the castle, and all the noise of shouting and celebration. Not once did he turn his head to look back at the place where he had so mightily defeated his enemy.

Soon you will hear of some pleasant and happy adventures that happened to him before he had finished all he meant to do. A man who is a king among men, as King Arthur was, has such a calm and steady nature that neither victory nor defeat can change him. Victory does not make him too proud of himself, and defeat does not trouble his spirit so much that he falls into despair. So if you want to become like King Arthur, take all your triumphs the way he took this victory. You will not be turned away from your final purposes by the loud praise of many people. Instead, you will first finish the work you set yourself to do, and only then allow yourself to sit down and enjoy the rewards of your victory.
Yes, a true king of men does not say to himself, “Look! I deserve to be crowned with laurels.” Instead he says to himself, “What more can I do to make the world a better place through my efforts?”

chapters.title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How King Arthur Met Four Knights and What Happened Because of It._

The day was wonderfully sweet and pleasant for a man as strong in body and light of heart as good King Arthur. Bright clouds sailed smoothly across the blue sky in huge billows of vapor. The wind blew across the long grass of the meadows and the fields of growing wheat, so that waves ran over the hills and valleys as if across a whole sea of green. At one moment the whole earth would be darkened by the wide shadows of those clouds, and the next moment everything would burst out again into a wonderful blaze of sunlight. The little birds sang merrily in the hedgerows and the leafy thickets, as though they would burst their tiny throats with singing. The rooster crowed, strong and bold, from the farmyard. All was so cheerful and lovely that the young King, with the visor of his helmet raised to feel the gentle breeze, would sometimes sing aloud for joy as he traveled. So King Arthur journeyed through that gay and tender summer season, when the earth was young and the time was long ago.

Now, remember that when King Arthur came from Carleon to the castle of Tintagalon, he had brought four young knights with him to keep him company. Those knights were these. There was Sir Gawaine, the son of King Lot and Queen Margaise. There was Sir Ewaine, the son of King Uriens and Queen Morgana la Fay (these two were nephews of the King, half related by blood). There was Sir Pellias, and there was Sir Geraint, the son of Erbin. These were the four noble young knights who had come with King Arthur from Camelot to Tintagalon.

As King Arthur rode along happily in the summer weather, he came to a place on the road where he saw a tall and handsome tower standing on a green hill right beside the road. And look! On the balcony of that tower stood three fair young ladies, all dressed in green taffeta. On the high road in front of the castle was a knight in very fine armor. He sat on a noble war-horse, and in his hands he held a lute. He played the lute and sang in a voice of wonderful sweetness. While he sang, the three ladies in green taffeta listened to him with cheerful faces. Whenever the knight stopped singing, the three ladies clapped their hands loudly and asked him to sing to them again, and he gladly did so.
King Arthur saw all this, and it seemed to him a very pleasant sight, so he was greatly delighted by it.

As he came closer, he saw that the knight who sat on his horse, playing the lute and singing to its music, was none other than Sir Geraint, the son of Erbin. That knight wore the figure of a gryphon on his crest, and the design on his shield was two gryphons standing on their hind legs, facing each other on a blue field. King Arthur knew that these were the crest and the shield of Sir Geraint. When the King saw who the singing knight was, he laughed to himself, quickly closed his visor, and made himself ready for whatever fight might come. Then he rode up to where the knight sang and the ladies listened.

When Sir Geraint saw King Arthur approaching, he stopped singing and hung his lute behind him across his shoulder. Then he looked up at the three fair ladies above him and said, “Ladies, you have been kind enough to listen to the song that I sang entirely in your honor. Now, in your honor as well, I will perform a deed of knightly courage, and I very much hope it will bring you great glory. If you will give me the encouragement that your great beauty can so easily offer, I have no doubt that you will see me defeat that knight over there completely. It will be to your great credit and fame.”

“Sir Knight,” said the lady who spoke for the others, “you are truly a lord of noble bearing and very pleasing manners, so we wish you great success in this task. We believe that you will succeed in what you attempt.”

Sir Geraint thanked the three young ladies warmly for their words, and then he closed the visor of his helmet. He lowered his spear, readied his shield, and bowed humbly to the three ladies. Then he rode out to meet King Arthur, who sat a short distance away, quietly and calmly waiting for him.

Sir Geraint did not recognize King Arthur, because the King wore no crest on his helmet and no design on his shield. As he saluted him, he spoke to him like this: “Ha! Good sir, I do not know who you are, since you carry neither crest nor shield design. Even so, I wish to do you the honor of riding a tilt with you on behalf of those three young ladies that you see on that balcony. I declare, and I am ready to defend my words in person as a knight, that those ladies are fairer than your lady, whoever she may be.”

“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I will gladly ride a course with you in honor of my lady. I can tell you that she is a princess, and many people consider her the most beautiful lady in all the world. But I will fight you only on one condition. The one who is thrown from his horse must give himself as a servant to the other for seven days, and during that time he must do everything that is asked of him.”

“I accept your challenge, Sir Unknown Knight,” said Sir Geraint, “and when I have thrown you down, I will hand you over to those fair ladies over there to be their servant for seven days. I tell you that many knights would certainly think that a pleasant and honorable task.”

“And if I should happen to throw you down,” said King Arthur, “I will send you to serve my lady for the same length of time. That will be an even more pleasant and honorable task than the one you have in mind for me.”

So each knight saluted the other, and then each took his place so that the clash would happen right below the balcony where the three fair young ladies looked down. Each knight lowered his spear and readied his shield, and when they were prepared, each sat still for a short moment. Then each shouted to his war-horse, dug his spurs into its flanks, and charged forward with amazing speed. They met in the very middle of the course with a force so fierce that the noise of it was terrifying to hear. Each knight struck the other in the very center of his defenses. And look! The spear of Sir Geraint burst into small pieces, all the way down to the stump. But the spear of King Arthur held firm, and Sir Geraint was thrown so violently backward that he and his horse both crashed into the dust with a noise like a huge roar of thunder.

When Sir Geraint got back on his feet, he was so astonished for a while that he did not know where he stood, because he had never been thrown like that in all his life. Then he quickly came to his senses, drew his sword at once, and called out fiercely for King Arthur to come down from his saddle and fight him on foot.

“No, Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I will not fight you that way. And do not forget that you promised to give yourself to me as my servant for seven days. I have clearly beaten you in this encounter, and now you are pledged to be my servant.”

Then Sir Geraint did not know what to say, for he was completely overcome with shame and anger at his defeat. Still, he saw that he must keep his knightly word and do what he had promised. So he put his sword away again, though he was very unhappy about it. “Sir Knight,” he said, “I admit that I have been beaten in this encounter, so I place myself under your commands, as I promised.”

“Then this is my command to you,” said King Arthur. “You must go at once to the Lady Guinevere at Cameliard and tell her that you were thrown down by the knight to whom she gave her necklace as a token. I also want you to obey her in everything she commands you to do, for the next seven days.”
“Sir Knight,” said Sir Geraint, “I will do what you ask of me, as you command.”

Then he mounted his horse and went on his way, and King Arthur went on his way too. The three ladies who stood on the balcony of the castle were very glad that they had seen such a noble contest of arms as the one they had looked down upon.

After King Arthur had traveled two or three leagues or more, he came to a place of moorland, where there were many ditches full of water and where the heron and the marsh-hen hid in the reeds. Here and there stood several windmills, their sails turning slowly in the sunlight before a wind that blew across the level plains of mud. At this place there was a long, straight causeway with two long rows of pollard willows, one on each side. When he had come near the middle of this causeway, King Arthur saw two knights sitting on their horses in the shade of a great windmill that stood beside the road. A large shadow of the sails moved across the road from time to time as the wheel of the mill turned slowly in the wind. All around the mill, and everywhere about, were great numbers of swallows that darted this way and that like bees around a hive in midsummer. King Arthur saw that the two knights, as they sat in the shadow of the mill, were eating a large loaf of rye bread, freshly baked with a crisp crust. They also ate fine white cheese, and the miller, all white with flour dust, served these things to them. But when the two knights saw King Arthur, they stopped eating the bread and cheese at once and quickly closed their helmets. When the miller saw them getting ready, he hurried back into the mill and shut the door. Then he went and looked out of a window above the place where the knights stood.

King Arthur was very amused when he saw that the two knights were Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine. He knew that one was Sir Gawaine because the crest of his helmet was a leopard standing on its hind legs, and because the design on his shield was a leopard standing on its hind legs on a red field. He knew that the other was Sir Ewaine, because his crest was a unicorn, and because the design on his shield was a lady holding a bare sword in her hand, on a gold field. So while he was still some way off, King Arthur closed his helmet so that the two young knights would not know who he was.

When he had come close to the two knights, Sir Gawaine rode forward a short way to meet him. “Sir Knight,” he said, “you must know that this is truly dangerous ground that you have ridden into. There is no side road from here across the swamp, and you may not go forward without riding a tilt with me.”

“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I am very willing to ride a tilt with you. But I will fight you only on one condition, and it is this: the one who is thrown down must serve the other fully for seven whole days.”
“I accept your challenge, Sir Knight,” said Sir Gawaine. For he said to himself, “Surely a knight as strong and skilled as I am will easily bring down this unknown knight.”

So each knight at once took his place. Each lowered his spear and readied his shield, made himself fully ready in every way, and rested for a short moment. Then each suddenly shouted to his horse, dug his spurs into its flanks, and rushed to the clash. Each knight struck the other in the middle of his defenses, and look! The spear of Sir Gawaine burst into pieces. But the spear of King Arthur held firm, so that Sir Gawaine was lifted right out of his saddle and over the back end of his horse. He fell into the dust with terrible force. He could not rise from that fall right away, but lay dazed for a little while. When he did get up, he saw that the white knight who had thrown him was sitting on his horse close beside him.
Then King Arthur spoke and said, “Sir Knight, I have completely beaten you, and so you must now serve me, as you promised on your knightly word.”

Then Sir Ewaine, who sat on his horse nearby, spoke up. “Not so, Sir Knight,” he said. “Not until you have dealt with me. I demand that you joust with me at once. If I throw you down, I will require you to release my cousin from the service he has promised. But if you throw me down, then I will serve you just as he has promised to serve you.”
“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “I accept your challenge with all my heart!”

So each knight took his place and made himself ready for the clash. Then they shouted and charged together, rushing at each other like two rams on a hillside. The spear of Sir Ewaine was also shattered into pieces. But King Arthur’s spear held firm, so that the straps of Sir Ewaine’s saddle burst apart, and both the saddle and the knight were swept off the horse’s back with such force that a falling tower could not have made a greater noise than Sir Ewaine did when he hit the dust of that causeway.

Then Sir Ewaine got to his feet and stared at him, filled with amazement. King Arthur came to him and spoke to him like this: “Ha, Sir Knight, it seems to me that you have been fairly beaten today. And so, as you promised, both you and that other knight must carry out all my commands for the next seven whole days. This is the command that I give to you both: you must go at once to the Lady Guinevere at Cameliard and bring her the greeting of her knight. Tell her that her knight, to whom she gave her necklace, has sent you, who are sons of kings, to do her service. And everything that she commands you to do in these next seven days, you must do down to the smallest detail.”

“Sir Knight,” said Sir Gawaine, “we will do as you command, since we have pledged ourselves to it. But when these seven days are over, I swear that I will seek you out and fight this combat to the very end. Any knight may be knocked from his horse, as I have been, yet I believe I may do better against you if I fight you with all my strength.”
“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “it shall be just as you wish. Yet I truly believe that when these seven days are over, you will not want to fight me as much as you do now.”

After saying this, King Arthur saluted the two knights, and they saluted him. Then he turned his horse and went on his way. Whenever he thought of how those two good knights had fallen before his attack, and how astonished and ashamed they had been at their defeat, he laughed aloud with pure fun. He promised himself that he had never in all his life taken part in so joyful an adventure as this.
When Sir Ewaine had mended the straps of his saddle, he and Sir Gawaine mounted their horses and set out toward Cameliard, very low in spirits.
Then the miller came out of the mill once more. He was greatly delighted to have watched such a wonderful knightly fight from so safe a place as the one where he had stood.

So King Arthur rode onward, very contented in his mind, until the afternoon was growing late. By that time he had come close to the arm of the forest that he had chosen as the proper place to leave his horse and his armor.

As he drew near this edge of the forest, he saw before him at the roadside a gnarled and stunted oak tree. He saw that a shield hung upon the oak, and that beneath the shield these words were written in fair, large letters:

“Whoever strikes this shield
Does so at the risk of his life.”
Then King Arthur felt a great spirit rise in him. He raised his spear and struck that shield so hard that it rang like thunder.

At once King Arthur heard a voice come out of the forest, crying, “Who has dared to attack my shield?” And immediately a large knight rode out from the trees upon a white horse, just like the one King Arthur himself rode. The trappings of the horse and of the knight were all white, like those of King Arthur and his horse. The knight wore on his helmet, as his crest, a swan with outspread wings. On his shield he bore the emblem of three swans on a silver field. From the crest and the emblem on the shield, King Arthur knew that this knight was Sir Pellias, who had come with him from Camelot to Tintagalon.

When Sir Pellias had come close to where King Arthur waited for him, he pulled up his horse and spoke to him in a very stern voice. “Ho! Ho! Sir Knight,” he said. “Why did you dare to strike my shield? Truly, that blow will bring you great danger and sorrow. Now get ready to defend yourself at once, because of what you have done.”

“Wait! Wait! Sir Knight,” said King Arthur. “It shall be as you wish, and I will fight you. But I will not try this adventure until you agree that the knight who is beaten in the fight shall serve the other in whatever way the other may wish, for one week from this time.”
“Sir Knight,” said Sir Pellias, “I accept that risk. So I now tell you to get ready for the fight at once.”

Then each knight took his place and set his spear and shield. When they were ready, they charged at each other at once, with a force like two stones hurled from a catapult. They met in the middle of the course, and once again King Arthur was entirely successful in his attack. The spear of Sir Pellias burst into pieces, but the spear of King Arthur held firm. Sir Pellias was thrown from his saddle with terrible force, more than half a spear’s length behind the rear of his horse. He did not fully recover from that fall for a long time. King Arthur had to wait beside him for quite a while before he was able to lift himself from the ground where he lay.

“Ha! Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “it has surely gone badly for you today. You have been completely overthrown, and now you must keep your pledge to serve me for seven days. So I command you to go at once to Cameliard and greet the Lady Guinevere from me. Tell her that her knight, the one to whom she gave her necklace, has won the fight against you. I also command you to obey her for seven days in whatever she may order you to do.”

“Sir Knight,” said Sir Pellias, “it shall be just as you order. But I wish I knew who you are, for I declare that in all my life I have never been overthrown as you have overthrown me. Indeed, I think there are very few men in the world who could have done to me what you have done.”
“Sir Knight,” said King Arthur, “some day you shall know who I am. But for now I am bound to complete secrecy.”
Then he saluted Sir Pellias, turned, rode into the forest, and was gone.
Sir Pellias mounted his horse and went to Cameliard, very downcast and troubled in spirit. He wondered greatly who that knight could be, who had treated him as he had just been treated.

That day four knights came to Cameliard: first Sir Geraint, then Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine, and last of all Sir Pellias. When these four saw one another, they were all so ashamed that hardly one of them dared to look another in the face. They came before the Lady Guinevere and explained their situation to her. They told her how the knight who wore her necklace had overthrown them all and sent them there to serve her for a week. She considered how great and famous those four knights were in deeds of chivalry, and she was overjoyed that her knight had proved himself so great in the feats of arms he had set out to perform. But she wondered greatly who that champion could be, and she turned the question over in her own mind. For it was entirely unheard of that one knight, in one day, with a single spear, should have overthrown five such proven and famous knights as Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, Sir Geraint, Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, and Sir Pellias. So she was very glad that she had given her necklace to such a worthy knight. She felt extraordinary pleasure and pride at the thought of the honor he had brought her.

After King Arthur had entered the forest, he soon came to the place where the woodcutters mentioned earlier were at their work. He stayed with them that night. When the next morning came, he left his horse and armor in their care, telling them to guard these things carefully and that they would be wonderfully rewarded for it. Then he left that place, meaning to return to Cameliard. He wore the rough jerkin of coarse cloth that he had worn ever since he left Tintagalon.

When he reached the edge of the forest, he put his cap of disguise on his head and so took on his humble appearance once more. With his knightly rank hidden completely, he returned to Cameliard to be the gardener’s boy, as he had been before.

chapters.title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 4
paragraphs: _How the Four Knights Served the Lady Guinevere._

When King Arthur returned to Cameliard (this was in the afternoon of the second day), he found the gardener waiting for him, very angry. The gardener had brought a long birch rod to punish his boy with when the boy came back to the garden. When he saw King Arthur, he said, “You rascal! Why did you leave your work and go wandering off?” King Arthur laughed and said, “Do not touch me.” This made the gardener so furious that he grabbed the King by the collar of his jacket, meaning to beat him. “Are you laughing at me, you rascal, and making fun of me? Now I will give you a good beating for what you have done.”

When King Arthur felt that man’s hand on him and heard the angry words of the gardener, his royal spirit swelled up within him, and he cried out, “Ha, wretch! Would you dare to lay your hands on my sacred person?” With that, he seized the gardener by the wrists, took the rod away from him, and struck him across the shoulders with it. The poor man felt himself held in the powerful grip of the angry King, and he felt the rod on his shoulders. He let out a great cry, although the blow did not hurt him at all. “Now get out of here!” said King Arthur. “Do not trouble me again, or I will treat you in a way you will not like at all.” With that, he let the poor man go. The gardener was so dazed with terror that the earth and the sky seemed to spin around him. King Arthur’s eyes had flashed at him like lightning, and those two hands had held his wrists with wonderful strength. So when the King let him go, he hurried away as fast as he could, trembling and sweating with fear.

He went straight to the Lady Guinevere and complained to her about how he had been treated. “Lady,” he said, weeping at the memory of his fright, “my boy goes away for a day or more, and I do not know where. When I tried to whip him for leaving his work, he took the rod right out of my hands and beat me with it. So now I beg you, deal with him as he deserves, and have several strong men chase him away from this place with rods.”

The Lady Guinevere laughed. “Leave him be,” she said, “and do not bother him anymore. He seems to me a very cheeky fellow. As for you, pay no attention to his coming or going, and perhaps I will deal with him in a way that suits him.”

The gardener went away, greatly wondering why the Lady Guinevere was so gentle with that insolent rascal. The Lady Guinevere went away too, in very good spirits. She had begun to think that there was surely a good reason for what had happened. When the White Champion, who did such wonderful deeds, came to the castle, the gardener’s boy went away. When the same Champion left, the gardener’s boy came back. So she suspected many things, and she felt wonderfully merry and cheerful.

That afternoon the Lady Guinevere happened to be walking in the garden with her damsels. With her walked the four noble knights whom her White Champion had sent there: Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Geraint, and Sir Pellias. The gardener’s lad was digging in the gardens, and as they passed him, the Lady Guinevere laughed aloud and cried out, “Look! Look! My lords and ladies! There is a very cheeky fellow for a gardener’s lad. He keeps his cap on all the time, even when he stands in front of lords and ladies.”

Then Sir Gawaine spoke up. “Is that so? Then I will go to that rascal right now and take his hat off for him. I will do it so roughly that I do not believe he will ever offend us again by wearing it in our presence.”

The Lady Guinevere laughed a great deal at this. “Leave him be,” she said, “leave him be! Sir Gawaine, it would not suit someone as gentle as you to have anything to do with that cheeky fellow. Besides, he has assured us all that he has an ugly sore on his head, so let him wear his cap, and God be merciful to him.”
So the Lady Guinevere, although she suspected a very great deal, was pleased to make fun of the very person she suspected.

That day Duke Mordaunt of North Umber had fully recovered from the painful injuries he had suffered when the White Champion overthrew him. So when the next morning came, he appeared before the castle again as he had done before, dressed in full armor. This time two heralds rode in front of him. When the duke and the two heralds reached the part of the meadows right in front of the castle of Cameliard, the heralds blew their trumpets very loudly. At the sound of the trumpets, many people came and gathered on the walls. King Leodegrance came too, and he took his place on a smaller tower that looked down on the plain where the Duke of North Umber and the two heralds stood. Then the Duke of North Umber looked up and saw King Leodegrance standing above him on top of that tower, and he cried out in a loud voice, “Hello there, King Leodegrance! Do not think that you are rid of me just because I fell from my horse by the bad luck of a fight. Nevertheless, I now make you this fair offer. Tomorrow I will appear before this castle with six fellow knights. If you have any seven knights who can stand against me and my companions in a fight, whether with spears or swords, on horseback or on foot, then I will give up every claim I have to the hand of the Lady Guinevere. But if you cannot find such champions to fight successfully against me and my fellow knights, then I will not only claim Lady Guinevere, but I will also seize and keep for myself three castles of yours that stand on the borders of North Umber. I will also seize and keep all the lands and church fields that belong to those same castles. Moreover, this challenge of mine will hold only until sunset tomorrow, and after that time it will be null and void. So, King Leodegrance, you had better see to it right away that you find champions who can defend you against these demands.”

Then the two heralds blew their trumpets once more, and Duke Mordaunt of North Umber turned his horse around and rode away. King Leodegrance went away too, very sorrowful and downhearted. He said to himself, “Is it at all likely that another champion will come to me like that wonderful White Champion who came two days ago, I do not know from where, to defend me against my enemies? And as for that White Champion, if I do not know where he came from, I also do not know where he has gone. How then can I know where to look for him to beg for his help again in this time of my great need?” So he went on his way, very sorrowful, and he did not know what to do to defend himself. Troubled to the depths of his spirit, he went straight to his own room and shut himself in. He would not see anyone or speak to anyone, but gave himself up completely to sorrow and despair.

In this great need, the Lady Guinevere thought of the four knights who had promised to serve her for seven days. She went to them where they were and spoke to them like this: “My lords, you were sent here, pledged to serve me for seven days. Now I order you to take up this challenge of Duke Mordaunt at my request. I very much want you to go out tomorrow and meet this Duke of North Umber and his fellow knights in battle. You are terribly powerful knights, and I believe you can easily defend us against our enemies.”

But Sir Gawaine said, “No, Lady, no! We are pledged to your service, but we are not pledged to the service of King Leodegrance, your father. We have no quarrel of any kind with this Duke of North Umber or with his six fellow knights. We are knights of King Arthur’s Court, and we may not take up a foreign quarrel in the service of another king unless he commands it.”

Then the Lady Guinevere became extremely angry, and she said hotly, “Either you are a wonderfully faithful lord to your King, Sir Gawaine, or else you are afraid to meet this Duke of North Umber and his fellow knights.”

At these words of the Lady Guinevere, Sir Gawaine also grew very angry, and he answered, “If you were a knight and not a lady, Dame Guinevere, you would think three or four times before you found the courage to say those words to me.” With that he rose and left the place, his face red with anger. The Lady Guinevere also left and went to her chamber, where she wept a great deal, both from sorrow and from anger.

All this while King Arthur had been well aware of everything that happened. So after a while he got up, went out, and found the gardener. He took the gardener firmly by the collar of his coat and held him where he stood. He said to him, “Fellow! I have an order to give you, and you will carry it out exactly, or else a great deal of pain may come to you.” As he spoke, he thrust his hand into the front of his jacket and brought out the necklace of pearls that the Lady Guinevere had given him from around her own neck. And he said to the gardener, “You will take this necklace to the Lady Guinevere and say this to her: she is to send me at once bread and meat and wine and sweets from her own table. Tell her that I want her to call those four knights, Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Geraint, and Sir Pellias, and that she is to order them to come and serve me with those things for my refreshment. Tell her also that she is to command those knights to go on serving me as I direct, and that from now on they are to be my servants and not hers. These are the orders I give you: you are to say these things to the Lady Guinevere.”

When the gardener heard those words, he was so astonished that he did not know what to think, for he believed the gardener’s lad had gone completely mad. He raised his voice and cried aloud, “What is this! What are you saying? Truly, if I do what you tell me, it will cost me my life or else it will cost you yours. Who would dare to say such words to the Lady Guinevere?”

But King Arthur said, “Nevertheless, you will do as I command you, fellow. If you fail in even one point, I assure you it will go very badly for you. I have the power to make you suffer as you have never suffered before.”

At this the gardener said, “I will go.” He said to himself, “If I do as this fellow tells me, the Lady Guinevere will have him severely punished, and so I will get my revenge for what he did to me yesterday. Besides, it annoys me very much to have a lad working in the garden who behaves as this fellow does. So,” he said, “I will go.” He took the necklace of pearls that King Arthur gave him and went out, and after a while he found the Lady Guinevere. When he had found her, he spoke to her like this:

“Lady, my garden boy has surely gone completely mad. He threatened to do me great harm if I did not carry out his errand, and he has sent me to give you a very grievous insult. He sent me with this string of large beads to give to you. He tells me to say that you are to send him bread and meat and sweets and wine, such as you use at your own table. He tells me to say that these things are to be served to him by the four noble knights who came here the day before yesterday. He says that you are to command those same knights to obey him in whatever he orders, for from now on they are to be his servants and not yours. And truly, Lady, he would listen to nothing I said against it, but threatened me with dire injury if I did not come here and deliver this message to you.”

When the Lady Guinevere heard what the gardener said, and when she saw the necklace that she had given to the White Champion, she knew that the White Champion and the gardener’s boy were one and the same. She was filled with such great joy that she did not know whether to laugh or to weep. She got up and took the necklace of pearls, and she told the gardener to come with her. Then she went until she found the four knights, and when she had found them, she spoke to them like this:

“My lords, a little while ago I commanded you to take up my quarrel with Duke Mordaunt of North Umber for my sake, and you would not do it. And you, my lord Gawaine, spoke such angry words as a servant should not speak to his mistress, still less a knight to the daughter of a king. So I have decided that you will do a certain thing as a penance. If you refuse, I will know very well that you do not mean to keep the promise you gave to my knight when he overthrew all four of you in fair combat. This is my command: you will take food prepared for my table, meats and white bread and sweets and wine, and you will take that food to my gardener’s boy, whose cap you so bravely threatened to take away this very morning, Sir Gawaine. All four of you are to serve the food to him as though he were a royal knight. And when you have served him, you are to obey him in whatever he orders. I put this on you as a penalty because you did not take up my quarrel as true knights should. From now on you are to be servants to that gardener’s boy and not to me. So go now to the buttery of the castle, and tell the steward to give you meats such as are served at my own table. You are to serve the food on silver plates, and the wine in silver cups and goblets. And you are to wait on that gardener’s boy as though he were a great lord of enormous fame and renown.”

So spoke the Lady Guinevere, and when she had finished speaking, she turned and left the four knights. She took the gardener with her, and he was so astonished at what he had heard that he did not know whether he had gone mad or whether the Lady Guinevere had gone mad. The Lady Guinevere told the gardener to go to the gardener’s boy and tell him that everything would be done as he commanded. And the gardener did as he was told.

Now let us turn to the four knights whom the Lady Guinevere had left behind. They were bewildered and ashamed at the strange commands she had given them. When they recovered from their amazement, they burned with such great anger that, for a while, they could not tell whether what they saw was daylight or complete darkness. None of them could look another in the face, so overcome were they with shame at the insult they had received. Then Sir Gawaine spoke up, and his voice shook so much with anger that he could hardly get the words out. “Messires,” he said, “do you not see how this lady has deliberately insulted us? She did it because we refused to do what she told us this morning, and because we would not take up her quarrel against the Duke of North Umber. Well, we will serve this gardener’s boy just as she has ordered. We will bring him food and drink as she commanded, and we will wait on him as she told us to. But mark this: we are no longer her servants. We are his servants, and so we may serve him in whatever way we choose. So when we have carried out her orders, and served him food and drink, and obeyed every command he gives us, then I make this vow. I will kill that gardener’s boy with my own hand. When he is dead, I will put his head into a bag, and I will send the bag to the Lady Guinevere by the humblest carrier I can find. In that way this proud lady will receive an insult as great as the one she has given us.” And they all agreed that everything should happen exactly as Sir Gawaine had said.

So the four lords went to the steward of the castle, and they asked for the best of the food that was to be served to the Lady Guinevere: meats and bread and sweet cakes and wine. Then they took silver plates and platters and set the food upon them. They took silver cups and goblets and poured the wine into them, and they went out carrying these things. Behind the castle, near the stables, they found the gardener’s boy, and they told him to sit down and eat and drink. They waited on him as if he were some great lord. Not one of the four knights knew who he really was. They did not know that he was the great King whom, in truth, they served. He wore his cap of disguise upon his head, and so they thought he was only a poor peasant.

Now Sir Ewaine saw that the boy still kept his cap on before them, and he spoke to him in great anger, saying, “Ha, villain! Would you keep your cap on even in the presence of great princes and lords such as we are?”
Sir Gawaine said, “Leave it, it does not matter.” Then he spoke very bitterly to the gardener’s boy. “Eat well, fellow! For you will hardly eat another meal on this earth.”

The gardener’s boy answered, “Sir Knight, perhaps that will be decided by a will other than yours. I may eat many more meals than this one. And perhaps you will wait on me at them, as you are waiting on me now.” The four lords were astonished beyond measure that he could speak to them so calmly and without any sign of fear.

When he had finished eating, the gardener’s boy said to the knights, “Look, Messires, I have had enough and I am done. Now I have other commands for you to carry out. My next command is that you get ready at once to ride out with me, and for that you must put on full armor. And you, Sir Gawaine, will go to the head stable-keeper of this castle and tell him to prepare the Lady Guinevere’s palfrey, so that I may ride out on it right away. When you are all dressed in your armor, and everything is ready as I have commanded, bring that palfrey to the back gate of the castle. I will meet you there, and we will ride out together.”
Sir Gawaine said, “It shall be done exactly as you command. But when we ride out from this castle, it will be a sorry journey for you.”
The gardener’s boy said, “I do not think so, Sir Gawaine.”

Then the four went away and did as the gardener’s boy had commanded. When they were dressed in full armor and had fetched the Lady Guinevere’s palfrey, they went to the back gate, and there the gardener’s boy met them. He saw that they stayed seated on their horses and did not move when he came. So he said, “Ha, Messires! Is this how you treat the one you have been ordered to serve? Now I command you, Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine, to come down and hold my stirrup for me. And I command you, Sir Geraint and Sir Pellias, to come down and hold my palfrey while I mount.”

Then the four noble knights did as they were told. And Sir Gawaine said, “You may give orders as you please, and I advise you to make the most of it while you can. You have only a little while left to enjoy the great honor that has come to you. For that honor, look you, will soon crush you to death.”
The gardener’s boy said, “Not so. I believe I will not die for a good while yet.” Again the four lords were greatly astonished at how calm he was.
So they rode out from that place. The gardener’s boy would not allow them to ride in front of him or beside him. He ordered them to ride behind him, since they were still his servants.

They rode that way, as he had arranged, for a long distance. After they had gone a great way forward, they came near a gloomy and dismal forest. It lay just beyond the lands that border Cameliard. When they were close to this forest, Sir Gawaine rode a little ahead and said, “Sir Gardener’s Boy, do you see that forest over there? When we enter it, you will die at once, and by a sword that has never been touched by anyone but noble or knightly blood.”
King Arthur turned around in his saddle and said, “Ha! Sir Gawaine! Would you ride ahead like this when I have told you to ride behind me?”
As he spoke he took the cap from his head, and then they all saw that it was King Arthur who rode with them.

Then a great silence of utter astonishment fell upon them all, and each man sat as still as if he had been turned into a stone statue. King Arthur was the first to speak. He said, “Ha! What is this, Sir Knights? Have you no words of greeting to offer me? Truly, you have served me very ungraciously this day. And you have even threatened to kill me. Now that I speak to you, you say nothing at all in reply.”

Then the four knights cried out at once. They leaped down from their horses and knelt in the dust of the road. When King Arthur saw them kneeling there, he laughed with great joy. He told them to mount their horses again, for time was passing and there was much to do.

So they mounted their horses and rode away. As they traveled, the King told them everything that had happened to him. They were greatly amazed, and they praised the knightly way he had behaved in all those fine adventures. They rejoiced that they had a king to rule over them who had such a high and knightly spirit.
So they rode to the part of the forest where King Arthur had left his horse and his armor.

chapters.title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 5
paragraphs: _How King Arthur defeated the enemies of King Leodegrance, and how his royalty was proclaimed._

The next day, the Duke of North Umber and six fellow knights appeared on the field in front of the castle of Cameliard, just as he had promised that he and they would. The seven champions arrived in great style. Seven heralds rode in front of them with trumpets and tabards, and seven squires rode behind. Each squire carried the spear, the shield, the crest, and the small banner of the knight he served. The seven heralds blew their trumpets so loudly that the sound reached the farthest corners of Cameliard, and people came running from everywhere. While the heralds blew, the seven squires shouted and waved the spears and banners. The seven knights rode so proudly that those who watched them had hardly ever seen such a splendid show of chivalry.

They paraded up and down the field three times, from one end to the other. Meanwhile a great crowd, called there by the blowing of the heralds’ trumpets, stood on the walls and gazed down at the noble sight. All the Court of King Ryence came too, and stood on the plain in front of the King’s pavilion. They shouted and cheered for the Duke of North Umber and his six fellow knights.

Meanwhile King Leodegrance of Cameliard was so weighed down with trouble and shame that he would not show his face. He hid himself away from all his Court, and he would not let anyone come into his presence that day.

Even so, the Lady Guinevere went to him with several of her damsels. When the King refused to let her in, she spoke to him through the door and tried to cheer him, saying: “My lord King and father, I beg you to look up and take heart. I promise you that there is one who holds our cause in his hands, and he is truly a most glorious champion. He will surely come before this day is over, and when he comes, he will certainly overthrow our enemies.”

But King Leodegrance did not open the door. He said: “My daughter, you say that only to comfort me. In this time of trouble I have no help except God, with His good, strong help and grace.” And she said: “No, I am telling you the truth. The help that God sends you, He will certainly send through a worthy champion who at this very moment holds our cause in his hand.”
So spoke the Lady Guinevere. King Leodegrance still did not come out, but he was greatly comforted by what she had said to him.

So passed all that morning and part of the afternoon, and still no one came to answer the challenge the seven knights had declared. But while the sun was still three or four hours high, a cloud of dust suddenly appeared in the far distance. Out of that cloud came five knights, riding at great speed toward the castle. When they drew near the walls, the people saw that the knight riding first of all was the same White Champion who had earlier overthrown the Duke of North Umber. They also saw that the four knights riding with him were very famous, with great skill and glory in arms. They were Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Geraint, and Sir Pellias. The people of the castle and the town knew those four knights, because they had stayed two days at Cameliard. They were so famous that folk crowded in from far and near to look at them whenever they walked abroad.

When the people on the walls saw who those knights were, and saw the White Champion who had earlier brought them such great honor, they shouted aloud a second time, with a voice mightier than the first.

King Leodegrance heard the people shouting, and hope suddenly woke within him. He came out at once, as fast as he could, to see what was happening. There he saw those five noble champions about to enter the field below the castle walls.

The Lady Guinevere also heard the shouting and came out as well. And behold, there was the White Champion with those four other knights. When she saw the White Knight and his four companions-at-arms, her heart nearly broke with pure joy and gladness. She wept from the strength of her feeling, and laughed while she wept. She waved her kerchief to those five noble lords and kissed her hand to them, and the five knights saluted her as they rode past her and into the field.

When the Duke of North Umber learned that five knights had come to answer the challenge against him and his companions, he came out of his pavilion at once and mounted his horse. His fellow knights came out and mounted their horses too, and he and they rode out to meet those who had come against them.

When the Duke of North Umber came close enough, he saw that the chief of the five knights was the White Champion who had earlier overthrown him. So he said to the White Champion: “Sir Knight, once before I lowered myself to fight you, though you were unknown to me and to everyone else here. I did not ask who you were. I rode a course against you, and by the chance of arms you overthrew me. This quarrel is more serious than that. So I and my companions-at-arms will not ride a course with you and your companions, and we will not fight you, until I first know the rank of the man I am fighting. I ask you now to declare who you are and what your standing is.”

Then Sir Gawaine opened the visor of his helmet and said: “Sir Knight, look at my face, and know that I am Gawaine, the son of King Lot. So you can see that my rank and standing are even better than your own. Now I tell you that the White Knight yonder is of such a rank that he lowers himself when he fights you, and you do not lower yourself by fighting him.”

“Ho, Sir Gawaine!” said the Duke of Umber. “That is a very strange thing to say, for there are few in this world so exalted that they would lower themselves to fight me. Nevertheless, since you vouch for him, I cannot deny what you say. Yet there is another reason why we cannot fight you. Look, we are seven well-proven and famous knights, and you are only five. Consider how unequal our forces are, and that you are in great danger in taking on so dangerous a fight.”

Sir Gawaine gave the Duke of North Umber a very grim smile. “Many thanks for your pity, Sir Duke, and for the tenderness you show for our safety,” he said. “But you may leave that matter to us and rest easy about it. I think the danger you seven are in is every bit as great as ours. Besides, if you were not a belted knight, a simple man might suppose you were more careful of your own safety in this matter than of ours.”

At these words the face of the Duke of North Umber turned completely red. He knew that he truly had no great wish for this battle, and he was ashamed of what Sir Gawaine had said to him. Each knight closed his helmet and all turned their horses. One party rode to one end of the field and the other party to the other end, and there each took its place.

They arranged themselves like this. In the middle was King Arthur, with two knights on either side. In the middle of the other party was the Duke of North Umber, with three knights on either side. When they had lined up, they readied their spears and shields and made themselves fully prepared for the charge. Then King Arthur and Duke Mordaunt each shouted aloud, and the two parties hurled themselves at each other with such violence that the ground shook and thundered under the horses’ hoofs, and clouds of dust rose up toward the heavens.
They met in the middle of the field with an uproar so dreadful that the crash of it could be heard more than a mile away.
When the two parties had passed each other and the dust of the clash had risen, behold, three of the seven had been overthrown, and not one of the five had lost his seat.

One of those who had been overthrown was Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, and he never rose from the ground where he lay. King Arthur had aimed his spear straight into the middle of his defenses, and the spear had held. Its point had pierced the Duke’s shield and his body armor, and the stroke was so violent that the Duke was lifted completely out of his saddle and thrown a full spear’s length behind his horse’s rump. So died that wicked man. As King Arthur rode past him, the evil soul of the Duke left his body with a faint noise like the squeak of a bat, and the world was well rid of him.

When King Arthur turned at the end of the course, he saw that only four knights were left on their horses out of all the seven he and his companions had charged. He raised his spear, drew rein on his horse, and spoke to his knights like this: “Messires, I am weary of all this noise and quarreling, and I do not care to fight any more today. So go at once and attack those knights. As for me, I will wait here and watch your adventure.”
“Lord,” they said, “we will do our best, as you command.”

So those four good knights did as he commanded. They rode straight against the other four, much encouraged that their King was watching their effort. King Arthur sat with the butt of his spear resting on his instep, and looked over the field with great calm and a steady face.

The four knights who remained of the Duke of North Umber’s party did not come out to this second clash as readily as they had before. They now knew how great the skill of the other knights was, and they saw that their enemies were coming at them very fiercely, with great courage and eagerness. So their hearts melted within them with doubt and worry about how this second clash would end.
Even so, they prepared themselves with what resolve they could find, and came forward as they were called to do.

Then Sir Gawaine rode straight at the foremost knight, a well-known champion named Sir Dinador of Montcalm. When he came close enough, he rose in his stirrups and struck Sir Dinador such a fierce blow that it split the knight’s shield in two and split his helmet as well. Part of the blade of Gawaine’s sword broke off and stayed in the helmet.

When Sir Dinador felt that blow, his brains swam like water, and he had to grab the horn of his saddle to keep from falling off. A great terror fell upon him, and he swerved his horse violently to one side. He fled from that place with the terror of death hanging over him like a black cloud of smoke. When his companions saw the stroke Sir Gawaine had dealt, and saw Sir Dinador flee from him, they also swerved to one side and fled at top speed, full of terror at their enemies. Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Geraint, and Sir Pellias chased them as they fled. They chased them straight through the Court of King Ryence, and the knights and nobles of that Court scattered this way and that like chaff as they came. They chased the fleeing knights in among the pavilions of King Ryence’s Court, and no man stopped them. When they had driven those knights completely away, they returned to the place where King Arthur still held his post, steadily waiting for them.

When the people of Cameliard saw their enemies overthrown, and saw them flee from their champions, they shouted with all their might and made a great cheer. They did not hold back their loud shouting when the four knights came back from chasing their enemies and rejoined the White Champion. They cheered even more when the five knights rode across the drawbridge and through the gateway into the town.
So ended the great combat, one of the most famous in all the history of chivalry in King Arthur’s Court.

When King Arthur had accomplished his purpose and come back into the town, he went to the merchant from whom he had borrowed the armor he wore, and gave the armor back to him. He said, “Tomorrow, Sir Merchant, I will send you two bags of gold for the rent of the armor you let me have.”
The merchant said: “Lord, there is no need to pay me for that armor, for you have done great honor to Cameliard by your skill in arms.”
But King Arthur said: “Enough, Sir Merchant, and do not forbid what I say. Take what I shall send you.”
Then he went on his way, and, having put his cap of disguise on his head, he came back into the Lady Guinevere’s gardens.

When the next morning came, the people of Cameliard looked out and saw that King Ryence had gone away from before the castle completely. That night he had taken down his pavilions, withdrawn his Court, and left the place where he and his people had camped for the past five days. He had taken with him the body of the Duke of North Umber, carrying it away in a litter surrounded by many lighted candles and borne with unusual pomp and ceremony. When the people of Cameliard saw that he was gone, they were overjoyed, and they made merry, shouting and singing and laughing. They did not know how deeply angry King Ryence was with them, for his old hatred of King Leodegrance was only a small flame compared with the anger that now possessed him.
That morning Lady Guinevere walked into her garden, and with her walked Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine. There she saw the gardener’s boy again.
Then she laughed aloud and said to the two knights, “Messires, look! There is the gardener’s boy, who wears his cap all the time because he has an ugly spot on his head.”

The two knights knew who that gardener’s boy was, and they were greatly embarrassed by her words, and did not know what to say or where to look. Sir Gawaine spoke aside to Sir Ewaine, saying: “By Heaven, that lady does not know what kind of man the gardener’s boy is yonder. If she did, she would be more careful of her words.”

The Lady Guinevere heard that Sir Gawaine was speaking, but she did not hear his words. So she turned to Sir Gawaine and said: “Sir Gawaine, perhaps it offends you that the gardener’s boy wears his cap in front of us. Maybe you will go and take it off his head, as you offered to do two or three days ago.”
And Sir Gawaine said: “Peace, Lady! You do not know what you are saying. Yonder gardener’s boy could more easily take my head off my shoulders than I could take his cap off his head.”
At this the Lady Guinevere laughed openly, but in her heart she secretly thought about that saying and wondered greatly what Sir Gawaine meant by it.

Around noon that day, a herald arrived from King Ryence of North Wales. He walked in boldly before King Leodegrance, who was sitting in his hall with a number of his people around him. The herald said: “My lord King, my master, King Ryence of North Wales, is greatly displeased with you. You sent certain knights against Duke Mordaunt of North Umber, and those knights killed that excellent nobleman, who was a close relative of King Ryence. Also, you have given no answer to the demands my master has made for certain lands and castles bordering North Wales to be handed over to him. For these reasons my master is insulted beyond measure. King Ryence orders me to give you two conditions, and they are these. First, you must immediately hand over to him the White Knight who killed the Duke of North Umber. Second, you must promise at once that those lands will be handed over to King Ryence immediately.”

Then King Leodegrance rose from his seat and spoke to the herald with great dignity. “Sir Herald,” he said, “the demands King Ryence makes of me are the height of insolence. The Duke of North Umber died because of his own pride and foolishness. I would not hand that White Knight over to your master even if I were able to. As for the lands your master demands, you may tell King Ryence that I will not give him so much as a single blade of grass, or a single grain of corn that grows there.”

The herald said: “If that is your answer, King Leodegrance, then I am ordered to tell you this. My master, King Ryence of North Wales, will soon come here with a great army, and he will take by force the things you will not give him peacefully.” With those words he left and went on his way.

After the herald had gone, King Leodegrance went into his private room. There he secretly sent for the Lady Guinevere, and she came to him. King Leodegrance said to her: “My daughter, a knight dressed all in white, with no crest or emblem of any kind, has come to our rescue twice and defeated our enemies. Everyone says that this knight is your own special champion. I also hear that he wore your necklace as a favor when he first went out against the Duke of North Umber. Now I beg you, daughter, tell me who the White Champion is, and where he can be found.”
Then the Lady Guinevere was overcome with confusion, and she looked away from her father’s face. She said: “Truly, my Lord, I do not know who that knight may be.”

Then King Leodegrance spoke very seriously to the Lady Guinevere. He took her by the hand and said: “My daughter, you are now old enough to think about marrying a man who will cherish you and protect you from your enemies. Look, I am growing old, and I cannot hope to defend you always from the dangers that surround people of our rank. Also, King Arthur (who is a very great King indeed) has brought peace to this realm. Because of that, all the noble court of knights that once gathered around me has scattered to other places, where greater adventures can be found than in my peaceful kingdom. So, as everyone has seen this past week, I now have not one single knight I can depend on to defend us in times of danger like these that now threaten us. It seems to me, my daughter, that you could not hope to find anyone who could protect you as well as this White Knight. He truly seems to be a champion of extraordinary skill and strength. So it would be good if you felt yourself drawn to him, as he seems to be drawn to you.”

Then the Lady Guinevere turned bright red, as if with fire, all the way down to her throat. She laughed, even as the tears overflowed her eyes and ran down her cheeks. So she wept, and yet laughed as she wept. She said to King Leodegrance: “My Lord and father, if I give my affection to anyone in the way you speak of, I will give it only to the poor gardener’s boy who digs in my garden.”
At these words King Leodegrance’s face twisted with fierce anger, and he cried out: “Ha, Lady! Would you make a mock and a joke of my words?”

Then the Lady Guinevere said: “Indeed, my Lord! I am not joking and I am not mocking. I tell you truly that the same gardener’s boy knows more about the White Champion than anybody else in the whole world.” Then King Leodegrance said: “What is this you are telling me?” And the Lady Guinevere said: “Send for that gardener’s boy and you will find out.” And King Leodegrance said: “Truly, there is more in this than I can understand right now.”
The King summoned his head page, a boy named Dorisand, and told him: “Dorisand, go to the Lady Guinevere’s garden and fetch the gardener’s boy to me.”

So Dorisand the page went as King Leodegrance had commanded, and in a little while he came back, bringing the gardener’s boy with him. With them came Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Pellias and Sir Geraint. Those four lords stood near the door where they had entered, but the gardener’s boy came and stood beside the table where King Leodegrance sat. The King looked up at the gardener’s boy and said: “Ha! Would you wear your cap in our presence?”
Then the gardener’s boy said: “I cannot take off my cap.”
But the Lady Guinevere, who stood beside King Leodegrance’s chair, spoke up and said: “I beg you, Messire, take off your cap to my father.”
At this the gardener’s boy said: “At your request I will take it off.”

So he took the cap off his head, and King Leodegrance saw his face and knew him. When he saw who stood before him, he cried out loud in utter amazement. He said: “My Lord and my King! What is this!” Then he rose from his seat, went and knelt on the ground before King Arthur. He pressed the palms of his hands together and placed his hands between the hands of King Arthur, and King Arthur took King Leodegrance’s hands in his own. King Leodegrance said: “My Lord! My Lord! Is it really you who have done all these wonderful things?”
Then King Arthur said: “Yes. Whatever those things were, I did them.” He bent down and kissed King Leodegrance on the cheek, lifted him to his feet, and spoke kind words to cheer him.

Now the Lady Guinevere, when she saw what was happening, was astonished beyond measure. All at once she understood everything with amazing clarity. A great fear came over her, so that she trembled terribly, and she said to herself: “What things have I said to this great King, and how I have mocked him and joked about him in front of everyone around me!” At the thought of it, she pressed her hand to her side to calm the terrible pounding of her heart. So, while King Arthur and King Leodegrance exchanged royal greetings and compliments, she slipped away and stood by the window near the corner of the wall.
After a while King Arthur looked up and saw her standing far off. He went straight to her, took her by the hand, and said: “Lady, how are you?”

She said: “Lord, I am afraid of your greatness.” He said: “No, Lady. It is I who am afraid of you. Your kind regard means more to me than anything else in all the world. Otherwise I would not have served for these twelve days as a gardener’s boy in your garden, all for the sake of your good will.” She said: “You have my good will, Lord.” He said: “Do I have your good will in great measure?” And she said: “Yes, you have it in great measure.”
Then he bent his head and kissed her in front of everyone there, and so they were promised to each other.
King Leodegrance was filled with such great joy that he did not know how to contain himself.

After these events, there was a war with King Ryence of North Wales. Sir Kay and Sir Ulfius had gathered a great army, as King Arthur had ordered them to do. So when King Ryence attacked Cameliard, he was completely defeated and his army scattered. He himself was chased into his mountains like an outcast.

Then there was great rejoicing in Cameliard. After his victory, King Arthur stayed there for a while with a splendid Court of noble lords and beautiful ladies. There was feasting and jousting and many famous contests of arms, the like of which that country had never seen before. King Arthur and the Lady Guinevere were perfectly happy together.

One day King Arthur sat at a feast with King Leodegrance, and the two of them were in very high spirits. King Leodegrance said to King Arthur: “My Lord, what shall I offer you as a dowry with my daughter, when you take her away from me to be your Queen?”
Then King Arthur turned to Merlin, who stood near him, and said: “Ha, Merlin! What shall I ask of my friend as that dowry?”

Merlin said to him: “My lord King, your friend King Leodegrance has one thing which, if he gives it to you, will greatly increase the glory and fame of your reign, so that it will never be forgotten.”
King Arthur said: “I ask you, Merlin, tell me what that thing is.”
So Merlin said: “My lord King, I will tell you a story:

“In the days of your father, Uther-Pendragon, I had a certain table made for him in the shape of a ring, and so men called it the ROUND TABLE. This table had seats for fifty men, and the seats were meant for the fifty knights who were the most worthy in all the world. The seats were made in such a way that whenever a worthy knight appeared, his name showed in letters of gold on the seat that belonged to him. When that knight died, his name would suddenly vanish from the seat he had once held.

“Now, forty-nine of these seats were all alike, except for one that was set aside for the King himself. That one was raised higher than the other seats, and was skillfully carved and inlaid with ivory and gold. The fiftieth seat was different from all the others, and it was called the SEAT PERILOUS. It was unlike the others both in how it was made and in what it meant. It was skillfully set with gold and silver in curious designs, and it was covered with a canopy of satin embroidered with gold and silver. It was altogether wonderful and magnificent to look at. No name ever appeared on this seat, because only one knight in all the world could hope to sit there safely. If any other dared to sit in it, either he would die a sudden and violent death within three days, or some great misfortune would fall upon him. That is why the seat was called the SEAT PERILOUS.
“In the days of King Uther-Pendragon, thirty-seven knights sat at the ROUND TABLE. When King Uther-Pendragon died, he gave the ROUND TABLE to his friend, King Leodegrance of Cameliard.
“At the beginning of King Leodegrance’s reign, twenty-four knights sat at the ROUND TABLE.

“But times have changed since then. The glory of King Leodegrance’s reign has paled beside the glory of your reign, and his noble Court of knights has left him completely. So now not one name is left on any of the fifty seats around the ROUND TABLE, except the name of King Leodegrance. The ROUND TABLE now lies under its pavilion, entirely unused.

“Yet if King Leodegrance will give you, my lord King, that ROUND TABLE as a dowry with the Lady Guinevere, it will bring your reign its greatest glory. In your day every seat at that TABLE will be filled, even the SEAT PERILOUS, and the fame of the knights who sit at it will never be forgotten.”
“Ha!” said King Arthur. “That would indeed be a dowry worthy of any king to have with his queen.”

“Then,” King Leodegrance said, “you shall have that dowry with my daughter. If it brings you great glory, then your glory will be my glory, and your fame will be my fame. For if my glory fades and yours grows, look, is not my child your wife?”
King Arthur said: “You speak well and wisely.”

So King Arthur became the master of that famous ROUND TABLE. The ROUND TABLE was set up at Camelot (which some men now call Winchester). Before long there gathered around it such a company of knights as the world had never seen before that time, and will never see again.
That was the story of the beginning of the ROUND TABLE in King Arthur’s reign.

chapters.title: The Winning of a Queen: Chapter 6
paragraphs: _How King Arthur Was Married in Royal State and How the Round Table Was Established._

Now the early fall of the year had come. It was that pleasant season when the meadows and the open country were still green with the summer that had just passed. The sky was still like summer, extraordinarily blue and full of large drifting clouds. A bird might sing here and another there, a short song in memory of spring. The air was warm, yet the leaves everywhere were turning brown and red and gold. When the sun shone through them, it was as though a cloth of gold, embroidered with brown and crimson and green, hung above your head. At this time of year it is wonderfully pleasant to be out in the fields among the nut trees with hawk and hound, or to travel through the yellow countryside, whether on horseback or on foot.

This was the time of year set for the marriage of King Arthur and the Lady Guinevere at Camelot, and the place was filled with extraordinary pomp and glory. All the world was stirring and bubbling with joy, for everyone was very glad that King Arthur was to have a Queen.

To prepare for that great occasion, the town of Camelot was decorated magnificently. The stony street along which the Lady Guinevere must travel to the King’s royal castle was strewn thickly with fresh-cut rushes, laid smooth. In many places it was also covered with carpets of excellent pattern, fit to lie on the floor of some splendid hall. All the houses along the way were hung with fine woven cloths shot through with threads of blue and crimson. Everywhere flags and banners floated in the warm, gentle breeze against the blue sky. The whole world seemed alive with bright colors, so that anyone looking down that street saw a winding path of wonderful beauty and gaiety stretched out before him.
So the King’s wedding day came—bright and clear and radiant.

King Arthur sat in his hall, surrounded by his Court, waiting for news that the Lady Guinevere was coming. About the middle of the morning, a messenger came riding in haste upon a milk-white horse. The messenger’s clothes and his horse’s trappings were all of cloth of gold embroidered with scarlet and white. His tabard was set with many jewels of different kinds, so that he glittered from far away as he rode, with a singular splendor.
This herald came straight into the castle where the King sat waiting, and he said: “Rise, my lord King, for the Lady Guinevere and her Court are drawing near.”

At this the King rose at once with great joy and went out with his Court of Knights, riding in great state. As he went down that marvelously decorated street, all the people shouted aloud as he passed by. He smiled and bowed his head from side to side, for that day he was very happy and loved his people with wonderful friendliness.

So he rode on to the town gate and out through it, and came into the countryside beyond. There the broad, well-worn highway ran winding down beside the shining river, between the willows and the osiers.

And behold! King Arthur and those with him saw the Princess’s Court far off in the distance. They rejoiced greatly and hurried forward with all speed. As they drew near, the sun fell upon the silk and cloth of gold, and upon the golden chains and the jewels that hung from them. All of that noble company surrounding the Lady Guinevere’s litter flashed and sparkled with dazzling radiance.

Seventeen of the noblest knights of the King’s Court, dressed in full armor, had been sent by him as an escort for the lady. They rode in great splendor around the litter in which the Princess lay. The frame of the litter was of richly gilded wood, and its curtains and cushions were of crimson silk embroidered with gold thread. Behind the litter rode the Princess’s Court in gay and joyful array, shining with many colors. There were her ladies-in-waiting, gentlemen, ladies, pages, and attendants.
So the King’s party and the Lady Guinevere’s party drew near to each other until they met and mingled together.

Then King Arthur at once got down from his noble horse. Dressed in all his royal robes, he went on foot to the Lady Guinevere’s litter, while Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine held his horse’s bridle. One of her pages drew aside the silken curtains of the litter, and King Leodegrance gave her his hand. She stepped down, wrapped, as it were, in wonderful beauty. King Leodegrance led her to King Arthur, and King Arthur came to her. He placed one hand beneath her chin and the other upon her head, bent his face to hers, and kissed her smooth cheek. It was warm and fragrant, as soft as velvet, and without any blemish at all. When he had kissed her cheek, everyone there lifted up their voices in a great cheer, shouting for joy that those two noble souls had met.

In this way King Arthur welcomed the Lady Guinevere and her father, King Leodegrance, on the highway beneath the walls of the town of Camelot, about half a league away. No one who was there ever forgot that meeting, for it was full of extraordinary grace and noble courtesy.

Then King Arthur and his Court of Knights and nobles led King Leodegrance and the Lady Guinevere with great ceremony to Camelot and the royal castle. Rooms were given to everyone, and the whole place was alive with joy and beauty.
When high noon came, the whole Court went in great state and ceremony to the cathedral. There, surrounded by wonderful magnificence, those two noble souls were married by the Archbishop.

All the bells rang joyfully, and all the people who stood outside the cathedral shouted with loud cheers. And look! The King and the Queen came out shining, like the sun for splendor and like the moon for beauty.

In the castle a great noontime feast was laid out. At it sat four hundred and eighty-six lords and noble folk—kings, knights, and nobles—along with queens and ladies in magnificent dress. Near the King and the Queen sat King Leodegrance and Merlin, Sir Ulfius, Sir Ector the trustworthy, Sir Gawaine, Sir Ewaine, Sir Kay, King Ban, King Pellinore, and many other famous and honored people. No one had ever seen such magnificent courtliness as was seen at that famous wedding feast of King Arthur and Queen Guinevere.

That day was also very famous in the history of chivalry, for in the afternoon the famous Round Table was established. That Round Table was at once the very flower and the greatest glory of King Arthur’s reign.

About the middle of the afternoon, the King and Queen walked in procession, led by Merlin and followed by that whole splendid Court of kings, lords, nobles, and knights in full dress. They went to the place where Merlin, partly by magic and partly by skill, had caused a very wonderful pavilion to be built above the Round Table where it stood.

When the King and the Queen and the Court had gone inside, they were amazed at the beauty of the pavilion. It seemed to them a great space, like a marvelous land of the Fairies. The walls were richly gilded and painted with wonderful figures of saints and angels, dressed in deep blue and crimson. All those saints and angels were shown playing upon various musical instruments that seemed to be made of gold. Overhead, the roof of the pavilion was made to look like the sky, all sky-blue and sprinkled with stars. In the middle of that painted sky was an image of the sun in his glory. Underfoot was a pavement all of marble, set in squares of black and white, and blue and red, and several other colors.

In the middle of the pavilion stood a Round Table with seats for exactly fifty people. At each of the fifty places was a golden cup filled with fragrant wine, and a golden plate bearing a small loaf of fine white bread. When the King and his Court entered the pavilion, music suddenly began to play with wonderful sweetness.
Merlin now stepped up, grasped King Arthur’s hand, and drew him aside from Queen Guinevere. He said to the King, “Look, here stands the Round Table.”
Then King Arthur said, “Merlin, what I see is more wonderful than words can tell.”

After that, Merlin showed the King the various marvels of the Round Table. First he pointed to a tall seat, wonderfully carved from precious woods and gilded so that it was exceedingly beautiful. He said, “Behold, lord King, that seat is called the ‘Seat Royal,’ and it is yours to sit in.” As Merlin spoke, look! Letters of gold suddenly appeared on the back of that seat, and the golden letters spelled out the name,
ARTHUR, KING.

And Merlin said, “Lord, that seat may well be called the center seat of the Round Table, for truly you are the very center of all that is most worthy in true knighthood. So that seat shall be called the center seat of all the other seats.”

Then Merlin pointed to the seat that stood opposite the Seat Royal. That seat also looked very wonderful, as was told earlier in this history. And Merlin said to the King: “My lord King, that seat is called the Seat Perilous. Only one man in all the world may sit in it, and that man has not yet been born. If any other man dares to sit in it, he will either die or suffer a sudden and terrible misfortune for his boldness. That is why the seat is called the Seat Perilous.”

“Merlin,” said the King, “everything you tell me is beyond understanding, it is so marvelous. Now I beg you to find, with all speed, enough knights to fill this Round Table, so that my glory will be complete.”

Then Merlin smiled at the King, though not cheerfully, and said, “Lord, why are you in such a hurry? Know that when this Round Table is completely filled in all its seats, then your glory will be fully achieved, and right after that your day will begin to decline. For when any man has reached the crowning of his glory, his work is done, and God breaks him, as a man might break a cup from which such perfect wine has been drunk that no baser wine may be allowed to spoil it. So when your work is done and ended, God will shatter the cup of your life.”

Then the King looked very steadily into Merlin’s face and said, “Old man, what you say is always full of wonder, for you speak words of wisdom. Even so, since I am in God’s hands, I wish my glory and His good will to be accomplished, even if He then breaks me completely when I have served His purposes.”

“Lord,” said Merlin, “you speak like a worthy king and with a very large and noble heart. Even so, I cannot fill the Round Table for you at this time. Though you have gathered about you the noblest Court of Chivalry in all of Christendom, there are only thirty-two knights here who may be thought worthy to sit at the Round Table.”
“Then, Merlin,” said King Arthur, “I ask you to choose those thirty-two for me right now.”
