“I will do so, lord King,” said Merlin.

Then Merlin looked around, and behold! He saw King Pellinore standing a little way off. Merlin went to him and took him by the hand. “Behold, my lord King,” he said. “Here is the knight in all the world who, next to yourself, is most worthy at this time to sit at this Round Table. He is very gentle in his manner toward the poor and needy, and at the same time so terribly strong and skillful that I do not know whether you or he would be more to be feared in a fight of knight against knight.”
Then Merlin led King Pellinore forward, and behold! Upon the high seat that stood to the left of the Royal Seat, a name suddenly appeared,
PELLINORE.

The name was blazoned in letters of gold that shone with extraordinary brightness. When King Pellinore took his seat, all those standing around gave him great and loud cheers that went on for a long time.

After Merlin had chosen King Arthur and King Pellinore in this way, he chose the following knights from King Arthur’s Court, thirty-two in all. These were the knights of great renown in chivalry who first established the Round Table. For this reason they were called “The Ancient and Honorable Companions of the Round Table.”

First there were Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine, who were the King’s nephews, and they sat near him on the right hand. There was Sir Ulfius (who held his seat only four years and eight months, until his death, after which Sir Geheris held that seat—he was squire to his brother, Sir Gawaine). There was Sir Kay the Seneschal, who was the King’s foster brother. There was Sir Baudwain of Britain (who held his seat only three years and two months, until his death, after which Sir Agravaine held that seat). There were Sir Pellias and Sir Geraint and Sir Constantine, son of Sir Caderes the Seneschal of Cornwall (who became king after King Arthur). There were Sir Caradoc and Sir Sagramore, called the Desirous, and Sir Dinadan and Sir Dodinas, called the Savage, and Sir Bruin, called the Black, and Sir Meliot of Logres. There were Sir Aglaval and Sir Durnure and Sir Lamorac (these three young knights were sons of King Pellinore). There were Sir Griflet and Sir Ladinas and Sir Brandiles and Sir Persavant of Ironside, and Sir Dinas of Cornwall, and Sir Brian of Listinoise. There were Sir Palomides and Sir Degraine and Sir Epinogres, the son of the King of North Umberland and brother of the enchantress Vivien. There were Sir Lamiel of Cardiff, and Sir Lucan the Bottler and his brother Sir Bedevere (who carried King Arthur to the ship of Fairies when he lay so badly wounded, close to death, after the last battle he fought). These thirty-two knights were the Ancient Companions of the Round Table. Others were added to them until there were forty-nine in all, and then Sir Galahad was added, and with him the Round Table was made completely full.
As Merlin chose each of these knights and took him by the hand, the knight’s name suddenly appeared in golden letters, very bright and shining, upon the seat that belonged to him.

But when all had been chosen, behold! King Arthur saw that the seat to the right of the Seat Royal had not been filled and had no name upon it. And he said to Merlin: “Merlin, how is it that the seat on my right hand has not been filled and has no name?”

And Merlin said: “Lord, there will be a name on it in a very little while. The one who sits in it will be the greatest knight in all the world, until the knight comes who will take the Seat Perilous. For the one who is coming will surpass all other men in beauty and in strength and in knightly grace.”
And King Arthur said: “I wish he were with us now.” And Merlin said: “He will come soon.”

So the Round Table was established with great pomp and ceremony. First the Archbishop of Canterbury blessed every seat, moving from place to place with his Holy Court around him. The choir sang most sweetly together, while others swung censers from which rose a wonderfully fragrant smoke of frankincense, filling the whole pavilion with a scent of Heavenly blessedness.

When the Archbishop had blessed every one of those seats, each chosen knight took his place at the Round Table. His squire came and stood behind him, holding the small banner with his coat of arms on the point of a spear above the knight’s head. And all those who stood about that place, both knights and ladies, lifted up their voices in loud cheers.

Then all the knights rose. Each knight held up the cross of his sword’s hilt in front of him, and each one repeated every word that King Arthur spoke. This was the covenant of their Knighthood of the Round Table. They promised to be gentle to the weak and brave against the strong. They promised to be terrible to the wicked and to anyone who did evil. They promised to defend the helpless who called on them for aid, and to hold all women sacred. They promised to stand up for one another whenever that help was needed, and to be merciful to all people. They promised to be kind in their deeds, true in friendship, and faithful in love. This was their covenant, and each knight swore to it on the cross of his sword. As a witness to his oath, he kissed the hilt. Then everyone standing nearby cheered loudly once more.

Then all the knights of the Round Table sat down. Each knight broke bread from the golden plate and drank wine from the golden cup that stood before him. They gave thanks to God for the food and drink they were having.
So King Arthur was married to Queen Guinevere, and so the Round Table was founded.

chapters.title: The Book of King Arthur: Conclusion
paragraphs: _So ends this Book of King Arthur. I have told it with such joy that it gives me great pleasure, as I close this first volume of my work, to look ahead to writing a second volume, which follows right away._

_That volume will tell the history of several very noble heroes who belonged to the Court of the King, and I think it is a good thing to write about such noble and honorable knights and gentlemen. Anyone might well enjoy reading such a history, hearing those heroes speak, and seeing how they behaved in times of trial and trouble. Their example will surely help us all to behave in the same way in a similar situation._

chapters.title: The Book of Three Worthies: Foreword
paragraphs: _Here begins the Second Book of the History of King Arthur, called The Book of Three Worthies. It is called this because it tells about three very excellent and honorable Lords of King Arthur’s court._
_The first of these three is Merlin the Wise. The second is Sir Pellias, who was known as the Gentle Knight. The third is Sir Gawaine, the son of King Lot of Orkney and the Isles._

_Next comes the story of the passing of Merlin the Wise. In it you will see how the very wisdom that Merlin had in such great measure brought about his own ruin. So I hope you will take that story to heart. Then you may see that the gifts of mind or body that God gives you must not be misused, by you or by others, so that they become the means of your own downfall._

_It will not excuse you in any way that, as you go forward in life, you will meet many men who are like Merlin. God has given them very great gifts of talent, which they could easily use for the great good of mankind. Instead they misuse those gifts, and so bring greater ruin upon themselves and greater harm to other men. Suppose you prove so weak or so wicked that you misuse your talents in that way, to the harm of others and of yourself. Your fault will be no less because others have done greater evil than you._

_So let this story of Merlin be a warning to you, I beg you all. I do not believe that Merlin meant his magic to harm anyone. Yet because of his folly, it did as much harm as if he had planned to do evil with it. Indeed, it is hard to say whether the wickedness or the foolishness of men does more harm in the world. So try to guard yourself well, not only against sin, but against folly and weakness as well._

chapters.title: The Book of Three Worthies: Prologue
paragraphs: One day King Arthur sat in the Royal Hall of Camelot with the Queen and all of his Court and all of her Court. There was great joy and laughter in that place.

While they sat there, an armed knight suddenly came into the Hall. His armor was covered with blood and dust, and his body had many wounds. Everyone in the room was astonished and afraid when they saw him, for his look promised no good news for King Arthur. The knight-messenger came to where the King sat. He was nearly fainting from weakness and from all the wounds he had taken. He told everyone there that five kings, all enemies of King Arthur, had suddenly entered the land, and that they were burning and plundering the country on every side.

The knight-messenger said that the five kings were the King of Denmark, the King of Ireland, the King of Soleyse, the King of the Vale, and the King of Longtinaise. They had brought a great army with them and were laying waste to the land all around. The whole realm was in terrible trouble and sorrow because of the damage they had done.

When King Arthur heard this news, he struck his palms together hard and cried out, “Alas! Who would want to be a king! Will the time never come when these wars and troubles will end, and we will have complete peace in this land!” Then he got up in great distress and left the room, and everyone who was there was deeply troubled.

King Arthur at once sent messengers to two friendly kings who were nearest to him, King Pellinore and King Uriens of Gore. He ordered them to come to his aid without losing any time. Meanwhile he gathered a large army himself, meaning to go out and meet his enemies right away.
So he rode out, and on the third day he came with his army to the forest of Tintagalon. There he stopped to rest for a little while, until King Pellinore and King Uriens could join him.

But the five kings, his enemies, heard that King Arthur was in that place. They made a forced march through North Wales, meaning to strike him before the other two kings could come to help him. They reached King Arthur by night and attacked so suddenly that his army was in great danger of being driven back and scattered by the assault.
But King Arthur pulled his army together through his own courage and generous spirit, and they defended themselves fiercely until King Pellinore arrived with his army and joined the battle.

In the end King Arthur won a great victory over his enemies, for they were beaten and scattered in every direction. Because of that war, and because the five kings had to submit to him, King Arthur won back all the land that had once belonged to his father, and more besides.
In that war eight of the knights of the Round Table lost their lives. King Arthur mourned them with great sorrow, for they were the first knights of the Round Table to die in battle defending him.

While King Arthur was grieving deeply for these eight knights, Merlin came to him and said, “Do not be downcast, my lord. Look, you still have many excellent knights around you, and you will surely have no great trouble filling the eight places that death has left empty. If you follow my advice, you must choose some very worthy adviser from the companion knights of your Round Table and talk this matter over with him (for two minds are better than one). Between the two of you, you can fill the places that the war has left vacant.”

King Arthur thought this was very good advice, so he did as Merlin said. That morning he called King Pellinore into his private room and laid the matter before him, and the two of them talked it over. In that talk King Pellinore advised King Arthur like this: four old and worthy knights should be chosen to fill four of the empty seats, and four young and eager knights should be chosen to fill the other four. In that way all eight seats would be filled.

King Arthur thought this was good advice, so he said, “Let it be done that way.” First the two of them chose the four old knights. They were King Uriens of Gore, King Lac, Sir Hervise de Reuel, and Sir Galliar of Rouge. From the younger knights of the Court they chose Sir Marvaise of Leisle, Sir Lionel, the son of King Ban of Benwick, and Sir Cadar of Cornwall. That left one place still to be filled.

It was very hard to decide who should fill that place, for at that time there were two very honorable young knights at the Court. One was Sir Baudemagus, a young knight who was the brother of Sir Ewaine and the son of King Uriens of Gore and Queen Morgana le Fay (who was King Arthur’s half-sister, as you have already been told). The other young knight was Sir Tor. He had come to the Court only lately, but he had already performed several very famous adventures. Sir Tor was a son of King Pellinore (though not by his Queen), and King Pellinore loved him very much.

Then King Pellinore said to King Arthur, “My lord, there are surely only two knights in all your Court to choose from for this eighth seat at the Round Table. One is your sister’s son, Sir Baudemagus, and the other is my son, Sir Tor. I cannot advise you in this matter, so you, my lord, must choose one or the other of these young knights to fill that place. But I will say this: it would please me greatly if your favor fell upon Sir Baudemagus. Then the whole world would believe that I acted honestly in this affair. If Sir Tor were chosen, all men would say that I favored my own son.”

Then King Arthur thought about the matter for a long while, and at last he spoke. He said, “Sir, I have weighed this whole affair, and I believe Sir Tor is the better knight of the two. He has performed several very excellent adventures, while Sir Baudemagus, though a worthy knight, has not yet shown any great achievement in the field of chivalry. So, in God’s name, let Sir Tor be seated as a companion of the Round Table.”
Then King Pellinore said, “So be it,” and the two of them got up and left that place.

And behold, at that very moment the names of the eight chosen knights appeared, each on the back of the seat at the Round Table that belonged to him. In this way the decision of the two men was confirmed in the sight of all the world.

When word of all this reached Queen Morgana le Fay, she was deeply insulted that her son, Sir Baudemagus, had been passed over and that another had been chosen in his place. So she cried out against King Arthur in the hearing of several people, saying, “Ha! What is this! Do blood and kinship count for nothing with this King, that he passes over so worthy a knight as his own nephew and chooses one who is not of lawful birth instead? My husband’s house has suffered many grievous wrongs at the hands of King Arthur. He has taken away our royal power and made us little better than prisoners in his own Court. That alone is as great an insult as if we were his bitter enemies instead of his close kin. But what he has now done to my son, by passing him over, is a greater insult than that.”

Queen Morgana le Fay spoke like this not only to King Uriens, her husband, but also to Sir Ewaine and Sir Baudemagus, her sons. King Uriens of Gore scolded her for her words, for he had grown to love King Arthur dearly because of the high nobility of his nature. Sir Ewaine scolded her too. He said he would listen to nothing bad said about King Arthur, for he loved the King better than anyone else in all the world, and the King was both the mirror of all knighthood and the very fountain of honor.

So these two spoke, but Sir Baudemagus listened to what his mother, Queen Morgana, said, for he was very angry with King Arthur because the King had passed him over. So he left the Court without asking King Arthur’s permission and went wandering in search of adventure, and King Arthur was very sorry for this.

As has been said, Queen Morgana le Fay told her anger to several other people of the Court, so that word of it reached King Arthur at last and grieved him very much. One day Queen Morgana came to him and asked his permission to leave the Court. He spoke to her with great sadness, saying, “My sister, I am very sorry that you are not pleased with what I have done in this matter, for God knows that I did the best I could. I would much rather have had Sir Baudemagus as a fellow of the Round Table. But I honestly believed that, for several reasons, Sir Tor had the best right to a seat at that Table. If I had chosen against my own right judgment, what worth would the Round Table have, when I would have shown favor to a man only because he was related to me?”

Then Queen Morgana le Fay said hotly, “Sir, everything you say only adds to the insult that our house has suffered at your hands. Now you not only refuse my son that seat, but you also shame him by comparing him unfavorably with this low-born knight you have chosen. The only pleasure I can have in talking to you is to beg you to let me go away from this place.”

Then King Arthur said, speaking with great dignity, “Lady, it shall be as you wish, and you may go wherever you please. God forbid that I should hold you back from your wishes. Moreover, I will see to it that you do not leave this place without a Court to accompany you that is fitting for the wife of one king and the sister of another.”

And he did just as he said, for he sent Queen Morgana le Fay away from his Court with great honor and in high style. But the more patient King Arthur was with her, and the more favor he showed her, the angrier Queen Morgana le Fay grew with him, and the more she hated him.

She made her way to an inlet of the sea. There she sent away those whom the King had sent with her, boarded several ships with her own Court, and sailed to the enchanted island called Avalon, which was her home.

The island of Avalon was a very strange and wonderful land, unlike anything else in all the world. It was as beautiful as Paradise, covered all over with many gardens of flowers mixed with groves of lovely trees, some bearing fruit and others in full blossom. There were also many terraces of lawns and smooth slopes of grass all around the edges of the island, looking out over the sea from tall white walls of pure marble. In the middle of these gardens and orchards and groves and lawns and terraces stood a great many castles and towers, built one above another. Some were as white as snow, and others were bright with many colors.

The greatest marvel of that wonderful island was this: in the middle of all those castles and towers stood a single tower built entirely of loadstone. In that tower lay the great mystery of the place.

For the island floated on the surface of the water, and the tower of loadstone had such power that Avalon would drift from place to place according to the will of Queen Morgana le Fay. Sometimes it would be here, and sometimes there, wherever that royal lady wished it to be.

Not many people had ever seen that island. At times it was covered with a mist of enchantment, shining like silver, so that no eyes could see it unless they belonged to the fay. But sometimes it had been seen, like a vision of Paradise. Then whoever saw it would hear gay voices sounding from its lawns and groves, thin and clear because of the great distance (for no one ever came near Avalon unless Queen Morgana le Fay allowed it). He would hear music so sweet that his soul might grow faint at the sound. Then Avalon would suddenly vanish in a marvelous way, and the one who had seen it would know that he would probably never see it again.
Such was the island of Avalon. If you want to read about it in more detail, you will find much about it in a certain book written in French and called “Ogier le Danois.”

Queen Morgana le Fay loved this island very much. Many people say that King Arthur is still alive there, lying in peace and quiet while he waits for the time when he will return to the world to set right everything that is wrong in it. That is why I have told you about the island with all these details here.

chapters.title: The Story of Merlin: Chapter 1
paragraphs: _This is an account of how Merlin was enchanted by a damsel named Vivien, and of everything that followed from it._
_It also tells how King Arthur was betrayed by his own sister, and how he would surely have been killed if not for the help of Vivien, the same enchantress who caused Merlin’s ruin._
_And it tells how the sheath of Excalibur was lost at that time._
_How Queen Morgana le Fay Plotted Evil Against King Arthur and Sent a Damsel to Trick the Enchanter Merlin._

Now Morgana le Fay was a very cunning enchantress. She was so skilled in magic that her powerful spells could bend all things to her will, whether living or dead. Merlin himself had once been her teacher. He had taught her his arts when she was still a young damsel at the Court of Uther-Pendragon. So, next to Merlin, she was at that time the most powerful enchanter in all the world. Still, she did not have Merlin’s foreknowledge of things to come, or his gift of prophecy. Merlin could not pass these gifts on to anyone, and so she had never learned them from him.

Now, after Queen Morgana le Fay had come to the Island of Avalon, as was told before, she brooded for a long time over the insult that she believed King Arthur had done to her house. The more she brooded, the bigger it grew in her mind. At last it seemed to her that she could have no joy in life unless she punished King Arthur for what he had done. Indeed, she would have been glad to see him dead at her feet, so great was her anger against him.

But Queen Morgana knew very well that she could never harm the King, her brother, while Merlin was there to protect him. Merlin would surely foresee any danger that threatened the King, and he would defeat it. So she knew that if she wanted to destroy the King, she must first destroy Merlin.

Now, at the Court of Queen Morgana le Fay there was a certain damsel whose beauty was so marvelous and bewitching that hardly her equal could be found in all the world. This damsel was fifteen years old and of royal blood, for she was the daughter of the King of Northumberland. Her name was Vivien. Vivien was wise and cunning beyond measure for one so young. She was also without any heart, and she was cold and cruel to anyone who stood against her wishes. Because she was so cunning and wise, Queen Morgana liked her and taught her many of the secrets of magic and sorcery that she knew. But in spite of all that Queen Morgana did for her, the girl felt no love for her mistress, for she had no heart at all.

One day this damsel and Queen Morgana le Fay sat together in a garden on the magic island of Avalon. The garden lay on a very high terrace and looked out over the sea. The day was very fair, and the sea was so wonderfully blue that it seemed as if the blue sky had melted into water and the water into sky. As Vivien and the Queen sat in this lovely place, the Queen said to the damsel, “Vivien, what would you rather have than anything else in all the world?” Vivien answered, “Lady, I would rather have wisdom like yours than anything else.”
Then Queen Morgana laughed and said, “You can be as wise as I am, and even wiser, if you will do as I direct you. For I know a way for you to gain wisdom.”
“How can I gain that wisdom, Lady?” asked Vivien.

Then Queen Morgana le Fay said, “Listen, and I will tell you. You must know that Merlin, whom you have seen several times at the Court of King Arthur, is master of all the wisdom that anyone can possess in this world. Everything I know of magic, Merlin has taught me. But he knows many things that he did not teach me, and he kept them back from me. Merlin taught me when I was a young damsel at the Court of my mother’s husband, because he found me beautiful. Merlin loves beauty above all other things in the world, and so he taught me many things of magic and was very patient with me.
“But Merlin has a gift that belongs to him alone and that he cannot give to anyone else, for it is born in him. That gift is the power of seeing into the future and of foretelling what will happen.
“Yet although he can foresee the fate of others, he is blind to his own. He admitted this to me several times: he cannot tell what will happen in his own life when it concerns only himself.

“Now you, Vivien, are far more beautiful than I was at your age. So I believe you will easily win Merlin’s favor. And if I also give you a certain charm that I own, I may make Merlin love you so much that he will share with you far more of his wisdom than he ever taught me when I was his pupil.

“But you must know, Vivien, that in winning this knowledge from Merlin you will put yourself in great danger. In time, when the charm of your beauty has faded for him, he may easily regret that he shared his wisdom with you. Then there will be great danger that he will cast a spell on you to take away your powers. For it would be impossible for both of you to live in the same world, each knowing so much of the cunning arts of magic.”

Vivien listened to all of this very closely. When Queen Morgana had finished, the damsel said, “Dear Lady, everything you tell me is very wonderful, and I feel a burning desire to gain such knowledge of magic. If you will help me in this, so that I may draw his wisdom out of Merlin, I will owe you a debt for as long as I live. As for any danger that may come to me, I am quite willing to take it on. I have great hope that I can protect myself from Merlin so that no harm will come to me. When I have drawn out all the knowledge I can from him, I will use that same knowledge to cast such a spell on him that he will never be able to harm me or anyone else again. In this I will match my wit against his wisdom and my beauty against his cunning, and I believe I will win the game.”

Then Queen Morgana burst into laughter beyond all measure. When she had stopped laughing, she cried, “Ha, Vivien! Truly you are more cunning than anyone I ever heard of, and I believe you are as wicked as you are cunning. For who ever heard of a child of fifteen years who would speak such words as you have just spoken? Who could imagine that so young a girl could think of bringing down the wisest magician who ever lived?”

Then Queen Morgana le Fay put a small whistle of ivory and gold to her lips and blew very shrilly upon it. In answer, a young page of her Court came running. Queen Morgana commanded him to bring her a certain alabaster casket, cunningly carved, decorated with gold, and set with several precious stones. She opened the box and took out two rings of pure yellow gold, beautifully made and set. One ring held a clear white stone of extraordinary brilliance, and the other held a stone as red as blood. Then Queen Morgana said, “Vivien, look at these two rings! Each one holds a spell of wonderful power. If you wear the ring with the white stone, whoever wears the ring with the red stone will love you with such a passion that you can make him do whatever you wish. So take these rings and go to King Arthur’s Court, and use them as your cunning sees fit.”
So Vivien took the two rings and thanked Queen Morgana le Fay again and again for them.

Now King Arthur took great pleasure in holding a grand feast every Pentecost, when his Court gathered around him with much joy and laughter. At such times he loved to have good entertainment to amuse himself and his Court, and so it happened that almost always something occurred that gave the King great delight. So the Feast of Pentecost came, and King Arthur sat at the table with a great many noble and lordly people and several kings and queens. As they all sat at the feast, their spirits lifted by merriment and good cheer, a very beautiful young damsel suddenly came into the hall. With her came a dwarf, wonderfully misshapen and hideous to look at. The maiden was dressed entirely in flame-colored satin, very rich, with beautiful embroidery of gold and silver. Her hair, which was red like gold, was coiled in a net of gold. Her eyes were black as coals and extraordinarily bright and glistening. Around her throat she wore a gold necklace of three strands. With all that gold and those bright clothes, she shone with wonderful splendor as she entered the hall. The dwarf who came with her was also dressed all in flame-colored clothing. In his hands he carried a cushion of flame-colored silk with tassels of gold, and on the cushion lay a ring of exceeding beauty set with a red stone.
When King Arthur saw this beautiful maiden, he thought it was nothing other than some fine entertainment, and he was very glad of it.

But when he looked at the damsel closely, her face seemed familiar to him. So he said to her, “Damsel, who are you?” “Sir,” she said, “I am the daughter of the King of Northumberland, and my name is Vivien.” At that, King Arthur was satisfied.

Then King Arthur said to her, “Lady, what is that on the cushion there, and why have you honored us by coming here?” Vivien answered, “My lord, I have here a very good entertainment to give you pleasure at this Feast of Pentecost. This is a ring of such a kind that only the wisest and most worthy of all the men here may wear it.” And King Arthur said, “Let us see the ring.”

So Vivien took the ring from the cushion that the dwarf held and brought it to King Arthur, and the King took it into his own hand. He saw that the ring was extraordinarily beautiful, and he said, “Maiden, may I try this ring on my finger?” And Vivien said, “Yes, my lord.”
So King Arthur tried to put the ring on his finger, but, behold, the ring shrank so that it would not go past the first joint. So King Arthur said, “It seems that I am not worthy to wear this ring.”

Then the damsel Vivien said, “Have I my lord’s leave to offer this ring to others of his Court?” And King Arthur said, “Let the others try the ring.” So Vivien carried the ring to the various people of the Court, both lords and ladies, but not one of them could wear it. Last of all, Vivien came to the place where Merlin sat. She knelt on the ground before him and offered him the ring. Because this concerned himself, Merlin could not look into the future to see that harm was meant for him. Even so, he looked sourly at the damsel and said, “Child, what is this silly trick you offer me?” “Sir,” said Vivien, “I beg you to try this ring on your finger.” Then Merlin looked at the damsel more closely, and he saw that she was very beautiful, and his heart softened toward her a great deal. So he spoke more gently to her and said, “Why should I take the ring?” She answered, “Because I believe you are the wisest and most worthy of any man in this place, and so the ring should belong to you.” Then Merlin smiled, and he took the ring and put it on his finger, and, behold, it fitted the finger exactly. Then Vivien cried out, “See! The ring fits his finger, and he is the wisest and most worthy!” And Merlin was greatly pleased that the ring the beautiful damsel had given him fitted his finger in that way.

Then, after a while, he wanted to take the ring off again, but, behold, he could not. The ring had grown onto his finger as if it were a part of the flesh and bone. At this Merlin became troubled in spirit and very anxious, for he did not understand what the magic of the ring might mean. So he said, “Lady, where did this ring come from?” And Vivien said, “Sir, you know all things. Do you not know, then, that this ring was sent here from Morgana le Fay?” Then Merlin was greatly in doubt again, and he said, “I hope there is no evil in this ring.” And Vivien smiled at him and said, “What evil could there be in it?”

By this time the great magic in the ring began to work upon Merlin’s spirit. He looked at Vivien steadily, and suddenly he took great pleasure in her beauty. Then the magic of the ring took full hold of him, and, behold, a wonderful passion seized his heart at once and wrung it until it was pierced as with violent pain.

And Vivien saw what was passing in Merlin’s mind, and she laughed and turned away. Several others who were there also noticed the very strange way that Merlin looked at her, and they said among themselves, “Surely Merlin is bewitched by the beauty of that young damsel.”

So, from that time on, the enchantment of the ring of Morgana le Fay worked so upon Merlin’s spirit that he could in no way free himself from Vivien’s witchery. From that day forth, wherever she went, he could be found not far away. If she was in the garden, he was there. If she was in the Hall, he was there also. If she went hawking, he rode along on horseback. All the Court observed these things, and many made merry and joked about it. But Vivien hated Merlin with all her might, for she saw that everyone laughed at Merlin’s folly, and his attention wearied her. But she hid her dislike when she was in front of him, and she behaved toward him in every way as though she had a great friendship for him.

Now it happened one day that Vivien sat in the garden. The summer weather was wonderfully pleasant, and Merlin came into the garden and saw Vivien where she sat. But when Vivien saw Merlin coming, she suddenly felt so great a dislike for him that she could not bear to be near him at that moment. So she rose in haste, meaning to escape from him. But Merlin hurried and caught up with her, and he said to her, “Child, do you hate me, then?” And Vivien said, “Sir, I do not hate you.” But Merlin said, “In very truth, I believe that you do hate me.” And Vivien was silent.

Then, after a little while, Merlin said, “I wish I knew what I could do for you so that you would stop hating me, for I find that I have a wonderful love for you.” At this Vivien looked at Merlin very strangely, and after a while she said, “Sir, if you would only share your wisdom and your cunning with me, then I believe I could love you very much. For, behold, I am only a young child in knowledge, and you are so old and so wise that I am afraid of you. If you would teach me your wisdom so that I might be your equal, then perhaps I could come to feel for you the regard that you wish me to feel.”

Merlin looked steadily at Vivien and said, “Damsel, you are certainly not the foolish child you claim to be. I can see that your eyes are bright with a cleverness far beyond your years. Now I doubt this: if I teach you the wisdom you want to have, it will either bring about your ruin or bring about mine.”
Then Vivien cried out in a loud, piercing voice, “Merlin, if you love me, teach me your wisdom and the cleverness of your magic! Then I will love you more than anyone else in all the world!”
But Merlin sighed deeply, for his heart was full of doubt. After a while he said, “Vivien, you shall have your way. I will teach you all the things of wisdom and magic that you wish to know.”

At this, Vivien was filled with such a fierce, painful joy that she did not dare let Merlin look at her face, for fear he would read what was written there. So she lowered her eyes and turned her face away from him. Then, after a little while, she said, “Master, when will you teach me that wisdom?”

Merlin answered, “I will not teach you today, or tomorrow, or in this place. I can only teach you such knowledge in a lonely spot, where nothing will disturb your studies. But tomorrow you must tell King Arthur that you need to return to your father’s kingdom. Then we will set out together with your attendants. When we have come to some hidden place, I will build a dwelling there by my magic, and we will stay in it until I have taught you wisdom.”
Then Vivien was overjoyed. She caught Merlin’s hand in hers and kissed it with great passion.

So the next day Vivien begged King Arthur to give her leave to return to her father’s Court. On the third day she and Merlin and a number of attendants who served the damsel left the Court of King Arthur. They rode out as though they were going to the Kingdom of Northumberland.

But when they had gone a little way from the King’s Court, they turned eastward and took the road toward a certain valley that Merlin knew. It was so fair and pleasant a place that it was sometimes called the Valley of Delight and sometimes the Valley of Joyousness.

chapters.title: The Story of Merlin: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How Merlin traveled with Vivien to the Valley of Joyousness, and how he built a castle for her there. Also, how he taught her the wisdom of magic, and how she used it to bring about his downfall._

So Merlin and Vivien and those with them traveled east for three days. Toward the end of the third day, they reached the edge of a very dark and gloomy forest. Before them stood trees so thickly woven together that no one could see any of the sky through the leaves. The branches and roots looked like serpents all twisted together. So Vivien said, “Sir, this is a very gloomy woodland.” “Yes,” said Merlin, “it does seem so. Nevertheless, inside this forest lies a place that some call the Valley of Joyousness and others call the Valley of Delight, because of its great beauty. Several paths run through this forest, and by them a man can reach that valley, whether on horseback or on foot.”

After a while they found that it was just as Merlin said. By and by they came upon one of those paths, entered it, and went deep into the forest. And look! Inside that gloomy woodland it was so dark that it seemed night had fallen, although it was bright daylight outside its borders. Because of this, many in the party were very frightened. But Merlin always gave them good cheer, and so they went forward on their way. At last they came out of that place and into the open again. They were greatly relieved and took much comfort.

By this time evening had come, very peaceful and calm, and wonderfully beautiful. In the center of the valley was a small lake, so smooth and clear, like crystal, that it looked like an oval shield of pure silver laid upon the ground. All around the edge of the lake were level meadows covered with a huge number of flowers of many colors and kinds, very beautiful to see.

When Vivien saw this place, she cried to Merlin, “Master, this is truly a joyous valley. I do not believe the blessed meadows of Paradise are more beautiful than this.” And Merlin said, “Very well; let us go down into it.” So they went down, and as they descended, night fell quickly and the round moon rose into the sky. It was hard to tell whether the valley was more beautiful in the daytime or when the moon shone down upon it like this.
So they all came at last to the edge of the lake, and they saw that there was neither house nor castle in that place.

Then the followers of Merlin murmured among themselves, saying, “This enchanter has brought us here, but how will he now provide us with a resting place to shelter us from the harsh changes of the weather? The beauty of this spot cannot shelter us from rain and storm by itself.” Merlin overheard their murmuring, and he said, “Peace! Do not trouble yourselves about that, for I will very soon provide you with a good resting place.” Then he said to them, “Stand a little distance aside until I show you what I will do.” So they withdrew a little, as he commanded, and he and Vivien stayed where they were. And Vivien said, “Master, what will you do?” And Merlin said, “Wait a little and you will see.”

With that, he began a very powerful conjuring, and the earth began to tremble and shake. Something like a great red dust rose into the air. In this dust, various shapes and forms began to appear, and they rose very high into the air. Soon those who watched saw that a great building was taking form in the middle of the cloud of red dust.

After a while, everything grew quiet and the dust slowly faded from the air. And behold! There stood a marvelous castle such as no one there had ever seen before, even in a dream. Its walls were of deep blue and bright red, decorated and adorned with figures of gold. In the moonlight that castle looked like a pure vision of great glory.

Vivien saw all that Merlin had done. She went to him, knelt on the ground before him, took his hand, and pressed it to her lips. While she knelt there, she said, “Master, this is surely the most wonderful thing in the world. Will you teach me such magic, so that I can build a castle like this one out of the elements?” And Merlin said, “Yes; I will teach you all this and more. I will teach you not only how to create such a building out of unseen things, but also how, with a single touch of your wand, to scatter that castle into the air in an instant. A child can do the same to a beautiful shining bubble with the stroke of a straw: one moment it is there, and the next moment it is gone. And I will teach you more than that. I will teach you how to change one thing into the likeness of a different thing, and I will teach you spells and charms such as you have never heard of before.”

Then Vivien cried out, “Master, you are the most wonderful man in all the world!” Merlin looked at Vivien. Her face was very beautiful in the moonlight, and he loved her very much. So he smiled at her and said, “Vivien, do you still hate me?” And she said, “No, master.”

But she did not tell the truth. In her heart she was evil, and Merlin’s heart was good, and what is evil will always hate what is good. Although Vivien hungered for the knowledge of dark magic, and although she spoke so lovingly with her lips, in her spirit she both feared and hated Merlin because of his wisdom. She knew very well that, if not for the enchantment of the ring he wore, Merlin would not love her any longer in that way. So she said in her heart, “If Merlin teaches me all his wisdom, then the world cannot hold both him and me.”

Merlin stayed with Vivien in that place for a year and a little more, and in that time he taught her all the magic he was able to give. At the end of that time he said to her, “Vivien, I have now taught you so much that I believe no one in all the world knows more than you do about the magic you have studied this past year. You have such power of sorcery that you can make the unseen elements take shape at your will. You can change one thing into the appearance of an altogether different thing. And you hold such strong magic that you can tangle any living soul in its web, unless that person has some very good charm to protect himself from your tricks. I myself have not much more power than what I have given to you.”
Merlin finished speaking, and joy swelled in Vivien. In her heart she thought, “Now, Merlin, if luck lets me trap you in my spells, you will never look upon the world again.”

When the next day came, Vivien had a very grand feast prepared for herself and Merlin. Using the knowledge Merlin had given her, she made a very powerful sleeping potion that had no taste at all. She mixed this potion into a fine wine herself, and she poured the wine into a golden cup of extraordinary beauty.

When the feast was over, while she and Merlin sat together, Vivien said, “Master, I wish to do you a great honor.” And Merlin said, “What is it?” “You will see,” said Vivien. With that she clapped her hands together, and at once a young page came to where they were. He carried that cup of wine in his hand and gave it to Vivien. Then Vivien took the cup, went to where Merlin sat, and knelt down before him. She said, “Sir, I beg you to take this cup and drink the wine in it. That wine is both very noble and very precious, and so is your wisdom. The wine is held in a cup of priceless cost, and your wisdom is held in a life that has been beyond all value to the world.” With that she touched her lips to the cup and kissed the wine in it.
Merlin suspected no evil. He took the cup and drank the wine cheerfully.

After a little while, the fumes of that strong drink began to rise into Merlin’s brain, and it was as though a cloud came down over his sight. When this came upon him, he soon knew he had been betrayed. He cried out three times in a bitter voice, full of pain, “Woe! Woe! Woe!” Then he cried out, “I am betrayed!” With that he tried to rise from where he sat, but he could not.

All this while Vivien sat with her chin upon her hands and watched him steadily, smiling strangely at him. Soon Merlin stopped struggling and sank into a sleep so deep that it was almost as though he were dead. When that had happened, Vivien rose and leaned over him and put a very powerful spell upon him. She stretched out her forefinger and wove an enchantment all around him, so that he seemed completely wrapped in a silver web of magic. When she was done, Merlin could move neither hand nor foot, not even a fingertip. He was like some great insect that a cunning and beautiful spider had tangled in a network of fine, strong web.

When the next morning came, Merlin woke from his sleep and saw that Vivien sat across from him, watching him very closely. They were in the same room where he had fallen asleep. When Vivien saw that Merlin was awake, she laughed and said, “Merlin, how are you?” And Merlin groaned with great passion, saying, “Vivien, you have betrayed me.”

At this Vivien laughed again, very shrilly and piercingly, and she said, “Behold! Merlin, you are completely in my power. You are wholly wound in the very enchantments you yourself taught me. See! You cannot move a single hair without my will. When I leave you, the world will see you no more. All your wisdom will be my wisdom, and all your power will be my power, and no one else in the whole world will have the wisdom that I have.”

Then Merlin groaned so fiercely that it seemed his heart would burst. And he said, “Vivien, you have brought me to such shame that even if I were freed from this spell, I could not bear for any man to see my face again. I do not grieve so much for my own ruin as for the folly that turned my own wisdom against me and destroyed me. So I forgive you everything you have done to betray me. Yet there is one thing alone that I ask of you.”
And Vivien said, “Does it concern you?” And Merlin said, “No, it concerns another.” Then Vivien said, “What is it?”

Then Merlin said, “It is this: I have received my gift of foresight again, and I see that King Arthur is in great danger of his life right now. So I beg you, Vivien, to go at once to where he is in danger and to use your powers of sorcery to save him. By doing this one good deed, you may perhaps lessen the sin of having betrayed me.”

At that time Vivien was not altogether as bad as she afterward became, for she still felt some small pity for Merlin and some small respect for King Arthur. So she laughed and said, “Very well, I will do as you ask in this matter. Where shall I go to save that King?”

Then Merlin replied, “Go into the West country, to the castle of a certain knight named Sir Domas de Noir. When you come there, you will see at once how you can help the good King.” Vivien said, “I will do this for you, for it is the last favor anyone can ever do for you in this world.”

With that Vivien clapped her hands together and called many of her attendants. When they had come in, she showed Merlin to them, and she said, “Behold how I have bewitched him. Go! See for yourselves! Feel his hands and his face and see if there is any life in him.” They went to Merlin and felt his hands and arms and his face, and they even plucked at his beard. Merlin could not move in any way but only groan in great sorrow. So they all laughed and made merry at his sad state.

Then Vivien used her magic to make a great stone chest appear in that place. She commanded those who were there to lift Merlin up and lay him in it, and they did as she commanded. Then, by her magic, she caused a huge slab of stone to be set upon that chest, so heavy that ten men could hardly lift it. Merlin lay beneath that stone like one who was dead.

Then Vivien caused the magic castle to vanish at once, and it happened just as she willed. Then she caused a mist to rise at that place, and it was of such a kind that no one could enter it or break it apart, nor could any human eye see what was within. When she had done all this, she left that valley with all her court, making great joy that she had triumphed over Merlin.
Nevertheless she did not forget her promise, but went to the castle of Sir Domas de Noir. After a while it will all be told how things turned out at that place.

Such was the passing of Merlin. May God grant that you never misuse the wisdom He gives you, so that it is turned against you and destroys you. For there can be no greater bitterness in the world than this: that a man should be betrayed by someone to whom he himself has given the power to betray him.
And now let us turn to King Arthur, to learn how things went with him after Merlin had been betrayed to his ruin.

chapters.title: The Story of Merlin: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How Queen Morgana le Fay Came Back to Camelot Meaning to Harm King Arthur. Also How King Arthur and Others Went Hunting, and What Happened Because of It._

After Merlin left the Court with Vivien in the way already told, Queen Morgana le Fay came back to Camelot. She went to King Arthur and knelt before him with her head bowed, looking very humble. She said, “Brother, I have thought a great deal about all that has happened. I see that I did wrong to speak against you as I did, and to rebel against your rule. So I ask you to forgive me for my wicked words and thoughts against you.”

King Arthur was deeply moved. He went to Queen Morgana, took her by the hand, lifted her to her feet, and kissed her forehead and her eyes. He said, “My sister, I hold no anger against you, only love for you in my heart.” So Queen Morgana le Fay stayed at the Court as she had before, for King Arthur believed that they were friends again.

One day Queen Morgana and the King were chatting in a friendly way about Excalibur. Queen Morgana said she very much wanted to see that noble weapon up close, and King Arthur promised to show it to her one day. The next day he said, “Sister, come with me, and I will show you Excalibur.” He took Queen Morgana by the hand and led her into another room, where there was a strong wooden chest bound with iron bands. The King opened the chest, and Queen Morgana le Fay saw Excalibur lying inside in its sheath. King Arthur said to her, “Lady, take this sword and look at it as you like.” Queen Morgana took Excalibur in her hands and lifted it out of the chest. She drew the sword from its sheath, and behold! The blade flashed like lightning. Then she said, “Sir, this is a very beautiful sword. I wish I could take it away and keep it for a little while, so that I could enjoy it fully.”

King Arthur wanted to show the Queen great kindness now that they had made peace. So he said to her, “Take it, and keep it for as long as you like.” Queen Morgana took Excalibur and its sheath and carried them away to her lodgings, where she hid the sword in the bed she slept in.

Then Queen Morgana sent for several goldsmiths, eight of them, and for some armorers, eight of them, and for some skillful jewelers, eight of them. She said to them, “Make me a sword exactly like the one I have here.” And she showed them Excalibur in its sheath. The goldsmiths, armorers, and jewelers worked very hard, and in two weeks they had made a sword so like Excalibur that no eye could tell one from the other. Queen Morgana le Fay kept both swords with her until her plans were ready to be carried out.
One day King Arthur announced a hunt, and he and all his Court were to take part in it.

The day before the hunt, Queen Morgana le Fay came to King Arthur and said, “Brother, I have a very beautiful and noble horse for you, which I mean to give you as a gift of love.” She called out, and two grooms came leading a horse as black as jet, covered with trappings and harness of silver. The horse was so extraordinarily beautiful that neither King Arthur nor anyone with him had ever seen one like it. The King was filled with wonder and delight at the sight of the horse, and he said, “Sister, this is the finest gift I have been given in a long time.” “Ha! Brother,” said Queen Morgana, “so you like the horse?” “Yes,” said King Arthur, “I like it better than any horse I have ever seen.” “Then,” said Queen Morgana, “think of it as a gift of peace between you and me. And as a sign of that peace, I ask you to ride this horse on the hunt tomorrow.” And King Arthur said, “I will.”
So the next day he rode out to the hunt on that horse, just as he had promised.

Some time after noon, the hounds startled a huge hart, and the King and all his Court chased it eagerly. But King Arthur’s horse soon left all the others behind, except the horse of one honorable and worthy knight of the Court named Sir Accalon of Gaul. Sir Accalon and the King rode fast through the forest, so caught up in the chase that they did not know where they were going. At last they caught up with the hart and found it hiding in a very thick, tangled part of the forest. There King Arthur killed the stag, and the chase was over.

After this, the King and Sir Accalon tried to go back the way they had come. But soon they saw that they were lost in the twisting paths of the woods, and they did not know where they were. They had chased the hart so far that they were in a completely strange country. They wandered this way and that for a long time until evening, and by then they were weighed down by hunger and tiredness. Then King Arthur said to Sir Accalon, “Sir, it seems to me that we will have nowhere to rest tonight except under a tree in this forest.”

Sir Accalon answered, “My lord, if you will follow my advice, we will let our horses find their own way through this wilderness. Perhaps, by the instinct that such animals have, they will bring us to some place where people live.”

King Arthur thought this was very good advice, so he did as Sir Accalon said. He dropped his reins and let his horse go wherever it wished. King Arthur’s horse took a certain path, and Sir Accalon followed behind the King. They went a long way like this, while night was falling over the forest.

But before it was fully dark, they came out of the forest into an open place. Before them lay a very wide estuary, like an arm of the sea. In front of them was a smooth, white beach of sand. The two of them went down to the beach and stood on the shore. They did not know what to do, for there was no house or village in sight in any direction.

While they stood there, unsure, they suddenly saw a ship far away. As it came closer, they saw that it looked very strange and wonderful. It was painted in many different colors, bright and brilliant, and its sails were all made of silk cloth woven in many colors and embroidered with figures like those in a tapestry. King Arthur was greatly amazed at the sight of that ship.
As they stood watching the ship, they saw it come nearer and nearer to where they were. After a little while it ran up onto the sandy shore, not far from them.
Then King Arthur said to Sir Accalon, “Sir, let us go down to the water’s edge and look into this ship. I have never seen anything like it in all my life, so I think it may be a ship of the fairies.”

So the two of them went to the ship and stood on the shore and looked down into it. At first they thought no one was aboard, for it seemed to be completely empty. But as they stood there, wondering at the marvel of the ship and at how it had come to them, they suddenly saw the curtains hanging before a room at the far end of the ship pulled apart. Twelve very beautiful damsels came out. Each wore a rich gown of bright, shining scarlet satin, each had a circlet of gold around her head, and each had many gold bracelets on her arms. The damsels came forward to where the two knights stood and said, “Welcome, King Arthur!” And they said, “Welcome, Sir Accalon!”

King Arthur was very surprised that they knew him, and he said, “Fair ladies, how is this? You seem to know me well, but I do not know you. Who are you, that you know me and my companion and call us by name?”

The chief of the damsels answered, “Sir, we are partly of the fairy kind, and we know all about you. We know that you have been following a very long chase. We know that you are tired, hungry, and thirsty. So we beg you to come aboard this ship and rest, and to refresh yourselves with food and drink.”

King Arthur thought this was a fine adventure, so he said to Sir Accalon, “Sir, I have a great wish to go aboard this ship and follow this adventure.” And Sir Accalon said, “My lord, if you go, I will go too.”

So the ladies lowered a gangplank from the ship, and King Arthur and Sir Accalon led their horses up the gangplank and aboard. Then the ship sailed away, just as it had come, very swiftly. It was now early night, and the moon hung round and full in the sky like a disk of pure shining silver.

Then the twelve damsels helped King Arthur and Sir Accalon down from their horses. Some of them took the horses away, and others led the two knights into a fine room at the end of the ship. In this room King Arthur saw a table set as if for their entertainment. It was spread with a linen cloth and laid with many tasty meats, with small loaves of white bread, and with several different kinds of excellent wine. At the sight of it, King Arthur and Sir Accalon were delighted, for they were very hungry.

They sat down at the table at once and ate and drank heartily. While they did so, some of the damsels served them food, others talked with them pleasantly, and others played lutes and citterns to entertain them. So they feasted and made merry.

But after a while, a great sleepiness began to come over King Arthur, though he thought it came only from the tiredness of the chase. So before long he said, “Fair damsels, you have refreshed us very much, and this has been a pleasant adventure. But now I wish you had a place for us to sleep.”
The chief of the damsels answered, “My lord, this boat has been made ready for your comfort, so everything has been prepared for you in full.”

Then some of the twelve damsels led King Arthur to a bedchamber that had been prepared for him, and others led Sir Accalon to another chamber prepared for him. King Arthur marveled at the beauty of his chamber, for he thought he had never seen a more splendidly furnished bedroom. He lay down in great comfort, and at once he fell into a deep, gentle sleep, without any dream or disturbance.

When King Arthur woke from that sleep, he was astonished beyond all measure, and he did not know whether he was still asleep and dreaming or awake. For behold! He lay on a straw bed in a very dark, gloomy room made entirely of stone. He saw that this room was a dungeon, and all around him he heard the sound of many voices crying out in misery. Then King Arthur said to himself, “Where is the ship I was on last night, and what has become of the ladies I spoke with?”

He looked around him, and behold! He saw that he was indeed in a dungeon, and that many knights were all around him in a sad state. So he understood that they were prisoners too, and that it was they who had made the sound of sorrowful crying that he had heard when he woke.

King Arthur got up from where he lay, and he saw that all the knights who were prisoners there were strangers to him. He did not know them, and they did not know him. There were twenty-two knights imprisoned in that place.

Then King Arthur said, “Sirs, who are you, and where am I now?” The chief of the knights who were prisoners answered, “Sir, we are prisoners like yourself in a dungeon of this castle, and the castle belongs to a knight named Sir Domas, who is also called le Noir.”

King Arthur marveled at what had happened to him, and he said, “Sirs, a very strange thing has happened to me. Last night I was asleep in a wonderful ship that I believe belonged to the fairies, and I had a knight with me as my companion. And behold! This morning I wake alone in this dungeon, and I do not know how I came here.”

“Sir,” said the knight who spoke for the others, “last night two men dressed in black brought you here and laid you on that straw bed while you slept. So it is plain to me that you are in the same trouble that we are in, and that you are a prisoner of this Sir Domas le Noir.”
Then King Arthur said, “Tell me, who is this Sir Domas? I declare that I have never heard of him before.” “I will tell you,” said the captive knight, and he told the story as follows:

“I believe,” said he, “that this Sir Domas is the falsest knight alive, for he is full of treachery and lies, and in his heart he is altogether a coward. Yet he is a man of very great wealth and very powerful in these parts.

“Now there are two brothers. Sir Domas is one, and the other is named Sir Ontzlake. Sir Domas is the elder, and Sir Ontzlake is the younger. When the father of these two knights died, he left each of them an equal share of his lands. But now Sir Domas has nearly all of those lands, and Sir Ontzlake has only one castle, which he holds by force of arms and by his own courage. Sir Domas is a complete coward in his heart, but he has more cunning and trickery than any man I have ever heard of. That is how it came about that Sir Domas has everything from his father’s estate, and Sir Ontzlake has nothing except that one castle and the land that goes with it.

“It seems very strange that Sir Domas is not satisfied with all this, yet he is not. He wants that one castle and that small estate that belong to his brother, and he can hardly enjoy life because of his greed. Yet he does not know how to get that estate from his brother. Sir Ontzlake is a very excellent knight, and the only way Sir Domas can lay hands on the estate is to face his brother man to man in a fight with weapons. This he is afraid to try.

“So for a long time Sir Domas has been looking for a knight who will take up his cause and fight against Sir Ontzlake for him. Every knight he can seize he brings to this castle and gives them a choice: either take up his cause against his brother, or stay here as his prisoner with no ransom. So he has seized all of us, and he has demanded of each of us that we fight for him. But not one of us will take up the cause of such a wicked knight as Sir Domas, so we all remain his prisoners.”

“Well,” said King Arthur, “this is a very strange case. But I think that if Sir Domas makes his appeal to me, I will take up his cause. I would rather do that than stay here a prisoner for the rest of my life. And if I take on this battle and win it, then I will deal with Sir Domas himself afterward, in a way I do not think he will like very much.”

A little while after this, the porter opened the door of the prison, and a very fair young damsel came in. She walked up to King Arthur and said, “How are you?” “I cannot say,” said King Arthur, “but it seems to me I am in a very bad spot in this place.” “Sir,” said the damsel, “I am sorry to see so noble a knight in such a sad state. But if you will agree to defend the cause of the lord of this castle against his enemy, then you will have leave to go wherever you please.” King Arthur answered, “Lady, this is a hard choice. Either I must fight a battle I do not care for, or I must stay here as a prisoner, with no ransom, for all my days. But I would rather fight than live here all my life, so I will take on that adventure as you ask. But if I fight for the lord of this castle, and if Heaven grants me the grace to win that battle, then all these companions of mine in prison must go free with me.”
The damsel said to this, “Very well, let it be so, for that will satisfy the master of this castle.”

Then King Arthur looked more closely at the maiden and said, “Damsel, it seems to me I should know your face, for I think I have seen you somewhere before this.” “No, sir,” she said, “that can hardly be, for I am the daughter of the lord of this castle.”

But in this she was lying. She was one of the damsels of Morgana le Fay, and one of those who had tricked King Arthur into the ship the night before. It was she who had brought him to that castle and handed him over to Sir Domas. She had done all these things on the orders of Queen Morgana le Fay.

Then King Arthur said, “But if I fight this battle, you must carry a message for me to the Court of King Arthur. That message must be delivered into the hands of Queen Morgana le Fay herself. Then, when that is done, I will fight this battle for the cause of Sir Domas.” And the damsel said, “It shall be done.”

So King Arthur wrote a sealed letter to Queen Morgana le Fay, asking her to send him his sword Excalibur, and he sent that message to her. When Queen Morgana received the letter, she laughed and said, “Very well, he shall have a sword that pleases his eye as well as Excalibur does.” And with that she sent him the other sword, which she had had made exactly like Excalibur.
So Sir Domas sent word to his brother, Sir Ontzlake, that he now had a champion to fight on his behalf. The battle was to win back the part of their inheritance that Sir Ontzlake still kept from him.

Now when Sir Ontzlake received this message, he was thrown into great distress. A little while before, he had been badly wounded in a tournament, where a spear had been thrust through both his thighs. He was now in bed with that wound and had no strength to get up from it. So he did not know what to do, for he could not fight on his own behalf, and he had no one to fight for him.

chapters.title: The Story of Merlin: Chapter 4
paragraphs: _What Happened to Sir Accalon, and How King Arthur Fought a Duel with Swords and Nearly Lost His Life._
Here is the account of what happened to Sir Accalon the morning after he went aboard the magic ship with King Arthur, as told before.

When Sir Accalon woke from that sleep, he felt just as King Arthur had felt. At first he did not know whether he was still asleep and dreaming or really awake. He found himself lying beside a marble basin of clear water, which gushed high into the air from a silver pipe. Not far from this fountain stood a large tent of many-colored silk, at the edge of a lovely green meadow.

Sir Accalon was astonished to find himself in this place when he had fallen asleep on board that ship. He feared that it was all the work of some very evil spell. So he crossed himself and said, “God save King Arthur from any harm. It seems to me that those damsels on the ship have worked some magic on us to separate us from each other.” With that, he got up from where he lay, meaning to find out more about the matter.

He made some noise as he stirred, and a very ugly dwarf came out of the tent. The dwarf greeted him politely and with great respect. Then Sir Accalon said to the dwarf, “Fellow, who are you?” The dwarf answered, “My lord, I belong to the lady of that tent over there. She has sent me to welcome you to this place and to invite you in to share a meal with her.” “Ha!” said Sir Accalon, “and how did I get here?” “Sir,” said the dwarf, “I do not know. But when we looked out this morning, we saw you lying here beside the fountain.”

Sir Accalon wondered greatly at what had happened to him. After a while he said, “Who is your lady?” The dwarf replied, “She is called the Lady Gomyne of the Fair Hair, and she will be very glad of your company in her tent.”

At this Sir Accalon got up. He washed himself at the fountain to refresh himself, and then he went with the dwarf to the lady’s tent. When he arrived, he saw that in the middle of the tent stood a silver table, spread with a fine white cloth and covered with excellent food for a man to break his fast.

As soon as Sir Accalon entered the tent, the curtains on the far side were parted. A very beautiful lady came in from another chamber and welcomed him to that place. Sir Accalon said to her, “Lady, I think you are very kind to invite me into your tent like this.” “No, sir,” said the lady, “it took no great effort to be kind to a knight as worthy as you.” Then she said to Sir Accalon, “Sir, will you sit here at the table with me and eat?”
At this Sir Accalon was very glad, for he was hungry, and the lady’s beauty pleased him greatly. It gave him great joy to be in her company.
So the two of them sat at the table in a cheerful and pleasant mood, and the dwarf waited on them.

After Sir Accalon and the Lady of the Pavilion had finished eating, she spoke to him like this: “Sir knight, you seem to be a very strong and worthy lord, and one well used to feats of arms and to bravery in battle.”

Sir Accalon replied, “Lady, it is not proper for me to speak of my own worth, but I may freely say this much. I have fought in several battles, as much as a knight with belt and spurs may do. I believe that both my friends and my enemies have had reason to say that I have always done my duty as well as I could.”
Then the damsel said, “I believe you are a very brave and worthy knight. Being such a man, you might be of help to a good knight who is in sad need of the kind of help one knight can give another.”

Sir Accalon said, “What is that help?” And the damsel replied, “I will tell you. Not far from here lives a knight named Sir Ontzlake, who has an older brother named Sir Domas. Sir Domas has treated Sir Ontzlake very badly in many ways. He has taken almost all of his inheritance, so that only a little is left to Sir Ontzlake of all the great possessions that once belonged to their father. But even that small holding is more than Sir Domas can stand to see him keep, so Sir Ontzlake must hold what he has by whatever force of arms he can manage himself. Now Sir Domas has found himself a champion, a man of great strength and skill in battle. Through this champion, Sir Domas challenges Sir Ontzlake’s right to hold even that small part of the lands that once were their father’s. So if Sir Ontzlake wants to keep what is his, he must fight for it right away.

“This is a very sad situation for Sir Ontzlake. A short time ago he was wounded by a spear at a tournament, and it pierced both of his thighs. So now he cannot sit on his horse and defend his rights against attack. It seems to me that a knight could have no better reason to show his courage than to defend so unlucky a man.”

So the lady spoke, and Sir Accalon listened closely to all she said. When she had finished, he said, “Lady, I would be very willing to defend Sir Ontzlake’s right, but I have no armor, and I have no weapons to fight with.”

Then the damsel smiled kindly at Sir Accalon and said to him, “Sir, Sir Ontzlake can easily provide you with armor that will suit you perfectly. And as for weapons, I have in this tent a sword that has only one equal in all the world.”

With this she got up and went back into the curtained room she had come from. Soon she returned, carrying something wrapped in a scarlet cloth. She opened the cloth before Sir Accalon’s eyes, and there was King Arthur’s sword Excalibur in its sheath! Then the damsel said, “This sword will be yours if you take up this quarrel on behalf of Sir Ontzlake.”

When Sir Accalon saw that sword, he did not know what to think. He said to himself, “Surely this is either Excalibur or its twin brother.” He drew the blade out of its sheath, and it shone with extraordinary brightness. Then Sir Accalon said, “I do not know what to think, I am so amazed. This sword is the very image of another sword I know.” When he spoke, the damsel smiled at him again and said, “I have heard that there is another sword in the world like this one.”

Then Sir Accalon said, “Lady, to win this sword for myself I would be willing to fight in any battle at all.” And the damsel replied, “Then if you will fight this battle for Sir Ontzlake, you are free to keep that sword as your own.” At this Sir Accalon was filled with joy beyond measure.

So it happened, through the tricks of Queen Morgana le Fay, that King Arthur was made to fight a battle without knowing it against a knight he dearly loved. And that knight held Excalibur to use against his own lord. All these things had come about through the cunning of Morgana le Fay.

A fine field was prepared for the battle, in a place convenient for both Sir Domas and Sir Ontzlake. They came there on the appointed day, each with his champion and his attendants. Sir Ontzlake was carried there on a litter because of the bad wound in his thighs. Many other people came to watch the fight too, for news of it had spread to a great distance around that place. When everything was ready, the two knights who were to fight were brought within the barriers of the field, each fully armed and each riding a very good horse.

King Arthur was dressed in the armor of Sir Domas, and Sir Accalon was dressed in the armor that belonged to Sir Ontzlake. Each man’s head was covered by his helmet, so neither of them knew the other.

Then the herald came forward and announced that the battle was about to begin, and each knight got ready at once for the charge. When the signal was given, the two knights rushed out from their places with such speed and fury that it was wonderful to see. They met in the middle of the field with a roar like thunder, and each knight’s spear burst into small pieces, until only the stump was left in his hand. Then each knight skillfully leapt from his horse and let it run free in the field. Each threw aside the stump of his spear and drew his sword, and they came at each other with the greatest fury of battle.

It was at this time that Vivien came to that place at Merlin’s command. She brought with her such a train of beautiful ladies, and such splendor, that a great many people looked at her with delight. Vivien and her train took their places at the barriers, where they could see everything that was happening. Vivien looked at the two knights, and she could not tell which was King Arthur and which was his enemy. So she said, “Well, I will do as Merlin asked me to do, but I must watch this battle for a while before I can tell which one is King Arthur. It would be a shame to cast my spells on the wrong knight.”

So the two knights fought each other on foot. First they thrust at each other, and then they both struck at the same time. And behold, the sword of King Arthur did not cut into Sir Accalon’s armor, but the sword of Sir Accalon cut very deep into King Arthur’s armor. It wounded him so badly that the blood ran down inside his armor in great streams. After that they struck many times, and very hard, and it went the same way as at first. Sir Accalon’s sword always cut into King Arthur’s armor, and King Arthur’s sword did not cut his enemy’s armor at all. So in a little while King Arthur’s armor was stained red all over with the blood that flowed from many wounds, while Sir Accalon did not bleed at all, because of the sheath of Excalibur that he wore at his side. King Arthur’s blood flowed down upon the ground until all the grass around him was soaked with it. When King Arthur saw the ground wet with his own blood, and saw that his enemy did not bleed at all, he began to fear that he would die in that battle. So he said to himself, “How is this? Has the power left Excalibur and its sheath? If not, I would think that the sword that cuts me so badly is Excalibur, and that this sword of mine is not.”
Then a great fear of death came over him. He ran at Sir Accalon and struck him such a hard blow on the helmet that Sir Accalon nearly fell to the ground.
With that stroke, King Arthur’s blade snapped off close to the handle and dropped into the bloody grass. Only the hilt, with its pommel and cross-guard, was left in his hand.

At that blow Sir Accalon grew furious, and he ran at King Arthur, meaning to give him some grievous stroke. But when he saw that King Arthur had no weapon, he stopped his attack and said, “Sir Knight, I see that you have no weapon and that you have lost a great deal of blood. So I demand that you yield to me as a beaten man.”

Then King Arthur again feared greatly that his death was near. Yet because he was a king, it was not possible for him to yield to any knight. So he said, “No, Sir Knight, I cannot yield to you, for I would rather die with honor than yield without honor. Though I have no weapon, there are special reasons why I cannot lack honor. So you may kill me while I am unarmed, and that will be your shame and not mine.”

“Well,” said Sir Accalon, “as for the shame, I will not spare you unless you yield to me.” And King Arthur said, “I will not yield.” Then Sir Accalon said, “Then stand away from me so that I may strike you.” When King Arthur had done as Sir Accalon told him, Sir Accalon struck him such a terrible blow that the King fell to his knees. Then Sir Accalon raised Excalibur to strike King Arthur again, and all the people who were there cried out to him to spare so honorable a knight. But Sir Accalon would not spare him.

Then Vivien said to herself, “Surely that must be King Arthur, who is so near to his death. I swear it would be a great shame for him to die after he has fought so fiercely.” So when Sir Accalon raised his sword that second time to strike his enemy, Vivien clapped her hands together with great force and sent out a spell so powerful that it seemed to Sir Accalon at that moment as if he had been struck a hard blow on the arm. For with that spell his arm went numb from his fingertips to the hollow of his armpit, and Excalibur fell out of Sir Accalon’s hands into the grass.

Then King Arthur saw the sword and knew that it was Excalibur, and so he knew that he had been betrayed. He cried out three times in a very loud voice, “Treason! Treason! Treason!” Then he set his knee upon the blade, and before Sir Accalon could stop him, he had seized it in his hands.

Then it seemed to King Arthur that a great power had come into him because of that sword. He rose from his knees and ran at Sir Accalon and struck him so hard that the blade went through his armor to the depth of half a palm’s breadth. He struck him again and again, and Sir Accalon cried out loudly and fell down on his hands and knees. Then King Arthur ran to him, seized the sheath of Excalibur, pulled it away from Sir Accalon, and flung it far from him. At once the wounds of Sir Accalon burst out bleeding heavily. Then King Arthur seized Sir Accalon’s helmet and tore it off his head, meaning to kill him.

Because King Arthur was blinded by his own blood, he did not recognize Sir Accalon. He said, “Sir Knight, who are you, who have betrayed me?” And Sir Accalon said, “I have not betrayed you. I am Sir Accalon of Gaul, and I am a knight in good standing at King Arthur’s Court.”

But when King Arthur heard this, he cried out loudly and said, “How is this? Do you know who I am?” And Sir Accalon said, “No, I do not know you.” Then King Arthur said, “I am King Arthur, your master.” And with this he took off his helmet, and Sir Accalon knew him.
When Sir Accalon saw King Arthur, he fainted and lay on the ground like a dead man. King Arthur said, “Take him away.”

When the people who were there understood who King Arthur was, they burst over the barriers and ran toward him, crying out in pity. King Arthur would have left that place, but then he too fainted because of the great loss of blood. All those around him were filled with sorrow, thinking that he was dying, and they wept and mourned without holding back.

Then Vivien came out into the field and said, “Let me take him. I believe I can cure his wounds.” She ordered two litters to be brought. She laid King Arthur in one and Sir Accalon in the other, and she carried them both away to a priory of nuns that stood not far from that place.
