When Vivien reached the priory, she examined King Arthur’s wounds and bathed them with a very precious balsam, and they began to heal at once. She would have nothing to do with Sir Accalon’s wounds. Instead she let one of her attendants wash him and bandage his injuries.

By the next morning King Arthur had recovered enough to get up, though he was still very weak and sick almost to death. He rose from his bed and would let no one stop him. He wrapped a cloak around himself and went to the place where Sir Accalon lay. There he questioned Sir Accalon closely, and Sir Accalon told him everything that had happened to him after he left that ship, and how the strange damsel had given him a sword to fight with. When King Arthur had heard all that Sir Accalon had to say, he told him, “Messire, I do not think you are to blame in this matter. But I greatly fear that there is treachery here, meant to bring about my ruin.”

Then he left that place, found Vivien, and said to her, “Damsel, I beg you to dress that knight’s wounds with the same balsam you used on mine.” “Lord,” said Vivien, “I cannot, for I have no more of that balsam.” But what she said was false. She did have more of the balsam, but she did not choose to use it on Sir Accalon.
So that afternoon Sir Accalon died of the wounds he had received in his battle with King Arthur.

That same day King Arthur called Sir Domas and Sir Ontzlake into his presence. They came and stood before him, so full of fear at his majesty that they could not stand, and they fell on their knees before him.

Then King Arthur said, “I will pardon you, for you did not know what you were doing. But you, Sir Domas, I believe, are a false and treasonous knight. Therefore I will take away all your possessions except the one castle that your brother had, and that castle I will leave to you. All your other possessions I will give to Sir Ontzlake. I further order that from now on you shall never have the right to ride any horse but a palfrey, for you are not worthy to ride a courser as a true knight has the right to do. I also command you to set free at once all those knights who were my companions in captivity. You shall repay them for all the harm you have done to them, as a Court of Chivalry shall decide.”
With that he sent the two knights away, and they were very glad that he had treated them so mercifully.

chapters.title: The Story of Merlin: Conclusion
paragraphs: Soon after the combat between King Arthur and Sir Accalon, the news of it was brought to Queen Morgana le Fay. The next day she heard that Sir Accalon was dead, and she could not understand how her plans had gone so wrong. Then she began to wonder how much King Arthur knew of her treachery. She said to herself, “I will go and see my brother, the King. If he knows about my treason, I will beg him to pardon my wrongdoing.” So she carefully asked where King Arthur was lying, gathered her Court of knights and esquires, and rode in that direction.

She came to that place on the fifth day after the battle. When she arrived, she asked the attendants how the King was doing. They answered her, “He is asleep, and he must not be disturbed.” Queen Morgana le Fay replied, “No matter. I will not be kept out, for I must see him and speak with him at once.” They did not dare to stop her, because she was the King’s sister.

So Queen Morgana went into the chamber where the King lay, and he did not wake when she came in. Then Queen Morgana was filled with hatred and a great desire for revenge. She said to herself, “I will take Excalibur and his shield and carry them away with me to Avalon, and my brother shall never see them again.” She went very softly to where King Arthur lay and looked at him as he slept. She saw that he had Excalibur beside him and that he held the handle of the sword in his hand while he slept. Then Queen Morgana said, “Alas! If I try to take Excalibur from him, he may wake, and he will kill me for my treason.” Then she looked and saw where the sheath of Excalibur lay at the foot of the couch. She took the sheath very softly and wrapped it in her mantle. Then she went out of the chamber, and King Arthur did not wake as she left.
Queen Morgana came out of the King’s chamber and said to the attendants, “Do not wake the King, for he is sleeping very soundly.” With that she mounted her horse and rode away from that place.

After a good while, King Arthur woke and looked for the sheath of Excalibur, but he saw that it was gone. At once he said, “Who has been here?” The attendants answered, “Queen Morgana le Fay was here. She came in and saw you, and then she went away without waking you.” Then King Arthur’s heart filled with dread, and he said, “I fear that she has dealt treacherously with me from the beginning to the end of these adventures.”

Then he got up and called together all his knights and esquires. He mounted his horse to chase Queen Morgana, although he was still very sick and faint from his painful wounds and the blood he had lost.

Just as the King was about to leave, Vivien came to him and said, “My lord, take me with you. If you do not, you will never get back the sheath of Excalibur, and you will never overtake Queen Morgana le Fay.” King Arthur said, “Come with me, damsel, in God’s name.” So Vivien went with him in pursuit of Queen Morgana.

After a while, as she fled, Queen Morgana le Fay looked behind her and saw that Vivien was with King Arthur’s party. Her heart failed her, and she said, “I fear I am now completely ruined. I helped that damsel gain so much knowledge of magic that I will have no spell left to save myself from her counter-spell. But at least King Arthur shall never have the sheath of Excalibur again to help him in his hour of need.”

At that moment they were passing beside the shore of a fairly large lake. Queen Morgana le Fay took the sheath of Excalibur in both hands and swung it by its belt above her head. Then she threw it far out into the water.

Then, behold, a very strange miracle happened. A woman’s arm suddenly appeared out of the water, dressed in white. It was decorated with many bracelets. The hand at the end of the arm caught the sheath of Excalibur and pulled it under the water, and no one ever saw that sheath again.
So the sheath of Excalibur was lost, and that was a terrible loss for King Arthur in later times, as you may read someday.

After Queen Morgana le Fay had thrown the sheath of Excalibur into the lake, she went on a little farther to a very lonely place with a great many rocks and stones lying on the ground. When she reached that place, she used powerful magic spells that Merlin had taught her. By means of those spells, she changed herself, all of her Court, and all of their horses into large round stones of many different sizes.

Soon King Arthur came to that place with his knights and esquires. He was very heavy of heart, for he had seen from a great distance how Queen Morgana le Fay had thrown the sheath of Excalibur into the lake.

When the King and his Court reached that spot, the damsel Vivien called out to him to stop. She said, “My lord, do you see all those great round stones?” “Yes,” said the King, “I see them.” Then Vivien said, “Behold, those stones are Queen Morgana le Fay and the Court who were with her. The magic she used to change herself and them into stones is something Merlin taught her. Now I know that magic myself, and I also know how to undo it whenever I wish. So if you will promise to punish that wicked woman at once for all her treason by taking her life, then I will bring her back to her true shape so that you may have her in your power.”

Then King Arthur looked at Vivien with great displeasure, and he said, “Damsel, you have a cruel heart! You yourself have suffered no harm from Queen Morgana. Why, then, would you have me kill her? If it were not for all you have done for me, I would be very angry with you. As for her, I forgive her for all of this, and I will forgive her again and again and yet again if she sins against me. Her mother was my mother, and the blood in her veins and in mine comes from the same source. So I will do no evil thing against her. Let us go back the way we came.”
Then Vivien looked at King Arthur with great bitterness. She laughed with great scorn and said, “You are both a fool and a doddering old man,” and with that she vanished from the sight of all.
From then on Vivien hated the King, for he had scolded her in front of others for her wickedness. Her hatred was even deeper than Morgana le Fay’s had ever been.
Some time later, King Arthur heard how Vivien had tricked Merlin, and he grieved bitterly that Merlin was lost to the world in that way.
So ends the story of the passing of Merlin.

chapters.title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 1
paragraphs: _Here begins the story of Sir Pellias, whom many called the Gentle Knight._
_Sir Pellias was so well loved that people said all women loved him without it harming them, and all men loved him to their great benefit._

_In the end he won the beautiful Lady of the Lake, one of the chief damsels of Faëry, as his beloved. He went to live as lord of her wonderful home, which no mortal except he and Sir Launcelot of the Lake had ever seen. Everyone was glad of his great good fortune—although the whole Court of King Arthur was sad that he had gone so far away and would never return._
_So I believe you will enjoy reading the account of Sir Pellias that is written here for your benefit._
_How Queen Guinevere Went Out to Gather May Blossoms, and How Sir Pellias Took On a Quest for Her._

It happened one pleasant spring day that Queen Guinevere went out to gather May blossoms with a fine company of Knights and Ladies of her Court. Among those Knights were Sir Pellias, Sir Geraint, Sir Dinadan, Sir Aglaval, Sir Agravaine, Sir Constantine of Cornwall, and several others. A court like that could hardly be found anywhere in the world, either then or before or since.

The day was lovely. The sunlight was golden yellow, and the breeze was soft and gentle. The little birds sang with great joy, and so many different flowers bloomed all around that the meadows were covered with their tender green. It seemed to Queen Guinevere very good to be out in the fields under the sky at such a season.

As the Queen and her Court walked happily among the blossoms, one of the damsels who served the Lady Guinevere suddenly cried out, “Look! Look! Who is that coming over there?” Queen Guinevere looked up and saw a damsel riding across the meadows on a milk-white horse. Three pages dressed in sky-blue clothes came with her. The damsel was also dressed all in blue. She wore a finely made gold chain around her neck and a gold band around her brow. Her hair was as yellow as gold and was wrapped all about with blue ribbons embroidered with gold. One of the pages who followed her carried a square frame, not very large, and the frame was wrapped and covered with a curtain of crimson satin.
When the Queen saw that fine company coming closer, she told one of the knights with her to go and meet the damsel. The knight who went out at her command was Sir Pellias.
When Sir Pellias met the damsel and her three pages, he spoke to her like this: “Fair damsel, the lady over there has told me to greet you and to ask you for your name and your purpose.”

“Sir Knight,” said the damsel, “I can see from your face and the way you speak that you are a lord of very high rank and great nobility. So I will gladly tell you that my name is Parcenet. I am a damsel of the Court of a very high lady who lives far from here, and she is called the Lady Ettard of Grantmesnle. I have come here hoping to be brought into the presence of Queen Guinevere. If you can tell me where I may find that noble lady, I will be very grateful to you.”
“Ha, Lady!” said Sir Pellias, “you will not have far to go to find Queen Guinevere. Look, there she walks, surrounded by her Court of Lords and Ladies.” Then the damsel said, “Please take me to her.”
So Sir Pellias led Parcenet to the Queen, and Queen Guinevere welcomed her very graciously. She said, “Damsel, what do you seek from us?”

“Lady,” said the damsel, “I will tell you gladly. The Lady Ettard, my mistress, is thought by everyone in the land where she lives to be the most beautiful lady in the world. Lately, such a report of your great beauty has reached her that the Lady Ettard decided to send me here to see with my own eyes whether what is told of you is really true. And indeed, Lady, now that I stand before you, I cannot deny that you are the fairest lady my eyes have ever seen, unless it is the Lady Ettard I spoke of.”

Then Queen Guinevere laughed with great delight. She said, “It seems to me a very funny thing that you should travel such a great distance for so small a matter.” Then she said, “Tell me, damsel, what is that your page is carrying, so carefully wrapped in the curtain of crimson satin?”
“Lady,” said the damsel, “it is a true and perfect portrait of the Lady Ettard, my mistress.”
Then Queen Guinevere said, “Show it to me.”

At this, the page who carried the picture got down from his horse and came to Queen Guinevere. He knelt on one knee and uncovered the picture so that the Queen and her Court could look at it. They all saw that the picture was painted with great skill on a panel of ivory framed in gold and set with many jewels of different colors. It showed a lady of such extraordinary beauty that everyone who saw it marveled. “Well, damsel!” said Queen Guinevere, “your lady is indeed blessed with wonderful beauty. If she truly looks like that picture, then I believe her equal in loveliness cannot be found anywhere in the world.”
Then Sir Pellias spoke up and said, “Not so, Lady. I declare, and I am willing to defend my words at the risk of my life, that you yourself are much more beautiful than that picture.”

“Well, Sir Knight!” said the damsel Parcenet, “it is lucky for you that you say this so far from Grantmesnle. In that place there is a certain knight named Sir Engamore of Malverat, who is a very strong knight indeed. He holds the opposite of what you say, in favor of the Lady Ettard, against all comers who dare to face him.”

Then Sir Pellias knelt before Queen Guinevere and pressed his palms together. “Lady,” he said, “I beg you to honor me by accepting me as your true knight in this matter. I would gladly try an adventure on your behalf, if you give me permission. If you grant me leave, I will ride out at once to meet this knight the damsel speaks of. I greatly hope that when I find him I will defeat him, to increase your glory and honor.”

Then Queen Guinevere laughed again with pure joy. “Sir,” she said, “it pleases me beyond measure that you would take up so small a quarrel for me. If you will take up so small a quarrel, how much more would you take up a serious one of mine? So I gladly accept you as my champion in this affair. Go now and arm yourself in the way that suits this adventure.”

“Lady,” said Sir Pellias, “if you allow it, I will go into this affair dressed as I am. I hope to win armor and equipment on the way. If I do, this adventure will bring you even more credit than it would otherwise.”

The Queen was very pleased that her knight would take on so serious an adventure dressed only in holiday clothes. So she said, “Let it be as you wish.” Then she told her page, Florian, to go and fetch the best horse he could find for Sir Pellias. Florian ran as fast as he could and soon came back with a noble horse, so black that I believe there was not a single white hair on him.

Then Sir Pellias said farewell to Queen Guinevere and her merry May Court. They bade him farewell and cheered him loudly. He mounted his horse and rode away with the damsel Parcenet and the three pages dressed in blue.
When they had gone some distance, the damsel Parcenet said, “Sir, I do not know your name or your rank, or who you are.”
To this Sir Pellias said, “Damsel, my name is Pellias, and I am a knight of King Arthur’s Round Table.”

Parcenet was very astonished, for many people considered Sir Pellias the best knight-at-arms alive, except only King Arthur and King Pellinore. So she cried out, “Messire, it will surely be a great honor for Sir Engamore to face so famous a knight as you.” To this Sir Pellias said, “Damsel, I think there are several knights of King Arthur’s Round Table who are better knights than I.” But Parcenet said, “I cannot believe that.”

After a while Parcenet said to Sir Pellias, “Messire, how will you get armor to fight Sir Engamore?” “Maiden,” said Sir Pellias, “I do not know right now where I will get armor. But before the time comes to face Sir Engamore, I trust I will find armor fit for my purpose. You must know that it is not always the armor a man wears on his body that brings him success. More often it is the spirit that lifts him up to his tasks.”

Then Parcenet said, “Sir Pellias, I do not think a lady often has so good a knight as you to fight for her.” Sir Pellias answered cheerfully, “Damsel, when your time comes, I wish you a much better knight to serve you than I.” “Sir,” said Parcenet, “that is not likely to happen to me.” At this Sir Pellias laughed with a light heart. Then Parcenet said, “Oh dear! I wish I had a good knight to serve me.”

To this Sir Pellias answered very seriously, “Maiden, the first one I catch I will give to you for your very own. Now would you like him fair or dark, short or tall? If you would rather have him short and fair, I will let the tall, dark one go. If you would have him tall and dark, I will let the other kind go.”

Then Parcenet looked very steadily at Sir Pellias and said, “I would have him about as tall as you are, with the same color of hair and eyes, a straight nose like yours, and a good wit such as you have.”

“Alas!” said Sir Pellias, “I wish you had told me this before we came so far from Camelot. I could easily have got you such a knight there. They have so many of them that they keep them in wicker cages and sell them two for a farthing.” At this Parcenet laughed cheerfully and said, “Then Camelot must be a very wonderful place, Sir Pellias.”

So with merry talk they went on their way, happy and content. They took great pleasure in the spring and the pleasant meadows they crossed, free of any care, with hearts full of cheerfulness and good will.

That night they stayed at a quaint, pleasant inn at the edge of the Forest of Usk. The next morning they left early, in the freshness of the new day, and went out of that place and into the shadows of the forest.

After they had traveled a long way in the forest, the damsel Parcenet said to Sir Pellias, “Sir, do you know what part of the woods this is?” “No,” said Sir Pellias. “Well,” said Parcenet, “this part of the woodland is sometimes called Arroy, and sometimes the Forest of Adventure. I must tell you it is a very wonderful place, full of many kinds of magic. It is said that no knight can enter this forest without some adventure happening to him.”
“Damsel,” said Sir Pellias, “what you tell me is very good news. Perhaps if we meet some adventure here, I may win armor suitable for my purpose.”

So they went straight into the Forest of Adventure and traveled in it for a long way, marveling at the look of the place they had come to. The Forest was very dark and silent, wonderfully strange and unlike any other place they had ever seen. It seemed to them that it would not be at all surprising if some extraordinary adventure should happen to them.

After they had traveled like this for some distance, they came suddenly out of the thicker part of the woods into a wide clearing. Before them they saw a violent stream that rushed along with great noise and turbulence. Beside the stream stood a thorn-tree, and under the thorn-tree was a bank of green moss, and on the bank of moss sat an old woman who looked very wretched. She was extraordinarily withered with age. Her eyes were red, as though she were always weeping. Many bristles grew on her cheeks and chin, and her face was covered with so many wrinkles that there was no spot without one.

When the old woman saw Sir Pellias and Parcenet and the three pages coming toward where she sat, she cried out in a loud voice, “Sir, will you not carry me over this water on your horse? Look, I am very old and weak and cannot cross this river by myself.”
Then Parcenet scolded the old woman, saying, “Quiet! Who are you to ask this noble knight to do you such a service?”

Sir Pellias was not pleased with Parcenet, so he said, “Damsel, you do not speak rightly in this matter. It is the duty of a true knight to help anyone who needs his aid. King Arthur is the perfect mirror of knighthood, and he has taught his knights to help all who ask for help, no matter what their condition.” With this, Sir Pellias got down from his horse and lifted the old woman onto the saddle. Then he mounted again and rode straight into the ford of the river, and so he carried the old woman safely across the torrent to the other side. Parcenet followed him, marveling greatly at his knightliness, and the three pages followed her.

When they had reached the other side of the water, Sir Pellias got down, meaning to help the old woman off the horse. But she did not wait for his help. She leaped down very lightly from where she sat. And behold! Sir Pellias saw that the woman he had thought only an old, withered hag was in truth a strange and wonderful lady of extraordinary beauty. Greatly amazed, he saw that she wore clothing of a kind that neither he nor anyone there had ever seen before. From her appearance he knew she was not an ordinary mortal, but surely a being of enchantment. Her face was wonderfully clear, as white as ivory. Her eyes were very black and extraordinarily bright, like two jewels set in ivory. She was dressed all in green from head to foot, and her hair was long and perfectly black, as soft and glossy as fine silk. Around her neck she wore a collar of opal stones and emeralds set in gold, and on her wrists were bracelets of finely made gold set with opal stones and emeralds. From all this he knew she must be a fay.
(For this was the Lady Nymue of the Lake. She had appeared to King Arthur in just this way, and so she appeared to Sir Pellias and those who were with him.)

Seeing the wonderful, magical nature of that lady, Sir Pellias knelt down before her and pressed his hands together, palm to palm. But the Lady of the Lake said, “Sir, why do you kneel to me?” “Lady,” said Sir Pellias, “because you are so wonderfully strange and beautiful.” “Messire,” said the Lady of the Lake, “you have done me a very good service, and you are truly an excellent knight. So rise, and kneel no longer!” Then Sir Pellias rose from his knees and stood before her, and he said, “Lady, who are you?” She answered him, “I am someone who holds a very kind regard for King Arthur and all his knights. My name is Nymue, and I am the chief of those Ladies of the Lake whom you may have heard about. I took the form of a poor old woman to test your knightliness, and behold! I have found nothing lacking in your worthy service.” Then Sir Pellias said, “Lady, you have truly done me a great favor in this.” At that the Lady of the Lake smiled at Sir Pellias very kindly, and she said, “Sir, I mean to do you an even greater favor than that.”

With those words, she at once took from around her neck the collar of opal stones, emeralds and gold. She hung it about the shoulders of Sir Pellias, so that it lay upon his chest with a wonderful glory of many colors.
“Keep this,” she said, “for it holds very powerful magic.”
Then she vanished at once from the sight of everyone there. She left them astonished and amazed beyond measure at what had happened.

Sir Pellias was like someone in a dream, for he did not know whether what he had seen was a vision or whether he had seen it with his waking eyes. So he mounted his horse in complete silence, as though he did not know what he was doing. In the same silence he led the way out of that place. None of the others spoke at that time. Only after they had gone a good distance did Parcenet say, in a fearful voice, “Messire, that was a very wonderful thing that happened to us.” To which Sir Pellias said, “Yes, maiden.”

Now the necklace that the Lady of the Lake had hung about the neck of Sir Pellias had such a power that whoever wore it was loved by everyone who looked upon him. The collar was enchanted with that special power, but Sir Pellias was completely unaware of it. He only took joy in the unusual beauty of the jewel that the Lady of the Lake had given him.

chapters.title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How Sir Pellias Defeated a Red Knight Named Sir Adresack, and How He Freed Twenty-Two Captives from That Knight’s Castle._

After that wonderful happening, they traveled on for a long while. They did not stop anywhere until, about an hour after sunrise, they came to a part of the forest where charcoal-burners were at work. Here Sir Pellias ordered them to pull up their horses and rest. So they got down to rest and refresh themselves, just as he had planned.

As they sat there eating and drinking, they suddenly heard loud crying and wailing from the forest. Almost at once a lady in sorry clothes rode out of the thickets into the clearing, on a spotted palfrey. Behind her rode a young squire dressed in green and white, on a reddish-brown horse. He also seemed full of grief, and his clothes were rumpled and his face was downcast. The lady’s face was swollen and red from weeping. Her hair hung loose on her shoulders, with no net or band to hold it, and her clothes were badly torn by brambles and stained from travel through the forest. The young squire who rode behind her came with his head drooping and his clothes in the same sad state. His cloak dragged behind him, fastened to his shoulder by only a single tie.

When Sir Pellias saw the lady and the squire in such a sad state, he got up at once, went straight to the lady, took her horse by the bridle, and stopped it. The lady looked at him but did not see him, for she was blinded by her grief and confusion. Then Sir Pellias said to her, “Lady, what troubles you, that you sorrow so greatly?” She answered, “Sir, it does not matter, for you cannot help me.” “How do you know that?” said Sir Pellias. “I truly mean to help you, if it is in my power.”

Then the lady looked more closely at Sir Pellias, seeing him as if through a mist of sorrow. She saw that he wore no armor, only holiday clothes of fine crimson cloth. So she began to weep again, even harder, for she thought he could give her no help in her trouble. She said, “Sir, your intentions are kind, but how can you hope to help me when you have neither weapons nor protection to take up such a quarrel?” But Sir Pellias said, “Lady, I cannot know how to help you until you tell me your sorrow. Still, I have good hope that I can serve you once I know what has upset you so.” Then, still holding the horse by the bridle, he led the lady to the place where Parcenet still sat beside the cloth spread with the food they had been eating. When they got there, he gently helped the lady down from her horse. Then, just as gently, he made her sit down on the grass and eat. When she had done so and had drunk some of the wine, she felt much refreshed and began to take heart. Seeing her so far recovered, Sir Pellias asked her again what her trouble was and begged her to open her heart to him.
Encouraged by his cheerful words, she told Sir Pellias the trouble that had brought her to this state.

“Sir Knight,” she said, “the place where I live is a long way from here. I came from there this morning with a very good knight named Sir Brandemere, who is my husband. We have been married only a little over four weeks, so our happiness was still quite new. This morning at daybreak Sir Brandemere wanted to take me hunting, and we set out with a hound of which my knight was wonderfully fond. We came to a certain place in the forest, and suddenly a doe sprang up in front of us. The hound chased her at once, barking wildly. My lord and I and this squire followed with great spirit and enjoyment of the chase. We followed the doe and the hound for a great distance, the hound running after the doe with fierce eagerness. Then we came to a place where we saw a rushing stream ahead of us, crossed by a long, narrow bridge. On the other side of the stream stood a strong castle with seven towers. It was built on the rocks in such a way that the rocks and the castle looked like one single rock.

“As we came near the bridge, behold! the castle’s portcullis was raised and the drawbridge was let down suddenly, with a great noise. At once a knight dressed all in red rode out of the castle. All the trappings of his horse were red too, and the spear in his hand was made of ash-wood painted red. He came out looking terrible and rode forward until he stood at the far end of that narrow bridge. Then he called out loudly to my husband, Sir Brandemere, saying: ‘Where do you think you are going, Sir Knight?’ Sir Brandemere answered him: ‘Sir, I want to cross this bridge, for my hound, which I love dearly, has crossed here chasing a doe.’ Then the Red Knight cried out in a loud voice, ‘Sir Knight, you come onto this bridge at your own peril. This bridge belongs to me, and whoever wants to cross it must first defeat me, or he cannot cross.’

“Now my husband, Sir Brandemere, was dressed at that time only in light clothes, such as one might wear for hunting or hawking, except that on his head he wore a light helmet wrapped with a scarf I had given him. Even so, he was so brave that he would not stand for a challenge like the one the Red Knight had given him. So he told me and this squire (whose name is Ponteferet) to stay on the near side of the bridge. Then he drew his sword and rode to the middle of the bridge, meaning to force his way across if he could. Seeing this, the Red Knight, who was dressed in full armor, threw aside his spear, drew his sword, and rode forward to meet my knight. They met in the middle of the bridge, and the Red Knight rose in his stirrups and struck my husband, Sir Brandemere, on the top of his helmet with his sword. I saw the blade cut through Sir Brandemere’s helmet and deep into his skull, so that blood ran down the knight’s face in great streams. Then Sir Brandemere fell straight from his horse and lay as though he were dead.

“Having beaten him, the Red Knight got down from his horse and lifted Sir Brandemere onto the horse from which he had fallen, so that he lay across the saddle. Then, taking both horses by the bridles, the Red Knight led them straight back across the bridge and into his castle. As soon as he had entered, the portcullis was closed behind him and the drawbridge was raised. He paid no attention to me or to the squire Ponteferet, but went away and left us without a single word of comfort. Even now I do not know whether my husband, Sir Brandemere, is alive or dead, or what has happened to him.”
As the lady spoke these words, behold! the tears again poured down her face.

Sir Pellias was deeply moved with pity, and he said, “Lady, your case is indeed a very sorrowful one, and I am greatly grieved for you. I would gladly help you as far as I am able. If you will lead me to this bridge and the grim castle you speak of, I promise you that I will do my very best to find out where your good knight is and what has happened to him.”

“Sir,” said the lady, “I am very grateful to you for your good will. But you cannot hope to succeed if you try so dangerous an adventure without weapons or armor to defend yourself. Think how badly that Red Knight treated my husband, Sir Brandemere, even though my husband had no arms or protection. So it is not likely he will treat you any more kindly.” Parcenet also raised her voice to the lady’s, telling Sir Pellias not to be so foolish as to do what he had in mind. The squire Ponteferet also called out to Sir Pellias that he should not do it, but should at least put on armor before he began this adventure.

But to all they said Sir Pellias replied, “Do not hold me back from what I mean to do. I tell you that I have several times undertaken adventures even more dangerous than this, and I have escaped without great harm.” He would not listen to anything the lady and the damsel said. Instead, he got up and helped the lady and the damsel onto their palfreys. Then he mounted his own horse, and when the squire and the pages had mounted theirs, the whole party left that place at once.

They traveled a long way through the forest, with the squire Ponteferet showing them the way that would bring them in time to the Red Knight’s castle. At last they came to a more open place in the wilderness, where a steep, bare hill lay before them. When they reached the top of the hill, they saw a wild, rushing river below. They saw that the river was crossed by a very straight, narrow bridge, and that on the far side of the bridge and the river stood a very strong castle with seven tall towers. The castle and its towers were built on very high, steep rocks, so that it was hard to tell where the rocks ended and the walls began. The towers and walls looked like one great rock of stone.

Then the squire Ponteferet pointed with his finger and said, “Sir Knight, there is the Red Knight’s castle, and he carried Sir Brandemere into it after wounding him so badly.” Then Sir Pellias said to the lady, “Lady, I will soon find out how your husband is.”

With that he spurred his horse and rode down the hill toward the bridge, very boldly. As he came closer to the bridge, behold! the castle’s portcullis was raised and the drawbridge was let down with a great noise and clamor. At once a knight dressed all in red armor and gear rode out of the castle and came quickly toward the end of the bridge. When Sir Pellias saw him approach so threateningly, he said to those who had followed him down the hill: “Stay where you are, and I will go forward to speak with this knight and ask about the injury he has done to Sir Brandemere.” Then the squire Ponteferet said to him, “Stop, Sir Knight, you will be hurt.” But Sir Pellias said, “No, I shall not be hurt.”
So he went boldly out onto the bridge, and when the Red Knight saw him come, he said, “Ha! Who are you, who dare to come onto my bridge like this?”

Sir Pellias answered him, “It does not matter who I am. But know this, you discourteous knight: I have come to ask you where you have put that good knight Sir Brandemere, and to ask why you treated him so cruelly a short time ago.”

At this the Red Knight grew full of rage. “Ha! ha!” he cried fiercely, “you will soon learn that to your great sorrow, for as I treated him, so I will soon treat you, and before long I will bring you to him. Then you may ask him whatever you like. But since you are unarmed and without protection, I do not wish to do you any bodily harm. So I demand that you surrender yourself to me at once. Otherwise it will be to your great pain and sorrow if you force me to use force to make you surrender.”

Then Sir Pellias said, “What! What! Would you attack a knight who is completely without weapons or protection, as I am?” And the Red Knight said, “Certainly I will, if you do not yield yourself to me at once.”
“Then,” said Pellias, “you are not fit to be treated as a proven knight deserves. So if I fight you, your defeat will be of a kind to shame any belted knight who wears golden spurs.”

Then he looked about for a weapon that would serve his purpose, and he saw a huge stone lying loose on the edge of the bridge. This stone was so large that five men of ordinary strength could hardly lift it. But Sir Pellias lifted it from its place with great ease, and, raising it in both hands, he ran quickly toward the Red Knight and hurled the rock at him with great force. The stone struck the Red Knight in the middle of his shield and drove it back against his chest with great violence. The force of the blow knocked the knight backward out of his saddle, so that he fell from his horse to the ground with a terrible crash and lay on the bridge as if he were quite dead.
The people in the castle who were looking out saw that blow, and they saw the Red Knight fall. They raised their voices in loud wailing, so that the outcry was terrible to hear.

But Sir Pellias ran as fast as he could to the fallen knight and set his knee on his chest. He unlaced the knight’s helmet and lifted it off. He saw that the knight’s face was strong and handsome, and that he was not quite dead.

When Sir Pellias saw that the Red Knight was not dead, and saw that he was about to get his breath back after the blow he had taken, he drew the knight’s dagger from its sheath and set the point at his throat. So when the Red Knight woke from his swoon, he saw death in the face of Sir Pellias and in the point of the dagger.

When the Red Knight saw how close death was, he begged Sir Pellias for mercy, saying, “Spare my life!” Sir Pellias said, “Who are you?” And the knight said, “I am called Sir Adresack, known as the Knight of the Seven Towers.” Then Sir Pellias said to him, “What have you done to Sir Brandemere, and how is that good knight?” And the Red Knight replied, “He is not as badly wounded as you suppose.”
When Sir Brandemere’s lady heard this, she was filled with joy, so that she clapped her hands together and cried out in thanksgiving.

But Sir Pellias said, “Now tell me, Sir Adresack, do you have other captives besides that knight, Sir Brandemere, at your castle?” Sir Adresack replied, “Sir Knight, I will tell you the truth. There are twenty-one other captives in my castle besides him: eighteen knights and squires of rank, and three ladies. For I have held this bridge for a long time, and everyone who tried to cross it I have taken captive and held for ransom. In this way I have gained great wealth and fortune.”

Then Sir Pellias said, “You are truly a wicked and discourteous knight, to treat travelers on your road this way. I would be right to kill you where you lie. But since you have begged me for mercy, I will grant it to you, though I do so only to the great shame of your knighthood. Besides, if I spare your life, there are several things you must do. First, you must go to Queen Guinevere at Camelot. There you must tell her that the knight who left her unarmed has taken your armor from you and has armed himself with it to defend her honor. Second, you must confess your faults to King Arthur, as you have confessed them to me, and you must beg his pardon for them. Ask him, in his mercy, to spare your life. These are the things you must do.”
To this Sir Adresack said, “Very well, I promise to do these things if you will spare my life.”

Then Sir Pellias let him get up, and he came and stood before Sir Pellias. Sir Pellias called the esquire Ponteferet to him and said, “Take this knight’s armor off his body and put it on mine, as you know how to do.” And Ponteferet did as Sir Pellias told him. He took the armor off Sir Adresack and dressed Sir Pellias in it, and Sir Adresack stood ashamed before them all. Then Sir Pellias said to him, “Now take me into your castle, so that I may free the captives you so wickedly hold as prisoners.” And Sir Adresack said, “It shall be done as you command.”

So they all went together to the castle and entered it, and it was an exceedingly stately place. There they saw a great many servants and attendants, who came at the command of Sir Adresack and bowed low before Sir Pellias. Then Sir Pellias told Sir Adresack to summon the keeper of the dungeon, and Sir Adresack did so. Sir Pellias ordered the keeper to lead them to the dungeon, and the keeper bowed before him and obeyed.
When they reached the dungeon, they saw that it was very tall and exceedingly strong. There they found Sir Brandemere and the others of whom Sir Adresack had spoken.

But when that sorrowful lady saw Sir Brandemere, she ran to him with a loud cry of joy, embraced him, and wept over him. He embraced her and wept too, and he forgot his wound entirely in the joy of seeing her again.

In the several rooms of that part of the castle, there were eighteen knights and esquires in all, and three ladies besides Sir Brandemere. Among those knights were two from King Arthur’s Court: Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte. When these two saw that Sir Pellias had set them free, they came to him, embraced him with great joy, and kissed him on both cheeks.
All those who were freed rejoiced greatly and gave Sir Pellias so much praise and honor that he was well pleased.

When Sir Pellias saw all the captives in the dungeon, he grew very angry with Sir Adresack. He turned to him and said, “Be gone, Sir Knight, and do the penance I gave you. I am very greatly displeased with you, and I fear I may regret my mercy to you.”
So Sir Adresack turned away and left that place at once. He called his esquire to him, and the two rode away to Camelot to do the penance he had promised Sir Pellias he would do.

After he was gone, Sir Pellias and the captives he had freed went through the various parts of the castle. There they found thirteen chests of gold and silver coins and four caskets of jewels, very fine and brilliant. All this treasure had been paid as ransom by the captives who had earlier been held prisoner there by force.
Sir Pellias ordered all the chests and caskets to be opened. When those who were there looked inside, their hearts were filled with joy at the sight of that great treasure.

Then Sir Pellias ordered all the gold and silver to be divided into nineteen equal parts. When it had been divided, he said, “Now let each of you who has been held captive in this place take one part of the treasure for his own, as payment for the sorrows he has suffered.” Then he gave each of the ladies who had been held captive a casket of jewels, saying to her, “Take this casket of jewels as payment for the sorrow you have suffered. And to Sir Brandemere’s lady he gave a casket of jewels for what she had endured.

But when those who were there saw that Sir Pellias kept no part of the great treasure for himself, they all cried out to him, “Sir Knight! Sir Knight! What is this? Look, you have set aside no part of this treasure for yourself.”

Then Sir Pellias answered, “You are right, I have not. I do not need any of this gold and silver, or any of these jewels, for myself. Look! You have suffered much at the hands of Sir Adresack, so you should receive payment for it. But I have suffered nothing at his hands, so I need no such payment.”
Then they were all astonished at his generosity and praised him greatly for his big heart. And all those knights swore to him loyalty until death.

When all these things were done, Sir Brandemere begged everyone there to come with him to his castle, so that they might refresh themselves with a time of merriment and good food. They all said they would go with him, and they did. At the castle of Sir Brandemere there was great rejoicing, with feasting and jousting for three days.

And everyone there loved Sir Pellias with an astonishing love because of that collar of emeralds and opals and gold. Yet no one knew the power of that collar, and Sir Pellias did not know of it either.

So Sir Pellias stayed in that place for three days. When the fourth day came, he got up early in the morning and ordered his horse saddled, along with the palfrey of the damsel Parcenet and the horses of their pages.
When everyone there saw that he meant to leave, they begged him not to go. But Sir Pellias said, “Do not stop me, for I must go.”

Then those two knights of Arthur’s Court, Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte, came to him and begged him to let them go with him on that adventure. At first Sir Pellias refused them, but they begged him all the more, until at last he was glad to say, “You shall go with me.”
So he left that place with his company, and all those who remained were deeply sorrowful that he had gone.

chapters.title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How Sir Pellias Fought Sir Engamore, Also Called the Knight of the Green Sleeves, and What Happened to the Lady Ettard._

Sir Pellias and his party, together with the damsel Parcenet and hers, traveled onward until, late in the afternoon, they came to the far edge of the forest. There the woods ended altogether. Before them, under the open sky, lay many fields and meadows, with farms, small cottages, and groves of trees all in bloom with tender leaves and sweet-smelling blossoms.

Sir Pellias said, “This is truly a beautiful land that we have come into.” The damsel Parcenet was very pleased, and she said, “Sir, I am glad that what you see pleases you. All this region belongs to the Lady Ettard, and it is my home. Besides, from the top of that hill over there you can see the castle of Grantmesnle, which lies in the valley below.” Then Sir Pellias said, “Let us hurry! I am eager to see that place.”

So they spurred their horses and rode up the hill at a steady gallop. When they reached the top, they saw the Castle of Grantmesnle lying below them, as small and clear as if it rested on the palm of a hand. Sir Pellias saw that it was a very fair castle. Its outer walls were built of red stone, and inside the walls stood many buildings of red brick. Behind the walls lay a little town, and from where they stood they could see its streets and the people coming and going about their business. Sir Pellias admired the castle and said, “Truly, maiden, that is a fine estate.”
“Yes,” said Parcenet, “those of us who live there think it a very fine estate indeed.”

Then Sir Pellias said to Parcenet, “Maiden, that glade of young trees near the castle looks like a cheerful spot. We will make our camp there, my companions in arms and I. We will also have three pavilions set up to shelter us by day and by night. In the meantime, I ask you to go to the lady, your mistress, and tell her that a knight has come here who does not know her, but who holds that the Lady Guinevere of Camelot is the fairest lady in all the world. Tell her also that I am here to defend those words against all comers, at the risk of my own life. So if the lady has any champion to fight for her, I will meet him in that field tomorrow at midday, a little before I eat my noon meal. At that time I mean to ride into the field and parade there until my friends call me in to dinner. I will take my stand in that place in honor of the Lady Guinevere of Camelot.”

“Sir Pellias,” said the damsel, “I will do just as you ask. I cannot wish for you to win that fight, and yet I am truly sorry to leave you. You are both a very brave and a very gentle knight, and I find that I have grown fond of you.”
Then Sir Pellias laughed and said, “Parcenet, you give me more praise than I deserve.” And Parcenet said, “Sir, that is not so. You deserve everything good I can say about you.”

Then the two of them parted with good will and much kindness. The maiden and the three pages went one way. Sir Pellias, his two companions, and the several attendants they had brought went into the glade of young trees, just as Sir Pellias had ordered.

There they set up three pavilions in the shade of the trees. The first was of fair white cloth, the second of green cloth, and the third of scarlet cloth. Over each pavilion they set a banner showing the device of the knight it belonged to. Above the white pavilion was the device of Sir Pellias, which was three swans on a silver field. Above the red pavilion, which belonged to Sir Brandiles, was a red banner showing his device, a mailed hand gripping a hammer. Above the green pavilion, which belonged to Sir Mador de la Porte, was a green banner with his device, a carrion crow holding a white lily in one claw and a sword in the other.

The next day, when midday was near, Sir Pellias rode out into the field before the castle, as he had promised. He was dressed from head to foot in the red armor he had taken from the body of Sir Adresack, and in that armor he looked terrifying. He rode up and down before the castle walls for a good while, crying in a loud voice, “Hear me! Hear me! Here stands a knight of King Arthur’s Court and of his Round Table. He declares, and is ready to defend with his own body, that the Lady Guinevere, King Arthur’s Queen of Camelot, is the most beautiful lady in all the world, without exception. So if any knight says otherwise, let him come out at once and defend his opinion.”

After Sir Pellias appeared in the meadow, a great stir rose inside the castle. Many people climbed onto the walls and looked down at Sir Pellias as he rode about the field. After a time the drawbridge of the castle was lowered, and a knight rode out, very large of body and very proud in manner. He was dressed from head to foot in green armor, and he wore a green sleeve on each arm. For this reason he was sometimes called the Knight of the Green Sleeves.

The Green Knight rode toward Sir Pellias, and Sir Pellias rode toward the Green Knight. When they met, they greeted each other with great politeness and knightly courtesy. Then the Green Knight said to Sir Pellias, “Sir Knight, will you do me the great favor of telling me your name?”
Sir Pellias answered, “Gladly. I am Sir Pellias, a knight of King Arthur’s Court and of his Round Table.”

Then the Green Knight replied, “Ha, Sir Pellias, it is a great honor to face so famous a knight. Who in the Courts of Chivalry has not heard of you? If I am lucky enough to overthrow you, all your honor will become mine. In return for your courtesy in telling me your name, I will give you mine and my title. I am Sir Engamore of Malverat, also known as the Knight of the Green Sleeves. I will also tell you that I am the champion of the Lady Ettard of Grantmesnle. For eleven months I have defended her claim to be the most beautiful lady alive, against all comers. If I defend it successfully for one month more, I will win her hand and all this fair estate. So I am ready to do everything in my power in her honor.”
Then Sir Pellias said, “Sir Knight, I thank you for your greeting, and I too will do all I can in this fight.” Then each knight saluted the other with his lance, and each rode to his appointed place.

A great crowd of people had come down to the lower walls of the castle and the town to watch the contest that was about to begin. It would be hard to imagine a finer occasion for knights to meet in a glorious joust. Each knight made himself ready in every way and set his spear and lance with great care. When all was ready, a herald who had come out from the castle into the field gave the signal to charge. In an instant each knight drove his spurs into his horse and rushed at the other with such terrible speed that the ground shook and trembled under the beating of the horses’ feet. They met exactly in the center of the field, each striking the other in the middle of his defenses with a force that was terrible to see. The spear of Sir Engamore burst into as many as thirty pieces. But the spear of Sir Pellias held firm, and the Green Knight was hurled out of his saddle so violently that he struck the ground more than a spear’s length behind his horse’s tail.

When the people on the walls saw how completely the Green Knight had been overthrown, they raised a great outcry, for there was no other knight in all those parts like Sir Engamore. The Lady Ettard cried out loudest of all, for she loved Sir Engamore dearly. Seeing him flung so violently to the ground, she thought he might have been killed.

Three squires ran to Sir Engamore, lifted him up, and unlaced his helmet to give him air. They saw that he was not dead, but only in a deep faint. After a while he opened his eyes, and Sir Pellias was very glad, for it would have grieved him to have killed that knight. When Sir Engamore came to his senses again, he demanded fiercely that he be allowed to continue the contest with Sir Pellias on foot, with swords. But Sir Pellias would not agree. “No, Sir Engamore,” he said, “I will not fight you over so serious a quarrel as that, for I have no ill will against you.” At this refusal Sir Engamore began to weep, out of sheer anger and shame at being so completely overthrown.

Then Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte came and praised Sir Pellias highly for the fine way he had fought in the contest. At the same time they spoke kindly to Sir Engamore and comforted him for his misfortune. But Sir Engamore took little comfort from their words.

While they were all standing together, the Lady Ettard came out from the castle with a very cheerful and handsome company of squires and ladies. They crossed the meadow toward the place where Sir Pellias and the others stood.
When Sir Pellias saw the lady approaching, he drew his dagger, cut the straps of his helmet, and took the helmet off his head. Then he went forward bareheaded to meet her.

But when he came close to her, he saw that she was many times more beautiful than the picture of her painted on the ivory panel that he had seen before. His heart went out to her with a very strong liking. So he knelt down on the grass and pressed his hands together, palm to palm, before her. He said, “Lady, I beg your forgiveness for having fought against your claim. I did it only for my Queen. Otherwise I would rather have been your champion than the champion of any other lady I have ever seen.”

At that time Sir Pellias wore around his neck the collar of emeralds, opals, and gold that the Lady of the Lake had given him. When the Lady Ettard looked at him, that necklace drew her heart toward him with a powerful enchantment. She smiled warmly at Sir Pellias, gave him her hand, and helped him rise from where he knelt. And she said to him, “Sir Knight, you are a very famous warrior. I think there is no one who knows anything of chivalry who has not heard of the fame of Sir Pellias, the Gentle Knight. My champion Sir Engamore of Malverat has overthrown every challenger until now, but he need not feel very ashamed to have been overthrown by so terribly strong a knight.”

Sir Pellias was very glad of the kind words the Lady Ettard spoke to him, and he introduced her to Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte. The Lady Ettard spoke very graciously to these knights too, moved by the great regard she felt for Sir Pellias. She invited them to come into the castle and refresh themselves with good cheer, and the knights said they would soon do so. They returned, each to his own pavilion, and there each dressed himself in fine clothing and ornaments of gold and silver, until he made noble company for any Court. Then the three knights went to the castle of Grantmesnle, and when they arrived, everyone was amazed at their noble appearance.
But Sir Engamore, who had by now recovered from his fall, was deeply discouraged. He said to himself, “Who am I, beside these noble lords?” So he stood apart, heavy-hearted and low in spirit.

Then the Lady Ettard held a very fine feast, and Sir Pellias, Sir Brandiles, and Sir Mador de la Porte were delighted with it. She seated Sir Pellias at her right hand and Sir Engamore at her left. This made Sir Engamore feel still worse, for until now he had always sat at the right hand of the Lady Ettard.

Because Sir Pellias wore the wonderful collar that the Lady of the Lake had given him, the Lady Ettard could not take her eyes from him. After they had refreshed themselves and gone out to walk in the warm sunshine of the castle gardens, she wanted Sir Pellias beside her constantly. When it came time for the visiting knights to leave the castle, she begged Sir Pellias to stay a while longer. Sir Pellias was very glad to do so, for he was delighted beyond measure by the kindness and the beauty of the Lady Ettard.
So after a while Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte went back to their pavilions, and Sir Pellias stayed on in the castle of Grantmesnle a little longer.

That night the Lady Ettard had a supper prepared for herself and Sir Pellias. She and Sir Pellias sat alone at the table, and the damsel Parcenet waited on the lady. While they ate, some young pages and squires played sweetly on harps, and some maidens of the lady’s Court sang so sweetly that it lifted the heart of anyone who heard them. Sir Pellias was so enchanted by the sweet music and by the beauty of the Lady Ettard that he did not know whether he was on earth or in Paradise. In his great happiness he said to the Lady Ettard, “Lady, I wish I could do something for you, to show you how high my regard and honor for you is.”

As Sir Pellias sat beside her, the Lady Ettard had kept her eyes on the wonderful collar of gold, emeralds, and opals that hung around his neck, and she wanted it very badly. So she now said to Sir Pellias, “Sir Knight, you could do me a great favor, if you are willing.” “What favor can I do you, Lady?” said Sir Pellias. “Sir,” said the Lady Ettard, “you can give me that collar that hangs around your neck.”
At this the face of Sir Pellias fell, and he said, “Lady, I cannot do that. That collar came to me in such an extraordinary way that I cannot part with it.”
Then the Lady Ettard said, “Why can you not part with it, Sir Pellias?”
Then Sir Pellias told her the whole of that extraordinary adventure with the Lady of the Lake, and how that fairy lady had given him the collar.

The Lady Ettard was greatly astonished at this, and she said, “Sir Pellias, that is a very wonderful story. Even so, though you cannot give that collar to me, you could let me wear it for a little while. I am charmed beyond all measure by the beauty of that collar, so I beg you to let me wear it for a little.”
At last Sir Pellias could not say no to her any longer. “Lady, you may wear it for a while,” he said. Then he lifted the collar from around his neck and hung it around the neck of the Lady Ettard.

After a short time the power of the jewel left Sir Pellias and passed into the Lady Ettard. She now looked at Sir Pellias with very different eyes than before. She said to herself, “Ha! What was wrong with me, that I let that knight enchant me, when my own champion has served me so faithfully? Has this knight not done me terrible wrong? Did he not come here for that very purpose? Did he not defeat my own true knight to show his scorn for me? Why did I ever treat him with such favor as I have?” Yet though she thought all this, she gave Sir Pellias no sign of it. She seemed to laugh and talk cheerfully. All the same, she began at once to search her mind for a way to take revenge on him. She said to herself, “Look! Is he not my enemy, and is my enemy not now in my power? Why should I not take full revenge on him for everything he has done to us of Grantmesnle?”

Soon she made an excuse, rose, and left Sir Pellias. She drew the damsel Parcenet aside and said, “Go and bring me a strong sleeping-draught right away.” Parcenet asked, “Lady, what do you mean to do?” The Lady Ettard answered, “Never mind.” Parcenet said, “Would you give that noble knight a sleeping-draught?” The lady said, “I would.” Then Parcenet said, “Lady, that would surely be a wicked thing to do to a man who sits peacefully at your table and eats your bread and salt.” The Lady Ettard replied, “Do not worry about that, girl. Just go at once and do as I tell you.”

Parcenet saw that it was not wise to disobey the lady, so she went at once and did as she was told. She brought the sleeping-draught to the lady in a cup of pure wine. The Lady Ettard took the cup and said to Sir Pellias, “Take this cup of wine, Sir Knight, and drink it to me, as much as you wish me well.” Parcenet stood behind her lady’s chair, and when Sir Pellias took the cup, she frowned and shook her head at him. But Sir Pellias did not see her. He was dizzy with the beauty of the Lady Ettard and with the enchantment of the collar of emeralds, opal stones, and gold that she now wore. So he said to her, “Lady, if there were poison in this cup, I would still drink the wine at your command.”
At that the Lady Ettard burst out laughing and said, “Sir Knight, there is no poison in that cup.”
Sir Pellias took the cup and drank the wine. Then he said, “Lady, what is this? The wine tastes bitter.” The Lady Ettard answered, “Sir, that cannot be.”

Soon Sir Pellias felt his head grow terribly heavy, as if it were made of lead, and he lowered it onto the table where he sat. The Lady Ettard kept watching him with a strange look. After a while she said, “Sir Knight, are you asleep?” Sir Pellias did not answer, for the fumes of the sleeping-draught had risen into his brain, and he was asleep.

Then the Lady Ettard rose laughing, clapped her hands together, and called her attendants. She said to them, “Take this knight away and carry him into an inner room. When you have brought him there, strip off his fine clothes and his ornaments, so that he has nothing left on but his underclothes. Then lay him on a pallet and carry him out of the castle, into the meadow below the walls where he defeated Sir Engamore. In the morning he will be a mockery and a joke to everyone who sees him. So we will shame him in the same field where he defeated Sir Engamore, and his shame will be greater than Sir Engamore’s.”
When the damsel Parcenet heard this, she was deeply grieved. She went off by herself and wept for Sir Pellias. But the others took Sir Pellias and did to him just as the Lady Ettard had ordered.

When morning came, Sir Pellias woke with the sun shining in his face. He did not know where he was at all, for his mind was clouded by the sleeping-draught he had drunk. He said to himself, “Am I dreaming, or am I awake? Truly, the last thing I remember is sitting at supper with the Lady Ettard, and yet here I am in an open field with the sun shining on me.”

He raised himself on his elbow, and he saw that he was lying beneath the castle walls, near the small back gate. Above him, on top of the wall, a great crowd of people had gathered. When they saw that he was awake, they laughed and jeered at him. The Lady Ettard also looked down at him from a window, and he saw that she was laughing at him and enjoying herself. Then he saw that he lay there dressed only in his linen undershirt and with bare feet, as if he were ready to sleep for the night. He sat up on the cot and said to himself, “Surely this must be some shameful dream that weighs on me.” He could not shake off his bewilderment.

As he sat there, the back gate suddenly opened, and the damsel Parcenet came out. Her face was wet with tears, and she carried a flame-colored cloak in her hand. She ran straight to Sir Pellias and said, “You good and gentle knight, take this and wrap yourself in it.”

Then Sir Pellias knew that this was no dream but a true and terrible disgrace. He was seized by such deep shame that he began to shake, and his teeth chattered as if he had a fever. He said to Parcenet, “Maiden, I thank you.” He could find no more words to say. He took the cloak and wrapped himself in it.

When the people on the walls saw what Parcenet had done, they booed her and shouted many cruel words at her. The maiden ran back into the castle. Sir Pellias got up and made his way toward his pavilion, wrapped in the cloak. As he went, he staggered and stumbled like a drunken man, for he carried a burden of shame that was almost too heavy to bear.

When Sir Pellias reached his pavilion, he went in, threw himself face down on his couch, and lay there without a word. Soon Sir Brandiles and Mador de la Porte heard of the trouble that had come upon Sir Pellias. They hurried to where he lay and grieved greatly over him. They were also very angry at the shame that had been put on him. They said, “We will get help from Camelot, break into that castle, and bring the Lady Ettard here to beg your pardon for this insult. We will do this even if we have to drag her here by the hair of her head.”

But Sir Pellias did not lift his head. He only groaned and said, “Leave it, good sirs. You must not do that, under any circumstances, because she is a woman. Even now I would defend her honor, even if I died doing it. I do not know whether I am bewitched or what is wrong with me, but I love her with a great passion, and I cannot tear my heart away from her.”
Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte were astonished at this. They said to each other, “Truly, that lady has put some powerful spell on him.”
After a while Sir Pellias asked them to go away and leave him alone. They did, though they did not go willingly.

Sir Pellias lay there all day until the afternoon came. Then he roused himself and told his squire to bring him his armor. When Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte heard of this, they went to him and said, “Sir, what do you mean to do?” Sir Pellias answered, “I am going to try to reach the Lady Ettard.” They said, “What madness is this?” “I do not know,” said Sir Pellias, “but it seems to me that if I do not see the Lady Ettard and speak with her, I will surely die of longing for her.” They said, “Truly, this is madness.” He replied, “I do not know whether it is madness or whether I am caught in some enchantment.”

The squire brought Sir Pellias his armor as he had ordered and dressed him in it, so that he was armed from head to foot. Then Sir Pellias mounted his horse at once and rode out toward the castle of Grantmesnle.

When the Lady Ettard saw Sir Pellias riding up and down the meadow below the castle again, she called six of her best knights to her. She said to them, “Look, good sirs, there is the knight who brought so much shame on us yesterday. Now I order you to go out against him and punish him as he deserves.”
The six knights went and put on their armor. When they were ready, they rode out at once against Sir Pellias.

When Sir Pellias saw them coming, his heart filled with fury. He shouted in a mighty voice and charged at them. For a while they stood against him, but he could not be stopped. He fought with such terrible fury that they soon broke away from him and fled. He chased them around that field and knocked four of them from their horses. Then, when only two of the knights were left, Sir Pellias suddenly stopped fighting. He called out to those two knights, “Good sirs, I surrender to you.”

The two knights were greatly astonished. They were still full of fear at his strength, and they did not know why he would yield to them. Even so, they came and took hold of him and led him toward the castle. Sir Pellias said to himself, “Now they will bring me to the Lady Ettard, and I will be able to speak with her.” For this was the very reason he had let those two knights capture him.

But things did not go as Sir Pellias wished. When they had brought him close beneath the castle, the Lady Ettard called down to them from a window in the wall. She said, “What are you doing with that knight?” They answered, “We are bringing him to you, Lady.” She cried out fiercely, “Do not bring him to me! Take him, tie his hands behind his back, tie his feet beneath his horse’s belly, and send him back to his friends.”
Sir Pellias lifted his eyes to that window and cried out in great despair, “Lady, it was to you that I surrendered, and not to these unworthy knights.”
But the Lady Ettard cried out even more fiercely, “Drive him away, for I hate the sight of him.”
So the two knights did as the Lady Ettard said. They took Sir Pellias and tied him hand and foot on his horse. When they had done this, they let his horse carry him back to his friends in that way.

When Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte saw Sir Pellias come to them with his hands bound behind his back and his feet tied beneath his horse’s belly, they were filled with grief and despair. They untied the cords from his hands and feet and cried out to him, “Sir Knight, Sir Knight, are you not ashamed to allow such disgrace as this?” Sir Pellias shook and trembled as if he had a fever, and he cried out in despair, “I do not care what happens to me!” They said, “We do not mean yourself, Sir Knight. Think of the shame you bring on King Arthur and his Round Table!” Then Sir Pellias cried aloud, in a great and terrible voice, “I do not care about them, either.”

All this happened because of the powerful enchantment of the collar of emeralds, opal stones, and gold that Sir Pellias had given to the Lady Ettard and that she wore all the time. No man could withstand the enchantment of that collar. That is how Sir Pellias came to be bewitched and brought to such a depth of shame.

chapters.title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 4
paragraphs: _How Queen Guinevere quarreled with Sir Gawaine, and how Sir Gawaine left the court of King Arthur for a while._

Queen Guinevere held Sir Pellias in high regard, and in just the same measure she disliked Sir Gawaine. Many people said Sir Gawaine had a silver tongue, and at times he could talk so well that he won others over to his wishes. But he was proud, stern, and haughty. So he did not always accept it when the Lady Guinevere ordered him about as she did the other knights of that court. She also could never forget how Sir Gawaine had refused her at Cameliard, when she begged him and his companions for help in her time of trouble. Nor could she forget how rudely he had spoken to her then. So there was little affection between these two proud people. Queen Guinevere held to her own way, and Sir Gawaine held to his, whatever happened.

One day Sir Gawaine, Sir Griflet, and Sir Constantine of Cornwall sat talking with five ladies of the Queen’s court. They were in a garden of woven branches that lay beneath the tower of the Lady Guinevere, and their talk was very pleasant. At times they told jokes and tales and made merry. At other times one of them would take up a lute they had brought with them, and play it and sing.

While these lords and ladies sat enjoying their conversation and songs, Queen Guinevere sat at a window that looked out over the garden. The window was not very high above the ground, so she could hear everything they said. But the lords and ladies had no idea that the Queen could hear them, so they talked and laughed very freely. The Queen greatly enjoyed their talk and the music they made.

That day was unusually mild, and it was well into the late afternoon. The lords and ladies were dressed in very bright clothes, and Sir Gawaine was the most brightly dressed of them all. He wore sky-blue silk embroidered with silver thread. He was playing the lute and singing a ballad in a most pleasing voice. Queen Guinevere sat beside the open window and was very glad to listen to him.

Queen Guinevere had a greyhound of which she was wonderfully fond. She was so fond of it that she had dressed its neck with a gold collar set with red jewels. At that moment the hound came running into the garden, and its feet were wet and muddy. When it heard Sir Gawaine singing and playing the lute, it ran to him and jumped up on him. Sir Gawaine was very angry at this. He clenched his fist and struck the hound on the head with his knuckles, and the hound cried out loudly.

When Queen Guinevere saw that blow, she was greatly offended. She called out from her window, “Why do you strike my dog, Messire?” The lords and ladies in the garden were very surprised. They were deeply embarrassed to find that the Queen had been so close by, and had heard everything they said and seen everything they did.
But Sir Gawaine answered boldly, “Your dog insulted me, Lady, and whoever insults me, I strike.”
Then Queen Guinevere grew very angry with Sir Gawaine. She said, “Your speech is too bold, Messire.” And Sir Gawaine said, “Not too bold, Lady, but only bold enough to defend my rights.”

At this the Lady Guinevere’s face burned like fire, and her eyes shone very bright. She said, “I am sure you have forgotten whom you are speaking to, Sir Knight.” At that, Sir Gawaine smiled bitterly and said, “And you, Lady, do not remember that I am the son of a king so powerful that he needs no help from any other king to defend his rights.”

At these words everyone there fell as silent as if they had been turned to stone, for that speech was extremely bold and proud. They all looked at the ground, for they did not dare to look at Queen Guinevere or at Sir Gawaine. The Lady Guinevere was also silent for a long time, trying to recover from what he had said. When she spoke, it was as though her anger half choked her. She said, “Sir Knight, you are proud and arrogant beyond measure. I have never heard of anyone who dared to answer his Queen as you have spoken to me. But this is my court, and I may command in it as I choose. So I now order you to leave, and to show your face no more, either here or in the Hall or in any place where I hold my court. You are an offense to me, and in none of these places will you be allowed to show your face until you ask my pardon for the insult you have given me.” Then Sir Gawaine stood up and bowed very low to Queen Guinevere, and he said, “Lady, I go. And I will not come back until you are willing to tell me that you are sorry for the rude way you have treated me, now and at other times in front of my peers.”

With these words Sir Gawaine left that place, and he did not turn his head to look back. Queen Guinevere went into her chamber and wept in secret, out of anger and shame. She was truly grieved at what had happened. Yet she was so proud that she would not have taken back the words she had spoken, even if she could have.

When the news of that quarrel had gone around the castle, it reached the ears of Sir Ewaine. He went straight to Sir Gawaine and asked what had happened. Sir Gawaine, who was like a man out of his mind and in deep despair, told him everything. Then Sir Ewaine said, “You were certainly wrong to speak to the Queen as you did. Still, if you are banished from this court, I will go with you, for you are my first cousin and my companion, and my heart is bound to you.” So Sir Ewaine went to King Arthur and said, “Lord, my cousin, Sir Gawaine, has been banished from this court by the Queen. I cannot say he has not earned that punishment, but I would gladly ask your leave to go with him.”

King Arthur was very sad at this, but he kept a steady face. He said, “Messire, I will not stop you from going where you wish. As for your kinsman, I suppose he gave the Queen such great offense that she could not do otherwise.”

So Sir Ewaine and Sir Gawaine both went to their lodgings and ordered their squires to help them put on their armor. Then they and their squires rode out of Camelot and took the road toward the forest lands.

The two knights and their squires traveled all that day until the gray of evening, when the birds were singing their last songs before closing their eyes for the night. As evening came quickly on, the knights feared they would not find friendly lodging before dark, and they spoke about this a good deal. But when they reached the top of a certain hill, they saw below them a valley, very fair and well farmed, with many cottages and small farms. In the middle of the valley stood a fine abbey, very beautiful to look at. Sir Gawaine said to Sir Ewaine, “If that abbey is a house of monks, I believe we will find excellent lodging there tonight.”
So they rode down into the valley to the abbey. At the small gate they found a porter, and from him they learned that it was indeed an abbey of monks. They were very glad and rejoiced greatly.

When the abbot of that abbey learned who they were and what high rank they held, he was delighted to welcome them. He brought them to the part of the abbey where he himself lived. There he bade them welcome and had a good supper set before them, and they were very glad of it. The abbot was cheerful and loved to talk with strangers. So he asked the two knights eagerly why they were wandering as knights-errant. But they told him nothing about the quarrel at court, only that they were looking for adventure. At this the abbot said, “Ha, Messires, if you are looking for adventures, you may find one not far from here.”

Sir Gawaine said, “What adventure is that?” And the abbot answered, “I will tell you. If you travel east from here, after a while you will come to a very fair castle of gray stone. In front of that castle you will find a good level meadow, and in the middle of the meadow a sycamore tree. On the tree hangs a shield, which certain ladies insult in a very strange way. If you forbid those ladies to insult that shield, you will find a very good adventure.”
Then Sir Gawaine said, “That is a very strange matter. Tomorrow morning we will go to that place and try to find out what sort of adventure it is.” And the abbot said, “Do so,” and laughed heartily.

When the next morning came, Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine said farewell to the abbot and left that place, riding east as the abbot had advised. After they had ridden that way for two or three hours or more, they saw ahead of them the edge of a forest, green and shady with leaves, and very cheerful in the warmth of the early summer day. And behold! Right at the edge of the woods stood a fair, strong castle of gray stone, with glass windows shining brightly against the sky.

Then Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine saw that everything was just as the abbot had said. In front of the castle was a smooth, level meadow with a sycamore tree in the middle of it. As they drew near, they saw that a black shield hung in the branches of the tree. Soon they could see that it bore the badge of three white goshawks with spread wings. But the most extraordinary thing was that in front of that shield stood seven young damsels, very fair of face, and they kept heaping insults on the shield. Some of the damsels struck it again and again with peeled willow rods, and others threw lumps of clay at it, so that the shield was badly spoiled. Close to the shield was a noble-looking knight dressed all in black armor and seated on a black war-horse. It was plain that the shield belonged to that knight, for he carried no other. Yet although it was very likely his own shield, the knight made no protest, by word or by action, to stop the damsels from insulting it.

Then Sir Ewaine said to Sir Gawaine, “That is a very strange thing I see over there. Perhaps one of us is meant to fight that knight.” And Sir Gawaine said, “Perhaps so.” Then Sir Ewaine said, “If so, then I will take the adventure.” “Not so,” said Sir Gawaine, “for I will take it myself. I am the elder of us two, and more experienced in knighthood.” So Sir Ewaine said, “Very well. Let it be that way, for you are a much more powerful knight than I, and it would be a pity if one of us failed in this task.” Then Sir Gawaine said, “So be it, and I will take it.”

He set spurs to his horse and rode quickly to where the damsels were insulting the black shield. He set his spear in position and shouted in a loud voice, “Get away! Get away!” When the damsels saw the armed knight riding at them like that, they fled from him, shrieking.

Then the Sable Knight, who had been sitting a short way off, rode forward in a very stately manner to Sir Gawaine. He said, “Sir Knight, why do you interfere with those ladies?” Sir Gawaine replied, “Because they were insulting what seemed to me a noble and knightly shield.” At this the Sable Knight spoke very proudly, saying, “Sir Knight, that shield belongs to me, and I assure you I am quite able to take care of it without the interference of any other defender.” To this Sir Gawaine said, “It does not seem so, Sir Knight.”
