Then the Sable Knight said, “Messire, if you think you can take better care of that shield than I can, I think you would do well to prove your words with your body.” To this Sir Gawaine said, “I will do my best to show you that I am better able to guard that shield than you, who own it.”

At this the Sable Knight, without further talk, rode to the sycamore tree and took down the shield that hung there. He fitted the shield to his arm, took his spear in hand, and made himself ready for defense. Sir Gawaine also made himself ready, and then each knight took whatever place on the field seemed fitting to him.

When the people of that castle saw that a fight with weapons was about to begin, they crowded in great numbers onto the walls. There were as many as forty ladies, squires, and people of different ranks looking down on the field of battle from the walls.

When the knights were fully ready, Sir Ewaine gave the signal for the charge. Each knight shouted aloud, drove his spurs into his war-horse, and rushed forward to the attack with a noise as loud as thunder.

Sir Gawaine thought he would easily defeat his opponent in this charge, and that he could throw him from the saddle without much trouble. Hardly any knight in that realm was equal to Sir Gawaine in strength and skill. Indeed, he had never yet been knocked from his horse in combat, except by King Arthur. So when the two rode at each other, Sir Gawaine was certain that his opponent would fall before him. But it was not so. In that charge Sir Gawaine’s spear broke into many pieces, but the spear of the Sable Knight held firm. Sir Gawaine was thrown violently out of the saddle and struck the dust with a terrible crash. He was so astonished by the fall that it seemed to him not that he had fallen from his saddle, but that the earth had risen up and struck him. He lay there for a while, stunned by the blow and by his astonishment.

But when he heard the shouts of the people on the castle wall, he quickly got up from the dust. He was so filled with rage and shame that he seemed like a man gone wild. He drew his sword and rushed furiously at his enemy, meaning to cut him down by sheer strength. The other knight, seeing him come at him like this, at once leaped from his own saddle, drew his sword, and set himself ready either to attack or to defend. They lashed at each other, wheeling this way and that, and struck with such fury that the blows were terrible to watch. When Sir Ewaine saw how fierce the fight was, he set spurs to his horse and pushed it between the two fighting knights. He cried out loudly, “Sir Knights! Sir Knights! What is this? There is no cause here for such a desperate battle.” But Sir Gawaine cried out furiously, “Let be! Let be! Stand aside! This quarrel is no business of yours.” And the Sable Knight said, “On horseback or on foot, I am ready to meet that knight at any time.”

But Sir Ewaine said, “Not so. You will fight no more in this quarrel. Shame on you, Gawaine! Shame on you for seeking such a desperate quarrel with a knight who only met you in a friendly way, in a fair contest!”

Then Sir Gawaine saw that Sir Ewaine was completely fair and right. So he put his sword away without a word, though he was close to tears at the shame of his defeat. The Sable Knight put his sword away too, and so peace was made between the two.

Then the Sable Knight said, “I am glad this quarrel is over. I can see, Messires, that you are knights of great nobility and fine breeding. So I would like us to be friends and companions from now on, not enemies. I beg you to come with me a short way from here, where I have set up my lodging. There we can rest and refresh ourselves in my pavilion.”
To this Sir Ewaine said, “I thank you for your courtesy, Sir Knight, and we will gladly go with you.” And Sir Gawaine said, “I agree.” So the three knights left the field of battle at once.

When they came to the edge of the forest, Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine saw a very fine pavilion of green silk set up beneath a tree. Around the pavilion were many attendants of all kinds, dressed in green and white. Sir Gawaine saw from this that the knight who had overthrown him must surely be a man of very high rank, and this comforted him greatly. Then the esquires of the three knights came and took off the helmets, each esquire for his own knight, so that the knights could be comfortable. When this was done, Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine saw that the Sable Knight had a very handsome face. It was ruddy, and his hair was as red as copper. Then Sir Ewaine said to him, “Sir Unknown Knight, my companion here is Sir Gawaine, son of King Urien of Gore, and I am Ewaine, the son of King Lot of Orkney. Now I ask you, in the same way, to tell us who you are.”
“Ha,” said the other, “I am glad you are such famous and royal knights, for I am also of royal blood. I am Sir Marhaus, the son of the King of Ireland.”

Sir Gawaine was very glad to learn how high in rank the knight was who had overthrown him. He said to Sir Marhaus, “Messire, I swear that you are one of the most terrible knights in the world. Today you have done to me what only one other knight in all the world has ever done, and that is King Arthur, who is my uncle and my lord. Now you must certainly come to the Court of King Arthur. He will be wonderfully glad to see you, and perhaps he will make you a Knight of his Round Table—and there is no honor in all the world that is so great.” He spoke without thinking, and then he remembered. He struck his fist against his forehead and cried out, “Aha! Aha! Who am I to invite you to the Court of King Arthur, when only yesterday I was disgraced and banished from it?”

Then Sir Marhaus felt very sorry for Sir Gawaine, and he asked about the trouble that weighed on him. Sir Ewaine told Sir Marhaus all about the quarrel, and at this Sir Marhaus felt even sorrier for Sir Gawaine. He said, “Messires, I like you both very much, and I would gladly join you as a companion in the adventures you are about to undertake. For now I need not stay here any longer. You must know that I was bound to defend those ladies who attacked my shield, until I had overthrown seven knights on their behalf. I must tell you that Sir Gawaine was the seventh knight I have overthrown. Now that I have overthrown him, I am released from my duty and may go with you.”

Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine were astonished that any knight should be under so strange a duty as to defend those who attacked his shield. They begged Sir Marhaus to tell them why he had been bound to such a pledge. So Sir Marhaus said, “I will tell you. This is how it happened. Some time ago I was traveling in these parts with a hawk on my wrist. I was dressed very lightly, in holiday clothes. I wore a tunic of green silk and hose, one leg green and one white. I had nothing to defend myself with but a light shield and a short sword. I came to a stream of water, very deep and swift, and I saw before me a stone bridge crossing it. The bridge was so narrow that only one horseman could cross at a time. So I rode onto the bridge, and I was partway across when I saw a knight in armor coming the other way. Behind the knight, on a pillion seat, sat a very fair lady with golden hair and a very proud manner. When that knight saw me on the bridge, he cried out, ‘Get back! Get back, and let me pass!’ But I would not do this. I said, ‘Not so, Sir Knight. I have come so far onto this bridge that I surely have the right of way to finish crossing, and it is for you to wait and let me cross.’ But the knight would not do so. He at once got ready to fight and came against me on the bridge, meaning either to kill me or to drive me back to the other end. But he could not do this, for I defended myself very well with my light weapons. I pushed my horse against his horse and drove him backward off the bridge and into the water. The horse, the knight, and the lady all fell into it together with a terrible uproar.

“At this the lady shrieked loudly, and both she and the knight were close to drowning. The knight was dressed completely in armor, so he could not lift himself above the water. Seeing their danger, I leaped from my horse into the water. With great effort, and at great risk to myself, I was able to bring them both to the shore.

“But that lady was very offended with me, for her fine clothes were wet through and spoiled by the water, and she scolded me fiercely. I knelt down before her and begged her pardon with all humility, but she kept on scolding me. Then I offered to do any penance she might set for me. At this the lady seemed to soften, for she said, ‘Very well, I will set you a penance.’ When her knight had recovered, she said, ‘Come with us.’ So I mounted my horse and followed them. After we had gone a long way, we came to this place, and here she gave me her command. ‘Sir Knight,’ she said, ‘this castle belongs to me and to this knight, who is my lord. This shall be your penance for the insult you have given me. You shall take your shield and hang it in that sycamore tree over there. Every day I will send some of my own damsels out from the castle, and they shall insult that shield. You shall not only put up with whatever insult they offer, but you shall defend them against all comers, until you have overcome seven knights.’
“So I have done until this morning, when you, Sir Gawaine, came here. You are the seventh knight I have fought, and since I have overcome you, my penance is now ended and I am free.”

Then Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine told Sir Marhaus how glad they were that his penance was complete, and all three were very well pleased with one another. Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine stayed that night in the pavilion of Sir Marhaus. The next morning they got up, washed themselves in a forest stream, and left that place.
So they entered the forest once more and made their way along certain paths, not knowing where they led. They traveled all that morning and until the afternoon came.

As they traveled, Sir Marhaus said suddenly, “Messires, do you know where we have come to?” “No,” they said, “we do not.” Then Sir Marhaus said, “This part of the forest is called Arroy, and it is also called ‘The Forest of Adventure.’ It is well known that when a knight, or a party of knights, enters this forest, they will surely meet with some sort of adventure. Some come out of it with honor, and others fail.” And Sir Ewaine said, “I am glad we have come here. Now let us go forward into this forest.”

So the three knights and their esquires went on through that woodland, where the silence was so deep that the tread of their horses on the ground was hardly heard. There was no song of any bird and no sound of any voice, and hardly any light reached into the gloom of that wood. The knights said to one another, “This is truly a very strange place, and perhaps a place of enchantment.”

When they had come into the very middle of these dark woods, they suddenly saw a fawn as white as milk on the path before them. Around the fawn’s neck was a collar of pure gold. The fawn stood and looked at them, but when they came near, it turned and ran along a very narrow path. Then Sir Gawaine said, “Let us follow that fawn and see where it goes.” And the others said, “Agreed.” So they followed the narrow path until they suddenly came to a little open lawn, bright with sunlight. In the middle of the lawn was a fountain of water. There was no fawn to be seen, but, behold, beside the fountain sat a wonderfully beautiful lady, dressed all in green. The lady was combing her hair with a golden comb, and her hair was as black as a raven’s wing. On her arms she wore marvelous bracelets of emeralds and opal stones set in finely worked gold. Her face was as white as ivory, and her eyes were as bright as jewels set in ivory. When the lady saw the knights, she stood up and laid aside her golden comb. She tied up the locks of her hair with ribbons of scarlet silk, and then she came to the knights and greeted them.

Then the three knights got down from their horses at once, and Sir Gawaine said, “Lady, I believe you are not of mortal kind, but of the fairy folk.” To this the lady said, “Sir Gawaine, you are right.” Sir Gawaine wondered that she knew his name so well. Then he said to her, “Lady, who are you?” and she answered, “My name is Nymue, and I am the chief of those Ladies of the Lake of whom you may have heard. It was I who gave King Arthur his sword Excalibur, for I am very friendly to King Arthur and to all the noble Knights of his Court. That is why I know you all. And I know that you, Sir Marhaus, will become one of the most famous Knights of the Round Table.” All three wondered at the lady’s words. Then she said, “Please tell me, what is it you seek in these parts?” And they said, “We seek adventure.” “Well,” she said, “I will lead you to an adventure, but it is Sir Gawaine who must take it on.” And Sir Gawaine said, “That is very glad news.” Then the lady said, “Take me up behind you on your saddle, Sir Gawaine, and I will show you that adventure.” So Sir Gawaine took the lady up behind him on the saddle, and behold, she brought with her a fragrance such as he had never known before. It was so delicate that it seemed to Sir Gawaine that the forest itself gave off the perfume the Lady of the Lake brought with her.

So the Lady of the Lake led them by many winding ways out of that part of the forest. She led them along various roads and paths until they came out into an open country, rich and pleasant to look at. She led them up a very high hill, and from the top they looked down on a fertile, level plain, like a table spread out before them. In the middle of the plain they saw a noble castle built all of red stone and red bricks. Beside it was a small town, also built of red bricks.

As they sat on their horses at the top of the hill, they suddenly saw a knight in red armor come out from a grove of trees. They saw him ride about the meadow in front of the castle, and they saw him challenge those inside the castle. Then the drawbridge of the castle was suddenly let down, and ten knights in full armor came out. They saw those ten knights attack the one knight in red armor, and they saw the one knight attack the ten. For a while the ten held out against the one, but he attacked them so fiercely that he struck down four of them very quickly. Then the rest broke and fled from him, and the Red Knight chased them about the meadow with great fury. They saw him strike one man out of his saddle, and then another, and another, until only two of the knights were left.
Sir Gawaine said, “What a wonderful thing to watch!” But the Lady of the Lake only smiled. “Wait a little longer,” she said.

So they waited, and they saw that the Red Knight struck down all his enemies except those two. When he had put those two in great danger of their lives, he suddenly sheathed his sword and gave himself up to them. They saw the two knights bring the Red Knight to the castle, and when they had brought him there, a lady on the castle wall shouted at him with great violence of language. They saw the two knights take the Red Knight and tie his hands behind his back. They tied his feet beneath his horse’s belly, and they drove him away from that place.

They saw all this from the top of that hill, and the Lady of the Lake said to Sir Gawaine, “There you will find your adventure, Sir Gawaine.” And Sir Gawaine said, “I will go,” and the Lady of the Lake said, “Do so.”
Then, behold, she vanished from their sight, and they were greatly amazed.

chapters.title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 5
paragraphs: _How Sir Gawaine met Sir Pellias, and how he promised to help him with the Lady Ettard._

After the wonderful lady had vanished from their sight, the three knights stood for a little while completely astonished. They could hardly believe what their eyes had seen. Then Sir Gawaine spoke. “Truly, that was a strange thing that happened to us. In all my life I have never known such a marvel. It is plain that some fine adventure lies in what we have seen. So let us ride down into that valley, where we will surely find out what it all means. I swear I have hardly ever seen a knight as fearsomely strong as the one who just fought that battle. So I cannot understand why he gave himself up to his enemies, when he had almost won the victory over them.”
Sir Ewaine and Sir Marhaus agreed that it would be good to go down and ask what the sight they had witnessed could mean.
So the three of them and their attendants rode down into the valley.
They rode on until they came to a clearing among the trees. There they saw three fine tents standing together. One was made of white cloth, the second of green cloth, and the third of scarlet cloth.

As the three companions came near the tents, two knights came out to meet them. Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine saw the shields of the two and knew at once that they were Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte. Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte knew Sir Gawaine and Sir Ewaine just as quickly. Each side was greatly surprised to meet the other in so strange a place. When they came together they greeted one another joyfully and clasped hands with warm love and good fellowship.

Then Sir Gawaine introduced Sir Marhaus to Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte. The five knights went together into the tents, talking happily and pleasantly as they walked. In the tent of Sir Brandiles they found a good meal laid out, with white bread and wine of excellent flavor.

After a while Sir Gawaine said to Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte, “Sirs, a little while ago we saw a very strange thing. We stood together on top of that hill and looked down into this plain. There we saw a single knight dressed all in red armor, fighting ten knights. That one knight in red fought the ten so fiercely that he drove them all away from him, though they were so many and he was alone. I swear I have hardly ever seen a knight show such great skill in arms. Yet when he had beaten all but two of those knights, and was well on his way to a clear victory, he suddenly gave himself up to those two. He let them take him, bind him, and drive him shamefully from the field. Now, I beg you, tell me what it meant. Who was that knight who fought so great a battle and then surrendered so shamefully?”

At this Sir Brandiles and Sir Mador de la Porte gave no answer. They looked the other way, for they did not know what to say. When Sir Gawaine saw that they were embarrassed, he began to wonder more than ever what the matter meant, and he said, “What is this? Why do you not answer me? I order you to tell me what your looks mean, and who that red knight is!”
After a while Sir Mador de la Porte said, “I will not tell you, but you may come and see.”

Then Sir Gawaine began to think that there might be something here that was better not made public. Perhaps, he thought, he had best look into the matter alone. So he said to the other knights, “Wait here a little, Sirs, and I will go with Sir Mador de la Porte.”
So Sir Gawaine went with Sir Mador de la Porte, and Sir Mador led him to the white tent. When they got there, Sir Mador drew aside the curtains of the tent. “Go in!” he said, and Sir Gawaine went in.

Inside the tent he saw a man sitting on a couch of rushes covered with blue cloth. Soon he saw that the man was Sir Pellias. But Sir Pellias did not see him at first. He sat with his head bowed, like a man completely crushed by despair.
When Sir Gawaine saw who it was sitting on the couch, he was greatly amazed and cried out, “Ha! Is it you, Sir Pellias? Is it you?”

But when Sir Pellias heard Sir Gawaine’s voice and saw who had spoken to him, he gave a very bitter cry. He sprang to his feet and ran as far away as the walls of the tent would allow. Then he turned his face to the wall.

After a while Sir Gawaine spoke very sternly to Sir Pellias. “Sir, I am astonished and deeply ashamed that a Knight of King Arthur’s Royal Court and of his Round Table should behave so dishonorably, as I saw you behave today. It is hard to believe that a knight of such fame and nobility as you would let two unknown knights take and bind him, as you did today. How could you bring yourself to accept such insult and shame? Now I demand that you explain this matter to me.”
But Sir Pellias was silent and would not reply. Then Sir Gawaine cried out fiercely, “Ha! Will you not answer me?” And Sir Pellias shook his head.

Then Sir Gawaine spoke again, still very fiercely. “Sir! You will answer me one way or another! Either you will tell me the meaning of your shameful conduct, or you will fight me to the death. I will not let you bring such shame on King Arthur and his Round Table without defending their honor and good name myself. Once you and I were dear friends. But unless you clear yourself at once, I will despise you and count you as my enemy.”

At this Sir Pellias spoke like a man nearly out of his mind. “I will tell you everything,” he said. Then he confessed it all to Sir Gawaine. He told everything that had happened to him since he left the May Court of Queen Guinevere to begin this adventure, and Sir Gawaine listened in great amazement. When Sir Pellias had finished telling all that had befallen him, Sir Gawaine said, “Truly, this is very strange. I cannot understand how you came to be so caught up in the charms of this lady, unless she has bewitched you with some powerful enchantment.”
To this Sir Pellias said, “Yes, I believe I have been bewitched. I am completely beside myself in this matter, and I cannot control my passion.”

Then Sir Gawaine thought for a long while, considering the matter very seriously. By and by he said, “I have a plan, and it is this. I will go to the Lady Ettard myself and look carefully into this affair. If I find that anyone has tangled you in enchantments, I will make that person suffer greatly for it. I will not allow another enchanter to trick you, as one has already tricked Merlin the Wise.”
Then Sir Pellias said to Sir Gawaine, “How will you manage to come into the presence of the Lady Ettard?”

Sir Gawaine replied, “I will tell you. We two will trade armor, and I will go to the castle wearing yours. When I get there, I will say that I beat you in a fight and took your armor from you. Then they will perhaps let me into the castle to tell my story, and I will have a chance to speak with her.”
Then Sir Pellias said, “Very well. It shall be as you say.”

So Sir Pellias called an esquire, and Sir Gawaine called his own esquire. The two of them took the armor off Sir Pellias and dressed Sir Gawaine in it. After that, Sir Gawaine mounted the horse of Sir Pellias and rode openly into the field where Sir Pellias had paraded before.

Now, the Lady Ettard happened to be walking at that time on a platform inside the castle walls, from which she looked down into the meadow. When she saw a red knight parading in the meadow, she thought Sir Pellias had come back again. She was annoyed and insulted beyond all measure. So she said to those near her, “That knight upsets me so badly that I fear I will fall ill from it if he comes here many more times. I wish I knew how to be rid of him. Only an hour ago I sent ten good knights against him, and he beat them all very swiftly, to their great shame and to mine.”

So she beckoned to the Red Knight, and when he had come near the castle walls, she said to him, “Sir Knight, why do you keep coming here to trouble and insult me like this? Can you not understand that the more often you come to tease me in this way, the more I hate you?”

Then Sir Gawaine lifted the visor of his helmet and showed his face, and the Lady Ettard saw that the Red Knight was not Sir Pellias. Sir Gawaine said, “Lady, I am not the one you take me for, but another. Look! I wear your enemy’s armor on my body, so you can see that I have beaten him. You must think it hardly likely that I could wear his armor unless I won it from him by force of arms. So you need trouble yourself no more about him.”

Then the Lady Ettard could only believe that this knight, whom she did not know, had truly defeated Sir Pellias in a fight and taken his armor from him. She was very astonished that such a thing could have happened. To her, Sir Pellias had seemed one of the greatest knights in the world, so she wondered who this knight could be who had beaten him in battle. She ordered several of her attendants to go out and bring that red knight into the castle and to treat him with great honor. He must surely be one of the greatest champions in the world.

So Sir Gawaine came into the castle and was brought before the Lady Ettard, who stood in a very large and noble hall. The hall was lit by seven tall windows of colored glass, and it was hung all around with rich tapestries of excellent quality. Sir Gawaine was greatly amazed at the splendor of everything he saw there.

Sir Gawaine had taken the helmet off his head and carried it under his arm, against his hip. His head was bare, so that everyone there could see his face plainly. They all saw that he was very handsome, with eyes as blue as steel, a high, curved nose, and dark, rich hair and beard. His bearing was steady and proud, so that those who looked at him were awed by his knightly appearance.

Then the Lady Ettard came to Sir Gawaine and gave him her hand, and he knelt and kissed it. The lady spoke to him very graciously. “Sir Knight, it would give me great pleasure if you would tell us your name and declare your rank to us.”
To this Sir Gawaine replied, “Lady, I cannot tell you these things at present, for I am just now bound by a vow of secrecy on those points. So I beg you to be patient with me for a little while.”

Then the Lady Ettard said, “Sir Knight, it is a great pity that we may not know your name and rank. Even so, though we do not yet know who you are, I hope you will give us the pleasure of your company for a while. I hope you will be kind enough to stay in this humble place for two or three days, while we offer you such refreshment as we are able to give.”

Now a very unfortunate thing happened. The Lady Ettard had grown so fond of the necklace of emeralds, opal stones and gold that she had borrowed from Sir Pellias that she never let it leave her, by day or by night. So she was wearing it at that moment, hanging about her neck and throat. As she talked with Sir Gawaine, he looked at that necklace, and its enchantment began to take a strong hold on him. He began to feel as though his heart were being drawn out of his chest toward the Lady Ettard, so that before long he could not keep his eyes from her. The more he looked at the necklace and the lady, the more the enchantment of the jewel took hold of his spirit. So when the Lady Ettard spoke so kindly to him, he was very glad to accept her kindness. Gazing at her with great longing, he said, “Lady, you are very gentle to offer me such courtesy. I will be glad beyond measure to stay with you for a short while.”

At these words the Lady Ettard was very pleased. She said to herself, “Truly, this knight, though I do not know who he may be, must be a champion of extraordinary strength and great achievements. If I can persuade him to stay in this castle as my champion, I will surely gain great credit by it. I will have someone to defend my rights who must surely be the greatest knight in all the world.” So she showed every charm and grace of manner to please Sir Gawaine, and Sir Gawaine was completely delighted by her kindness.

Sir Engamore was there at that time, and he was deeply troubled. The more courtesy Sir Gawaine received from the Lady Ettard, the more Sir Engamore sank into sorrow and distress, so much so that it was pitiful to see. He said to himself, “Before these foreign knights came here, the Lady Ettard was very kind to me, and was willing to take me as her champion and lord. But first Sir Pellias came and beat me, and now this strange knight comes and beats him. In the presence of such a great champion as this, I have become nothing in her sight.” So Sir Engamore left that place and went to his private room, where he sat down alone in great sorrow.

The Lady Ettard had ordered a very noble and splendid feast to be prepared for Sir Gawaine and herself. While it was being made ready, she and Sir Gawaine walked together in the pleasure garden of the castle. It was a pleasant, shady place where flowers grew in great numbers, and many birds sang sweetly among the blossoms of the trees. As Sir Gawaine and the lady walked there together, the attendants stood a little way off and watched them. They said to one another, “It would surely be a very good thing if the Lady Ettard took this knight as her champion, and if he stayed here in Grantmesnle forever.”

Sir Gawaine and the lady walked together, talking cheerfully, until sunset. By then supper was ready, and they went in and sat down to eat. While they ate, a number of handsome pages played harps before them, and several damsels sang sweetly to the music. Sir Gawaine’s heart swelled with joy. He said to himself, “Why should I ever leave this place? Look, I have been banished from King Arthur’s Court. Why should I not set up a Court of my own here, one that might in time be as glorious as his?” The Lady Ettard looked so beautiful to him that this seemed a wonderfully pleasant idea.
Now let us turn to Sir Pellias.

After Sir Gawaine had left him, Sir Pellias began to fear that he had not been wise. At last he said to himself, “Suppose Sir Gawaine forgets his duty to me when he meets the Lady Ettard. It seems she may have some powerful charm that could draw Sir Gawaine’s heart to her. If he comes under the spell of such enchantment, he may forget his duty to me and betray the honor of his knighthood.”

The more Sir Pellias thought about this, the more troubled he became. So when evening had fallen, he called an esquire to him and said, “Go and bring me the clothing of a black friar, for I want to go to the castle of Grantmesnle in disguise.” The esquire did as he was told and brought him the clothing, and Sir Pellias dressed himself in it.

By that time darkness had covered the whole earth, so no one could have recognized Sir Pellias even if they had seen his face. He went to the castle, and the people there, who thought he was a black friar, as he looked to be, let him in by the small back gate.

As soon as Sir Pellias was inside the castle, he began to ask carefully where he could find the knight who had come there that afternoon. The people in the castle still thought he was a friar of the black order, and they said to him, “What do you want with that knight?” Sir Pellias answered, “I have a message for him.” They said, “You cannot see that knight just now. He is at supper with the Lady Ettard, and he is talking pleasantly with her.”

At this Sir Pellias grew very angry, for he hated the thought that Sir Gawaine was making merry with the Lady Ettard at that very moment. He said sternly, “I must speak with that knight right now, so I order you to take me to him without delay.” Then the people of the castle said, “Wait here, and we will see whether that knight is willing to have you come to him.”

One of the attendants went to the place where Sir Gawaine sat at supper with the Lady Ettard, and he said, “Sir Knight, a black friar has come here who demands to speak with you right away. He will not be refused, and he keeps repeating his demand.”

At this Sir Gawaine felt a great pang of conscience, for he knew he was not treating Sir Pellias honorably. He wondered whether this black friar might be a messenger from his friend. Yet he could not see how he could refuse to speak with such a messenger. So after thinking for a while, he said, “Bring the black friar here, and let him give me his message.”

So the attendants brought Sir Pellias, dressed as a black friar, to the outer room next to where Sir Gawaine sat at supper with the lady. For a little while Sir Pellias did not go in. He stood behind the curtain of the ante-room and watched them, because he wanted to be sure whether Sir Gawaine was true to him or not.

Everything in the room where the knight and the lady sat was decorated with extraordinary splendor. It was lit by several score of wax candles, which gave off a delightful perfume as they burned. As Sir Pellias stood behind the curtains, he saw Sir Gawaine and the Lady Ettard sitting at the table together, and he saw how happy they were in each other’s company. He saw that Sir Gawaine and the lady drank wine from the same cup, and that the cup was made of gold. As he watched the two of them making merry together, he was filled with great anger and outrage, for now he understood that Sir Gawaine had betrayed him.

After a while he could hold himself back no longer. He took five steps into the room and stood before Sir Gawaine and the Lady Ettard. They looked up at him in great surprise, and he threw back the hood from his face, and they knew him. The Lady Ettard shrieked loudly, crying out, “I have been betrayed!” Sir Gawaine sat completely silent, for he had not a single word to say to the lady or to Sir Pellias.

Then Sir Pellias went close to the Lady Ettard with such a fierce look on his face that she could not move for fear. When he stood next to her, he seized the necklace of emeralds, opal stones and gold so violently that the clasp broke and he pulled it from her neck. He said, “This is mine, and you have no right to it!” And with that he thrust it into his bosom. Then he turned on Sir Gawaine where he sat and said, “You are false both to your knighthood and to your friendship, for you have betrayed me completely.” Then he raised his arm and struck Sir Gawaine in the face with the back of his hand so hard that the mark of his fingers was left in red across Sir Gawaine’s cheek.

Sir Gawaine turned pale as ashes and cried out, “Sir, I have truly betrayed you, but you have insulted me so much that we are even.” Sir Pellias answered, “Not so. The injury I gave you is only on your cheek, but the injury you gave me is on my heart. Nevertheless, I will answer to you for the insult I have done you. But you must also answer to me for the wrong you have done me by betraying me.”

Then Sir Gawaine said, “I am willing to answer to you in full.” And Sir Pellias said, “You will indeed.” With that he turned and left the place, and he did not even look back at Sir Gawaine or at the Lady Ettard.

But now that the Lady Ettard no longer wore the magic collar around her neck, Sir Gawaine felt nothing of the great enchantment that had drawn him so strongly to her before. He now disliked her as much as he had liked her before. So he said to himself, “How could I have betrayed my knighthood for this lady, and done so much harm to my friend?” He pushed back his chair violently and rose from the table, meaning to leave her.

But when the Lady Ettard saw what he meant to do, she spoke to him in great anger. She was deeply insulted that he had deceived her when he said he had defeated Sir Pellias. She said hotly, “You may go, and I am quite willing for you to do so, for you lied when you told me you had defeated Sir Pellias. Now I see that he is both a stronger and a nobler knight than you. He struck you as if you were his servant, and you still wear the marks of his fingers on your cheek.”

At this Sir Gawaine was furiously angry and filled with shame at what had happened to him. He said, “Lady, I think you have bewitched me and brought me to this point of dishonor. As for Sir Pellias, look out into that meadow tomorrow and see whether I do not leave a deeper mark on him than he ever left on me.” Then he left the room, went down into the courtyard, and called to the attendants there to bring him his horse. They did as he ordered, and he rode out into the night at once.

He was very glad of the darkness of the night, for it seemed easier to bear his shame in the dark. When he came to the glade of trees, he would not enter the pavilion where his friends were. When Sir Ewaine and Sir Marhaus came out to him and told him to come in, he would not, but stayed outside in the darkness. He said to himself, “If I go in where there is light, perhaps they will see the mark of Sir Pellias’s hand on my face.”
So he stayed outside in the darkness and told them to go away and leave him alone.

Once they had gone, Sir Gawaine summoned his esquire and said, “Help me out of this red armor and carry it to the pavilion of Sir Pellias, because I hate the sight of it.” The esquire obeyed, and Sir Gawaine paced back and forth all night long, his mind and heart heavy with trouble.

chapters.title: The Story of Sir Pellias: Chapter 6
paragraphs: _How the Lady of the Lake Took Back Her Necklace From Sir Pellias._

When the next morning came, Sir Gawaine called his esquire to him and said, “Bring me my armor and help me put it on.” The esquire did so. Then Sir Gawaine said, “Help me onto my horse,” and the esquire did that as well. It was still very early. The grass was bright and sparkling with dew, and the little birds sang so loudly and gladly that anyone would have been glad to be alive. So once Sir Gawaine was in his armor and on horseback, he began to feel braver, and the dark clouds that had hung over him lifted a little. He spoke to his esquire in a stronger voice. “Take this glove of mine to Sir Pellias and tell him that Sir Gawaine is riding in the meadow in front of the castle, and that he challenges Sir Pellias to meet him there, on horseback or on foot, whichever that knight prefers.”

The esquire was very surprised. Sir Gawaine and Sir Pellias had always been such close friends that there were hardly any friends like them in all that land, and everyone spoke of their love for one another. But the esquire kept his thoughts to himself and only said, “Will you not eat something before you go to battle?” Sir Gawaine answered, “No, I will not eat until I have fought. Now go and do as I told you.”

So Sir Gawaine’s esquire went to Sir Pellias in his tent. He gave the knight Sir Gawaine’s glove and told him the message. Sir Pellias said, “Tell your master that I will come out to meet him as soon as I have eaten my breakfast.”

News of the challenge reached Sir Brandiles, Sir Mador de la Porte, Sir Ewaine and Sir Marhaus, and these knights were very troubled by it. Sir Ewaine said to the others, “Gentlemen, let us go and find out what this is about.” So the four knights went to the white tent where Sir Pellias was eating his breakfast.
When they stood before Sir Pellias, Sir Ewaine said to him, “What is this quarrel between my kinsman and you?” Sir Pellias answered, “I will not tell you. Leave it alone and do not meddle in it.”
Then Sir Ewaine said, “Would you really fight your friend in earnest?” Sir Pellias replied, “He is no friend of mine any longer.”

Then Sir Brandiles cried out, “It is a great pity that a quarrel should come between friends like you and Sir Gawaine. Will you not let us make peace between you?” But Sir Pellias answered, “You cannot make peace. This quarrel cannot be stopped until it has been fought to its end.”
Then the knights saw that their words were useless, and they left Sir Pellias and went away.

When Sir Pellias had finished his breakfast, he called an esquire named Montenoir and ordered him to help him put on the red armor that he had worn all this time. Montenoir did so. Then, dressed in that armor, Sir Pellias rode out into the meadow before the castle, where Sir Gawaine was riding up and down. The four other knights came to him once more and begged him to make peace with Sir Gawaine. But Sir Pellias would not listen to them, so they left him again, and he rode out into the field before the castle of Grantmesnle.

By now a great crowd of people had gathered on the castle walls to watch the combat, for the news had spread all around the place. People had also learned that the knight who would fight Sir Pellias was the famous royal knight Sir Gawaine, the son of King Lot of Orkney and a nephew of King Arthur. So everyone was eager to see such a famous knight in battle.

The Lady Ettard also came down to the walls and stood in a smaller tower that looked over the field. From there she saw that Sir Pellias wore the necklace of emeralds, opals and gold over his armor. Her heart went out to him because of it, and she hoped that he would win.

Then each knight took his place where he thought best. They set their spears and shields and made themselves ready. When they were fully prepared, Sir Marhaus gave the signal to begin. At once each knight left his place and charged at the other as fast as lightning, so fiercely that the ground thundered and shook under their horses’ hooves. They met squarely in the middle of the field, each striking the other right in the center of his shield. In that clash the spear of Sir Gawaine broke all the way to the hand-guard, but the spear of Sir Pellias held firm. Sir Gawaine was thrown from his saddle with terrible force. He hit the ground so hard that he rolled three times in the dust, and then he lay completely still, as though he were dead.
At this, all the people on the walls shouted aloud, for it was a truly splendid combat.

Then the four knights who had been watching hurried to Sir Gawaine where he lay, while Sir Pellias rode back and waited on his horse close by. Sir Ewaine and Sir Gawaine’s esquire quickly unlaced Sir Gawaine’s helmet. And, look! His face was the color of ashes, and they could not see that he was breathing.

Then Sir Marhaus said, “I believe you have killed this knight, Sir Pellias.” Sir Pellias said, “Do you think so?” “Yes,” said Sir Marhaus, “and I think it a great pity.” Sir Pellias answered, “He has not suffered more than he deserved.”

At these words Sir Ewaine was filled with anger and cried out, “Sir Knight, I think you forget who this knight is. He is not only a fellow companion of the Round Table, to whom you have sworn complete brotherhood. He is also the son of a king and the nephew of King Arthur himself.”
But Sir Pellias kept a very steady face and answered, “I would not be sorry for this even if that knight were a king in his own right instead of the son of a king.”
Then Sir Ewaine raised his voice in great anger and shouted at Sir Pellias, “Go away, or something terrible will happen to you!” “Very well,” said Sir Pellias, “I will go.”
With that he turned his horse and rode away. He entered the woods and was soon out of their sight.

Then the others lifted up Sir Gawaine and carried him to the tent that had lately been Sir Pellias’s, and they laid him on Sir Pellias’s bed. It was more than an hour before he came to himself again, and for much of that time those beside him believed that he was dead.

But none of those knights knew the truth. Sir Pellias had been so badly wounded in the side in that fight that there was no hope he would live beyond that day. Although Sir Gawaine’s spear had broken, and Sir Pellias had thrown him down completely, the head of Sir Gawaine’s spear had pierced Sir Pellias’s armor. It had gone into his side and broken off there, so that a piece of iron as long as the breadth of a palm was left inside his body, a little above the waist. So, while Sir Pellias sat talking so firmly to those four knights, he was in terrible pain, and blood was running down inside his armor in great amounts. Because of the blood he had lost and the great agony he suffered, his head swam and felt as light as a feather the whole time he talked with them. But he said not a word to them about the terrible wound he had received. Instead he rode away proudly into the forest.
But once he was in the forest, he could hold back no longer. He began to groan bitterly and cried out, “Alas! Alas! I have surely received my death-wound in this battle!”

That morning the damsel Parcenet had ridden out to fly a young falcon, and a dwarf who belonged to the Lady Ettard had ridden with her for company. They were riding along the edge of the forest, not far from Grantmesnle, where the thick woods began and the thin woods ended. There the damsel heard a voice in the woods, crying out in great sorrow. She stopped and listened, and soon she heard the voice again, moaning loudly. Then Parcenet said to the dwarf, “What is that I hear? Surely it is someone crying in grief. Let us go and see who is making such a sad moan.” The dwarf said, “It shall be as you say.”

So the damsel and the dwarf went a little farther, and there they saw a knight sitting on a black horse beneath an oak tree. The knight was dressed completely in red armor, so Parcenet knew that it must be Sir Pellias. She saw that he was leaning the butt of his spear on the ground to hold himself up on his horse, for he would otherwise have fallen from weakness. And all the while he made the great moan that Parcenet had heard. Seeing him in such a sorry state, Parcenet was filled with pity and hurried to him, crying out, “Alas! Sir Pellias, what is wrong?”

Sir Pellias looked at her as though she were very far away. Because he was so faint, he saw her as if through thin water. He said very weakly, “Maiden, I am badly hurt.” She said, “How are you hurt, Sir Pellias?” He answered, “I have a terrible wound in my side. The point of a spear is still stuck there, about a palm’s breadth deep, so that it reaches almost to my heart. It seems to me that I will not live very long.”
At this the maiden cried out, “Alas! Alas! What is this!” She wept bitterly and wrung her hands in sorrow that such a noble knight should have come to such a terrible state.

Then the dwarf, seeing how deeply she was troubled by grief, said, “Damsel, I know of a place in this forest, though it is quite far from here, where a very holy hermit lives who is an exceptionally skilled healer. If we can bring this knight to the chapel where that hermit lives, I believe he may be helped back to health and comfort.”

Then Parcenet said, “Gansaret”—for Gansaret was the dwarf’s name—“Gansaret, let us take this knight there as quickly as we can. I tell you truly that I care for him very much.” “Very well,” said the dwarf, “I will show you where the chapel is.”

So the dwarf took the bridle of Sir Pellias’s horse and led the way through the forest, while Parcenet rode beside Sir Pellias and held him up in his saddle. From time to time Sir Pellias fainted from sickness and pain, and he would have fallen if she had not held him. So they went forward very sadly and so slowly that it was noon before they came to the thick and lonely part of the forest where the hermit lived.
When they reached that place, the dwarf said, “There, damsel, is the chapel I told you about.”

Then Parcenet lifted her eyes and saw a little chapel in the woods, built among the leafy trees. Around it was a small open lawn decked with flowers, and near the door of the hermitage was a fountain of water as clear as crystal. It was a hidden, lonely place, and very quiet and peaceful. In front of the chapel they saw a wild doe and her fawn grazing on the tender grass and herbs, without any fear of harm. When the dwarf, the maiden and the wounded knight came near, the doe and the fawn looked up with wide eyes and pricked up their large ears in wonder. But they did not run away, for they feared no harm, and soon they began to graze again. All around the chapel, in the branches of the trees, were great numbers of birds, singing and chirping cheerfully. The birds were waiting for the midday meal that the hermit used to throw to them.
(This was the same forest sanctuary where King Arthur had come when he was so badly wounded by Sir Pellinore, as was told earlier in this history.)

As the maiden, the dwarf and the wounded knight came near the chapel, a little bell began to ring very sweetly, and its sound echoed all through the quiet woods, for it was now the hour of noon. Sir Pellias heard the bell as though from far away. First he said, “Where have I come?” and then he managed to make the sign of the cross. Parcenet crossed herself, and the dwarf knelt down and crossed himself. When the bell stopped ringing, the dwarf cried out in a loud voice, “Hello! Hello! Here is someone who needs help!”

Then the door of the sanctuary opened, and a very old and respected man came out, with a long white beard like finely combed wool. And look! As he came out, all the birds that had been waiting flew around him in great numbers, for they thought he had come to feed them. So the hermit had to brush the little birds away with his hands as he walked over to the place where the three stood.

When he reached them, he asked who they were and why they had brought the wounded knight there. Parcenet told him how things stood with them, and how they had found Sir Pellias so badly wounded in the forest that morning and had brought him here.

When the hermit had heard her whole story, he said, “It is well, and I will take him in.” He took Sir Pellias into his cell, and when they had helped lay him on the bed, Parcenet and the dwarf went home again.

After they had gone, the hermit examined Sir Pellias’s wound, and Sir Pellias lay in a deep faint. The faint was so deep that the hermit saw it was the faint of death and that the knight was close to the end. He said, “This knight must surely die very soon, for I can do nothing to save him.” So he left Sir Pellias’s side at once and hurried to prepare the last sacrament, as is given to a noble knight who is dying.

While the hermit was busy with this, the door suddenly opened, and a very strange lady came into the room. She was dressed all in green, and around her arms she wore bracelets of emeralds and opals set in gold. Her hair was very soft and entirely black, and it was tied with a cord of crimson ribbon. The hermit saw that her face was as white as ivory and that her eyes shone like jewels set in ivory, and so he knew that she was no ordinary mortal.

The lady went straight to Sir Pellias and leaned over him so that her breath touched his forehead. She said, “Alas! Sir Pellias, that you should lie like this.” “Lady,” said the hermit, “you may well say ‘Alas,’ for this knight has only a few minutes left to live.” The lady answered, “Not so, holy man, for I tell you that this knight will live a long while yet.” When she had said this, she bent down and took from around his neck the necklace of emeralds, opals and gold that circled it, and she hung it around her own neck.
When the hermit saw what she did, he said, “Lady, what is this that you are doing, and why do you take that ornament from a dying man?”

But the lady answered very calmly, “I gave it to him, so I am only taking back what is mine. Now please let me stay with this knight for a little while, because I have great hope that I can bring him back to life.”
Then the hermit was doubtful and said, “Will you try to heal him by magic?” And the lady said, “If I do, it will not be black magic.”
So the hermit was satisfied. He went away and left the lady alone with Sir Pellias.

Once the lady was alone with the wounded knight, she began to do several very strange things. First she brought out a loadstone of great power and held it to the wound. And behold, the iron of the spear-head came out of the wound, and Sir Pellias groaned with great pain as it came. When the spear-point was out, blood burst from the wound like a crimson fountain. But the lady quickly pressed a fragrant napkin of fine linen against the wound and stopped the blood. It bled no more, for she held it inside the veins with powerful spells of magic. With the blood stopped, the lady took a small crystal bottle from her bosom. It was filled with a blue elixir that had a very unusual fragrance. She poured some of this elixir between the cold, gray lips of the knight. As soon as it touched his lips, life began to enter his body once more. In a little while he opened his eyes and looked about him with a very strange expression. The first thing he saw was the lady dressed in green standing beside him. She was so beautiful that he thought he might have died and gone to Paradise, so he said, “Am I dead, then?”

“No, you are not dead,” said the lady, “but you have been terribly close to death.” “Then where am I?” said Sir Pellias. She replied, “You are in a deep part of the forest, and this is the cell of a saintly hermit.” At this Sir Pellias said, “Who has brought me back to life?” The lady smiled and said, “I did.”

For a little while Sir Pellias lay very quiet. Then after a time he spoke and said, “Lady, I feel very strange.” “Yes,” said the lady, “that is because you now have a different life.” Then Sir Pellias said, “What has happened to me?” And the lady said, “This is how it is. To bring you back to life, I gave you a drink of an _elixir vitæ_. So now you are only half what you were before. By one half you are mortal, and by the other half you are fay.”

Then Sir Pellias looked up and saw that the lady wore around her neck the collar of emeralds, opals and gold that he had worn before. And behold, his heart went out to her with great warmth, and he said, “Lady, you say that I am half fay, and I can see that you are wholly fay. Now I beg you to let me stay near you from now on.” And the lady said, “It will be as you ask. That is the very reason I let you come close to death and then brought you back to life.”

Then Sir Pellias said, “When may I go with you?” And she said, “In a little while, when you have had something to drink.” “How can that be?” said Sir Pellias. “I am as weak as a little child.” The lady answered, “When you have drunk some water, your strength will return to you, and you will be completely well and whole again.”

So the Lady of the Lake went out and soon came back, carrying an earthen jug filled with water from the fountain close by. When Sir Pellias had drunk that water, he felt his strength suddenly come back to him entirely.

Yet he was not at all as he had been before. His body now felt as light as air, and his soul was filled with a pure joy such as he had never felt in his life. So he got up at once from his bed of pain and said, “You have given life to me again, and now I give that life to you forever.”

Then the lady looked at him and smiled with great kindness. She said, “Sir Pellias, I have thought tenderly of you ever since the day I saw you, in your young knighthood, drink a cup of milk at a cottager’s hut in this forest. The day was warm and you had set aside your helmet. A young milkmaid, brown-faced and barefoot, came and brought you a bowl of milk, and you drank it with great appetite. That was the first time I saw you, although you did not see me. Since then I have felt great friendship for all your fellowship at King Arthur’s Court, and for King Arthur himself, all for your sake.”

Then Sir Pellias said, “Lady, will you accept me as your knight?” and she said, “Yes.” Then Sir Pellias said, “May I kiss you?” And she said, “Yes, if it pleases you.” So Sir Pellias kissed her on the lips, and so they pledged themselves to each other.
Now let us return to Parcenet and the dwarf:

After those two had left the hermitage in the woodland, they made their way again toward Grantmesnle. When they had almost come out of the forest, at a place not far from the glade of trees where those fellow knights had made their camp, they met one of those knights in half-armor. That knight was Sir Mador de la Porte. Parcenet called to him by name and said, “Alas! Sir Mador, a short time ago I left a hermit’s cell in the forest, where I left Sir Pellias wounded almost to death. I fear he has only a little while to live.”
Then Sir Mador de la Porte cried out, “Ha! Maiden, what is this you tell me? That is very hard to believe, for when Sir Pellias left us this morning he showed no sign of any wound or sickness.”
But Parcenet replied, “All the same, I saw him myself, lying in great pain and sorrow. Before he fainted into the sleep of death, he told me himself that he had the iron of a spear in his side.”
Then Sir Mador de la Porte said, “Alas! Alas! That is sad news! Now, damsel, with your leave, I will go and hurry to my companions to tell them.” And Parcenet said, “Please do.”
So Sir Mador de la Porte hurried to the pavilion where his companions were, and he told them the news he had heard.

By this time Sir Gawaine had fully recovered from the violent fall he had suffered that morning. So when he heard the news that Sir Mador de la Porte brought, he struck his hands together and cried out loud, “Woe is me! What have I done! First I betrayed my friend, and now I have killed him. I will go out at once to find him and beg his forgiveness before he dies.”
But Sir Ewaine said, “What are you going to do? You are not yet fit to make any journey.”

Sir Gawaine said, “I do not care, for I am determined to go and find my friend.” He would not allow any of his companions to go with him. He called his esquire to bring his horse, mounted it, and rode away alone into the forest, heading west and mourning with great sorrow as he went.

Late in the afternoon, when the sun was sinking toward its setting and the light fell as red as fire through the forest leaves, Sir Gawaine came to the hermit’s cell, which stood in a silent and lonely part of the forest. He saw that the hermit was outside his cell, digging in a little garden of lentils. When the hermit saw the armed knight ride onto the lawn in the red light of the setting sun, he stopped digging and leaned on his trowel. Then Sir Gawaine came closer, and from his horse he told the holy man what business had brought him.

To this the hermit said, “A lady came here several hours ago. She was dressed all in green and looked very unusual, so it was easy to see that she was fay. By certain charms of magic that lady cured your friend, and after she had healed him, the two of them rode away into the forest together.”

Then Sir Gawaine was greatly amazed and said, “This is a very strange thing you tell me, that a dying knight should be brought back to life in so short a time, and should ride away so suddenly from his bed of pain. Now please tell me where they went.” The hermit said, “They went west.” When Sir Gawaine heard this, he said, “I will follow them.”

So he rode away and left the hermit gazing after him. As he rode on, twilight began to fall quickly, and soon the woods grew very dark and strange all around him. But as the darkness came down, a wonderful marvel happened. Behold, a pale blue light appeared in front of Sir Gawaine. It went ahead of him and showed him the way, and he followed it, full of wonder.

After he had followed the light for a very long time, he suddenly came to the place where the woods ended and a wide, open plain of great size began. The whole plain was lit by a strange glow like the light of a clear full moon, although no moon was shining at that time. In that pale, silver light Sir Gawaine could see everything with wonderful clearness. He saw that he was on a plain covered all over with flowers of many kinds. Their scent so filled the night that it seemed to press on his chest with a great pleasure. He saw that a great lake lay in front of him, very wide and still. All these things looked so strange in that light that Sir Gawaine knew he had come into a land of faëry. So he rode among the tall flowers toward the lake, half afraid, for he did not know what was going to happen to him.

As he drew near the lake, he saw a knight and a lady coming toward him. When they came close, he saw that the knight was Sir Pellias, and that his face looked exceedingly strange. He saw that the lady was the one he had seen before, dressed all in green, when he had traveled in the Forest of Adventure with Sir Ewaine and Sir Marhaus.

When Sir Gawaine first saw Sir Pellias, he was filled with great fear, for he thought he was looking at a spirit. But when he saw that Sir Pellias was alive, a joy as great as that fear came into his heart, and he hurried toward Sir Pellias. When he came near, he leaped from his horse, crying out, “Forgive me! Forgive me!” with great passion. Then he would have taken Sir Pellias in his arms, but Sir Pellias drew away from Sir Gawaine’s touch, though not in anger. Sir Pellias spoke in a voice that was thin and clear as silver, as though it came from far away. He said, “Do not touch me, for I am not as I was before. I am not all human, but part fay. As for my forgiveness, I forgive you whatever harm I may have suffered at your hands. And more than that, I give you my love, and I hope greatly for your joy and happiness. But now I am going away from you, dear friend, and perhaps I will not see you again. So I leave this with you as my last request: go back to King Arthur’s Court and make your peace with the Queen. Then you can bring them news of all that has happened to me.”
Then Sir Gawaine cried out in great sorrow, “Where are you going?”
And Sir Pellias said, “I am going to that wonderful city of gold and blue that lies in that valley of flowers.”
Then Sir Gawaine said, “I see no city, only a lake of water.”
Sir Pellias replied, “Even so, there is a city there, and I am going to it, so now I say farewell to you.”

Then Sir Gawaine looked into the face of Sir Pellias and saw again the strange light in it. It looked very unusual, for it was white like ivory, and his eyes shone like jewels set in ivory. A smile lay on his lips and never grew or faded but always stayed the same. (For those of that kind always looked this way and smiled in this manner. They were the Lady of the Lake, Sir Pellias, and Sir Launcelot of the Lake.)

Then Sir Pellias and the Lady of the Lake turned and left Sir Gawaine where he stood. They went toward the lake and entered it. When the feet of the horse of Sir Pellias touched the water of the lake, behold, Sir Pellias was gone, and Sir Gawaine saw him no more. He stood there for a long time, weeping with great passion.
So ends the story of Sir Pellias.

But Sir Gawaine returned to the Court of King Arthur as he had promised Sir Pellias he would. He made his peace with Queen Guinevere, and after that, although the Queen did not love him, there was peace between them. And Sir Gawaine told these things to the Court of King Arthur, and all men marveled at what he said.
And only twice after that was Sir Pellias ever seen by any of his former companions.
And Sir Marhaus was made a Companion of the Round Table and became one of its foremost knights.
And the Lady Ettard took Sir Engamore back into favor, and that summer they were married, and Sir Engamore became lord of Grantmesnle.
So ends this story.

chapters.title: The Story of Sir Gawaine: Chapter 1
paragraphs: _Here is the story of Sir Gawaine, and how he showed such wonderful loyalty to King Arthur, his lord, that I do not believe anyone has ever seen the like of it before._

_Sir Gawaine could be very rough and harsh in his manner, and he spoke so bluntly that his words hid the gentle nature within him. Yet beneath that proud manner he had much courtesy. At times he was so polished in his bearing and so soft in his speech that many people called him the Knight of the Silver Tongue._
_So here you will read how his loyalty to King Arthur brought him such high reward that almost anyone in the world might envy his great good fortune._
_How a White Hart Appeared Before King Arthur, and How Sir Gawaine and His Brother Gaheris Went After It, and What Happened to Them on That Quest._

One time King Arthur, together with Queen Guinevere and all his Court, was traveling through a part of his kingdom that lay far from Camelot. The King journeyed in very great state, and Queen Guinevere had her own Court about her, with many esquires and pages. With the knights, lords, and ladies who attended them, there were more than a hundred and twenty people with the King and Queen.

It happened that the weather was very warm at that time. When midday came, the King commanded his people to put up a number of pavilions where they could rest until the heat of the day had passed. So the attendants set up three pavilions in a pleasant glade at the edge of the forest.

When this was done, the King ordered the tables for their midday meal to be set in the shade of the trees in that glade. A gentle wind was blowing and many birds were singing, so it was very pleasant to sit in the open air.

The attendants of the Court did as the King commanded. The tables were set on the grass in the shade, and the King and Queen and all the lords and ladies of their Courts sat down to that cheerful meal.

They were feasting happily, with much laughter and pleasant talk among themselves, when all at once a great outcry came from the woods nearby. A very beautiful white hart burst out of the leafy thicket, chased by a white hound just as beautiful. There was not a hair on either animal that was not as white as milk, and each wore a gold collar around its neck that was lovely to see.

The hound chased the white hart with a great deal of barking and bellowing, and the hart fled in terror. In this way they ran three times around the table where King Arthur and his Court sat at their meal. Twice during that chase the hound caught the hart and bit its haunch, and each time the hart leaped away. Everyone at the table saw blood in two places on its haunch where the hound had bitten it. Each time the hart escaped from the hound, and the hound ran after it with such yelling that King Arthur and Queen Guinevere and all their Court were annoyed by the noise and uproar the two creatures made. Then the hart fled back into the forest by another path, and the hound chased it, and both were gone. The baying of the hound grew fainter and fainter as it ran away into the woods.

The King and Queen and their Court had not yet recovered from their astonishment when a knight and a lady suddenly appeared at the place in the forest where the hart and the hound had come out. The knight had a very lordly bearing, and the lady was exceedingly beautiful. The knight wore half-armor, and the lady was dressed in green as though for the hunt. The knight rode a dapple-gray war horse, and the lady rode a spotted palfrey. Two esquires, also dressed for the hunt, were with them.

Seeing the large company gathered there, they stopped as though surprised. While they stood so, another knight suddenly appeared on a black horse. He was dressed in full armor, and he seemed very angry. He charged at the knight in half-armor and struck him such a bad blow with his sword that the first knight fell from his horse and lay on the ground as though dead. The lady who was with him shrieked in great grief.

Then the knight in full armor on the black horse rode to the lady and seized her. He lifted her from her palfrey and laid her across the front of his saddle, and then he rode back into the forest. The lady screamed so violently that it was pitiful to hear her. But the knight paid no attention to her shrieking, and carried her away by force into the forest.
Once the knight and the lady had disappeared, the two esquires hurried over and helped the wounded knight onto his horse. Then they too rode off into the forest and vanished.

King Arthur and his Court saw all this from a distance. They were too far away to stop the knight on the black horse from carrying the lady off into the forest, and they could not help the knight in half-armor whom they had seen struck down. So they were deeply grieved at what they had seen, and did not know what to think of it. Then King Arthur said to his Court, “Messires, is there not one of you who will follow this adventure and find out what it means? Will someone make that knight tell us why he behaved as he did?”

Then Sir Gawaine said, “My lord, I would be very glad to take this adventure upon myself, if I have your leave.” King Arthur said, “You have my leave.” Then Sir Gawaine said, “My lord, I would also like you to let me take my younger brother, Gaheris, with me as my esquire on this task. He is growing quickly toward manhood, and yet he has never seen any great adventure in arms.” So King Arthur said, “You have my leave to take your brother with you.”
Gaheris was very glad at this, for he had an adventurous spirit, and the thought of going with his brother on this quest gave him great pleasure.
So the two of them went to Sir Gawaine’s pavilion, and there Gaheris helped Sir Gawaine put on his armor, as his esquire should. Then they rode out on the quest Sir Gawaine had taken up.

They traveled onward for a long distance, following the direction the hart had taken when it ran away from the hound. From time to time they met some of the forest folk, and they asked them where the white hound and the white hart had gone, and where the knight and the lady had gone. In this way they followed the adventure steadily.

After a long ride, late in the afternoon, they suddenly heard a great uproar of fighting, like a fierce battle in progress. They followed the sound, and after a while they came to an open meadow with fair, level grass. There they saw two knights fighting with great fury and a deadly purpose. Sir Gawaine said, “What is this? Let us go and see.” So he and Gaheris rode forward to where the two knights were fighting. As they came near, the two knights stopped their combat and rested on their weapons. Then Sir Gawaine said, “Ha! Messires, what is going on? Why do you fight each other so fiercely?” One of the knights answered Sir Gawaine, “Sir, this does not concern you.” The other said, “Do not meddle with us, for this battle is our own choice.”

“Messires,” said Sir Gawaine, “I would be very sorry to interfere in your quarrel. But I am chasing a white hart and a white hound that came this way, and also a knight who has carried off a lady along the same road. I would be greatly in your debt if you would tell me whether you have seen either of them.”

Then the knight who had spoken first said, “Sir, this is a very strange matter, for we were fighting just now, as you saw, over that very white hart and hound, and the knight and the lady. This is how it happened. We two are brothers, and we were riding together in great friendship when that hart and that hound came this way. My brother said he very much hoped the white hart would escape from the hound, and I said I hoped the hound would catch the hart and bring it down. Then that knight came by with the lady as his captive, and I said I would follow that knight and rescue the lady, and my brother said that he would take on that adventure.

“We fell into a dispute over these points. I felt great affection for the hound, and my brother felt just as great a regard for the white hart. I thought that since I had spoken first, I should have the right to follow the adventure. But my brother was fond of the hart, and he thought that since he was the elder of us two, he had the better right to the adventure. So we quarreled, and soon we began the fight you saw us in.”

Sir Gawaine was greatly astonished at this. He said, “Messires, I cannot understand how so great a quarrel could arise from so small a dispute. Truly, it is a great pity for two brothers to quarrel as you have done, and to give each other such painful cuts and wounds as I see you have both received.”
“Messires,” said the second knight, “I think you are right, and I am now very ashamed of that quarrel.” The other said, “I too am sorry for what I have done.”

Sir Gawaine then asked, “Sirs, would you be so kind as to tell me your names?” The first knight answered, “My name is Sir Sorloise of the Forest.” The other said, “And mine is Sir Brian of the Forest.”
Then Sir Sorloise said, “Sir Knight, I would think it a great courtesy if you would tell me who you are.”

“I would be very glad to,” said Sir Gawaine, and he told them his name and rank. When they heard who Sir Gawaine was, the two knights were astonished and delighted, for no one in all the courts of chivalry was more famous than Sir Gawaine, the son of King Lot of Orkney. So the two brothers said, “It is truly a great joy to us to meet so famous a knight as you, Sir Gawaine.”

Then Sir Gawaine said, “Sir Knights, that hart and that hound came only a short while ago to where King Arthur and Queen Guinevere and their Courts of lords and ladies were feasting. There we all saw that knight seize the lady and carry her off as his captive. So my brother and I have come out on King Arthur’s command to find out what we saw. I would think it a great courtesy if you would give up this fight and go peacefully to the King’s Court. Tell him what you saw, and how you quarreled, and how we met. Otherwise I will have to fight you both myself, and that would be a great pity, for you are weary from battle and I am fresh.”
Then the two knights said, “Sir, we will do as you wish, for we have no desire to fight so powerful a knight as you.”
So the two knights left and went to the Court of King Arthur as Sir Gawaine had ordered, and Sir Gawaine and his brother rode on with their adventure.

Soon they came near a great river, and there they saw a single knight ahead of them in full armor. He carried a spear in his hand and had a shield hanging from his saddle-bow. Sir Gawaine hurried forward and called out to the knight, and the knight stopped and waited until Sir Gawaine caught up with him. When Sir Gawaine reached him, he said, “Sir Knight, have you seen a white hart and a white hound pass this way? And have you seen a knight carrying off a captive lady?”

The knight answered, “Yes, I saw them both, and I am following them right now, meaning to find out where they are going.” Then Sir Gawaine said, “Sir Knight, I ask you not to follow this adventure any farther, for I have taken it up myself. I want you to give it up so that I may take it on in your place.” “Sir,” said the other knight, speaking very hotly, “I do not know who you are, nor do I care very much. As for following this adventure, I tell you that I intend to follow it to the end, and I will do so, no matter who tries to stop me.”
Then Sir Gawaine said, “Messire, you will not go forward on this adventure unless you first deal with me.” The knight said, “Sir, I am quite willing.”

So each knight took the position on the field that seemed best to him. Each got ready to defend himself and set his shield and his spear. When they were fully prepared, they charged at each other, rushing together at great speed and with such an uproar that the ground trembled and shook beneath them. They met in the middle of the course, and the strange knight’s spear burst into small pieces, but Sir Gawaine’s spear held. So he hurled that knight out of his saddle with such force that he struck the ground with a blow like an earthquake.
Then Sir Gawaine rode back to where his enemy lay, for that knight was unable to get up. He took the helmet from the fallen knight’s head and saw that the knight was very young and handsome.

When the fresh air touched the knight’s face, he soon woke from his faint and came back to his senses. Sir Gawaine said, “Do you yield to me?” The knight said, “I do.” Then Sir Gawaine said, “Who are you?” The knight said, “I am called Sir Alardin of the Isles.” “Very well,” said Sir Gawaine. “Then I command you to do this. You shall go to the Court of King Arthur and give yourself up to him as a captive of my skill in arms. You are to tell him all you know about the hart and the hound and the knight and the lady. And you shall tell him everything that has happened to you in this attack.”
The knight promised that he would do as he was told. Then the two parties parted, one going one way and the other going the opposite way.

After that, Sir Gawaine and his brother Gaheris rode a long distance, until at last they came out of a woodland onto an open plain. It was now about sunset. In the middle of the plain they saw a very stately and noble castle with five towers, and it was very strong.

Right there they saw a sight that filled them with great sorrow. They saw the dead body of the white hound lying beside the road like any carcass. The hound had been pierced through with three arrows, so they knew it had been killed very violently.

When Sir Gawaine saw the beautiful hound lying dead, he was filled with sorrow. “What a pity,” he cried, “that this noble hound has been killed! I think it was the most beautiful hound I have ever seen in my whole life. Someone has certainly done a terrible and treacherous thing to it, because of the white hart it was chasing. Now I make a vow. If I can find that hart, I will kill it with my own hands, because the hound met its death in that chase.”
After that they rode on toward the castle. As they came close, they saw the white hart with the golden collar grazing on the meadow in front of it.

As soon as the white hart saw the two strangers, it fled at great speed toward the castle and ran into its courtyard. When Sir Gawaine saw the stag, he chased after it as fast as he could, and Gaheris followed his brother.

So Sir Gawaine chased the white hart into the courtyard of the castle, and from there it could not escape. Then Sir Gawaine jumped down from his horse, drew his sword, and killed the hart with a single blow.
He did this in great haste. But when it was done, and too late to undo, he was very sorry for what he had done.

All this noise brought out the lord and the lady of the castle. The lord had a proud and noble look, and the lady was graceful and very beautiful. Sir Gawaine looked at her and thought he had hardly ever seen so lovely a lady. For that reason he was sorrier than ever that he had killed the white hart in his haste.

But when the lady of the castle saw the white hart lying dead on the stone pavement of the courtyard, she clapped her hands together and screamed so shrilly and so loudly that it hurt the ears to hear it. She cried out, “Oh, my white hart, are you dead?” And then she burst into passionate weeping. Sir Gawaine said, “Lady, I am very sorry for what I have done, and I wish I could undo it.” Then the lord of the castle said to Sir Gawaine, “Sir, did you kill that stag?” “Yes,” said Sir Gawaine. “Sir,” said the lord of the castle, “you have done very wrong in this, and if you will wait a little, I will take full revenge on you.” Sir Gawaine answered, “I will wait for you as long as you please.”

Then the lord of the castle went into his chamber and put on his armor, and in a little while he came out looking very fierce. “Sir,” said Sir Gawaine, “what is your quarrel with me?” The lord of the castle said, “You have killed the white hart that was so dear to my lady.” Sir Gawaine replied, “I would not have killed the white hart, except that because of it the white brachet was treacherously killed.” At this the lord of the castle grew angrier than ever. He rushed at Sir Gawaine and struck him by surprise. The blow cut through the shoulder plate of his armor, and through the flesh to the bone of his shoulder, so that Sir Gawaine was in terrible pain. Then Sir Gawaine was filled with rage at the pain of the wound, and he struck the knight such a blow that it cut through his helmet and into the bone beneath. The knight fell to his knees from the force of the blow, and he could not get up again. Then Sir Gawaine seized his helmet and ripped it off his head.
Then the knight said in a weak voice, “Sir Knight, I beg mercy of you, and I yield myself to you.”
But Sir Gawaine was furious with anger because of the unexpected blow he had received and the great pain of his wound. So he would not show mercy, and instead raised his sword to kill the knight.

Then the lady of the castle saw what Sir Gawaine meant to do. She broke away from her damsels, ran forward, and threw herself upon the knight to shield him with her own body.
