At that moment Sir Gawaine was already striking and could not stop his blow. Even so, he managed to turn his sword in his hand so that its edge did not strike the lady. But the flat of the sword hit her on the neck with a very painful blow, and the blade cut her a little, so that blood ran down her smooth white neck and over her kerchief. With the force of the blow, the lady fell and lay on the ground as though she were dead.
When Sir Gawaine saw this, he thought he had killed the lady in his haste, and he was terrified at what he had done, so he cried, “Woe is me! What have I done?”
“Alas!” said Gaheris. “That was a very shameful blow you struck, and the shame of it is mine too, because you are my brother. Now I wish I had not come with you to this place.”
Then Sir Gawaine said to the lord of the castle, “Sir, I will spare your life, for I am very sorry for what I have done in my haste.”

But the knight of the castle was filled with bitterness, because he thought his lady was dead. He cried out in despair, “I do not want your mercy now, for you are a knight without mercy and without pity. Since you have killed my lady, who is dearer to me than my life, you may kill me too. That is the only service you can do me now.”

But by now the lady’s damsels had come to where she lay, and the chief among them cried out to the lord of the castle, “Ah, sir, your lady is not dead. She has only fainted, and she will soon recover.”

When the lord of the castle heard this, he wept with pure joy, for now that he knew his lady was alive he could not contain himself. Sir Gawaine came to him, lifted him up from the ground, and kissed him on the cheek. Then some others came and carried the lady to her chamber, and there in a little while she woke from her faint and was hardly the worse for the blow she had received.

That night Sir Gawaine and his brother Gaheris stayed with the knight and the lady. When the knight learned who Sir Gawaine was, he felt it a great honor to have so famous a knight in his castle. So they feasted together that evening in great friendship.
When they had eaten and rested, Sir Gawaine spoke. “Sir, please explain to me what the white hart and the white brachet meant, since they are what drew me into this adventure.”
The lord of the castle, whose name was Sir Ablamor of the Marise, said, “I will.” And he spoke as follows:
“You must know, sir, that I have a brother who has always been very dear to me. When I took this lady as my wife, he married her sister.

“My brother lived in a castle near this one, and we were close friends. But one day my lady and my brother’s lady were riding together through this forest, talking pleasantly. Just then a lady appeared before them. She was very beautiful and had a very strange look, for I do not think that either my lady or her sister had ever seen anyone like her.

“This strange lady brought the two ladies a white hart and a white brachet. She held the hart and the hound each by a silver chain fastened to a golden collar around its neck. She gave the white hart to my lady and the white brachet to my lady’s sister. Then she went away, leaving them very glad.

“But their gladness did not last long. Ever since then there has been nothing but quarreling between my brother and me, and between my lady and her sister. The white hound has always hunted the white hart to destroy it, so my lady and I have been deeply angry with my brother and his lady for not keeping the white brachet at home. Several times we have tried to kill the hound, and so my brother and his lady have been just as angry with us.

“Today it happened that I was near the edge of the forest to the east of us when I heard a great uproar in the woods. Soon the white hart that belonged to my lady came fleeing through the trees, with the white brachet that belonged to my brother’s lady chasing it. My brother and his lady and two squires followed swiftly after the hart and the brachet.
“I was very angry, for it seemed to me they were chasing the white hart to spite my lady and me, so I followed them as fast as I could.

“I came upon them at the edge of the woods, near some pavilions pitched in the shade of a grove of trees in the middle of the meadow. There, in my anger, I struck my brother such a blow that I knocked him from his horse. Then I seized his lady, threw her across the front of my saddle, and carried her here to this castle. I have kept her here out of revenge, because they chased the white hart that belonged to my lady. My lady loved that hart more than anything else in the world except myself.”

“Sir,” said Sir Gawaine, “this is a very strange matter. Now I ask you to tell me what that lady looked like, the one who gave the white hart and the white hound to those two ladies.” “Messire,” said the knight, “she was dressed all in crimson. Around her throat and arms she wore many gold ornaments set with stones of many colors. Her hair was red like gold and was held in a net of gold, her eyes were very black and shone brightly, and her lips were like coral. She had a very strange look.”

“Ha!” said Sir Gawaine. “From this description I think that lady could be none other than the sorceress Vivien. She spends all her time doing mischief like this by her enchantments, out of pure spite. Indeed, I think it would be a very good thing if she were put out of this world, so that she could do no more such mischief. But tell me, Messire, where is that lady now, your wife’s sister?” “Sir,” said the knight, “she is in this castle, a prisoner of honor.” “Well,” said Sir Gawaine, “now that both the hart and the hound are dead, surely you can have no more anger toward her and your brother. So I beg you to let her go free, and to return to friendship and good will with each other, as it was between you before.” And the lord of the castle said, “Sir, it shall be so.”
So he set the lady free then, and afterward there was friendship between them, just as Sir Gawaine had arranged.
The next day Sir Gawaine and his brother Gaheris returned to the King’s Court, and he told King Arthur and his Court everything that had happened, hiding nothing from them.

Queen Guinevere was very displeased when she heard how Sir Gawaine had shown no mercy to that knight and how he had struck the lady with his sword. She said quietly to one of those standing near her, “It seems to me a very strange thing for a belted knight to do, to refuse mercy to a fallen enemy and to strike a lady with his sword. I think any sword that had drawn blood from a lady in such a way would be dishonored forever. And I cannot believe that anyone who would strike a lady like that could think himself free of blame before his vow of knighthood.”

Sir Gawaine overheard this and was very angry about it, but he hid his anger at that time. Only after he had gone away did he say to his brother Gaheris, “I believe that lady hates me with all her heart. But some day I will show her that I have more courtesy and gentleness in me than she thinks. As for my sword, since she believes it was dishonored by that blow, I will not use it any more.” So he took the sword out of its sheath, broke it across his knee, and flung it away.

All this has been told to prepare for what follows, for there you will learn what great deeds of nobility Sir Gawaine could do when he had to. Those of you who have read this story may feel, as Queen Guinevere did, that Sir Gawaine was not truly courteous, as a belted knight should have been, in the adventure told above.

chapters.title: The Story of Sir Gawaine: Chapter 2
paragraphs: _How King Arthur Got Lost in the Forest, and How He Met with a Very Strange Adventure in a Castle He Came To._

Some time after this, King Arthur was at Tintagalon on certain business of state. Queen Guinevere and her Court, together with the King’s Court, traveled from Camelot to Carleon. There they stayed until the King should finish his business at Tintagalon and join them.

It was springtime, and everything felt bright and cheerful, so King Arthur was seized by a great longing for adventure. He called a favorite esquire named Boisenard and said, “Boisenard, this day is so pleasant that I can hardly hold myself still for the joy of it. My heart feels ready to burst with wanting something. So I am of a mind to go wandering about the countryside, with only you for company.”
Boisenard answered, “My lord, I know of nothing that would please me more.”
King Arthur said, “Very well. Let us leave this place so that no one knows we have gone. We will ride to Carleon and surprise the Queen by arriving when she does not expect us.”
So Boisenard fetched armor that carried no coat of arms and dressed the King in it. Then the two of them rode out together, and no one knew that they had left the castle.

When they reached the open fields, King Arthur whistled and sang and joked and laughed and made merry. He was like a war-horse let loose on the grass, which loves the sunshine and the warm air and becomes a colt again.

After a while they came to the forest and rode on in great content. They took this path and then that path, for no reason except that the day was so bright and cheerful. Before long they had lost their way in the tangle of the woods and did not know where they were.

Finding themselves lost, they rode more carefully, trying first one way and then another. But they could not find their way out of the tangle. Night fell, and they still did not know where they were. Everything grew dark and gloomy, and the woods all around them were full of strange and unfamiliar sounds.
Then King Arthur said, “Boisenard, this is a very puzzling situation, and I do not know how we will find a place to sleep tonight.”
Boisenard said, “My lord, if you give me leave, I will climb one of these trees and see whether I can spot any sign of a home in this wilderness.” King Arthur said, “Do so, I ask you.”
So Boisenard climbed a very tall tree, and from the top he saw a light a long way off. He said, “My lord, I see a light in that direction.” Then he climbed down from the tree again.

King Arthur and Boisenard rode toward the place where Boisenard had seen the light. Soon they came out of the forest into an open place, where they saw a huge castle with several tall towers. It looked grim and forbidding. The light Boisenard had seen came from this castle. The two rode up to it, and Boisenard shouted and pounded on the castle gate. At once a porter came and asked what they wanted. Boisenard said to him, “Fellow, we want to come in and stay tonight, for we are weary.” The porter asked, “Who are you?”—speaking roughly and rudely, for in the darkness he could not tell what sort of men they were. Then Boisenard said, “This is a knight of very high rank, and I am his esquire. We have lost our way in the forest, and now we have come here looking for shelter.”
“Sir,” said the porter, “if you know what is good for you, you will sleep in the forest rather than come into this place. This is no good shelter for wandering knights.”
At this King Arthur spoke to the porter, for what the porter had said made him very curious. He said, “No, we will not go away. We demand to stay here tonight.”
Then the porter said, “Very well, you may come in.” He opened the gate, and they rode into the courtyard of the castle.

At the noise of their arrival, many lights appeared inside the castle, and a number of servants came running out. Some helped King Arthur and Boisenard to get down from their horses, and others led the horses away. Still others brought basins of water for them to wash in. When they had washed their faces and hands, other servants led them into the castle.

As they entered, they heard a great noise of many people talking and laughing together, mixed with the sound of singing and harp music. They came into the great hall and saw that it was lit by a great number of candles and tapers and torches. A crowd of people sat at a table spread for a feast. At the head of the table sat a knight who was well along in years, with hair and beard as white as milk. Yet he was very strong and sturdy, with wonderfully broad shoulders and a deep chest. He looked stern and forbidding. He was dressed completely in black, and around his neck he wore a gold chain with a gold locket hanging from it.

When this knight saw King Arthur and Boisenard come into the hall, he called out to them in a booming voice and told them to come and sit with him at the head of the table. They did so, and those sitting there made room for them, so that they sat beside the knight.

King Arthur and Boisenard were very hungry, so they ate eagerly and enjoyed the entertainment they were given. All the while the knight kept them company with pleasant talk, speaking of whatever would amuse them most. After a while the feast ended, and they stopped eating.

Then, all of a sudden, the knight said to King Arthur, “Messire, you are young and high-spirited, and I do not doubt that you have a great heart. What do you say to a little sport between the two of us?” King Arthur looked at the knight very steadily. He thought the man’s face was not as old as it seemed, for his eyes were very bright and shone like sparks of light. So he was doubtful, and he said, “Sir, what sport do you have in mind?” At this the knight burst into laughter and said, “It is a very strange sport. You and I will test each other to see how much courage each of us has.” King Arthur asked, “How will we test that?” The knight answered, “This is what we will do. You and I will stand in the middle of this hall, and you will have leave to try to cut off my head. If I can take that blow without dying of it, then I will have leave to cut off your head in the same way.”
At these words King Arthur felt great dread, and he said, “That is very strange sport for two men to take part in.”

When King Arthur said this, everyone in the hall burst out laughing, and they laughed as though they would never stop. When they had grown a little quieter, the knight of the castle said, “Sir, are you afraid of that sport?” King Arthur grew angry and said, “No, I am not afraid. No man has ever had reason to say that I showed fear of anyone.” “Very well,” said the knight of the castle. “Then let us try the sport I spoke of.” And King Arthur said, “I am willing.”

Then Boisenard came to King Arthur where he stood and said, “My lord, do not agree to this. Let me take on this challenge in your place, for I am sure that some great treachery is planned against you.” But King Arthur said, “No. No man will take my danger upon himself. I will face my own danger without asking anyone else to bear it.” Then he said to the knight of the castle, “Sir, I am ready for the sport you spoke of. But who is to strike the first blow, and how shall we draw lots for it?” “Messire,” said the knight of the castle, “we will draw no lots. Since you are the guest in this place, you will have the first try at this sport.”

With that, the knight stood up and took off his black robe. Underneath he wore a shirt of fine linen, very skillfully worked, and red hose. Then he opened the linen shirt at the throat and turned the collar down, to leave his neck bare for the blow. He said, “Now, Sir Knight, you will have to strike well if you want to win at this sport.”

But King Arthur showed no fear of the task. He stood up and drew Excalibur, so that the blade flashed with dazzling brightness. Then he measured his distance, raised the sword, and struck the knight of the castle on the neck with all his might. And behold! The blade cut through the knight’s neck with wonderful ease, and the head flew from the body and landed far away.

But the knight’s body did not fall. Instead it stood up and walked to where the head lay. The hands of the body picked up the head and set it back on the shoulders, and behold! The knight was as sound and whole as he had ever been in his life.

At this all the people in the castle shouted and made great merriment. They told King Arthur that it was now his turn to try the sport. So the King got ready, taking off his surcoat and opening his shirt at the throat, as the knight of the castle had done. Boisenard cried out in great sorrow. Then the knight of the castle said, “Sir, are you afraid?” King Arthur said, “No, I am not afraid. Every man must die some time, and it seems that my time has now come. I am to give up my life in this foolish way, through no fault of my own.”
Then the knight of the castle said, “Well, stand back a little way, so that I do not strike you too close and so spoil the power of my blow.”

So King Arthur stood in the middle of the hall, and the knight of the castle swung his sword several times without striking. Several times he also laid the blade on King Arthur’s neck, and it was very cold. Then King Arthur cried out in great anger, “Sir, it is your right to strike, but I beg you not to torment me like this.” “No,” said the knight of the castle. “It is my right to strike when it pleases me, and I will not strike before then. If it pleases me, I will torment you for a long while before I kill you.” So he laid his sword on King Arthur’s neck several more times, and King Arthur said no more but bore the torment with a very steady spirit.

Then the knight of the castle said, “You seem to be a very brave and honorable knight, and I have a mind to make an agreement with you.” King Arthur asked, “What is that agreement?” “It is this,” said the knight of the castle. “I will spare your life for a year and a day, if you will give me your knightly word to return here at the end of that time.”
King Arthur answered, “Very well, I agree.” He promised on his knightly honor that he would come back when the year was over, and he swore this oath upon the cross-shaped hilt of Excalibur.

Then the knight of the castle said, “I will make another agreement with you.” “What is it?” said King Arthur. “My second agreement is this,” said the knight of the castle. “I will give you a riddle. If you can answer it when you return here, and make no mistake in your answer, then I will spare your life and set you free.” King Arthur asked, “What is the riddle?” The knight answered, “The riddle is this: What is it that a woman wants most of all in the world?”

“Sir,” said King Arthur, “I will try to find the answer to that riddle, and I thank you for sparing my life for so long and for giving me a chance to escape my death.” At this the knight of the castle smiled a very sour smile and said, “I do not offer this out of mercy toward you, but because I take pleasure in tormenting you. What joy can you have in living your life when you know you must surely die at the end of one short year? And what pleasure can you have even in that year, when you will be tormented by worry to find the answer to my riddle?”
Then King Arthur said, “I think you are very cruel.” And the knight said, “I do not deny it.”

So that night King Arthur and Boisenard slept at the castle, and the next day they went on their way. King Arthur was heavy at heart and troubled. Even so, he ordered Boisenard to say nothing of what had happened and to keep it secret. Boisenard did as the King commanded and said nothing about that adventure.

In the year that followed, King Arthur put his affairs in order. He also searched everywhere for the answer to the riddle. Many people gave him plenty of answers. One said that a woman most wanted wealth, and another said beauty. One said she wanted the power to please, and another said she most wanted fine clothes. One said this and another said that, but none of the answers seemed to King Arthur good or right for his purpose.

So the year went by until only two weeks remained. Then King Arthur could not bear to stay where he was any longer, for it seemed to him that his time was very near. He was filled with bitter anxiety, and he was restless to be gone.
So he called Boisenard to him and said, “Boisenard, help me put on my armor, for I am going away.”
Then Boisenard burst into tears and said, “My lord, do not go.”

At this King Arthur looked sternly at his esquire and said, “Boisenard, what is this? Would you tempt me to break my honor? It is not very hard to die, but it would be very bitter to live my life in dishonor. So tempt me no more, but do as I order and keep quiet. And if I do not return within a month from now, then you may tell everything that has happened. You may tell Sir Constantine of Cornwall that he is to search the papers in my cabinet, and there he will find everything that must be done if death should overtake me.”

So Boisenard put a plain suit of armor on King Arthur, though he could hardly see what he was doing for the tears streaming from his eyes. He fastened a surcoat with no coat of arms over the King’s armor and gave the King a shield with no device. Then King Arthur rode away without thinking where the road led him. Of everyone he met he asked what it was that a woman most wanted, and no one could give him an answer that seemed to be the right one. So he was in great doubt and anguish of spirit.

The day before King Arthur was to keep his promise at that castle, he was wandering through the nearby forest, deeply troubled in spirit, because he did not know what he could do to save his life. As he wandered, he suddenly came upon a small hut built beneath a spreading oak tree. The tree and the hut were so tangled together that it was hard to tell where one ended and the other began. Many large, mossy rocks lay all around it, and the King might easily have walked past the hut. But he saw smoke rising from it, as from a fire burning inside. So he went to the hut, opened the door, and stepped in. At first he thought no one was there. Then he looked again and saw an old woman sitting hunched over a small fire on the hearth. King Arthur had never seen such an ugly old hag as the one bending over that fire. Her ears were huge and flapped about, and her hair hung down around her head like snakes. Her face was so covered in wrinkles that there was not a single spot without one. Her eyes were watery and clouded over, and her eyelids were red, as if she were always weeping. She had only one tooth in her mouth, and the hands she held out to the fire were like claws of bone.
Then King Arthur greeted her, and she greeted him in return. She said to him, “My lord King, where do you come from? And why have you come to this place?”

King Arthur was greatly astonished that the old woman knew who he was. He said, “Who are you, that you seem to know me?” “That does not matter,” she said. “I am someone who wishes you well. So tell me what trouble has brought you here at this time.” So the King told the old woman all his trouble, and he asked her if she knew the answer to the riddle, “What is it that a woman most desires?” “Yes,” said the old woman, “I know the answer to that riddle very well. But I will not tell it to you unless you promise me something in return.”

At this King Arthur was filled with great joy that the old woman knew the answer to the riddle. But he was also full of doubt about what she would ask of him. So he said, “What must you have in return for that answer?”
Then the old woman said, “If I help you guess your riddle correctly, you must promise that I will become the wife of one of the knights of your Court. I will choose him when you return home again.”

“Ha!” said King Arthur. “How can I promise that on behalf of anyone else?” Then the old woman said, “Are the knights of your Court not noble enough to do that to save you from death?” “I believe they are,” said King Arthur. With that he thought for a long while, saying to himself, “What will my kingdom do if I die now? I have no right to die.” So he said to the old woman, “Very well, I will make that promise.”
The old woman spoke to the King again. “Here is the answer to your riddle: a woman most wants to have her own way.” King Arthur felt sure the answer was right.

Then the old woman said, “My lord King, you have been tricked by the knight who led you into this trouble. He is a great conjurer and a very wicked magician. He carries his life not in his body, but in a crystal globe that he wears in a locket hanging around his neck. That is why, when you cut the head from his body, his life stayed in the locket and he did not die. If you had destroyed that locket, he would have died at once.”
“I will remember that,” said King Arthur.

So King Arthur stayed with the old woman that night, and she refreshed him with food and drink and looked after him very well. The next morning he set out for the castle where he had made his promise, and his heart was more cheerful than it had been for a whole year.

chapters.title: The Story of Sir Gawaine: Chapter 3
paragraphs: _How King Arthur Defeated the Knight-Enchanter, and How Sir Gawaine Showed the High Nobility of His Knighthood._

When King Arthur came to the castle, the gate was opened to him at once, and he went in. Servants came and led him into the hall where he had been before. There he saw the knight of that castle, and a great crowd of people who had come to see how the adventure would end. When the knight saw King Arthur, he said, “Sir, have you come to keep your promise?” “Yes,” said King Arthur, “for that is the vow I made to you.” Then the knight of the castle said, “Sir, have you solved the riddle?” King Arthur said, “I believe I have.” The knight said, “Then let me hear your answer. But if you make any mistake, or if you guess wrongly, your life is forfeit.” “Very well,” said King Arthur. “So be it. This is the answer to your riddle: what a woman most desires is to have her own way.”
When the lord of the castle heard that King Arthur had guessed correctly, he did not know what to say or where to look. The others who were there saw too that the King had guessed right.

Then King Arthur stepped very close to the knight, with a stern look, and said, “Now, you traitor knight! A year ago you asked me to play a game with you. Now it is my turn to ask you to play a game with me. This is the game I want: you will give me the chain and locket that hang around your neck, and I will give you the collar that hangs around mine.”

At this, the knight’s face turned pale as ashes, and he made a sound like a hare when the hound seizes it. Then King Arthur grabbed him roughly by the arm, and he took hold of the locket and tore it from the knight’s neck. The knight shrieked very loudly, fell down upon his knees, and begged the King for mercy, and there was a great uproar in the hall. Then King Arthur opened the locket, and behold! Inside was a ball like crystal, very clear and shining. King Arthur said, “I will show no mercy,” and with that he hurled the ball down hard upon the stone floor, so that it broke with a loud crash. At that very moment the knight-conjurer gave a piercing, bitter cry and fell to the ground. When people ran to lift him up, they found that he was quite dead.

When the people of that castle saw their knight suddenly dead, and saw King Arthur standing there in the fury of his kingly majesty, they were so frightened that they shrank away from him. Then the King turned and walked out of the castle, and no one stopped him. He mounted his horse and rode away, and no one tried to block his path.

When the King had left the castle in this way, he went straight to the hut where the old hag lived, and he said to her, “You helped me greatly in my hour of need, so now I will keep the promise I made to you. I will take you to my Court, and you shall choose one of my knights for your husband. I think there is not one knight in all my Court who would not gladly do whatever is in his power to reward someone who has saved me as you have done today.”

With that he took the old woman and lifted her up onto the back of his horse behind the saddle. Then he mounted himself, and they rode away from that place. All the way, the King treated the old woman with the greatest courtesy, as though she had been a beautiful lady of the highest rank in the land. He showed her as much respect as if she had been a lady of royal blood.
In due time they reached the Court, which was then at Carleon. They arrived there about midday.

About that time, the Queen, a number of the lords of the Court, and a number of the ladies of the Court were out in the fields, enjoying the pleasant weather of Maytime. No one in all the world, except the squire Boisenard, knew of the danger that had threatened King Arthur, so everyone was happy in the beauty of the season. As King Arthur drew near, they looked up and saw him coming. They were astonished beyond measure to see King Arthur riding toward them across the field with that old hag behind him on the saddle, and they stood still and waited until he reached them.

But when King Arthur came up to them, he did not get down from his horse. He sat there and gazed at them all very steadily. Then Queen Guinevere said, “Sir, what is this? Do you mean to play some merry joke on us today, that you have brought that old woman here?”

“Lady,” said King Arthur, “if it were not for this old woman, it would have been a very sorry joke for you and for me. If she had not helped me, I would be a dead man now, and in a few days you would all be sunk in grief.”
Then everyone who was there was greatly amazed at the King’s words. The Queen said, “Sir, what has happened to you?”

Then King Arthur told them everything that had happened to him, from the very beginning, when he and Boisenard had left the castle of Tintagalon. When he had finished his story, they were greatly amazed.

There were seventeen lords of the Court present. When King Arthur had finished his story, he said to them, “Messires, I have given my promise to this old woman that any one of you whom she chooses shall take her as his wife and treat her with all the respect he possibly can. That was the condition she set for me. Now tell me, did I do right to promise her that I would do what she asked?” And all who were there said, “Yes, lord, you did right, for we would do anything in the world to save you from such a danger as the one you have escaped.”

Then King Arthur said to the old woman, “Lady, is there any one of these knights whom you would choose to be your husband?” At this, the old woman pointed her long, bony finger at Sir Gawaine and said, “Yes, I would marry that lord. I can tell by the chain around his neck, by the golden circlet upon his hair, and by the proud nobility of his look that he must be the son of a king.”

Then King Arthur said to Sir Gawaine, “Sir, are you willing to keep my promise to this old woman?” Sir Gawaine said, “Yes, lord, whatever you ask of me, I will do.” So Sir Gawaine went to the old woman, took her hand in his, and raised it to his lips. Not one of all those present so much as smiled. Then they all turned and went back to the King’s castle. They were very silent and downcast, for a bitter trouble had come upon that Court.

After they had returned to the Court, they gave the old woman rooms of her own. They dressed her in rich clothing such as a queen might wear, and they gave her a household fit for a queen. It seemed to everyone that, in those rich robes, she looked ten times uglier than before. When eleven days had passed, Sir Gawaine was married to the old woman in the chapel of the King’s Court, with great ceremony and splendor. Everyone there was as sad and sorrowful as if Sir Gawaine had been condemned to die.

After they were married, Sir Gawaine and the old woman went to Sir Gawaine’s house. There he shut himself away from the whole world and would let no one come near him. He was proud beyond measure, and in this great humiliation he suffered so much that words cannot tell how great it was. So he hid himself from the world, so that no one might see his grief and his shame.

All the rest of that day he paced up and down his chamber, in such despair that it came into his mind that it would be better to take his own life, for it seemed impossible to bear such shame as had come upon him. After a while the early night fell dark, and with it a certain strength came to Sir Gawaine. He said, “It is a shame for me to behave this way. Since I have married that lady, she is my true wedded wife, and I am not treating her with the respect she deserves.” So he left that place and went to the rooms of the old woman who was his wife. By then it was fully dark. But when Sir Gawaine came to where she was, the old woman scolded him, crying out, “So, Sir! You have treated me badly on our wedding day. You have stayed away from me all afternoon, and now you only come to me when it is dark night.” Sir Gawaine said, “Lady, I could not help it, for I was weighed down with many cares. If I have neglected you today, I beg your forgiveness, and I will do everything in my power to make up for any neglect I have shown you.” Then the lady said, “Sir, it is very dark in here. Let us have a light.” “It shall be as you wish,” said Sir Gawaine, “and I myself will go and fetch a light for you.”

So Sir Gawaine went out and brought two wax candles, one in each hand, set in candlesticks of gold, for he wanted to show the old woman every respect. When he came back into the room, he saw that she was at the far end of the chamber, and he went toward her. She rose and stood before him as he came near.

But when the circle of light fell upon the old woman, and Sir Gawaine saw who stood before him, he cried out in a loud voice, amazed at the wonder of what he saw. For instead of the old woman he had left, he saw a lady of extraordinary beauty, in the very flower of her youth. Her hair was long, glossy and very black. Her eyes were black too, like black jewels. Her lips were like coral, and her teeth were like pearls. For a while Sir Gawaine could not speak. Then he cried out, “Lady! Lady! Who are you?”

Then the lady smiled upon Sir Gawaine with such loving-kindness that he could think only that this was an angel who had come down from paradise. He stood before her for a long time and could find no words to say, and she kept smiling at him kindly. After a while Sir Gawaine said to her, “Lady, where is the woman who is my wife?” The lady said, “Sir Gawaine, I am she.” “It is not possible,” cried Sir Gawaine, “for she was old and extraordinarily ugly, and I believe you are more beautiful than any lady I have ever seen.” The lady said, “Nevertheless, I am she. Because you took me for your wife of your own free will and with great courtesy, part of the enchantment that lay upon me has been lifted. Now I can appear before you in my own true shape. For half of each day I may look as you see me now, but for the other half I must be as ugly as I was before.”

Then Sir Gawaine was filled beyond all words with joy, and with that joy came a great rush of love for the lady. He cried out aloud several times, “This is surely the most wonderful thing that ever happened to any man in all the world.” With that he fell upon his knees, took the lady’s hands in his own, and kissed them warmly, and all the while she smiled upon him as she had at first.

Then the lady said again, “Come, sit down beside me, and let us decide which part of the day I shall have the one appearance and which part the other. For all day I may look one way, and all night the other.”

Then Sir Gawaine said, “I would have you like this during the night, for then we are together in our own home. And since you are as I see you now, I do not care at all what the world may think of you.”

At this the lady spoke with great spirit. “No, sir, I would not have it that way, for every woman loves to be admired by the world. I would gladly enjoy my beauty in front of everyone, and not suffer the scorn and contempt of men and women.”
Sir Gawaine said to this, “Lady, I would have it the other way.”
And she said, “No, I would have it my way.”
Then Sir Gawaine said, “So be it. Since I have taken you for my wife, I must show you respect in all matters. Therefore you shall have your way in this and in all other things.”
Then the lady burst into laughter and said, “Sir, I only set this as one last test for you. As I am now, so I shall always be.”
At this Sir Gawaine was so full of joy that he did not know how to hold it in.

So they sat together for a long time, hand in hand. After a while Sir Gawaine said, “Lady, who are you?” She answered, “I am one of the Ladies of the Lake. But for your sake I have become mortal like other women, and I have left the beautiful home where I once lived. I have kept you in my heart for a good while, for I was not far away when you said farewell to Sir Pellias beside the lake. I saw how you wept and mourned when Sir Pellias left you, and my heart went out to you with great pity. So after a while I left that lake and became mortal for your sake. Then, when I learned of the trouble King Arthur had fallen into, I took the chance to have him bring me to you. I wished to test the full nobility of your knighthood. And behold, I have found it to be all that I hoped it could be. Though I appeared to you so old, so ugly and so foul, you treated me with great kindness. I do not believe you could have been more courteous to me if I had been the daughter of a king. So it gives me such joy to have you as my knight and my true lord that I can hardly tell you how great my happiness is.”
Then Sir Gawaine said, “Lady, I do not think it can be as great as my joy in having you.” With that he went to her, laid his hand upon her shoulder, and kissed her on the lips.

After that, he went out and called in a great voice all through the house, and the people of the house came running from every direction. He commanded them to bring lights and refreshments. They brought the lights, and when they saw a beautiful lady where the old woman had been, they were filled with wonder and joy. They cried out loud, clapped their hands together, and made a great noise of rejoicing. Then they set out a grand feast for Sir Gawaine and his lady. Where there had been sorrow and darkness, there were now joy and light, music and singing. Those of the King’s Court, watching this from a distance, said, “It is very strange that Sir Gawaine should take so much joy in having married that old hag.”

The next morning, the lady dressed herself in robes of yellow silk. She hung many strands of precious stones of several colors about her neck, and she set a golden crown upon her head. Sir Gawaine called for his horse, and he called for a snow-white palfrey for the lady, and then they rode out from that place and came to the Court of the King. When the King and the Queen and their Courts saw that lady, they were so astonished that they did not know what to say. When they heard all that had happened, they cheered with great joy and loud praise, and all their mourning turned into rejoicing. Indeed, there was not one knight in all that Court who would not have given half his life to be as fortunate in that matter as Sir Gawaine, the son of King Lot of Orkney.

That is the story of Sir Gawaine, and this is the lesson I take from it. The poor ugly old woman looked ugly to Sir Gawaine, and in the same way a man’s duty sometimes looks ugly and very unpleasant to his own desires. But when he has married himself to that duty, and made it one with himself as a bridegroom makes himself one with his bride, then that duty suddenly becomes very beautiful to him and to others.

So may it be with you, that you will take up your duty no matter how much you dislike doing so. A man will hardly find any real pleasure in his life unless his own wishes are wedded to his duty and cling to it as a husband clings to his wife. When wishes and duty are joined in this way, the soul takes great joy in itself, as though a wedding had taken place between a bridegroom and a bride within its dwelling.

In the same way, when you have become entirely wedded to your duty, you will be as worthy as that good knight and gentleman Sir Gawaine. A man does not need to wear armor to be a true knight. He needs only to do his best with all patience and humility, as it has been appointed for him to do. So when your time comes to show your knighthood by taking up your duty, I pray that you may prove yourself as worthy as Sir Gawaine proved himself in this story I have told you.

chapters.title: The Book of Three Worthies: Conclusion
paragraphs: _This is the end of the book, which has told in full detail the history of the Three Worthies of the Court of King Arthur._
_And now, if God will give me the grace to do it, I will write before very long the further history of several other knights and worthies whom I have not yet spoken of._

_The first of these will be Sir Launcelot, whom everyone knows to have been the greatest knight in feats of arms who ever lived, except for his son, Sir Galahad. I will also tell you the story of Sir Ewaine and Sir Geraint, of Sir Percival, and of several others._
_But that is for another time. For now, with great regret, I say farewell and bring this history to a close._
_May God allow us to meet again in such happiness and prosperity that your heart is free and untroubled, ready to enjoy the history of those excellent men that I will then set before you. Amen._
